sentences.text: One of the most prominent design issues in pharmacy is that of drug packages and the patient information leaflets (PILs) included in them.
Many pharmacists are concerned that current designs are 'accidents waiting to happen'.

The UK government shares this concern and, in 2003, the National Patient Safety Agency created a new role, appointing Colum Lowe, who has 14 years' experience as a designer in the private sector, as head of design and human factors.
Packaging design in the pharmaceutical industry is handled by either in-house teams or external design agencies.

For packaging design of over-the-counter medicines, which do not have to be dispensed by a pharmacist but can be bought directly from a sales assistant, characteristics such as attractiveness and distinguishability are important and so these are usually commissioned from an external design team.
The marketing team prepares the initial brief and the designers come up with six or seven designs.
Two or three of these are then tested on a consumer group.
In contrast, most designs for prescription-only products are created in-house.
In some cases, this may simply involve the company's design team applying the house design and then handing it over to design engineers rather than testing the design on a consumer group.
Clearly this process cannot adequately address the needs of the wide variety of patients using medication.
Design considerations
In her book Information Design for Patient Safety, Thea Swayne highlighted a multitude of design problems.
For example, drugs that look or sound alike can lead to confusion; small type sizes and even the glare on silver-foil packaging can lead to names or instructions being misread.
One such example is a drug that was accidentally injected into a patient through the spine (intrathecally) rather than through the veins (intravenously).
Investigations following this tragedy attributed some blame to the poor choice of typescript used on the drug container.

Furthermore, according to Swayne, real situations in which medicines are used include a parent giving a cough medicine to a child in the middle of the night; packaging should be designed for moments such as these rather than for the ideal world of a hospital.
Safety and compliance
Child protection is another area that gives designers opportunities to improve safety.

According to the Child Accident Prevention Trust, 70% of children admitted to hospital with suspected poisoning have swallowed medicines, and although child-resistant lids have helped, they are not yet fully effective.
There is scope for improving what is currently available, according to Richard Mawle, a freelance product designer who feels it is not just children who are blocked by child-proof closures.

'Many child-resistant packs are based on strength but older people may have the same level of strength as a child,' he explained, and suggested that better designs could rely on cognitive skills (e.g.
removing the lid using a three-step process).
Mawle also worked on a project which involved applying his skills to packaging and PILs.
Commenting on the information presented, he said: 'There can be an awful lot of junk at the beginning of PILs.
For example, why are company details towards the beginning of a leaflet when what might be more vital for the patient is that the medicine should not be taken with alcohol?'
Design principles and guidelines
Most designers work according to basic principles; for example, certain print styles are known to be more difficult to read than others.
Look-alike boxes present the potential for errors and an obvious solution would be to use colours to highlight a larger dosage of a drug.
However, according to Thea Swayne, designating a colour to a particular dosage is not recommended because this could lead to the user not reading the text on a box.
Design features can provide the basis for lengthy debates.
One argument is that if all packaging was white with black lettering, people would have no choice but to read every box carefully.
The problem is that trials of drug packaging are few – common signage studies concern road-traffic signs and visual-display units.
Although some designers take results from such studies into account, proving that a particular feature is beneficial can be difficult.

For example, current UK legislation requires packaging to include the name of the medicine in Braille, but, according to Karel van der Waarde, a design consultant to the pharmaceutical industry, 'it is not known how much visually impaired patients will benefit nor how much the reading of visually able patients will be impaired'.
Van der Waarde is sceptical about current legislation and says that many regulatory authorities do not have the resources to handle packaging information properly.
'They do not look at the use of packaging in a practical context – they only see one box at a time and not several together as pharmacists would do,' he said.
Innovation
On a positive note, a recent innovation exhibition revealed several new designs.

'The popper' aims to help arthritis sufferers remove tablets from blister packs , and 'Pluspoint' is an adrenaline auto-injector (a device that allows diabetics to inject themselves) aimed at overcoming the fact that many patients do not carry their medication due to its prohibitive size.
The aim of good design is to try to make things more user-friendly as well as safer.
The guidelines in Information Design for Patient Safety are not intended to be legally binding.
Rather, the book's purpose is to create a basic design standard and to stimulate innovation.
The challenge for the pharmaceutical industry is to adopt such a standard.

transcript.text: You will hear part of a presentation given by a business student on an assignment about absence from work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on page 7.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For my assignment, I did a review of the literature concerning absence in the workplace, and I'm going to present a summary of what I found.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I looked at some research on absence from work, that is, the number of days' work people miss for various reasons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers refer to 2 types of absence: frequent absence, which is obviously a more serious problem, and occasional absence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A lot of studies look at the factors involved in absence from work, and several have been identified.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, the gender of the employee may influence his or her ability to attend work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, a female is more likely to have childcare responsibility and so could be absent as a result of that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The next factor that has been identified is the attitude of employees toward their work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But there has been a lot of debate about the extent to which this actually does influence absence, and some people argue that the research hasn't been conclusive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some researchers have suggested that another reason for high levels of absence is that some organizations have a culture in which absence is accepted, but others have criticized this model, arguing that it's too much of a generalization.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And then there are factors related to the type of work the employee does.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's been claimed that workers in industry are more likely to have high absence rates than people who work in offices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's also important to recognize that groups within a single organization might behave differently.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, one of the other underlying themes in the literature is that there is a connection between how often an employee is absent and what size of work group he or she belongs to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Specifically, it's been found that the bigger the group, the higher the levels of absence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On a related theme, some writers have focused on a comparison between public sector organizations and private sector ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is some evidence that absence levels are higher in the public sector.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's not exactly clear why this should be the case, but one explanation that has been often put forwards is that in some cases, public sector organizations may not be as efficient.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This might be because their systems are more bureaucratic due to factors which are external rather than internal, like the degree of control the government imposes on the public sector.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, most recent literature suggests a number of other explanations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, a public sector organization tends to have a workforce which is larger.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, it tends to employ a higher number of female and older employees, both of which groups are likely to record higher absence rates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is also suggested that public sector organizations are more likely to give their absent employees benefits for a longer period and are less likely to place restrictions on these.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, it's been found that public sector employers have less of a tendency to dismiss employees for being absent, and all of these could be additional or alternative reasons for higher absence rates in the public sector.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now I'd like to talk about the management of absence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.content:
Absence From Work
Absence may be frequent or occasional.
Main factors involved
- the {{31}} of employees (e.g. females are likely to have responsibility for children)
- employees’ {{32}} (but the evidence is inconclusive)
- the {{33}} of the organisation (absenteeism may be acceptable)
- the type of work (higher absence among employees in {{34}} )
- the {{35}} of an employee’s work group
Public sector versus private sector
- Public sector has higher absence levels
- Possible explanation: the public sector is less {{36}}
- Systems may be more bureaucratic because of {{37}} factors(state controls)
More recent literature suggests public sector organisations usually:
- have a {{38}} workforce
- provide {{39}} for longer, with fewer restrictions
- are less likely to {{40}} employees

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到影响出勤的第一个因素是员工的“gender（性别）”，并且用女性照顾孩子的例子对应了题目括号里的举例。

questions.quote: Firstly, the gender of the employee may influence his or her ability to attend work. For example, a female is more likely to have childcare responsibility and so could be absent as a result of that.

questions.explanation: 录音中紧接着说到的下一个影响出勤的因素是员工对工作的“attitude（态度）”。
questions.tip: 录音后半句提到的debate和hasn't been conclusive是对题干中inconclusive（无定论的）的同义替换，如果没有听懂这层替换，你可能会因为怀疑自己而不敢填入attitude。
questions.quote: The next factor that has been identified is the attitude of employees toward their work. But there has been a lot of debate about the extent to which this actually does influence absence, and some people argue that the research hasn't been conclusive.

questions.explanation: 录音提到另一个原因是有些组织拥有允许缺勤的“culture（文化）”，完全对应题干的organisation以及括号里的可接受缺勤。
questions.tip: 你可能会被后面的generalization干扰，但这句话的核心主干就是在说机构的文化，抓准核心名词即可。
questions.quote: Some researchers have suggested that another reason for high levels of absence is that some organizations have a culture in which absence is accepted, but others have criticized this model, arguing that it's too much of a generalization.

questions.explanation: 在提到工作类型后，录音对比了“industry（工业/制造业）”和办公室，指出前者的缺勤率更高。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到offices就填进去，但要注意录音中明确说了是industry的缺勤率比offices高，填offices语义完全相反。
questions.quote: And then there are factors related to the type of work the employee does. It's been claimed that workers in industry are more likely to have high absence rates than people who work in offices.

questions.explanation: 录音提到缺勤频率和员工所属工作小组的“size（规模/大小）”有关。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到后面的bigger而错填成big，但题干中“the... of”的结构需要填入的是表示属性的名词。
questions.quote: For example, one of the other underlying themes in the literature is that there is a connection between how often an employee is absent and what size of work group he or she belongs to. Specifically, it's been found that the bigger the group, the higher the levels of absence.

questions.explanation: 录音直接给出了原因解释，说公共部门可能没有那么“efficient（高效）”，对应题干的less efficient。
questions.tip: 此处用not as efficient替换了less efficient，如果你死等less这个词，很容易就错过了真正的答案。
questions.quote: It's not exactly clear why this should be the case, but one explanation that has been often put forwards is that in some cases, public sector organizations may not be as efficient.

questions.explanation: 录音解释系统官僚化的原因是基于“external（外部的）”因素，例如政府的控制。
questions.tip: 录音中同时出现了external和internal，但原话说的是“external rather than internal（是外部而不是内部）”，如果不理解rather than的否定意味，很容易因为听到internal就填反。
questions.quote: This might be because their systems are more bureaucratic due to factors which are external rather than internal, like the degree of control the government imposes on the public sector.

questions.explanation: 在引入新文献的观点后，第一点就明确指出公共部门往往拥有“larger（更大的）”劳动力队伍。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为句子语序和题干不同（录音是workforce which is larger，题干是larger workforce）而产生犹豫，从而导致漏听。
questions.quote: However, most recent literature suggests a number of other explanations. Firstly, a public sector organization tends to have a workforce which is larger.

questions.explanation: 录音提到公共部门更有可能给缺勤员工提供较长时期的“benefits（福利）”。
questions.tip: 你可能会把注意力放在后面的restrictions上，但题干中fewer restrictions对应的是录音里的less likely to place restrictions，空格处要填的是provide对应的直接宾语。
questions.quote: It is also suggested that public sector organizations are more likely to give their absent employees benefits for a longer period and are less likely to place restrictions on these.

questions.explanation: 录音提到公共部门的雇主不太倾向于“dismiss（解雇）”缺勤员工，对应题干的less likely to dismiss。
questions.tip: 如果你没能把录音中的less of a tendency和题干里的less likely进行同义替换对应，就很容易在长句中跟丢节奏，导致错过动作词。
questions.quote: In addition, it's been found that public sector employers have less of a tendency to dismiss employees for being absent, and all of these could be additional or alternative reasons for higher absence rates in the public sector.

r1.title: A Brief History of Humans and Food

sentences.text: During the journey from our hunter-gatherer ancestors to the present day, there have been three seismic changes that have impacted the food we eat: the discovery of cooking, the emergence of agriculture, and the invention of methods of preserving food.
The 19th-century scientist Charles Darwin thought that cooking, after language, was the greatest discovery made by man.
All of us eat some raw food, such as fruit and vegetables, but the great majority of food we consume is cooked.
Cooking can turn plants that are inedible into edible food by destroying toxic chemicals that plants often manufacture to protect themselves against attack by insects or other herbivorous animals.

These toxic chemicals are referred to as “plant secondary compounds” because they are not directly involved in the plant's normal growth, development, and reproduction, and are produced purely as chemical defenses.
They give many of the plants we consume, such as coffee or Brussels sprouts, their bitter taste.
Cooked food is often more digestible because heat breaks down tough cellulose cell walls in plants or tough connective tissue in animals.
Chewing raw turnip, a plate of uncooked rice, or a raw leg of lamb is much harder work than eating the cooked equivalent.

The energy expended in chewing to break down the tough material is replaced by energy from the fuel used in cooking the food, so the ratio of energy gained to energy expended by the body is greater when food is cooked.
Until the development of agriculture, hunter-gatherers spent up to seven hours a day gathering food.
This all began to change around 10,500 years ago with the advent of farming, which led to dramatic changes in human societies.
People began to create a variety of new tools to aid survival, and in turn, populations increased in size.
These changes led to the possibility of specialization of different tasks within society.
Around this time, writing became more sophisticated and allowed people to maintain records of the harvest and taxes.
Eventually, formalized structures of government were established as people settled in one area.
The arrival of agriculture meant that, for the first time, our ancestors had more food than they could eat immediately.
This, combined with the seasonality of production, led them to discover methods of preserving food: smoking, drying, adding acid by fermentation, or adding salt.
These four methods all share one feature in common—they make the food a more hostile environment for bacteria that can cause it to spoil.
They also tend to slow down natural chemical reactions in the food that would cause decay.
Although foods today are still preserved in these ancient ways, two more recent methods of preserving food have become more common: canning and freezing.
Canning was invented by a Frenchman, Nicolas Appert, in the early 19th century.
He sealed food in bottles fabricated from glass and then heated them in boiling water to cook the contents.
Appert's method had great advantages over older methods of food preservation: it could be applied to a wide range of foods, and the flavor and texture were similar to freshly cooked products.
His idea was soon copied by an Englishman, Peter Durand.
Until this point, containers had been too heavy to be widely used, but Durand produced the first ones which were lightweight and resistant to damage.

Two years later, in 1812, two Englishmen, Bryan Donkin and John Hall, started the commercial canning of food, although the real rise in popularity of canning had to wait until the invention of the can opener in 1855.
Until then, cans were opened with a chisel and hammer.
Canning is an extremely effective way of preserving food: one can containing meat, dating back to 1824, was opened in 1939, and the contents were still in good condition.
In the 21st century, the dominance of canning as a method of food preservation has been overtaken by freezing.
Chilling food to keep it fresh is an old idea.
The earliest mentions of icehouses, thick-walled buildings, half underground, date back to 1700 BC in northwest Iran.
In early 16th-century Italy, water was mixed with chemicals to lower its freezing point to -18 degrees Celsius.
Several centuries later, frozen fish and other goods were transported by ship from Australia to England.
However, the modern frozen food industry was started in the 1920s by an American, Clarence Birdseye.

While on a fishing trip with the Inuit in the Canadian Arctic, Birdseye observed that rapid freezing creates smaller ice crystals and therefore causes less damage to food—a discovery he had not expected.
Nevertheless, the major growth in demand for frozen food came with the arrival of freezers in ordinary people's homes.
The advantages of frozen over canned food include the fact that the flavor and consistency are often identical to the fresh product, and freezing can be used to preserve a wide variety of foods.

questions.prompt: According to Darwin, cooking was the most significant development in human history.
questions.explanation: 题目说根据达尔文，烹饪是人类历史上**最重要（most significant）**的发展。原文A段说达尔文认为烹饪是“after language, was the greatest discovery（仅次于语言的最伟大发现）”，即语言才是第一，烹饪第二，所以不是“最重要”，选 FALSE。
questions.tip: 题目中的“the most significant”忽略了原文的限定词“after language”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “...cooking, after language, was the greatest discovery made by man.”

questions.prompt: The process of cooking gets rid of some plant poisons.
questions.explanation: 题目说烹饪过程会去除一些植物毒素。原文A段提到烹饪通过“destroying toxic chemicals（破坏有毒化学物质）”将不可食用的植物变成可食用的，选 TRUE。
questions.tip: “Gets rid of” 对应 “destroying”，“poisons” 对应 “toxic chemicals”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “Cooking can turn plants... by destroying toxic chemicals...”

questions.prompt: Eating cooked food is more energy efficient than eating raw food.
questions.explanation: 题目说吃熟食比吃生食更节能（energy efficient）。原文B段末尾说由于烹饪节省了咀嚼和消化的能量，身体获得的能量与消耗的能量之比在吃熟食时“is greater（更大）”，即更高效，选 TRUE。
questions.tip: “More energy efficient” 对应 “ratio of energy gained to energy expended... is greater”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...so the ratio of energy gained to energy expended... is greater when food is cooked.”

questions.prompt: Clarence Birdseye had previously worked in the Australian food industry.
questions.explanation: 题目说Clarence Birdseye此前曾在澳大利亚食品工业工作。原文F段虽然提到了从澳大利亚运冷冻鱼到英国（transported from Australia），但这是在他出场之前的历史背景描述，并未提及Birdseye本人是否在澳大利亚工作过，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.tip: 不要把“提到澳大利亚”和“提到Birdseye”强行关联，文中两者无交集。
questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “Several centuries later, frozen fish... from Australia... However, the modern frozen food industry was started... by... Clarence Birdseye.”

questions.prompt: Birdseye's trip with the Inuit confirmed what he already believed about rapid freezing.
questions.explanation: 题目说Birdseye与因纽特人的旅行证实了他**已经相信（already believed）**的关于快速冷冻的看法。原文F段说这是一个“discovery he had not expected（他未曾预料到的发现）”，即他之前并不相信或知道，选 FALSE。
questions.tip: “Confirmed what he already believed” 与 “had not expected” 矛盾。
questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “...a discovery he had not expected.”

The changes agriculture brought about were:

Food preservation

sentences.text: It seems that our current society cannot get enough information about the daily lives of celebrities.
But how did celebrities become such an important force in our culture?

While people have always shared a certain obsession with the fantastic and the famous, the notion of celebrity, as well as the types of people termed 'celebrities', has evolved greatly throughout the ages.
The word 'celebrity' has its roots in the language of the ancient Roman civilization.
The word we now know to mean 'a condition of being famous' or 'a famous person' is derived from the Latin word 'celeber', meaning 'frequented or populous'.

The celebrities of the ancient world were the powerful and awesome deities of Greece and Rome, and the citizens of these civilizations believed in a vast number of immortals who had a direct impact on their lives.
It was, therefore, important to know about these figures' personal lives.
This need to know led to the creation of myths, which personalized the gods and involved them in ancient celebrity scandals that thrilled and excited the common people.
During ancient times, amateur and professional athletes also began to make an impact on the celebrity culture.
Victors in the ancient Olympic Games were treated as heroes and were often elevated to god-like status.
In the ancient Roman civilization, gladiators – the equivalent of today's professional athletes – were also revered by the common people for their heroics and seemingly superhuman strength.

As Europe moved into the Dark Ages (the years spanning approximately 400–1300 AD) and a time when athletics and the arts were largely forgotten, monarchs and rulers continued to maintain celebrity status, while religious figures took on newfound fame.

The miraculous lives and fascinating deaths of spiritual figures lent excitement to the lives of common people when there was often little else to be excited about, as they faced war, disease and food shortages.
During the period 1300–1600 AD, or the Renaissance period as it is known, interest in ruling figures faded.
As Europe emerged from its long neglect of the arts, there was greater appreciation for portraits, statues and stone carvings.
This period of appreciation for the arts lent a sense of celebrity to artists who were noted for their works and their personal achievements.
It was a time when artists began to surpass political and religious individuals for supreme celebrity – a trend that would continue into later centuries.
While the figures of the ancient and early modern civilizations were able to achieve moderate and sometimes lasting celebrity within particular cultures, the global reach of their fame was limited.
It was not until the 1700s, when technological advances made publishing commercially viable, that the extent of a person's fame could spread further.

The increase in the availability of the written word was accompanied by a huge rise in the number of common people who could read, allowing a mass audience to find out about celebrities for the first time.
Suddenly, the lives of authors, politicians, war heroes, and other celebrities could now be read about in newspapers around the world.
These gave ordinary people the opportunity to become intimately knowledgeable about the figures they most admired.
In the modern era, particularly as radio and film took off in the 1900s, things really began to change.
First, radio began to make its way into the average home in the 1920s and 1930s.
Professional athletes also began to be regarded as stars, as their games and exploits could be broadcast over the air for an entirely new audience.
Then, the rise of television in the 1950s only cemented the premier level of celebrity that film stars, athletes and television actors were beginning to share.
This also meant a huge increase in the individual salaries of these celebrities.
Even a few animals gained fame through children's TV shows.
The emergence of reality television shows in the late 1990s allowed all kinds of people with little ability to enjoy a short burst of fame on the television screen.
All you needed, it seemed, was an attractive appearance.

Today, reality television programmers make it possible to be famous not for doing anything in particular, but simply for being, with the audience deciding whether someone deserves to become a celebrity or not.
As the meaning of celebrity continues to evolve and redefine itself in a quickly changing world, there is no telling who will become of interest next.

r3.title: Research into the effects of different teaching styles

sentences.text: Prior to 1960, most inquiries into pupils' learning skills explored the relationship between factors such as children's social background, personality or measured intelligence and their achievement in various school subjects.
Studies of teachers were largely a quest for criteria of effectiveness, and numerous investigations sought links between personality or attitude and 'success' at teaching.
By 1950, Domas and Tiedeman were able to survey 672 such studies of teacher effectiveness.
Yet there was widespread disappointment with such research, partly because so little of value seemed to emerge.
First of all, there was little agreement about what constituted 'good' teaching or who the good teachers were.
Secondly, there were numerous conflicting and contradictory findings.
No sooner had one investigator found a relationship which appeared to be significant, than another discovered the opposite effect.
For example, in 1945, two American researchers, Rostker and Rolfe, both using standardized testing techniques and broad samples of teachers, reached exactly opposite conclusions.

Rostker concluded that the intelligence of the teacher is the most important single factor conditioning teaching ability, and that there is no significant relationship between personality and teaching ability.
Rolfe, however, found no correlation between intelligence and teaching efficiency: he claimed that the teacher's personality was what produced good teaching.

Another American writer, Barr (1961), summarized a massive amount of American research and underlined the chaos in the research literature on effectiveness: “Some teachers were preferred by administrators, some were liked by the pupils, and some taught in classes where there were substantial pupil gains, and generally speaking these were not the same teachers.”

One of the earliest pieces of research dates from 1912, when Stevens made 100 random observations of lessons in a variety of subject areas, in order to analyze the number and nature of questions being asked by teachers.
Stevens's overall total was 64% teacher talk and 36% pupil talk, figures which are remarkably similar to a number of findings half a century later.
For many years in the first half of the 20th century, so-called 'formal' teaching was the norm.

Teachers taught their classes as a whole group, gave out information, asked questions which predominantly required factual recall, and frequently set a common written task for the children to complete in a prescribed period of time.
It was hardly surprising, therefore, that one focus of classroom interaction research in the decades following Stevens's inquiry was on the phenomenon of 'attentiveness'.

A number of studies in the 1920s and 1930s, by Morrison and others, sought relationships between the degree of attention being paid by children and the amount they subsequently appeared to have learnt.

Such research was usually based on observing teachers at work, a technique which was also employed extensively by United States administrators in the 1920s and 1930s, in order to assess teachers' competence and allocate merit payments to so-called 'superior' teachers.

As the 1930s came to an end, it was partly the emergence of totalitarian regimes in Europe which led to a shift in interest in the United States away from attentiveness, with its emphasis on the authority of the teacher, and towards a scrutiny of authoritarianism itself.
A number of people began to feel that if dictatorship were to be avoided, children must learn in school how to handle democracy.
Several investigators examined the processes taking place within small discussion groups, and tried to establish superiority for discussion groups over lecture classes, but with conflicting results.

The movement towards what was becoming known as child-centred education was gathering momentum, and as interest in child development increased, investigators began to discover the usefulness of direct observation and the categorization of child behavior.
This was when systematic observation of teacher-pupil interaction began in earnest.
Anderson (1939) studied what he called 'domination' and 'integration' amongst kindergarten children.

Dominative acts by children included blaming and snatching toys, and such acts by teachers included restricting children's activities; while children's integrative acts included sharing facilities and playing harmoniously, and those of teachers included expanding opportunities for self-direction and co-operation.
Anderson then attempted to measure what is now commonly called 'classroom climate'.
Lewin, Lippitt and White (1939 and 1943) studied the effects of different teaching styles.
They arranged for three groups of five boys each to be taught in very different ways: these were labelled 'authoritarian', 'democratic' and 'laissez-faire'.
The first two of these were similar to Anderson's concept of dominative and integrative teachers.
Beginning with Withall's work in 1949, there was much greater interest in interaction within the classroom.

Withall used the term 'social-emotional climate' to describe the emotional tone created as a result of face-to-face interaction in groups, and, like many who followed him, concentrated his analysis of this climate on the study of teachers' verbal behavior.

Withall also made efforts towards increasing the reliability of analyses, and this important pioneering work in the development of classroom observation methodology was followed by many others during the 1950s.

Partly because of the disappointing results of the teacher-effectiveness research, and partly because of the general neglect in earlier work of the variables of actual classroom behavior, the decade 1960–70 produced a large number of studies of classroom processes, based on observation of teachers at work.

transcript.text: I sure am.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Tucson's not my hometown, though, but it's definitely worth seeing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I was wondering what to take with me.

questions.tip: 你可能会把后面补充的 courses（球场）当作答案填进去，但结合题目“playing（玩/打）”的语境，这里填具体的运动项目 golf 才是合乎逻辑的。
questions.quote: Any chance of a game of golf? Oh, absolutely. There are loads of courses around Tucson.

questions.explanation: 女士直接报出了街道数字和名称，并在男士的请求下对 Fearnleigh 进行了逐字母拼读。
questions.tip: 你可能会在拼写时漏掉中间不发音的 n 或者把 e 和 i 的顺序弄反，听到逐个字母拼读时一定要专注并迅速写下。

questions.quote: So is it full of old buildings? Well, the post office is the oldest, as it was built in eighteen eighty-one, but there was a big fire in nineteen oh one, and most of the town was burnt down. But it didn't take them long to rebuild.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear the manager of a bookshop called Bibliostack talking to a group of young people about the way the bookshop is organized.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and a big welcome to Bibliostack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, I'll explain the plan of the store to you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The building is on seven floors and is circular, as you can see, and we're here on the ground floor in its entrance hall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right in the center of this floor, but behind the bookshelf, so you can't see it very well from here, is our main seating area, where people are encouraged to sit and read for as long as they like.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But they're under no pressure to buy what they're reading.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's not how we operate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And if you look to your immediate left, past the first double row of shelves, you'll see piles of colored cushions in front of the window there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We provide those so that people can sit wherever they want.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lots of people like to sit close to the bookshelves, and if they want to sit on the floor there, we want them to be as comfortable as possible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On your right, between the two larger bookshelves, you'll see the computer bench, where our visitors can search through our entire catalog.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We pride ourselves in being the largest bookshop in the country, so our sales assistants can't possibly know all the available titles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although the room in front of you is dominated by the bookshelves, at the far end, just in front of the lift, you'll see that we provide a small café bar here, too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And just to your right, there's a door to the cloakroom, where people can leave their coats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then after that, there's a stand where we keep a selection of local and national newspapers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Customers are welcome to browse through them, and we also have some for sale.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We really want people to feel as though they're browsing through books in the comfort of their own home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I suggest we walk slowly up through the building, and I'll give you more information as we go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're open twelve hours a day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We don't mind if people spend the whole day here, but leave without buying anything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, we hope they'll buy something, but our purpose is to draw people in, to provide the kind of environment which makes them want to stay and read.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Look at how busy each floor is, but how quiet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You may be wondering whether there are any children in the building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We debated about locating children's books on the ground floor or halfway up the building, like the third or fourth floor, but in the end, we decided to put them on the very top level, and I can assure you, it's not the least bit quiet up there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, many parents would prefer to spend time on other floors, and so we provide a supervised area for children under two in the basement, so parents can wander around the shop for a few hours and not worry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But they do have to pay for this service, because although we thought about using some of our own assistants, we decided to employ qualified nursery staff for parents' complete peace of mind.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, we're just passing the fiction section, and you've probably noticed a small crowd of people beginning to gather.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's because a well-known author is going to read from her latest novel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We try to hold events like this at least once or twice a week, and as you can imagine, they're very popular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We don't make a charge for people to attend, but we obviously hope that some of them will want to purchase the book after listening to part of it being read aloud.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other events which are proving to be very popular are our workshops.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Last week, we held a poetry workshop, and people came along with poems that they'd written.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the country's best-known poets ran the workshop, and the participants read their poems aloud to him.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He was kind and encouraging, and many people felt inspired by his advice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's extremely difficult to earn your living as a professional poet, and even published poets have other jobs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now we're going to take a look at our section on audiobooks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.tip: 你可能会只听到“center”就想随便选，但一定要听完“behind the bookshelf”，明确是在中央短书架的后面，而且你是从最下面的 entrance 入口进入的，从而精准锁定C而不是前方的E。
questions.quote: The building is on seven floors and is circular, as you can see, and we're here on the ground floor in its entrance hall. Right in the center of this floor, but behind the bookshelf, so you can't see it very well from here, is our main seating area, where people are encouraged to sit and read for as long as they like. questions.explanation: 从入口立刻向左看（immediate left），越过第一组并排的双列书架（past the first double row），在窗户前面的区域就是F。
questions.tip: 地图题很容易因为干扰物跟错路线，你必须严格跟随“左转”且“越过第一组并排书架”的行进绝对动作，不能停留在起点附近的无关字母上。
questions.quote: And if you look to your immediate left, past the first double row of shelves, you'll see piles of colored cushions in front of the window there. We provide those so that people can sit wherever they want. Lots of people like to sit close to the bookshelves, and if they want to sit on the floor there, we want them to be as comfortable as possible.

questions.prompt: Computer bench

questions.tip: 不要在右侧一大堆书架里迷失，你只要抓住“on your right（在右边）”并锁定“between（在...两者之间）”这个核心方位词，就能直接把目标锁定在两个大书架之间的空隙D点。
questions.quote: On your right, between the two larger bookshelves, you'll see the computer bench, where our visitors can search through our entire catalog. We pride ourselves in being the largest bookshop in the country, so our sales assistants can't possibly know all the available titles.

questions.prompt: Café bar
questions.explanation: 目光直接看向地图的最远端（at the far end），正对着电梯（lift）前方的区域就是咖啡吧A。
questions.tip: 这道题很直接，但你要快速在图表顶部找到“lift”这个大参照物，没跟上这个词就会在满屏幕的书架中跟丢。
questions.quote: Although the room in front of you is dominated by the bookshelves, at the far end, just in front of the lift, you'll see that we provide a small café bar here, too.

questions.prompt: Newspapers
questions.explanation: 入口右侧是衣帽间（cloakroom）的门，顺着外围路线继续往后走（after that），放置报纸的架子就是H。
questions.tip: 你可能会在G和H之间犹豫，但录音强调了是在衣帽间的门“之后（after that）”，说明你的行进路线要在图上继续延伸，所以要排除紧挨着门的G，选择更靠后的H。
questions.quote: And just to your right, there's a door to the cloakroom, where people can leave their coats. Then after that, there's a stand where we keep a selection of local and national newspapers. Customers are welcome to browse through them, and we also have some for sale. We really want people to feel as though they're browsing through books in the comfort of their own home.

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: The bookshop aims to
questions.explanation: 书店的目的是吸引人们进来，并提供一种能让大家“想要留下来阅读（stay and read）”的环境，对应选项C。
questions.tip: 你可能想选A，但录音明确说“不介意大家不买东西就离开”；也可能想选B，但录音最后强调环境是“安静的（quiet）”而不是充满活力的（energetic）。
questions.quote: We're open twelve hours a day. We don't mind if people spend the whole day here, but leave without buying anything. Of course, we hope they'll buy something, but our purpose is to draw people in, to provide the kind of environment which makes them want to stay and read. Look at how busy each floor is, but how quiet.

options.text: sell as many books as possible.
attract people to remain in the shop.

questions.prompt: Children’s books are located
questions.explanation: 虽然讨论过其他楼层，但书店最终决定（in the end）把儿童书籍放在“最顶层（very top level）”，对应选项B。
questions.tip: 你很容易一听到 ground floor 或 halfway up 就立刻选A或C，但这只是他们“曾经讨论过”的方案，单选题里听到讨论过程一定要耐心等到表结论的转折词（but in the end）出现。
questions.quote: We debated about locating children's books on the ground floor or halfway up the building, like the third or fourth floor, but in the end, we decided to put them on the very top level, and I can assure you, it's not the least bit quiet up there.

questions.prompt: For parents to relax, the bookshop provides
questions.explanation: 书店最终雇佣了“有资质的托儿所员工（qualified nursery staff）”来照顾孩子，完美对应专业儿童看护（professional child care）。
questions.tip: 你可能想选A，但录音说“想过用自己的普通店员但最终没用”；也极容易想当然选B，但录音明确点出这项服务是“必须要付费的（pay for this service）”，直接一击排除了免费选项。
questions.quote: ...and so we provide a supervised area for children under two in the basement, so parents can wander around the shop for a few hours and not worry. But they do have to pay for this service, because although we thought about using some of our own assistants, we decided to employ qualified nursery staff for parents' complete peace of mind.

options.text: trained floor staff to take care of children.

questions.prompt: The aim of the regular book reading is
questions.explanation: 书店举办阅读活动的目的是希望有人听完后会“想要买这本书（want to purchase the book）”，直指选项A。
questions.tip: 你可能看都没看仔细就想选C，但录音直接用“不收门票费（don't make a charge）”一脚踢开了靠卖票赚钱的干扰，听出否定词就能果断排除。
questions.quote: Now, we're just passing the fiction section, and you've probably noticed a small crowd of people beginning to gather. That's because a well-known author is going to read from her latest novel. We try to hold events like this at least once or twice a week, and as you can imagine, they're very popular. We don't make a charge for people to attend, but we obviously hope that some of them will want to purchase the book after listening to part of it being read aloud.

options.text: to generate income by charging for tickets.

questions.prompt: Participants at the poetry workshops were able to
questions.explanation: 在诗歌工作坊上，知名诗人非常和蔼并给予鼓励（encouraging），很多人也因为他的“建议（advice）”而受到启发，对应选项C。
questions.tip: 录音里抛出了 published（出版） 和 professional poet（职业诗人）这两个原词来诱导你选A或B，但仔细听就会发现，这是为了强调“哪怕出版过书的职业诗人也要做兼职谋生”，绝不是说你参加个工作坊就能立刻出书或变成全职诗人。
questions.quote: Other events which are proving to be very popular are our workshops. Last week, we held a poetry workshop, and people came along with poems that they'd written. One of the country's best-known poets ran the workshop, and the participants read their poems aloud to him. He was kind and encouraging, and many people felt inspired by his advice. It's extremely difficult to earn your living as a professional poet, and even published poets have other jobs.

options.text: receive feedback and encouragement from an expert.

18.s: for parents' complete peace of mind

19.s: at least once or twice a week

20.s: One of the country's best-known poets

transcript.text: Part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a trainee teacher called Eve talking to her university tutor about her preparations for teaching practice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Before you listen, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, Eve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Come in and sit down.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How's it going?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fine, thanks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'm looking forward to my teaching practice next week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, you've got two classes, haven't you?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Year three and year six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Have you done your lesson plans?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I've decided to take the topic of renewable energy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I haven't done a lesson plan for year six yet, but I thought I'd base their lesson on an example of very simple technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So I've brought this diagram to show you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I got it from the Internet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Let's see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A biogas plant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So this is equipment for producing fuel from organic waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The smaller container on the left is where you put the waste you've collected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And from there, it's piped into the larger tank.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And that's slurry on the base of the larger tank.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And what exactly is slurry?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a mixture of organic waste and water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So is that pipe at the bottom where the water comes in?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, it is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As the slurry mixture digests, it produces gas, and that rises to the top of the dome.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then, when it's needed, it can be piped off for use as fuel in homes or factories.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's very simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I suppose there's some kind of safety valve to prevent pressure buildup.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's the overflow tank.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That container on the right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As the slurry expands, some of it flows into that, and then once some of the gas has been piped off, the slurry level goes down again, and the overflow tank empties again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I think that's suitably simple for the age level it's for.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I look forward to seeing the whole lesson plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And can I show you my ideas for the year three lesson?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Of course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's look.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you listen to the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: I thought I'd introduce the topic by writing the word energy on the board and reinforcing the spelling and the pronunciation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then I'll do a little mime, you know, run on the spot or something to convey the sense.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'd keep it brief at this stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, I will.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then I'll wipe the word off and write the question, where does energy come from?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And see what the pupils come up with.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Fine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'd suggest that you just brainstorm at this stage and don't reject any of their suggestions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, that's what I was going to do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then I've produced a set of simple statements like, energy makes cars move along the road, and energy makes our bodies grow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There are eight altogether.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Are you going to give them out as a handout or write them up on the board?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, put them up on the board, and then I'll read them out loud.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And I'll get the pupils to copy them out in their notebooks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'll also ask them to think up one more similar statement by themselves and add it to the list.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After that, I thought I'd vary things a bit by sticking some pictures up of things like the sun and plants and food and petrol and a running child.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And I'll get the pupils to work out what order the pictures should come in in terms of the energy chain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I think that's a very good idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You could move the pictures around as the pupils give you directions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, I think they'd enjoy that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And to finish off, I've made a gap fill exercise to give out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They'll be doing that individually, and while they're writing, I'll walk around and check their work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And have you worked out the timing of all that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It'll probably take you right through to the end of the lesson.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.instructions:
What part of Kathy's dissertation has the tutor just read? Label the diagram below.
Write the correct letter, A-G, next to questions 21–25 below.

questions.prompt: Waste container
questions.explanation: 录音明确指出左边较小的容器（smaller container on the left）是用来放收集来的废物的，对应图中的C。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为没重点听方位词“on the left”，而在图左侧的几个箭头和部件中犹豫不决。
questions.quote: Yes. The smaller container on the left is where you put the waste you've collected.

questions.prompt: Slurry
questions.explanation: 录音提到在这个较大水箱的底部（base of the larger tank）有泥浆（slurry），对应图中大水箱最底部的G。
questions.tip: 听到“larger tank”时你可能会直接想选代表整个大水箱的D，但关键定位词其实是表示具体位置的“base（底部）”。
questions.quote: That's right. And that slurry on the base of the larger tank.

questions.prompt: Water inlet
questions.explanation: 男生提问证实了底部的那个管子就是水进来的地方（pipe at the bottom where the water comes in），对应图中底部代表水入口的A。
questions.tip: 你可能没反应过来“water comes in（进水）”就是题目中“inlet（入口）”的直接同义替换。
questions.quote: So is that pipe at the bottom where the water comes in?

questions.prompt: Gas
questions.explanation: 录音提到消化过程会产生气体（gas），并且气体会上升到圆顶的顶部（rises to the top of the dome），对应图中最上方的E。
questions.tip: 由于前两题都在看水箱底部，你可能会被惯性思维困住，忽略了动词“rises（上升）”指引你立刻把视线转移到图的顶端。
questions.quote: Yes, it is. As the slurry mixture digests, it produces gas, and that rises to the top of the dome.

questions.prompt: Overflow tank
questions.explanation: 男生猜测有安全阀，女生直接纠正说那是溢流罐（overflow tank），就是右边的那个容器（container on the right），对应图中的F。
questions.tip: 你可能会被男生提问时抛出的“safety valve（安全阀）”干扰，跑去图里乱找，其实只要稳住听女生紧接着给出的方位词“on the right”就能锁定答案。
questions.quote: I suppose there's some kind of safety valve to prevent pressure buildup. That's the overflow tank, that container on the right.

questions.explanation: 录音提到老师写完单词后，会做一些模仿动作（mime）来传达意思（convey the sense），完美对应选项D的“展示含义（Demonstrate meaning）”。
questions.tip: 你可能会把录音举例的“run on the spot（原地跑步）”当成一项单纯的体育活动，而没理解这只是为了“convey the sense（表达意思）”。
questions.quote: I thought I'd introduce the topic by writing the word energy on the board and reinforcing the spelling and the pronunciation. Then I'll do a little mime, you know, run on the spot or something to convey the sense.

questions.explanation: 录音顺着教学流程说到，老师接下来准备了一组简单的陈述句（a set of simple statements），对应选项G的“展示句子（Present sentences）”。
questions.tip: 这里的教学步骤比较长，你可能会把前面提到的写出问题（write the question）误当成这一步的答案而选错。
questions.quote: Yes, that's what I was going to do. Then I've produced a set of simple statements like, energy makes cars move along the road, and energy makes our bodies grow.

questions.explanation: 老师说明会把句子写在黑板上，然后让学生抄写到他们的笔记本上（copy them out in their notebooks），动作要求直接对应选项C。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到老师要“read them out loud（大声读出来）”就去选项里找听或读的动作，而漏听了紧接着针对学生的指令是“copy（抄写）”。
questions.quote: Are you going to give them out as a handout or write them up on the board? First, put them up on the board, and then I'll read them out loud, and I'll get the pupils to copy them out in their notebooks. I'll also ask them to think up one more similar statement by themselves and add it to the list.

questions.explanation: 贴出图片后，老师明确会让学生弄清楚这些图片应该以什么顺序出现（work out what order the pictures should come in），“order（顺序）”对应选项A的sequence。
questions.tip: 录音里罗列了一大堆图片内容（太阳、植物、食物等），你可能会陷入这些名词细节里，而没抓住动词短语“work out what order”才是任务核心。
questions.quote: After that, I thought I'd vary things a bit by sticking some pictures up of things like the sun, and plants, and food, and petrol, and a running child. And I'll get the pupils to work out what order the pictures should come in in terms of the energy chain.

questions.explanation: 录音提到最后老师做了一个填空练习来分发给学生（give out），“give out”是选项E“Distribute（分发）”的同义替换。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为没听懂“gap fill exercise（填空练习）”其实就是“worksheet（工作纸/练习卷）”的具体形式而不敢选E。
questions.quote: Yes, I think they'd enjoy that. And to finish off, I've made a gap fill exercise to give out. They'll be doing that individually, and while they're writing, I'll walk around and check their work.

21.s: where you put the waste you've collected

25.s: safety valve to prevent pressure buildup

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about factors you should consider when creating advertising materials and the effects they can have on your product sales.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, class, and welcome back to Marketing Strategies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This week, I will expand upon last week's lecture by talking about factors you should consider when creating advertising materials and the effects they can have on your product sales.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lesson one: limit your advertising to the geographic area of your target market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though you may have a product that people want in a large area, the distance that customers are willing to travel is a significant factor in their choice of where to purchase that product.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Take this example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you're really hungry and decide you want a burrito, would you choose the restaurant that is a block from your apartment or the one that is just as good, or even slightly better, across town?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, you'd pick the closer restaurant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, there's the method of communication to your target market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How do you decide among radio ads, TV commercials, flyers, or even word of mouth?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While we often think of the visual presentation of ads, there's much more to advertising than the look.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Studies show that consumers are much more likely to remember advertising slogans if there's also a sound played.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Did you know that your sense of smell is closely linked with memory?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Think about Mandy's Candy Store up the road.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Every time you walk past it, you can just smell the chocolate, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I bet you can almost smell it now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Just mentioning the name brings about the smell memory and, in turn, a chocolate craving.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What better way to sell chocolate bars?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Obviously, sometimes appealing to the senses isn't the most practical way to advertise.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, it's a good idea to come up with a marketing strategy that adapts to the product, especially digital products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The flexibility of this kind of products is extremely important, so it's very common for advertisers to form one single layout for all of their ads, the visual, the medium, even the majority of the content, and simply update the ad each time they come out with a new version.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember, advertising is all about stirring up the right feeling in your potential customers, whether by stimulating the senses, appealing to the intellect, and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once the customer experiences the ad, the important thing is his or her reaction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Someone could love the ad you made, but unless he or she considers buying the product, you failed to get the reaction you were looking for.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So once you have successfully reached your target customer and you have his or her business, often you'll want to expand to a larger market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: More often than not, the same marketing strategies you used in your small campaign may not work for a larger audience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The larger you scale your product, the more factors you must consider.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, Apple operates worldwide, so they must tailor their advertising for each market they enter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Often you'll see Apple ads on international flights that appear not only in English, which is the lingua franca of most regions, but also in the native languages of the majority of passengers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I traveled to Russia last week, and it was really interesting to see the same Nike ad that I've seen a hundred times, except this time it was in Russian.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, going back to the medium of the advertisement, even after choosing to create print ads instead of radio announcements, television commercials, et cetera, there is more to consider.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you print your ad in a newspaper, it will be read by a far different audience than if you print your ad in a popular magazine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Would you put an ad for the new Justin Bieber album in a newspaper?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Probably not, because that product is most suitable for youths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's face it, do you know anyone under the age of twenty-five that buys a newspaper?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let's try a few strategy exercises.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Imagine you are a company that is aiming to improve the environment by making products that reduce human waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How would you advertise your product?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Clearly, it would send the wrong message if you put up flyers or other materials that caused lots of waste paper.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Consider instead putting commercials on the health channel or buying ad space on websites like UNESCO.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Or here's another example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What is one great place to advertise suntan lotion?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How about a swimming pool?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has the exact group of people that need the product.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All right, one last thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's say you're filming a commercial for a water filter pitcher.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What would be good scenery to use for the background?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Think about somewhere calm and relaxing with clean, fresh water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Can't you see how much more effective a commercial with the beautiful scenery and flowing rivers of a national park would be than, say, water dripping from a tap?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So to wrap things up today, think about the geography of your target market, the type of marketing material you should use, and the most effective way to appeal to the customer in order to make a successful ad campaign.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is all I have for you today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Make sure to read through chapter eight for Monday if you have not done so already.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, now I'd be happy to answer any questions you may have.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到顾客愿意出行的“distance（距离）”是他们选择去哪里购买产品的重要因素，这直接对应了题干中的“affects the probability”。
questions.tip: 你可能在后面听到了关于餐厅远近的例子，但填空考查的是概括性的核心词，不要被具体的场景例子（如restaurant、apartment）带跑偏。

questions.explanation: 录音指出，如果广告标语播放时伴随着“sound（声音）”，消费者会更容易记住，完美契合题干的“easier to remember”和“played with”。

questions.quote: Studies show that consumers are much more likely to remember advertising slogans if there's also a sound played.

questions.explanation: 录音用Mandy's Candy Store作为例子，说明了嗅觉（sense of smell）能唤起记忆并引发对巧克力的渴望，从而吸引顾客。

questions.quote: Did you know that your sense of smell is closely linked with memory? Think about Mandy's Candy Store up the road. Every time you walk past it, you can just smell the chocolate, right? I bet you can almost smell it now. Just mentioning the name brings about the smell memory and, in turn, a chocolate craving.

questions.explanation: 录音直接点明，对于数字产品（digital products）这类商品来说，其“flexibility（灵活性）”是极其重要的（extremely important）。

questions.quote: For example, it's a good idea to come up with a marketing strategy that adapts to the product, especially digital products. questions.quote: Once the customer experiences the ad, the important thing is his or her reaction. Someone could love the ad you made, but unless he or she considers buying the product, you failed to get the reaction you were looking for.

sentences.text: As an island country with a fauna dominated by birds, New Zealand was once home to an owl species which is now extinct, the laughing owl, named for its distinctive cry.
This bird was widespread throughout the islands when European settlers arrived in the middle of the 19th century and it remained in good numbers for some years thereafter.
Where other native birds suffered from predation by the Polynesian rat, the laughing owl turned the tables and adapted its diet to include the rodent.
It was also capable of catching and killing the other New Zealand owl, the morepork, and even larger birds, such as the weka.
However, the laughing owl was wiped out around the beginning of the 20th century, its demise caused by specimen collectors, habitat changes, and non-native predators including cats and stoats.
Surprisingly, it is the smaller owl, the morepork, that has managed to survive until this day.
Speckled dark brown, with yellow eyes and long tails, they are around 29 centimetres long from head to tail and 175 grams in weight.
Moreporks have fringes on the edge of their feathers, so they can fly almost silently and not alert potential prey.
They have acute hearing and their large eyes are very sensitive to light.
Moreporks nest in tree hollows, in clumps of plants, or in cavities among rocks and roots.
In the wild, moreporks usually start nesting in October, although two specimens have been recorded nesting in mid-winter, possibly stimulated by an ample food supply.
The female lays up to three white eggs, which she incubates for 20 to 30 days.
During this time, she rarely hunts, and the male brings food to her.
Once the chicks hatch, she stays mainly on the nest until the young owls are fully feathered.
When hatched, chicks are covered in light grey down and have their eyes closed.
The eyes do not open until the eighth day after hatching.
They can fly at around 35 days.
By day, moreporks sleep in roosts.
By night, they hunt a variety of animals – mainly large invertebrates including scarab and huhu beetles, moths, caterpillars and spiders.
They also take small birds and mice.
They can find suitable food in pine forest as well as native forest.
A morepork uses its sharp talons to catch or stun its prey, which it then carries away in its bill.
Moreporks are clever hunters, and birds such as robins, grey warblers and fantails can end up as their prey.
In the day, these small birds sometimes mob drowsy moreporks and chase them away from their roosts; they force the sleepy predators to search for a more peaceful spot.
Moreporks have proved to be ungracious hosts.
Scientists trying to establish a population of plovers on Motuora Island in New Zealand’s Hauraki Gulf were mystified as to why only two birds survived out of the 75 placed there.
The culprits turned out to be five pairs of moreporks that ate or chased away the new arrivals.
Although moreporks are still considered to be relatively common, it is likely that numbers are in gradual decline due to predation and loss of habitat.
As the female is a hole-nester, she is vulnerable to predators such as stoats and possums during the breeding season, and eggs and chicks will also be at risk from rats.
The use of pesticides is another possible threat to the owls, though not a direct one.
As moreporks are at the top of the food chain, they could be affected by an accumulative poison by consuming prey that has ingested poison.
The New Zealand Department of Conservation is taking steps to ensure the preservation of New Zealand’s only native owl.
The department is involved in measuring the population of moreporks and has put transmitters on a number of birds to determine survival and mortality.
As well as being New Zealand’s only native owl, the morepork has symbolic and spiritual importance, so in monitoring the birds it is hoped that the morepork will continue to survive and thrive.
At dusk, the melancholy sound of the morepork can be heard in forests and parks as it calls to other moreporks and claims territory.
Its Māori name (ruru) echoes its two-part cry.
In the tradition of the Māori people of New Zealand, the morepork, or ruru, was often seen as a careful guardian.
A number of sayings referred to the bird’s alertness.
As a bird of the night, it was associated with the spirit world.
Moreporks were believed to act as messengers to the gods in the heavens, flying along spiritual paths in the sky.
They were the mediums used to communicate with the gods.
The occasional high, piercing call of the morepork signified bad news, but the lower-pitched and more common “ruru” call heralded good news.

sentences.text: A  A rare textile made from the silk of more than a million wild spiders has been on display at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City.

To produce this golden cloth, 70 people spent four years collecting golden-orb spiders from telephone poles in Madagascar, while another dozen workers carefully extracted about 80 feet of silk filament from each of the arachnids.
The resulting 11-foot-by-4-foot textile is the only large piece of cloth made from natural spider silk in the world today.
B  Spider silk is very elastic and strong compared with steel or Kevlar, said textile expert Simon Peers, who co-led the project.
Kevlar is a lightweight synthetic fabric, chemically related to nylon, that is used in bullet-proof vests.
Kevlar is resistant to wear, tear and heat and has virtually no melting point.
But the tensile strength of spider silk is even greater than Kevlar’s aramid filaments and higher than that of high-grade steel.
Most importantly, spider silk is extremely lightweight: a strand long enough to circle the Earth would weigh less than 500 grams (18 oz).

It is also especially ductile, able to stretch up to 140 percent of its length without breaking and to retain its strength below –40 °C, giving it toughness equal to that of leading commercial fibres.
C  Researchers have long been intrigued by the unique properties of spider silk.
Unfortunately, spider silk is extremely hard to mass-produce.
Unlike silkworms—easy to raise in captivity—spiders have a habit of biting off each other’s heads when housed together.

According to Peers, there is intensive research worldwide aimed at replicating spider-silk tensile properties for use in medicine and industry, but no-one has yet reproduced all the qualities of natural silk.
D  Peers conceived the idea of weaving spider silk after reading about French missionary Jacob Paul Camboué, who worked with spiders in Madagascar during the 1880s and 1890s.
Camboué built a small hand-driven machine to extract silk from up to 24 spiders at once, without harming them: the spiders were briefly restrained, their silk collected, then released.
Peers built a replica of this 24-spider “silking” machine, said co-leader Nicholas Godley.
As a test the pair collected about 20 spiders.
“When we stuck them in the machine and started turning it, lo and behold, this beautiful gold-coloured silk started coming out,” Godley recalled.
E  To make a textile of any significant size, the scale had to increase dramatically.
Fourteen thousand spiders yield about an ounce of silk, Godley said, and the finished textile weighs about 2.6 pounds.
By the end, handlers had worked with more than one million female golden-orb spiders—abundant in Madagascar and famed for their golden thread.
Because the spiders produce silk only in the rainy season, all were collected between October and June.
An additional 12 workers used hand-powered machines to extract the silk and twist it into 96-filament yarn.
After “silking”, the spiders were released; within a week they regenerate their silk, allowing the same individuals to be used again—“the gift that never stops giving,” said Godley.
F  Spending four years to produce a single piece of cloth is hardly practical for scientists or companies hoping to exploit spider silk in biomedicine or as a Kevlar alternative.
Several groups have inserted spider genes into bacteria and even goats to make silk, but results have been only partly successful.
One reason is that spider silk begins as a liquid protein produced in a special gland in the abdomen.
Using the spinneret, the spider applies force that rearranges the protein’s molecular structure, transforming it into solid fibre.

“When we talk about a spider spinning silk, we’re talking about how it applies forces to convert liquid to solid,” explained spider-silk expert Todd Blackledge of the University of Akron, who was not involved in the project.
“Every year we get closer to mass production, but we’re not there yet.”
For now, we must be content with one extraordinarily beautiful cloth—courtesy of more than a million spiders.

questions.tip: 不要被“scientific analysis”迷惑，这里讲的是历史故事和一个机械装置的复原，重点在于“复活旧点子（old idea）”。

questions.tip: 不要看到“genes”和“bacteria”就只关注“advances（iii）”，本段后半部分详细分析了“从液体变固体”的生物物理过程，这才是“科学分析”。
