transcript.text: Now, you wanted to organize a formal discussion of some sort in the class.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Is that right, Daniel?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We thought it would be really good to end our psychology course with a formal debate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You know, where there's a statement, and people argue for or against it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Mm, good idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Where did the enthusiasm come from?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Have either of you organized debates before?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fiona?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No, but one of my friends did in his last year at secondary school, and he says he got a lot out of doing it, and I know they have debates in lots of other departments here at the university.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what do you think the students, you and the others, would get out of this?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, a debate will encourage people to study all sides of the subject matter, and I also think listening to other people's ideas can have a focusing effect on your own.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Sometimes you kind of don't know what you truly believe until you hear something you disagree with.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: [laughs] Okay, what about the topic for the debate?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We've got three to choose from.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We'll show you in a minute to check they're okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: At first, we thought we'd ask the other students to suggest something, but we were afraid we'd get thirty different topics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: [laughs]
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So instead, we brainstormed some, just the two of us, then made a shortlist, and we'll get them to vote for the one they like best.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the thing is, if people don't know how debates work, they could feel at a disadvantage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I mean, it wouldn't affect their grades or anything, but it could put them off.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So we thought we should have a meeting beforehand to make sure everyone's clear about what's involved in a debate and how to prepare for it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I think that's a good idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And we thought we could establish some key points of a successful debate there, like that debates are effective methods for considering an issue and that you need to understand both sides of an argument in order to support one side effectively.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We think it'll be best if we can use an issue that the students already have strong opinions about.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Then some people will be happy to speak in support of it and others to oppose it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What else do you want to do at the meeting?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, we've got to think about how people will do the background research for the debate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We could organize everyone into two teams.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That should save time for the main speakers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They won't have to do it on their own.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And we'll need to decide on some rules, like how long each person speaks for, and to select a chair for the debate, someone who's really confident.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Fine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I think you should have some sort of follow-up to the debate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: After it's over, I'd like you to get everyone to write a short essay focusing on what they gained from participating in it, and in turn, that can feed into the work we've been doing on learning and motivation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But would you be willing to read them and report back?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I mean, give some feedback on them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: [laughs] I wouldn't have made the suggestion if I wasn't.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, now let's think a bit more about the meeting.

transcript.text: You need to decide exactly how you'll introduce the students to different features of a debate.

transcript.text: Yes, okay.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, but we do need to talk about body language as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yes, that's a very important tool.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've got an interesting article on that with some good diagrams of techniques for things like eye contact.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll make some copies for you to give out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So they'll need to know where to look for the information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, get everyone involved.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: What about preparation for asking and answering questions?

transcript.text: We could try to demonstrate that, but I'm not sure how.

transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.text: Okay.

l4.title: Antarctica Field Trip To Mertz Glacier

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a talk given by a researcher about a recent field trip to a glacier in Antarctica.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'd like to talk to you about our recent field trip to the Mertz Glacier in Antarctica, and to place it in the wider context of research and international cooperation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: According to the Antarctic Treaty, the whole region was designated for the advancement of science and maintaining global peace.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This decision was a milestone in international cooperation, preventing conflict in one of the world's most isolated areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The treaty has provided a framework that allows nations to collaborate rather than compete, and it is one of the reasons why Antarctica remains such a unique site for fieldwork.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, preparing for an expedition to such an environment requires great care.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The explorers always had to pack spare batteries to keep their instruments functioning in the harsh climate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Without them, they risked losing valuable data during research missions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, it was equally important that they could operate a radio device in case of emergencies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Radios were often the only way to contact nearby stations for help, so every member of the team was given basic communication training before departure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The journey itself began with sea travel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The team traveled aboard the Aurora Australia, a modern research vessel that even has its own library for study and reference.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This facility allowed the scientists to continue reading, analyzing, and preparing reports while at sea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On arrival, the schedule was filled with both practical work and training.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During their stay, they attended specialized workshops that offered guidance on managing and preserving scientific data.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These sessions helped ensure that valuable findings would be stored accurately and shared effectively with other researchers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once the field activities began, the scientists undertook a variety of monitoring tasks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of their tasks involved monitoring water pollution, particularly measuring how much acid was present in the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Careful recording of acidity levels was essential for tracking long-term changes in ocean health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Alongside this, they also carried out inspections of the instruments used in a penguin study, including checking that the cameras were functioning correctly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Reliable footage was vital for observing penguin behavior without disturbing the animals directly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Speaking of penguins, one of the most fascinating observations came from their movements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers observed that penguin colonies often advance across the ice, forming a pattern like a wave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This movement not only creates rhythm in their march but also provides protection and energy efficiency for the group.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The recordings captured by the cameras gave the team new insights into these collective behaviors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, environmental issues were also a major focus.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Scientists carefully recorded the specific types of rubbish discovered in the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Analyzing this debris allowed them to identify the zones most seriously affected by human pollution and to make recommendations for cleaning and protecting sensitive areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, we should mention the plans for the future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Plans are underway for an additional ship that will serve future expeditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This modern vessel is expected to provide improved laboratories and accommodation, making research far more efficient.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It will also allow larger teams to visit Antarctica and extend the reach of collaborative projects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So to summarize, the trip to the Mertz Glacier was not only about data collection, but also about training, cooperation, and planning for sustainable research in one of the harshest environments on Earth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

Antarctica Field Trip to the Mertz Glacier
Background to the Antarctic Treaty
•　Under the Antarctic Treaty, the continent is dedicated to science and {{31}} .
•　The scientists had to take extra {{32}} for equipment.
•　They had to learn how to use a {{33}} for emergencies.
Recent research
•　They travelled on the Aurora Australia, which has its own {{34}} .
•　They attended workshops e.g. advice on managing and preserving {{35}} .
•　Monitoring water pollution especially how much {{36}} there was.
•　Checking the equipment for a penguin study, for example, the {{37}} .
Penguin behaviour and future plans
•　Penguin groups move in the shape of a {{38}} .
•　Noting details of {{39}} to understand which areas are most affected.
•　A new {{40}} is planned and this will benefit researchers.

questions.explanation: 录音里明确提到南极条约（Antarctic Treaty）将该地区用于科学发展（science）和维护全球和平（peace），刚好对应题目的两个并列信息。
questions.tip: 你可能会把“global peace”都写上，但注意题目字数要求是“ONE WORD ONLY”，所以只能填最核心的名词“peace”。
questions.quote: Today, I'd like to talk to you about our recent field trip to the Mertz Glacier in Antarctica, and to place it in the wider context of research and international cooperation. According to the Antarctic Treaty, the whole region was designated for the advancement of science and maintaining global peace.

questions.explanation: 录音中用“pack spare（打包备用的）”替换了题干的“take extra（带额外的）”，后面紧跟着的“batteries”就是设备所需带上的物品。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到后面的“data”而填错，但“data”是没带电池会导致丢失的东西，而不是为了设备额外带的东西。
questions.quote: Now, preparing for an expedition to such an environment requires great care. The explorers always had to pack spare batteries to keep their instruments functioning in the harsh climate. Without them, they risked losing valuable data during research missions.

questions.explanation: 录音中说的“operate a radio device in case of emergencies（在紧急情况下操作无线电）”完美对应了题干的“use a _____ for emergencies”。
questions.tip: 你可能想填“device”，但“radio”才是体现具体沟通用途的核心词，且填入“radio”更符合语境。
questions.quote: In addition, it was equally important that they could operate a radio device in case of emergencies. Radios were often the only way to contact nearby stations for help, so every member of the team was given basic communication training before departure.

questions.explanation: 录音里提到Aurora Australia这艘船“has its own library”，这跟题干上的“has its own”一模一样，听到就可以直接锁定答案。
questions.tip: 这里基本就是送分题，别被后面补充说明的“study and reference”分散注意力导致漏听或拼错即可。
questions.quote: The journey itself began with sea travel. The team traveled aboard the Aurora Australia, a modern research vessel that even has its own library for study and reference. This facility allowed the scientists to continue reading, analyzing, and preparing reports while at sea.

questions.explanation: 题干里的“advice”在录音里换了个说法变成了“guidance”，紧随其后的“managing and preserving”原词重现，顺理成章带出答案“data”。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到完整的“scientific data”而不知道怎么填，但字数限制只有一个词，所以果断舍弃形容词提取核心名词“data”即可。
questions.quote: On arrival, the schedule was filled with both practical work and training. During their stay, they attended specialized workshops that offered guidance on managing and preserving scientific data. These sessions helped ensure that valuable findings would be stored accurately and shared effectively with other researchers.

questions.explanation: 录音用“measuring”替换了题目的“monitoring”，紧跟着的“how much acid was present”直接解答了“how much ______ there was”的疑问。
questions.tip: 注意不要填成后面补充说明里出现的“acidity levels”，根据疑问词“how much”锁定不可数名词“acid”是最稳妥的。
questions.quote: One of their tasks involved monitoring water pollution, particularly measuring how much acid was present in the environment. Careful recording of acidity levels was essential for tracking long-term changes in ocean health.

questions.explanation: 录音先提到了“penguin study”，然后用“including checking”引出具体检查的设备，答案“cameras”呼之欲出。
questions.tip: 这题答案带有复数“s”，听的时候一定要注意抓尾音，别只写了单数“camera”导致冤枉扣分。
questions.quote: Alongside this, they also carried out inspections of the instruments used in a penguin study, including checking that the cameras were functioning correctly. Reliable footage was vital for observing penguin behavior without disturbing the animals directly.

questions.explanation: 题干的“in the shape of（以...的形状）”被替换成了“forming a pattern like（形成像...一样的图案）”，后面紧跟的“a wave”就是正确答案。
questions.tip: 你可能只顾着死等“shape”这个词而错过了“pattern”这种换汤不换药的说法，导致跟丢了后面的正确答案。
questions.quote: Speaking of penguins, one of the most fascinating observations came from their movements. Researchers observed that penguin colonies often advance across the ice, forming a pattern like a wave. This movement not only creates rhythm in their march but also provides protection and energy efficiency for the group.

questions.explanation: 题干的“Noting details of（记录...的细节）”换了个说法变成了“carefully recorded the specific types of”，直接引出后面的记录对象“rubbish”。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到下一句出现的“debris”或者后面的“human pollution”，但只有“rubbish”是紧跟在“记录”这个动作后面的第一对象。
questions.quote: Of course, environmental issues were also a major focus. Scientists carefully recorded the specific types of rubbish discovered in the environment. Analyzing this debris allowed them to identify the zones most seriously affected by human pollution and to make recommendations for cleaning and protecting sensitive areas.

questions.explanation: 录音明确提到正在计划一艘额外的船（an additional ship），这里的“additional”和后面说的“modern vessel”都对应题干的“new”，所以填“ship”或“vessel”都对。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到后面的“laboratories”并想把它填进去，但实验室是这艘船提供的内部设施，而题目问的是整体计划了一个新的“什么”。
questions.quote: Finally, we should mention the plans for the future. Plans are underway for an additional ship that will serve future expeditions. This modern vessel is expected to provide improved laboratories and accommodation, making research far more efficient.

sentences.text: Katherine Mansfield Beauchamp Murry was born in 1888, into a prominent family in Wellington, New Zealand.
She became one of New Zealand's best-known writers, using the pen name of Katherine Mansfield.
The daughter of a banker, and born into a middle-class family, she was also a first cousin of Countess Elizabeth von Arnim, a distinguished novelist in her time.
Mansfield had two older sisters and a younger brother.
Her father, Harold Beauchamp, went on to become the chairman of the Bank of New Zealand.

In 1893, the Mansfield family moved to Karori, a suburb of Wellington, where Mansfield would spend the happiest years of her childhood; she later used her memories of this time as an inspiration for her Prelude story.
Her first published stories appeared in the High School Reporter and the Wellington Girls' High School magazine in 1898 and 1899.
In 1902, she developed strong feelings for a musician who played the cello, Arnold Trowell, although her feelings were not, for the most part, returned.
Mansfield herself was an accomplished cellist, having received lessons from Trowell's father.

Mansfield wrote in her journals of feeling isolated to some extent in New Zealand, and, in general terms, of her interest in the Maori people (New Zealand's native people), who were often portrayed in a sympathetic light in her later stories, such as How Pearl Button Was Kidnapped.
She moved to London in 1903, where she attended Queen's College, along with her two sisters.
Mansfield recommenced playing the cello, an occupation that she believed, during her time at Queen's, she would take up professionally.
She also began contributing to the college newspaper, with such a dedication to it that she eventually became its editor.

She was particularly interested in the works of the French writers of this period and in the 19th century British writer, Oscar Wilde, and she was appreciated amongst fellow students at Queen's for her lively and charismatic approach to life and work.
She met fellow writer Ida Baker, a South African, at the college, and the pair became lifelong friends.
Mansfield did not actively support the suffragette movement in the UK.
Women in New Zealand had gained the right to vote in 1893.
Mansfield first began journeying into other parts of Europe in the period 1903–1906, mainly to Belgium and Germany.
After finishing her schooling in England, she returned to her New Zealand home in 1906, only then beginning to write short stories in a serious way.
She had several works published in Australia in a magazine called The Native Companion, which was her first paid writing work, and by this time she had her mind set on becoming a professional writer.
It was also the first occasion on which she used the pseudonym “K.
Mansfield”.
Mansfield rapidly grew discontented with the provincial New Zealand lifestyle, and with her family.
Two years later she headed again to London.
Her father sent her an annual subsidy of £100 for the rest of her life.
In later years, she would express both admiration and disdain for New Zealand in her journals.
In 1911, Mansfield met John Middleton Murry, the Oxford scholar and editor of the literary magazine Rhythm.
They were later to marry in 1918.
Mansfield became a co-editor of Rhythm, which was subsequently called The Blue Review, in which more of her works were published.
She and Murry lived in various houses in England and briefly in Paris.
The Blue Review failed to gain enough readers and was no longer published.
Their attempt to set up as writers in Paris was cut short by Murry's bankruptcy, which resulted from the failure of this and other journals.
Life back in England meant frequently changed addresses and very limited funds.
Between 1915 and 1918, Mansfield moved between England and Bandol, France.
She and Murry developed close contact with other well-known writers of the time such as D.
H.
Lawrence, Bertrand Russell and Aldous Huxley.
By October 1918 Mansfield had become seriously ill; she had been diagnosed with tuberculosis and was advised to enter a sanatorium.
She could no longer spend winters in London.
In the autumn of 1918 she was so ill that she decided to go to Ospedaletti in Italy.
It was the publication of Bliss and Other Stories in 1920 that was to solidify Mansfield's reputation as a writer.
Mansfield also spent time in Menton, France, as the tenant of her father's cousin at “The Villa Isola Bella”.
There she wrote eight stories including Miss Brill and The Daughters of the Late Colonel, the latter of which she pronounced to be “…the only story that satisfies me to any extent”.
Mansfield produced a great deal of work in the final years of her life, and much of her prose and poetry remained unpublished at her death in 1923.
After her death, her husband, Murry, took on the task of editing and publishing her works.

His efforts resulted in two additional volumes of short stories, The Doves' Nest and Something Childish, published in 1923 and 1924 respectively; the publication of her Poems; as well as a collection of critical writings (Novels and Novelists) and a number of editions of Mansfield's previously unpublished letters and journals.

groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 1–6 on your answer sheet, write:

questions.prompt: The name Katherine Mansfield, which appears on the writer's books, was exactly the same as her original name.
questions.explanation: 题目说她书上的名字和原名“完全一样（exactly the same）”，原文A段说她用笔名Katherine Mansfield，而原名是“Katherine Mansfield Beauchamp Murry”，显然不同，选 FALSE。
questions.tip: 原文明确区分了“pen name（笔名）”和出生时的全名，长度都不一样，绝非“exactly the same”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “She became one of New Zealand's best-known writers, using the pen name of Katherine Mansfield... born... Katherine Mansfield Beauchamp Murry.”

questions.prompt: Mansfield won a prize for a story she wrote for the High School Reporter.
questions.explanation: 原文B段只提到她的首批故事“发表（appeared）”在High School Reporter上，完全没有提及她是否因此“得奖（won a prize）”，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.tip: “发表”不等于“获奖”，不要因为她是著名作家就默认她小时候一定得过奖。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “Her first published stories appeared in the High School Reporter...”

questions.prompt: How Pearl Button Was Kidnapped portrayed Maori people in a favourable way.
questions.explanation: 题目说《Pearl Button》这篇故事以“有利/正面（favourable）”的方式描绘毛利人。原文B段说毛利人在她后来的故事中常以“同情/好感的光环（sympathetic light）”被描绘，选 TRUE。
questions.tip: “Sympathetic light” 在文学批评中通常指带有同情、理解和好感的正面描写，对应 “favourable way”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...Maori people... who were often portrayed in a sympathetic light in her later stories, such as How Pearl Button Was Kidnapped.”

questions.prompt: When Mansfield was at Queen's College, she planned to be a professional writer.
questions.explanation: 题目说她在Queen's College时计划成为职业作家。原文C段说她在那里时相信自己会职业从事“大提琴（playing the cello）”，成为职业作家是回新西兰后的事（1906年），选 FALSE。
questions.tip: 注意时间点“during her time at Queen's”，那时的目标是音乐（cello），不是写作。
questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “Mansfield recommenced playing the cello, an occupation that she believed, during her time at Queen's, she would take up professionally.”

questions.prompt: Mansfield was unpopular with the other students at Queen's College.
questions.explanation: 题目说她在Queen's College不受其他学生欢迎（unpopular）。原文C段说她因活泼和魅力被同学“欣赏（appreciated）”，即受欢迎，选 FALSE。
questions.tip: “Appreciated amongst fellow students” 直接反驳了 “unpopular”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “...she was appreciated amongst fellow students at Queen's for her lively and charismatic approach...”

questions.prompt: In London, Mansfield showed little interest in politics.
questions.explanation: 原文C段只说她“没有积极支持（did not actively support）”英国的妇女参政运动，但这不代表她对政治“几乎没兴趣（little interest）”，可能只是不支持该特定运动或方式，信息不充分，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.tip: 这道题有另外一个版本，原文对应答案句为“Mansfield did not become involved in much political activity when she liveed in London. For example, although at that time in London many women were demonstrating for votes for women, Mansfield did not actively support the suffragette movement in the UK...”，所以答案选 A。
questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “Mansfield did not actively support the suffragette movement in the UK.”

questions.explanation: 题目说____阻止了二人在巴黎待在一起，原文E段说他们在巴黎的尝试被Murry的“bankruptcy（破产）”打断了，填 bankruptcy。

questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “She and Murry developed close contact with other well-known writers of the time...”

questions.explanation: 题目说随着《Bliss》出版，她的____被巩固了，原文F段说这本书的出版“solidify Mansfield's reputation（巩固了曼斯菲尔德的声誉）”，填 reputation。
questions.tip: 动词“consolidated”是原文“solidify”的同义替换。
questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “It was the publication of Bliss... that was to solidify Mansfield's reputation as a writer.”

questions.explanation: 题目说曼斯菲尔德的____在她死后出版了更多作品，原文G段说她死后，她的“husband（丈夫）”Murry承担了编辑出版的任务，填 husband。
questions.tip: 虽然原文也给了名字 Murry，但题目结构是“Mansfield's ______”，填身份词 husband 最为准确。
questions.quote: (Paragraph G) “After her death, her husband, Murry, took on the task of editing and publishing her works.”

sentences.text: There is an age-old practice of harvesting plants and herbs in their natural environment for use as medicines.

And today there is huge potential for New Zealand to develop a herb industry based on the excellent growing conditions and expertise there, according to Phil Rasmussen, a pharmacist and medical herbalist.
Take arnica, for example, a popular pharmaceutical herb used to treat bruises and joint problems.
Traditionally collected by Romany communities in Europe, it is now in high demand worldwide as interest develops in the capabilities of the small alpine plant.
A 2008 report for the Plant and Food Research organisation concluded that New Zealand has a good opportunity to cultivate arnica flowers and roots for the international markets.
However, the initiative was stopped in its tracks when the government abruptly halted funding for the research programme.
It was an unjustified move, according to agronomist Malcolm Douglas, based on a number of inaccurate views about weed invasion.
The history of herbal medicines in New Zealand has long featured disagreements of this sort.

For the early Maori people – the original inhabitants of New Zealand – the forest was well stocked with edible plants that were an obvious source of nutrition, but that were taken for the relief of pain as well.

While the earliest European doctors in New Zealand relied on imported dried herbs, many were keen to include native plants in their practices: in his book published in 1891, herbalist James Neil described manuka and koromiko as among New Zealand's most valuable herbs.
Despite its popularity among some, however, herbalism continued to have its detractors.
In 1907 Neil, president of the then very young New Zealand Association of Medical Herbalists (NZAMH), petitioned parliament for legal status for herbalists, but he was unsuccessful.
The Evening Post newspaper perhaps summed up the opposing position by claiming that herbalism 'is obsolete'.
In fact, traditional Maori medicine faced a more determined challenge.
In 1908 the government passed a controversial law that had the effect of restricting traditional herbal practice, or pushing it underground.
Then for a brief period in the mid-20th century, herbal medicine was largely ignored, shunned by the majority of the medical profession, and absent from medical school curricula.

But a centuries-old tradition was not going to disappear so easily, and in the 1980s the NZAMH was revived, and it became possible to complete a course in herbal medicine at several polytechnics around the country.
However, the problem remained of how to connect the culture of plant-based medicine with conventional scientific thinking in order to promote herbal use within the general population.
For many years, the limited evidence there was that herbal medicines worked was undermined by lack of interest among general practitioners and within the scientific community.

Today, the ideas of herbalists in the 1980s – eat a varied diet, include lots of fresh fruit and vegetables, recognise stress – are completely accepted by the medical establishment and widely practised in society as a whole.
Natural health products are big sellers in pharmacies, and global pharmaceutical companies are buying up natural supplement brands or developing their own.
What's more, according to Rasmussen, robust clinical trials show that herbal medicine is generally safe – safer than most drugs.
'It doesn't do everything,' he says, 'but there's a lot it does do, particularly in terms of preventative health care.'
One significant issue for today's export-oriented herbal medicine producers is the question of how to guarantee standards for consumers in different countries.
In other words, there is the need for some form of globally recognised system of documentation.
Rasmussen's range of extracts are produced under the Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) scheme, which is respected around the world.
So too is the range produced by Sandra Clair, who says that such assurance is expensive but necessary if you want to export herbal remedies to the rest of the world.

Moves to launch a joint Australia–New Zealand agency to regulate herbal remedies under a single, streamlined licensing process have recently been revived, after being abandoned in 2007 through lack of support in parliament.
There are those in the industry who support further regulation still.
According to Rasmussen, some herbs should require a prescription from a suitably qualified medical herbalist or doctor.

For example, consumers shouldn't be able to go to their local supermarket and buy St John's Wort, according to Rasmussen, because it can interact in harmful ways with at least ten pharmaceutical drugs.
Isla Burgess, who is part of the International Research Group for the Conservation of Medicinal Plants, agrees that tighter regulation is necessary, but for a different reason.
'More than 400,000 tonnes of medicinal and aromatic plants are traded in the world each year,' says Burgess.
'The great majority of these are harvested from the wild, so they each have an impact on their local ecosystem.'
She gives the example of elm trees in the USA, ringbarked and stripped for the growing market for a product called 'slippery elm': this endangered tree should be protected.
But others argue that more regulation would be prohibitively expensive for all but the largest manufacturers – a change, cautions Clair, that would probably put some local companies out of business.
So, for the time being at least, it seems that the topic of herbal medicines will continue to provoke debate.

groups.instructions:
Reading Passage 2 has five paragraphs, A-E.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A-E, in boxes 14–17 on your answer sheet.

questions.prompt: a reference to the interest shown by large corporations in herbal remedies
questions.explanation: 题目提到大公司对草药疗法的兴趣，D段指出“全球制药公司（global pharmaceutical companies）”正在收购天然补充剂品牌或开发自己的产品，对应选项 D。
questions.tip: 关键词“Large corporations”对应原文的“global pharmaceutical companies”，且动作是“buying up... or developing”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph D) “Natural health products are big sellers in pharmacies, and global pharmaceutical companies are buying up natural supplement brands or developing their own.”

questions.prompt: examples of the uses of one particular herbal medicine
questions.explanation: 题目要求一种特定草药用途的例子，A段以“山金车（arnica）”为例，说明它被用于治疗“瘀伤和关节问题（bruises and joint problems）”，对应选项 A。
questions.tip: 看到“Take arnica, for example”就能直接锁定这是关于“examples”的段落。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “Take arnica, for example, a popular pharmaceutical herb used to treat bruises and joint problems.”

sentences.text: O’ Connell-Rodwell, a post-doctoral fellow at Stanford University, has traveled to Namibia’s first-ever wildlife reserve to explore the mystical and complicated realm of elephant communication.
She, along with her colleagues, is part of a scientific revolution that started almost 20 years ago.

This revolution has made a stunning revelation: elephants are capable of communicating with one another over long distances by means of low-frequency sounds, also known as infrasound, which are too deep for humans to hear.
As might be expected, African elephants’ ability to detect seismic sound may have something to do with their ears.
The hammer bone in an elephant’s inner ear is proportionally huge for a mammal, but it is normal for animals that use vibrational signals.
Thus, it may be a sign that elephants can use seismic sounds to communicate.
Other aspects of elephant anatomy also support this ability.

First, their massive bodies, which enable them to give out low-frequency sounds almost as powerful as the sound a jet makes during take-off, serve as ideal frames for receiving ground vibrations and transmitting them to the inner ear.
Second, the elephant’s toe bones are set in a fatty pad, which might help focus vibrations from the ground into the bone.
Finally, the elephant has an enormous brain that sits in the cranial cavity behind the eyes, in line with the auditory canal.
The front of the skull is riddled with sinus cavities, which might function as resonating chambers for ground vibrations.
It remains unclear how elephants detect such vibrations, but O’ Connell-Rodwell suggests that the pachyderms are ‘listening’ with their trunks and feet instead of (or in addition to) their ears.
The elephant trunk may be the most versatile appendage in nature: it is used for drinking, bathing, smelling, feeding and scratching.
Both trunk and feet contain two types of nerve endings that are sensitive to pressure—one detects infrasonic vibration and the other responds to vibrations of slightly higher frequencies.
As O’ Connell-Rodwell sees it, this research has a boundless and unpredictable future.
‘Our work is really at the interface of geophysics, neurophysiology and ecology,’ she says.
‘We’re raising questions that have never even been considered before.’

Scientists have long known that seismic communication is widespread among small animals such as spiders, scorpions, insects and many vertebrates, including white-lipped frogs, blind mole-rats, kangaroo rats and golden moles.
Nevertheless, O’ Connell-Rodwell was the first to argue that a giant land animal is also sending and receiving seismic signals.

‘I used to lay a male planthopper on a stem and replay the calling sound of a female; the male would exhibit the same kind of behaviour that happens in elephants: he would freeze, press down on his legs, move forward a little, then stay still again.
I found it fascinating, and it made me think that perhaps auditory communication is not the only thing going on.’

Scientists have confirmed that an elephant’s capacity to communicate over long distances is essential for survival, especially in places like Etosha, where more than 2,400 savanna elephants range over an area larger than New Jersey.
It is already difficult for an elephant to find a mate in such a vast wilderness, and elephant reproductive biology only complicates matters.
Breeding herds also adopt low-frequency sounds to warn of predators.
Even though adult elephants have no enemies other than human beings, calves are vulnerable and susceptible to attacks from lions and hyenas.
At the sight of a predator, older herd members clump together to protect the young before running away.
We now know that elephants can respond to warning calls in the air, but can they detect signals transmitted solely through the ground?
To investigate, the research team designed an experiment in 2002 that used electronic devices to send signals through the ground at Mushara.
‘The outcomes of our 2002 study revealed that elephants could indeed sense warning signals through the ground,’ O’ Connell-Rodwell observes.
Last year, an experiment was set up to pursue the problem further.
It used three different recordings: the 1994 warning call from Mushara, an anti-predator call recorded by scientist Joyce Poole in Kenya, and a made-up warble tone.
‘The data I’ve observed so far imply that the elephants responded exactly as I expected.
However, the fascinating finding is that the anti-predator call from Kenya—unfamiliar to them—caused them to gather, tense up and rumble aggressively as well; but they didn’t always flee.
I didn’t expect the results to be that clear-cut.’

transcript.text: Around ten years ago, Australia Zoo, the University of Queensland, and Queensland Parks and Wildlife undertook a project to monitor the movements and behavior of the crocodiles in Lakefield National Park.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The aim of the study was to provide better information on how adult crocodiles there interact within a river system, enabling people to have better decisions on how to manage crocodile populations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This project can lead the world in crocodile management because of the use of satellite, which enables scientists to stably receive accurate information being sent back to them on the computer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even though the crocodiles can travel very long distances, scientists can still know where they are and study their habits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The study is going to help scientists gain further knowledge on crocodile behavior, which can help make informed decisions on the management plans for crocodiles, not only in Australia, but around the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Crocodile tracking isn't a new idea in Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Crocodile studies have been previously conducted by radio.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A miniature electronic device was implanted under the skin of these animals, and they were released back into the river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These tags enabled scientists to track the movements of these particular crocodiles over the next ten years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, there are some unexpected challenges.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The data transmitted from each receiver is recorded by some devices employed in the receiving stations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, some devices are too old that they always lose signals due to a variety of reasons,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: so they can't track those animals which they have been studying for months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to study the crocodiles, they must first be captured so that the device can be put on them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But this is a very difficult task because they are alert and afraid of being followed by humans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it might take the team several hours to capture one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The tracking device has signal transmitters inside, and it's waterproof.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is attached to the head of the crocodile, so the crocodile cannot remove the device with its feet or tail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The research has begun to reveal the movements of crocodiles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Data showed that crocodiles tend to be more active at nighttime.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The GPS sometimes shows that in some areas the crocodiles are overpopulated, so scientists at the park have to use a helicopter to relocate the crocodiles in order to control their population in the area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A crocodile would be taken many kilometers away from its original place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, scientists found that the relocation methods were ineffective because the relocated crocodiles will return to their original location following the most direct route within one week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The tracking data shows that the crocodiles swim right back to where they came from when moved.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Crocodiles sometimes travel hundreds of kilometers from Indonesia to Australia in order to reproduce.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is interesting to see that they can always find their way, and they will not get lost in the ocean.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Scientists realized the crocodiles are able to navigate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is an important ability for them when they have to migrate for very long distances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We may wonder if human beings can learn from the crocodiles and find our way without using technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, through lots of research and experiments, scientists conclude that crocodiles can tell directions by using their senses to the sun so that they know where they're going.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is an ability which human beings don't possess.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another finding is that like the migration of birds who can travel thousands and thousands of kilometers, crocodiles have the same system to help them travel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The research is still going on in northern Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Scientists are working hard to gather more information about this amazing creature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.

sentences.text: A The oceans cover more than 70 per cent of the planet's surface, yet until quite recently we knew less about their depths than about the surface of the Moon.
The Moon has been far more accessible to study because astronomers have long been able to look at its surface, first with the naked eye and then with the telescope, both instruments that focus light.

Until the twentieth century, however, no instruments were available for the study of Earth's oceans: light, which can travel trillions of kilometres through the vast vacuum of space, cannot penetrate very far in seawater.
B It turns out that for penetrating water the best instrument is sound.
Curious investigators have long been fascinated by sound and the way it travels in water.

As early as 1490, the artist and scientist Leonardo da Vinci observed: 'If you cause your ship to stop and place the head of a long tube in the water and place the outer extremity to your ear, you will hear ships at a great distance from you.'
It was not until 1826 that two scientists, Colladon and Sturm, accurately measured the speed of sound in water.
Using a long tube to listen under water (as da Vinci had suggested), they recorded how fast the sound of a submerged bell travelled across Lake Geneva in Switzerland.
What these investigators demonstrated was that water is an excellent medium for sound, transmitting it almost five times faster than its speed in air.
C A number of factors influence how far sound travels under water and how long it lasts, including particles, salinity, temperature and pressure.

Particles in seawater can reflect, scatter and absorb certain frequencies of sound, just as certain wavelengths of light may be reflected, scattered and absorbed by specific types of particles in the atmosphere.
In 1943, Maurice Ewing and J.
L.

Worzel conducted an experiment to test the theory that low-frequency waves, which are less vulnerable than higher frequencies to scattering and absorption, should be able to travel great distances, if the sound source is placed correctly.
The researchers set off an underwater explosion and learned that it was detected easily by receivers 3,200 kilometres away.
In analysing the results of this test, they discovered a kind of 'sound pipeline', known as the 'deep sound channel'.
Sound introduced into this channel of water could travel thousands of kilometres with minimal loss of signal.
D The US Navy was quick to appreciate the usefulness of low-frequency sound and the deep sound channel.

They developed the Sound Surveillance System (SOSUS), which involved underwater microphones, called hydrophones, that were placed on the ocean bottom and connected by cables to on-shore processing centres.
It was Christopher Clark of Cornell University who soon realised that SOSUS could be used to listen to whales.
Using a SOSUS receiver in the West Indies, he could hear whales that were 1,770 kilometres away.
E Whales are the biggest of Earth's creatures, yet these animals are also remarkably elusive.
Scientists wishing to observe blue whales must simply wait in their ships for the whales to surface.
A few whales have been tracked briefly in the wild in this way but not for very great distances, and much about them remains unknown.
But by using SOSUS, scientists can track the whales and position them on a map.
Moreover, they can track not just one whale at a time, but many creatures simultaneously.

They can also learn to distinguish whale calls; researchers have detected changes in the calls of finback whales as the seasons change, and have found that blue whales in different regions of the Pacific Ocean have different calls.
F SOSUS has also proved instrumental in obtaining information crucial to our understanding of climate.

The system has enabled researchers to begin making ocean temperature measurements on a global scale, measurements that are key to understanding the workings of heat transfer between the ocean and the atmosphere.
The ocean plays an enormous role in determining air temperature — the heat capacity in only the upper few metres of ocean is thought to be equal to all of the heat in the entire atmosphere.
For sound waves travelling horizontally in the ocean, speed is largely a function of temperature.
Thus, the travel time of a wave of sound between two points is a sensitive indicator of the average temperature along its path.
Transmitting sound in numerous directions through the deep sound channel can give scientists measurements spanning vast areas of the globe.

Thousands of sound paths in the ocean can be pieced together into a map of global ocean temperatures, and by repeating measurements along the same paths over time, scientists can track changes in temperature over months or years.
G Researchers are also using other acoustic techniques to monitor climate.
Oceanographer Jeff Nystuen, for example, has explored the use of sound to measure rainfall over the ocean.
Monitoring changing global rainfall patterns will contribute to understanding major climate change as well as the weather phenomenon known as El Niño.
Since 1985, Nystuen has used hydrophones to listen to rain over the ocean, acoustically measuring not only the rainfall rate but also the rainfall type, ranging from drizzle to thunderstorms.
By using the sound of rain under water as a 'natural' rain gauge, the measurement of rainfall over the oceans will become available to climatologists.
In this way, modern society continues to benefit from the investigations of those who, like Leonardo da Vinci, pursued the answers to some basic questions of nature.

sentences.text: A Do you read while listening to music?
Do you like to watch TV while finishing your homework?
People who have these kinds of habits are called multitaskers.
Multitaskers are able to complete two tasks at the same time by dividing their focus.
However, Thomas Lehman, a researcher in psychology, believes people never really do multiple things simultaneously.
Maybe a person is reading while listening to music, but in reality the brain can only focus on one task.
Reading the words in a book will cause you to ignore some of the words of the music.
When people think they are accomplishing two different tasks efficiently, what they are really doing is dividing their focus.
While listening to music, people become less able to focus on their surroundings.
For example, we all have experienced times when we talk with friends and they are not responding properly.
Maybe they are listening to someone else talk, or maybe they are reading a text on their smartphone and don’t hear what you are saying.
Lehman called this phenomenon “email voice.”
B The world has been changed by computers and their spin-offs such as smartphones or cellphones.
Now that most individuals have a personal device, like a smartphone or a laptop, they are frequently reading, watching or listening to virtual information.
This increases the occurrence of multitasking in our day-to-day life.
Nowadays, when you work, you may use your typewriter, your cellphone, and speak with colleagues who may drop by at any time.

In professional meetings, when one would normally focus on and listen to one another, people are more likely to have a cellphone in their lap, reading or communicating silently with more people than ever.
Even inventions such as the cordless phone have increased multitasking.
In the old days, a traditional wall phone would ring, and the housewife would have to stop her activities to answer it.
When it rang, the housewife would sit down with her legs up and chat, with no laundry, sweeping or answering the door.
In the modern era, our technology is convenient enough not to interrupt our daily tasks.
C Earl Miller, an expert at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, studied the prefrontal cortex, which guides the brain while a person is multitasking.
According to his studies, the size of this cortex varies between species.
He found that for humans, it constitutes one-third of the brain, whereas it is only 4 – 5 percent in dogs and about 15 percent in monkeys.
Because this cortex is larger in humans, it allows a person to be more flexible and accurate in multitasking.
However, Miller wanted to know whether the cortex was truly processing information about two different tasks simultaneously.
He designed an experiment in which he presented visual stimuli to his subjects in a way that mimicked multitasking.
Miller then attached sensors to the patients’ heads to pick up the electrical patterns of the brain.
These sensors would show whether the neurons were truly processing two different tasks.
What he found was that the brain neurons lit up in singular areas one at a time—never simultaneously.
D David Meyer, a professor at the University of Michigan, studied young adults in a similar experiment.
He instructed them to solve math problems while simultaneously classifying simple words into different categories.
Meyer found that when you think you are doing several jobs at the same time, you are actually switching between jobs.
Even though the participants tried to do the tasks at the same time and both tasks were eventually accomplished, overall the task took more time than if the person had focused on a single task.
E People sacrifice efficiency when multitasking.
Gloria Mark used office workers as her subjects.
She found that they were constantly multitasking.
She observed that nearly every 11 minutes people at work were disrupted.
She found that doing different jobs at the same time may actually save time.
However, despite the fact that they are faster, it does not mean they are more efficient.
We are equally likely to self-interrupt as to be interrupted by outside sources.
She found that in the office nearly every 12 minutes an employee would stop and, with no reason at all, check a website on their computer, call someone or write an email.
If they concentrated for more than 20 minutes, they would feel distressed.
She suggested that the average person may suffer from a short concentration span.
This short attention span might be natural, but others suggest that new technology may be the problem.
With cellphones and computers at our sides at all times, people will never run out of distractions.
The format of media—such as advertisements, music, news articles and TV shows—is also shortening, so people are used to paying attention to information for a very short time.
F Even though focusing on a single task is the most efficient way for our brains to work, it is not always practical in real life.
According to human nature, people feel more comfortable and efficient in environments with a variety of tasks.
Edward Hallowell said that people are losing a lot of efficiency in the workplace due to multitasking, outside distractions and self-distractions.
In fact, the changes made to the workplace do not have to be dramatic.
No one is suggesting we ban e-mail or make employees focus on only one task.
However, certain common workplace situations—such as group meetings—would be more efficient if we banned cellphones, a common distraction.
A person can also apply these tips to prevent self-distraction.
Instead of arriving at the office and checking all of your e-mails for new tasks—a common ritual—you could dedicate an hour to a single task first thing in the morning.
Self-timing is a great way to reduce distraction and finish tasks one by one, instead of slowing ourselves down with multitasking.

sentences.text: A A tiny insect navigates its way across featureless salt-pans.
A cockroach successfully works out how to scramble over an obstacle.
The mantis shrimp scans its aquatic world through hyperspectral eyes.

Using the most basic of equipment and brains tinier than a pin-head, insects constantly solve complex problems of movement, vision and navigation – processing data that would challenge a super-computer.
How they do it is driving one of the most exciting new fields of technology – biomimetics and biorobotics, the imitation of insect systems to control man-made machines.
Delegates at a recent conference presented some outcomes of their work in this area.
B Dr Alex Zelinsky suggested that the method by which wasps use landmarks to find their way back to the nest may one day be part of a system for navigating cars that know where to go.
A research team led by Dr Zelinsky has shown that a robot can navigate its way among 50 different landmarks by recognising them individually using a panoramic camera.
“The inspiration came from biology, where wasps use a practical method turn back and look to orient themselves as they emerge from their nest.
By flying to and fro, they look at the wasp nest from different angles and perspectives so they can recognise it again,” he explained.
The robot’s panoramic camera logs the surrounding area and its key landmarks, which are then stored in its computer according to how reliable they are as navigational aids.
The landmarks are then scaled, from small to large, so that the robot can recognise whether it is getting closer to or further away from them.
Their location is built into a map in its mind, which operates at different scales and instructs the robot whether to turn left or right at a particular mark.
The technology provides a general way for a machine to navigate an unknown landscape.

C For three decades, Professor Ruediger Wehner has journeyed from Switzerland to the Sahara Desert where Cataglyphis, a tiny ant with a brain weighing just 0.1 mg, performs acts of navigational genius when it leaves its nest, forages for food and returns successfully.
Cataglyphis uses polarised light, caused when air molecules scatter light, to orient and steer itself.
Wehner’s team found that the ant has a set of specialised photoreceptors along the upper rim of its eyes that detect polarised light, while other receptors perform different navigational tasks.
As the sun moves, the ant notes its direction each time it leaves the nest and updates its internal compass.
Using other eye receptors it stores a snapshot image of landmarks close to the nest entrance in its eyes and compares this with what it sees as it returns.
The ant also has a way of measuring distance travelled, while a path integrator periodically informs the ant of its current position relative to its point of departure.
Rather than integrate all the information it receives in its brain, the ant actually performs a number of complex calculations in different organs.
Like a super-computer, the ant has many separate sub-routines going on simultaneously.

Using the ant’s ability to steer by polarised light and to store and reuse landscape images, Wehner and colleagues have built “Sahabot,” a small vehicle that uses polarisers and a CCD camera to store 360° images of its surroundings.
It navigates by using polarised sunlight and comparing the current images of landmarks to the ones in its memory.
D Professor Robert Michelson had a different desert challenge – to design a flying robot that can not only navigate but also stay aloft and hover in the thin atmosphere of Mars.
Drawing inspiration from insect flight, he has gone beyond nature to devise a completely new concept for a flying machine.
The “Entomopter” is a sort of double-ended dragonfly whose wings beat reciprocally.

Michelson says that the flapping-wing design gives the craft unusually high lift compared with a fixed-wing flyer, enabling it to fly slowly or hover in the thin Martian air – whereas a fixed-wing craft would have to move at more than 400 km/h and could not stop to explore.
E Engineer Roger Quinn and entomologist Professor Roy Ritzmann are taking their inspiration from cockroaches.

According to Quinn and Ritzmann, the ability of cockroaches to run very fast over rough terrain may one day give rise to a completely new all-terrain vehicle with six legs, or maybe even wheel-like legs called “whegs.”
The key to the cockroach’s remarkable cross-country performance lies partly in the fact that its legs do a lot of the thinking without having to consult the brain.

Quinn and Ritzmann are drawing on cockroach skills to create robotic walkers and control strategies that capture the remarkable capacity of these insects to traverse complex terrain and navigate safely toward goals while avoiding obstacles.
The team has already designed a series of robots that run on six legs or on whegs, enabling them to handle surprisingly rugged terrain.
F International experts believe there are tremendous opportunities in biorobotics.
However, delegates at the conference had differing visions for the future of the science.

While some were concerned that the initial applications of biorobotics may be military, others, such as Dr Barbara Webb, predicted swarms of tiny, cheap, insect-like robots as society’s cleaners and collectors.
Sonja Kleinlogel hoped the study of the hyperspectral eyes of the mantis shrimp might yield remote sensors that can watch over the environmental health of our oceans.
Several delegates were concerned about the ethical implications of biorobotics and urged that close attention be paid to this as the science and technologies develop.

transcript.text: To begin with, we ask you to make a phone call to our vetting people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We need to know some basic information about you, like how long you're intending to be in this country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The minimum time limit is three months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Whether you're working or studying, we require a reference which must be from the person in authority who you're working with or studying under.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This will be used for an identity check.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Once that's been sent to the authorities and approved, we'll email you an application form which you can download.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You should complete this and return it with two recent passport-sized photographs of yourself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One photo will be held in our records, and the other will be sent to your host family prior to your first weekend visit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Our center manager will get back to you within a week of receiving your form to let you know that we have it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And if we think there's a suitable match on our files, someone from our interview team will contact you for a face-to-face meeting with a member of staff.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: At that point, you should have some idea of weekend dates when you're free, which we can put to the host family.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: However, decisions are not made at the meeting, but you can expect to hear the result from us in a couple of days.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, the process for those of you interested in welcoming someone...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a discussion between two students called Mark and Fran about their presentation on some dolphins which are unique to New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-four on page five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hi, Mark.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thanks for coming around.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hi, Fran.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: No problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We need to try and get this presentation finished.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Mark, let's start with the way dolphins make sounds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, we all know that dolphins make clicking noises to communicate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They have tongues and larynxes as humans do, but what's really strange about the dolphin is that the sounds are focused through an extraordinary organ called the melon, which most other sea mammals don't have.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So shall I take over from there and speak about the different dolphin types?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I want to share what we found out about those rare dolphins that are special just to New Zealand in particular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, great.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Put the emphasis on them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The rarest of all is the Hector's dolphin, isn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are endangered, aren't they?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think that's mainly because so many of them get tangled up in fishing gear, especially gill nets, and die.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I know that some conservationists are worried about the impact of the tourism industry on dolphin numbers, but I don't think that's a problem yet here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, remember that this species has a very long reproductive cycle, so their numbers don't get replenished quickly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yeah, that's really sad.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But at least the New Zealand government established a sanctuary for them, didn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The fishing industry was against it, but I remember reading that the general public were very supportive of the decision.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It was a consequence of a study done by some marine biologists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Having a protected breeding area has made a big difference to the dolphin population already.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, I think their numbers have swelled to over seven thousand in total, with a tiny group of just eighty-nine living down off Southland, nearly two thousand living near Christchurch on the East Coast, and the biggest group surviving off the West Coast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's pretty wild country over there, so I guess there aren't as many tourists and fishermen to disturb them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-five to thirty on page six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-five to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, so how do you suggest I structure my part of the talk?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, you could start with the common dolphin, which inhabits the whole of the sea around New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And once you've covered everything to do with them, feeding and so on, you could go on to the more unusual types.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The dusky dolphin is especially interesting because you know how all the dolphins travel in small social groups called pods?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the dusky dolphins travel in pods as big as eight hundred members.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And I think the duskies like to travel along beside fishing and tourist boats, don't they?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Whereas the Hector's dolphins are different in that they prefer to go in the wake of boats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is, coming along in the rear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, they do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But they also dive down deep to avoid fast boats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, let's not forget the Māui because they are endangered too, aren't they?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There are only a hundred and fifty of them left, and they inhabit only the western coastal waters off the North Island of New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, it's a pity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also face problems because of their tiny size.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hmm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the orca is actually a dolphin too, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, surprisingly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So I'll include that in my talk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: People call them killer whales, but in fact they're not whales.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They're a huge and very fierce type of dolphin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In New Zealand, Kaikoura in the South Island is the best place to spot orcas swimming by.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So people mistakenly think that's where they live.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But actually, orcas cover vast distances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Let's not forget to mention the bottlenose.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's bigger than nearly all the other dolphins, even the common dolphin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, but still not as big as the orca, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I think that's our presentation done now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about native citrus plants in Australia, known as lemon myrtle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we're going to explore a few remarkable native citrus species found in Australia, which are not only important ecologically, but also increasingly popular in culinary and commercial industries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's begin with one of the most well-known examples, lemon myrtle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This evergreen tree, native to the subtropical rainforests of Queensland, is widely appreciated for its strong lemon aroma.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People often use lemon myrtle in cooking, but one of its more traditional applications is steeping the leaves to create herbal tea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Aside from its pleasant flavor, it's also believed to have antimicrobial properties, which makes it popular in natural remedies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, lemon myrtle isn't the only citrus-like tree found in Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although desert lemon trees resemble other native citrus types, they won't develop properly unless there is consistent and sufficient rain available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This need for regular water supply makes them more challenging to grow in areas prone to long dry spells, despite their name suggesting otherwise.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another fascinating species is the finger lime, sometimes referred to as citrus caviar due to its tiny bead-like juice vesicles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These are often used in gourmet dishes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, finger lime trees, known for their culinary appeal, often struggle in wet climates where fungal and bacterial diseases tend to spread quickly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This sensitivity has made commercial cultivation a bit risky, especially in regions with poor drainage or unpredictable weather.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When it comes to cultivation practices, timing is everything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Farmers usually begin planting during the spring months, as unexpected frost later in the year can severely damage young trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This seasonal strategy helps to maximize growth while avoiding environmental stressors that could affect survival rates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Speaking of safety, it's also important to mention that not every part of these trees is edible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While generally safe, certain areas of the plant, especially the leaves, can be considered slightly toxic when eaten in significant amounts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For this reason, growers and chefs alike must take precautions when handling or preparing these native ingredients.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As for processing, there's more than one way to use the harvest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In some recipes, the dried form, commonly referred to as a powder, is preferred over using the fully ripened fruit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This allows the flavor to be preserved and used in spice blends, marinades, or even herbal teas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From a geographical standpoint, distribution of these plants varies depending on species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These plants are naturally found in extremely dry ecosystems, with the desert landscape being one of their most common habitats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their resilience to harsh conditions has made them well suited for outback environments, although they still need proper care.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even so, not all environments are equal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ideal growth occurs in consistently hot and humid environments, particularly in tropical zones where temperatures remain stable throughout the year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is why some commercial farms are now being established further north, where these conditions are more reliable year-round.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Beyond function, some species are valued for aesthetics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Chefs often enhance the look of seafood dishes by adding colorful citrus zest, especially when presenting grilled fish to guests.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This decorative touch adds both flavor and visual appeal, making native citrus a favorite in high-end cuisine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, cultivation is not without its challenges.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Pests pose a significant challenge to these trees, with certain species of insects like borers and mites causing serious leaf damage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Farmers often need to monitor their orchards closely and use eco-friendly pest control methods to maintain healthy crops.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That brings us to the end of our overview.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you can see, Australia's native citrus species offer a mix of culinary richness, ecological uniqueness, and agricultural complexity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
