r1.title: The Early History of Olive Oil

sentences.text: Olive oil is produced from the fruit of the olive tree, which is a member of the Oleaceae plant family.
The trees require some cold weather during the year, but also tolerate hot, dry conditions, and do not like moisture when they are flowering.
They actually produce better when subjected to these stressful conditions, and as a result, olive trees have traditionally been grown on land where little else will survive.

Archaeologists today are divided over exactly where the first domestication of the olive occurred: some say it was in the area which is now Iran, Syria, Jordan and Egypt, while others contend it was in mainland Greece or on the island of Crete.
The one thing that can be said with certainty is that cultivation began at least 6,000 years ago and spread slowly westward across the lands bordering on the Mediterranean Sea.
Olive oil was used for a variety of purposes during these early times, including as a pharmacological ointment and in rituals for anointing royalty.
The ancient Greeks believed the olive tree was a priceless gift from the goddess Athena and used its oil in sacred religious rituals.
In fact, the Greek poet Homer called olive oil ‘liquid gold’, and during the 6th and 7th centuries BC, Greek law forbade the cutting down of olive trees and made it punishable by death.
The ancient Middle Eastern ruler King David valued his groves of olive trees and his olive oil warehouses so much that he posted guards around the clock to protect them.
Over the years, olive oil developed other uses.
Its employment in cooking dates at least as far back as the 5th century BC, as described by the Greek philosopher Plato.
Its use as an aid to beauty and health later became ingrained in many Mediterranean cultures.
The Romans, for example, are said to have used generous amounts on their bodies to moisturise their skin after bathing.
With the spread of the Roman Empire, olive oil became a major commodity, and its trade promoted commerce throughout the ancient world.
It is generally believed that in the 1st–2nd centuries BC, olive trees were taken to North Africa and then to Spain, which was later to become the world’s largest producer of olive oil.
Artefacts found at various Mediterranean archaeological sites include olive oil storage vessels with olive plant residue still in them.

Historical evidence still in existence in the form of wall paintings and ancient manuscripts (including the works of the Roman naturalist and philosopher, Pliny the Elder) all record production techniques and the various uses of olive oil.
Making olive oil in those early days was a laborious process accomplished without mechanisation.
Processing or milling the fruit involved several distinct stages to extract the liquid.
The olives were harvested from the trees by hand or by beating the fruit from the trees with long sticks.
The olives were then rinsed and crushed to separate out the large seed found in the centre of each.
The remaining seedless flesh was put in woven bags and pressed.
Hot water was then poured over the bags to separate the oil from the solid bits of olive.
The liquid produced in this process, consisting of oil and water, was drained into stone basins or tanks, where it was allowed to settle and separate.
In cold weather, a bit of salt was added to speed up the process.
As much oil as possible was drawn off the water, but the result was still not pure oil.
Therefore, this impure mixture was allowed once more to settle in vats and then separated in order to refine the product.
The waste water from the milling process, which is called amurca, is a bitter-tasting and foul-smelling liquid.
In many ancient civilisations it was often simply discarded, causing serious pollution because of its acidity and high salt content.
However, in the Roman period it was regarded as a very useful substance.
When spread on surfaces, amurca forms a hard finish and therefore it was often applied to the floors of grain storage buildings where it hardened, keeping out water, mud and pests.
When boiled down, amurca was applied to leather to soften it so that it was easier to shape into articles of clothing and shoes.
It could also be eaten by farm animals and was, in fact, fed to livestock suffering from malnutrition.
According to ancient texts, amurca was also utilised in moderate amounts by farmers as a fertiliser or as a pesticide, helping them to protect their crops from insects and even small rodents.

sentences.text: How busy is too busy?
For some it means sometimes having to have a short lunch; for others it may mean missing lunch altogether.
For a few, it is not being able to take a day off once a month.
Then there is a group of people for whom working every evening and weekend is normal, and feeling stressed is taken for granted.
For most senior executives, workloads swing between extremely busy and frenzied.
Neil Plumridge, vice-president of a management consultancy company, says that his weeks vary from a ‘manageable’ 45 hours to 80 hours, but average 60 hours.
Three signs warn Plumridge about his workload: sleep, scheduling and family.

He knows he is doing too much when he gets less than six hours’ sleep for three consecutive nights, when he is constantly having to reschedule appointments, and when he misses a family birthday or anniversary.
‘Then,’ he says, ‘I know things are out of control.’
Plumridge states that stress is often caused by his having unrealistic expectations of himself.
‘I’ll promise a client that I’ll do something tomorrow, and then I’ll promise another client that I’ll do the same thing, when I know it’s not going to happen.
I could have said: “Why don’t I give that to you in 48 hours?”
The client wouldn’t care.’
Over-committing is something people experience as an individual problem.
However, new research indicates that people may be designed to over-commit.
A study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology shows that people always believe that they will be less busy in the future.
This is a misapprehension according to the authors of the report, Gal Zauberman of the University of North Carolina and John Lynch of Duke University.
‘On average, an individual will be just as busy two weeks or a month from now as he or she is today.
But that is not how it appears in everyday life,’ they say.
‘People make commitments long in advance that they would never make if the same commitments required immediate action.
They discount future time investments relatively steeply.’
Being ‘too busy’ is highly subjective, but for any individual there are some concrete signs of stress: disturbed sleep and declining mental and physical health are the most common examples.

Figures for National Workers’ Compensation (insurance against injury caused by work) show that stress causes the most loss of time of any workplace injury: employees suffering stress are absent from work for an average of 16.6 weeks.
The effects of stress are also expensive.

The Australian Government insurer reports that, in 2003–2004, claims for stress-related psychological injury accounted for 7% of insurance claims, but almost 27% of the amount paid out in claim payments.
Experts say the key to dealing with stress is not to focus on relief — a game of golf or a massage — but to reassess workloads.
Neil Plumridge says he makes it a priority to work out what has to change: that might mean allocating extra staff to a job, allowing more time, or changing expectations.
He also relies on the advice of colleagues, saying that his peers coach each other on business problems: ‘Just a fresh pair of eyes over an issue can help,’ he states.
Executive stress is not confined to big organisations.
Vanessa Stoykov has been running her own advertising agency and public relations business for seven years.
Her company has grown so fast that it appeared on the Business Review Weekly ‘Fast 100’ list of fastest- growing small enterprises in 2004, just after Stoykov had her first child.
In 2005, revenue was projected to double to $2.4 million.
She had just had her second child.
With a fast- growing business and two small children, Stoykov says she has mastered the art of caring for children, typing, and talking on the phone at the same time.
But, unlike many others, she appears to thrive on the mental stimulation of running her own business, despite the stress.
Jan Elsner, a psychologist who specialises in executive coaching, says that doing well on a demanding workload is typical of senior executives.
Some people work best with high- adrenaline periods followed by quieter times, while others thrive under sustained pressure.

Elsner’s practice is based on a movement known as positive psychology, a school of thought that argues that positive experiences — feeling engaged and challenged, for example — do not balance out negative experiences such as stress; instead they help people increase their resilience over time.
Elsner says that many of the senior business people she coaches are increasingly relying more on regulating stress through methods such as meditation.
She points to research showing that meditation can alter the biochemistry of the brain and the way that brains and bodies react to stress.
Some experts believe there is too much emphasis on treating job stress as an individual problem.

Tony LaMontagne, of the University of Melbourne, says that while personality traits do have some effect on stress, it is systemic stressors — qualities of job roles and organisations themselves — that have a far greater effect.
His recent research shows that the major predictor of stress is the level of job control a person has.
The best type of job combines challenging work with high autonomy.
The worst jobs combine challenging work and low control.
People with demanding jobs but little autonomy have up to four times the probability of depression and more than double the risk of heart attack.

Stress: its effects and how to reduce it
Statistics on workers’ compensation show that people take more time off work due to stress than for any other {{22}} at work. On average, workers who take time off because of stress stay away for {{23}} . This absence comes at a high price — while the number of insurance claims due to stress amount to only {{24}} of the total, they account for a much higher proportion of the cost of claim payments.
Experts believe that seeking to relieve stress through physical therapies such as sport or {{25}} may be less effective than simply reviewing your {{26}} .

sentences.text: To most of us, termites are destructive insects which can cause damage on a devastating scale.
But according to Dr Rupert Soar of Loughborough University's School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering, these pests may serve a useful purpose for us after all.

His multidisciplinary team of British and American engineers and biologists has set out to investigate the giant mounds built by termites in Namibia, in sub-Saharan Africa, as part of the most extensive study of these structures ever taken.
Termite mounds are impressive for their size alone; typically they are three metres high, and some as tall as eight metres have been found.
They also reach far into the earth, where the insects 'mine' their building materials, carefully selecting each grain of sand they use.
The termite's nest is contained in the central cavity of the mound, safely protected from the harsh environment outside.
The mound itself is formed of an intricate lattice of tunnels, which split into smaller and smaller tunnels, much like a person's blood vessels.
This complex system of tunnels draws in air from the outside, capturing wind energy to drive it through the mound.
It also serves to expel spent respiratory gases from the nest to prevent the termites from suffocating, so ensuring them a continuous provision of fresh, breathable air.

So detailed is the design that the nest stays within three degrees of a constant temperature, despite variations on the outside of up to 50 °C, from blistering heat in the daytime to below freezing on the coldest nights.
The mound also automatically regulates moisture in the air, by means of both its underground 'cellar', and evaporation from the top of the mound.
Some colonies even had 'chimneys' at a height of 20 m to control moisture loss in the hottest regions of sub-Saharan Africa.
Furthermore, the termites have evolved in such a way as to outsource some of their biological functions.
Part of their digestive process is carried out by a fungus, which they 'farm' inside the mound.
This fungus, which is found nowhere else on earth, thrives in the constant and optimum environment of the mound.

The termites feed the fungus with slightly chewed wood pulp, which the fungus then breaks down into a digestible sugary food to provide the insects with energy, and cellulose which they use for building.
And, although the termites must generate waste, none ever leaves the structure, indicating that there is also some kind of internal waste-recycling system.

Scientists are so excited by the mounds that they have labelled them a 'super organism' because, in Soar's words, “They dance on the edge of what we would perceive to be cool or, if you're too cold, you need to thrive: that's called homeostasis.”
What the termites have done is to move homeostatic function away from their body, into the structure in which they live.
“As more information comes to light about the unique features of termite mounds, we may ultimately need to redefine our understanding of what constitutes a 'living' organism.”
To reveal the structure of the mounds, Soar's team begins by filling and covering their plaster of Paris, a chalky white paste based on the mineral gypsum, which becomes rock-solid when dry.
The researcher then carves the plaster of Paris into half-millimetre thick slices, and photographs them sequentially.
Once the pictures are digitally scanned, computer technology is able to recreate complex three-dimensional images of the mounds.
These models have enabled the team to map termite architecture at a level of detail never before attained.

Soar hopes that the models will explain how termite mounds create a self-regulating living environment which manages to respond to changing internal and external conditions without drawing on any outside source of power.
If they do, the findings could be invaluable in informing future architectural design, and could inspire buildings that are self-sufficient, environmentally friendly, and cheap to run.
“As we approach a world of climate change and temperatures rise,” he explains, “there will not be enough fuel to drive air conditioners around the world.”

It is hoped, says Soar, “that the findings will provide clues that aid the ultimate development of new kinds of human habitats, suitable for a variety of arid, hostile environments not only on the earth but maybe one day on the moon and beyond.”

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.explanation: A段开头说大家通常认为白蚁是破坏性的，但转折说它们可能有“有用（useful purpose）”的一面，即重新评估它们的名声，对应选项 iii。
questions.tip: 不要看到“Namibia”就以为要选地点分布（v），重点在于作者对白蚁看法的转变（从有害到有用）。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “To most of us, termites are destructive... But... these pests may serve a useful purpose for us after all.”

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.explanation: B段全段都在描述白蚁丘的物理特征，如“三米高（three metres high）”、“复杂网络（intricate lattice）”等，对应选项 vii（惊人的物理尺寸）。
questions.tip: 虽然段落提到了“tunnels”，但那是为了说明其结构的复杂和规模，主要还是在讲它的“physical dimensions”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “Termite mounds are impressive for their size alone; typically they are three metres high...”

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.explanation: C段详细解释了白蚁丘如何吸入空气、排出废气、调节温度和湿度，这些都是它的功能，对应选项 iv（主要功能）。这一段是讲它“做什么（functions）”，而上一段B是讲它“长什么样（dimensions）”，注意区分。
questions.tip: 这一段是讲它“做什么（functions）”，而上一段B是讲它“长什么样（dimensions）”，注意区分。
questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “This complex system of tunnels draws in air... expel gases... regulates moisture...”

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.explanation: D段描述了白蚁“种植（farm）”真菌，白蚁给真菌木浆，真菌给白蚁提供消化的食物，这是典型的互利共生，对应选项 ix（互利关系）。
questions.tip: 哪怕你不懂“symbiosis”这个词，看到互相喂食（feed... provide...）也能明白这是双方受益的关系。
questions.quote: (Paragraph D) “The termites feed the fungus... which the fungus then breaks down into a digestible sugary food to provide the insects with energy...”

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.explanation: E段科学家称其为“超级生物（super organism）”，并提出可能需要“重新定义（redefine）”我们对生物体的理解，对应选项 ii（挑战我们对生命本质的假设）。
questions.tip: “Redefine our understanding” 就是 “challenging our assumptions” 的完美同义替换。
questions.quote: (Paragraph E) “...we may ultimately need to redefine our understanding of what constitutes a 'living' organism.”

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.explanation: F段按步骤介绍了研究结构的方法：填充石膏、切片、拍照、电脑建模，对应选项 i（用于调查白蚁丘形成的方法）。
questions.tip: 这一段全是动作描述（begins by filling, carves, photographs），显然是在讲具体的“methods”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “To reveal the structure of the mounds, Soar's team begins by filling... carves... photographs...”

questions.prompt: Paragraph G
questions.explanation: G段讨论了这些研究发现可能启发未来的建筑设计，实现自给自足和节能，对应选项 vi（了解白蚁建筑的一些潜在好处）。
questions.tip: 虽然提到了“global climate change”，但它是作为背景来强调这种建筑节能的好处，而不是说白蚁丘正受到气候变化的威胁（viii）。
questions.quote: (Paragraph G) “...the findings could be invaluable in informing future architectural design, and could inspire buildings...”

questions.quote: Something to do with sun, sunshine, is it? I think you meant the Sunshade Apartments.

questions.explanation: 在介绍The Grand公寓时，提到每个房间都有希腊画作（Greek paintings），并且外面有一个“balcony”（阳台）。
questions.tip: 只要跟上卷面上的“Greek paintings”这个并列的定位词，紧接着听连词“and”后面的信息就能轻松抓取答案，切忌走神。
questions.quote: The Grand? Actually, it's quite reasonable. It's an older style house with Greek paintings in every room and a balcony outside.

questions.explanation: 提问景色（views）如何时，工作人员回答四周都是“forests”，对应了题干中的“overlooking”（俯瞰）。
questions.tip: 听到“supermarket”时要区分，它是被森林藏起来在路边的（hide a supermarket），不是用来俯瞰的自然景色。
questions.quote: What are the views like? Well, there are forests all around, and they hide a supermarket just down the road, so that's very useful for all your shopping needs.

questions.explanation: 问及价格时，录音清晰回答了你想要去的那个时间段对应的价格是“Three hundred and nineteen pounds”。
questions.tip: 后面提到的“forty percent”（40%）是如果你11月份去才有的折扣，不要把这个折扣干扰项当成最终的费用填进去。
questions.quote: And the price? Three hundred and nineteen pounds at that time. But if you leave it till November, it goes down by forty percent.

questions.explanation: 工作人员明确表示，针对希腊岛屿的度假项目，他们保险的最高理赔额度是“ten thousand pounds”。
questions.tip: 原有的保险理赔额是“eight thousand pounds”，这是你自己说的条件，千万别把客人自己现有的额度当作题目中对应机构的额度。
questions.quote: Well, the first thing is cancellation. If the holiday's canceled on the policy I've got, you can claim eight thousand pounds. We can improve on that, Miss Nash. Uh, for Greek Island holidays, our maximum is ten thousand pounds.

questions.explanation: 在听到“hospital”的600英镑定位点后，顺着往下听，录音明确说到额外允许一名“relative”（亲属）前往度假地。
questions.tip: 这是一道非常顺畅的推导题，跟住600磅后立刻抓取后面的名词，不要把听到的动词（如travel）错填进去。
questions.quote: Now, if you go to hospital, we allow six hundred pounds. Yes, mine's similar. And we also allow a relative to travel to your holiday resort.

questions.explanation: 工作人员先询问没登上飞机（don't get on the plane）怎么办，随后直接点出了专有名词“missed departure”。
questions.tip: 注意录音一开始利用了同义替换（没登上飞机）来引出这个话题，随后才报出标准术语，别因为开头没听到直白的“departure”就漏掉答案。
questions.quote: And what happens if you don't get on the plane? Uh, nothing as far as I can see on this form. Don't you have, uh, missed departure?

questions.explanation: 录音讲完个人物品最高赔付3000英镑后，补充说明单件物品（a single item）的赔付不超过500英镑。
questions.tip: 题干上的“one”对应的就是录音里的“a single”，抓住了这个显而易见的同义替换就能精准捕捉到紧跟在后面的“item”。
questions.quote: And we're particularly generous about loss of personal belongings, up to three thousand pounds, but not more than five hundred pounds for a single item.

questions.explanation: 工作人员做自我介绍时说出了自己的名字“Ben Ludlow”，并且非常贴心地顺便拼写了姓氏。
questions.tip: 这种送分题只要按照录音中一个字母一个字母的拼写“L-U-D-L-O-W”无脑记录下来即可，注意不要产生拼写手误。
questions.quote: Ben Ludlow. That's L-U-D-L-O-W.

7.s: to travel to your holiday resort

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a supervisor at Holly's Supermarket talking to a group of new employees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome to Holly's Supermarket.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm sure you'll all enjoy working in our dedicated team here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, what will you be doing?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, we're open Monday through Sunday, so you'll need to be able to work weekends as well as irregular weekday shifts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These sometimes start at five AM or finish at eleven PM.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Your duties will include checking and unpacking lorry deliveries, as well as working on the shop floor, stocking shelves and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But you'll only be required to do manual lifting if the goods are light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When the store is very busy, you'll also have to assess changing priorities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, if there's a queue at the tills, you'll jump on a spare one to help.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you notice something's been spilt and the surface is a little bit wet, you'll get a mop to clean it up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No need to check with a manager first.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Similarly, if bakery items are selling quickly, you'll help cook some more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And if a customer can't find, say, the apples, you'll instantly leave what you're doing and show them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But you'll still get time off to relax too, of course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We pride ourselves on a positive attitude here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A little small talk shows you're interested in the customers and are providing excellent service, just as long as you don't overdo it and keep another customer waiting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And always smile.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It forces you to stay positive, and being generally upbeat makes your whole team happy too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This increases efficiency and gives a good impression to customers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If it's quiet, help someone pack their bags.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Customers really appreciate it, especially when they've bought more than they expected to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Staying calm is also a necessity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If a customer's unhappy for any reason, keep cool and call for a supervisor to help diffuse the situation if things are getting out of hand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Occasionally, when working tills, you'll find yourself waiting for someone to extract their wallet from the bottom of a cluttered bag while a long queue of annoyed customers builds up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You have to make sure, however hard it might be, that you remain composed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So now let's look at the plan of the supermarket.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Have you all got your plans?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll start with the staff entrance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, you came in through the customer entrance, clearly marked on the bottom of your plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in future, you'll enter through the door in the top left-hand corner of the diagram.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please don't confuse this with the emergency exits in the top right-hand corner and bottom left.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's very important that these are kept clear at all times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Regarding the manager's office, some of you may have attended interviews here when it was next to the newspaper and magazine sales area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it's recently been moved and is now the circular space marked on the right of your plans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When the manager's not on the shop floor, that's where you'll find her.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The storage and unpacking area, you may be asked to help out here both before and after opening hours.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is represented by the largest of the four rectangles in the top section of the plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It tends to get very busy there at times, so please be careful on entering and leaving this area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a kitchen on site where food and drinks are prepared for customers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has specialist staff, but some of you may have to fill in occasionally.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the plan, it's shown by the triangular shape to the left of the tinned goods aisle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's very busy as many customers like to take a break in the cafe and read a newspaper before or after doing their shopping.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cleaning equipment is stored in a cupboard.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's the smaller of the two squares marked near the vegetable and fruit section and can come in very handy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'd be surprised how often we have to mop up squashed tomatoes or grapes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, you'll be pleased to know there's a separate staff relaxation area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is at the top of your plan between the frozen goods section and the exit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As well as comfortable chairs, there's also a microwave for heating up snacks and a drinks dispenser.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's go there now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part two.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a presentation about prehistoric cave paintings and the symbols found within or near them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My presentation today is about the cave paintings produced by prehistoric artists about thirty thousand years ago, and in particular, the symbols that appear in or near these paintings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These symbols are found deep in caves in many countries around the world, but the ones I'm going to talk about today are mainly European.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, a little about the most common symbols.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The symbols that have been discovered are of different shapes and sizes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some are easily recognizable as they're quite simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most basic are just a series of dots, but they may also include forms such as the triangle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, other symbols are more complex.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A case in point is the wavy line.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is sometimes used on its own, but the same wavy line is also used as part of a larger picture of a horse.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we think this is what the wavy line represents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One very important symbol is what's called the hand symbol.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This frequently appears on the walls of caves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll talk about it in a bit more detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, how it was made.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The paint itself was made up from a variety of things that cave artists would have had access to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They had fire, so charcoal was one ingredient.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another was the fat from the animals they would have hunted, and lastly, the saliva from their own mouths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then there's the question of how they actually applied the runny paint onto the walls of the cave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It certainly wouldn't have been easy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They would have had to use something hollow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, it's likely to have looked like a straw, you know, like the kind we use for drinking nowadays.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They'd have sucked the paint up into it, then blown it out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers have recently recreated both the paint and the processes used to make the hand symbols.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The artist would have first put his hand flat against the wall, then blown the paint onto the wall, creating an outline of the hand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The researchers who've tried to recreate the process have said that not only is it a difficult technique to master, but also that a strange noise is produced.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It also led them to feel light-headed, so we can only imagine that these cave artists felt the same.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm sure you'll agree that these symbols are really interesting, but they're also of vital importance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers have now identified a total of twenty-six symbols commonly used in France and Spain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We only have this knowledge thanks to a database that's been created and which is being added to all the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It clearly demonstrates that many symbols are often used in particular combinations, even if they're in different places.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is significant as it looks like different tribes of cave people who lived and traveled through the area at that time would have seen these markings as well as adding to them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although researchers don't believe that these symbols are a language as such, they are happy to call them a type of code.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is evidence to support this idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One sequence of five symbols is particularly common in caves in Spain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Exactly the same sequence of five symbols has been found carved into a necklace made from the teeth of a red deer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it appears that this combination of symbols may have had a special meaning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, many of these explanations are theory as opposed to hard facts, which is why there is disagreement among researchers about the significance of what we are seeing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One theory is called The Great Leap Forward.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The idea is that around thirty-five thousand years ago, there was a sudden increase in creativity which led to the invention of the boat, among other things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, not everyone agrees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, many scientists believe that what has been found in Africa seems to indicate that this increase in creativity happened much earlier, around seventy to ninety thousand years ago, and more gradually.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One example of an artifact that is offered to support the idea is the discovery of different sorts of arrows, which would have been used for hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These scientists suggest that the reason more symbols haven't been found from this earlier time is because they would have been painted on things that did not survive, such as wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, we are very lucky that caves have protected these specimens as well as they have, or we might never have known what these artists were capable of.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

r1.title: The History Of The Bar Code V2

sentences.text: A Barcodes may seem common enough today that it is difficult to imagine a shopping trip without them.
However, barcodes were not of much importance until the 1970s.
The first product to be barcoded and scanned with the first barcode scanner ever used was in 1974.
The idea of barcodes, on the other hand, is not quite as recent.
In 1932, Wallace Flint suggested that it might be feasible to create an automated retail checkout system.
Even though his idea was not considered practical at the time, Flint continued to support the development of automated checkouts throughout his working life.
He later became a key figure in the development of the UPC code and went on to become vice-president of an association of food chains about forty years later.
B There is a common misunderstanding that the retail UPC barcode was the first barcode.
In fact, the first barcode symbology was not referred to as a barcode when it was first invented.
At that time, it resembled a bull’s-eye target consisting of a set of concentric circles.
This design was chosen because it could be scanned from any direction, later gaining the nickname the "Bullseye barcode".
Two college students, Joseph Woodland and Bernard Silver, created this design after realising that something similar was needed to track huge inventories in rapidly growing supermarkets.
Woodland later joined IBM in 1951 and persuaded the company to bring in a consultant to study barcodes.
As he considered the future needs of grocery stores, he based his initial idea on Morse Code.
Instead of using dots and dashes, however, he lengthened them into a series of wide and narrow lines, creating the first linear barcode.
This vertical pattern of lines was then arranged into a circle.
C Meanwhile, a scanner that could read these codes was also being developed.
Finally, in 1952, the Bullseye code and the linear version were patented, along with the mechanical and electrical scanner systems designed to read them.
IBM suggested that it buy the patent, but did not agree to match the asking price because the company did not think the product was marketable enough at that time.
Philco, however, did agree to the price and later sold the patent to RCA.
This event marked the beginning of a new era in automatic identification and electronics as a whole.
D It was not until 1967, when RCA started promoting the Bullseye to the grocery industry, that the code was actually used.
One Kroger grocery store agreed to be the first to try the Bullseye, while RCA attempted to highlight the potential savings made possible by automating the checkout counter.
However, although the Bullseye required less scanner orientation, the code occupied a large amount of space, and its circular design restricted the quantity of data that could be encoded.
The Bullseye therefore needed further refinement, since the technology at that time could not yet manage variable printing effectively, and scanners were still being improved.

E At the same time, as developers were increasing the capabilities of scanning equipment and computer technology, progress in automatic identification began to focus on the railroad system that supported the retail and manufacturing industries.
Freight cars often travel from one end of the country to the other, and they are sometimes borrowed by one rail line from another.
As a result, tracking freight trains as they move around the country is extremely challenging.
F Barcodes were first applied in the American railroad system in the late 1960s.
At that time, the Association of American Railroads introduced a system called KarTrak, designed by a railroad employee and MIT graduate named David Collins.
The system used blue and red reflective stripes painted on steel plates attached to the sides of railroad cars.
The plates had thirteen horizontal labels, which closely resembled barcodes.
They included start labels, stop labels and check numbers.
The placement of these stripes encoded a four-digit railroad company identifier as well as a six-digit car number.
When railcars passed through rail yards, this information could be scanned and used to identify them.
G Around ten years later, the same program fell into disuse after an economic downturn.
The system was also considered unreliable and error-prone because the stripes could become contaminated with dirt.
By the 1980s, radio tags had become the dominant method of tracking railroad cars.
Collins, however, still saw other possible uses for barcodes, especially in industrial settings.
He went on to establish a company called Computer Identics Corporation.
General Motors became one of the first companies to monitor the production and distribution of car parts using these barcodes, while another early system was used in a distribution facility.

r2.title: The Constant Evolution of the Humble Tomato

sentences.text: Famous for their taste, color, and organic appearance, heirloom tomatoes are favorites of gardeners and advocates of locally grown foods.

The tomato enthusiast might conclude that, given the immense varieties, heirlooms must have a more diverse and superior set of genes than the tomatoes available in grocery stores, those ordinary hybrid varieties such as cherry and plum.

However, their seeming diversity is only skin- deep: heirlooms are actually feeble and inbred—the defective product of breeding experiments that began hundreds of years ago, and exploded thanks to enthusiastic backyard gardeners.
“The irony of all this,” says Steven Tanksley, a geneticist at Cornell University, “is that all that diversity of heirlooms can be accounted for by a handful of genes.
There are probably no more than 10 mutant genes that create the diversity of heirlooms you see.”

But rather than simply proving that the myth about the heirlooms’ diversity is wrong, Tanksley’s deconstruction of the tomato genome, along with work by others, is showing how a small berry-like fruit from the Andes became one of the world’s top crops.

The cultivated tomato is a member of the nightshade family that includes New World crops such as the potato, which spread around the globe after Christopher Columbus brought them back to Spain in the 15th century.
But whereas scientists have uncovered a wealth of archaeological evidence on early farming practices in the New World, the record is blank when it comes to the tomato.
The modern tomato seems to have its origins in the Andes in South America and may have been domesticated in Veracruz, Mexico.
Primitive varieties still grow throughout the Americas.
All told, botanists call as many as 13 species “tomatoes” and consider an additional four to be closely related.
One might assume that one of these known wild species became today’s cultivated crop, but that’s not the case: the Mother Tomato has never been found.
The closest relative is the currant tomato, which, based on genetic comparisons, split from today’s tomato some 1.4 million years ago.
So researchers like Tanksley have to work backward, crossing tomato varieties and species in order to understand how various genes influence shape and size.
Once isolated, Tanksley later inserts those genes into other tomato varieties to make his case with a dramatic transformation.
Tanksley concludes from his analyses that in their effort to make bigger, tastier, and faster-growing fruit, our ancestors ultimately exploited just 30 mutations out of the tomato’s 35,000 genes.
Most of these genes have only small effects on tomato size and shape, but recently Tanksley and his colleagues reported that they found a gene that increases fruit size by 50 percent.
It was probably the most important event in domestication.

The first written record of tomatoes—from Spain in the 1500s—confirms that this mutation, which enlarges tomatoes by producing compartments known as locules, existed back in the same yellow tomatoes that gave Italians the word pomodoro, or golden apple.
Besides size, tomato farmers also selected for shape.
To discover those genes, Esther van der Knaap, a Tanksley alumna now at The Ohio State University, took a gene from one heirloom tomato and inserted it into a wild relative.
She observed that, as a result, the tiny fruits became shaped like pears.
The selection of these traits has, however, affected the heirlooms’ hardiness.
They often suffer from infections that cause the fruit to crack, split, and otherwise rot quickly.
Wild plants must continuously evolve to fend off such infections, points out Roger Chetelat of the Tomato Genetics Resource Center at the University of California.
But in their quest for size, shape, and flavor, humans have inadvertently eliminated defensive genes.
As a result, most possess only a single disease-resistant gene.
Chetelat elaborates that heirlooms’ taste may have less to do with their genes than with the productivity of the plant and the growing environment.
Any plant that produces only two fruits, as heirlooms sometimes do, is highly likely to produce juicier, sweeter, and more flavorful fruit than varieties that produce 100, as commercial types do.
In addition, heirlooms are sold ripened on the vine, a certain way to get tastier results than allowing them to mature on the shelf.
This means breeders feel confident that getting germ-beating genes back into heirlooms won’t harm the desirable aspects of the fruit.
Modern breeding has resuscitated grocery-store tomatoes with an influx of wild genes; in the past 50 years, as many as 40 disease-resistant genes have been bred back into commercial crops.
In 1996, a tomato breeder and former Tanksley student named Doug Heath began a favorite project.
After 12 years of traditional breeding with the help of molecular markers, he created a new multi-colored tomato less prone to cracking and also endowed with 12 disease-resistant genes.
The original heirloom plant, Heath explains, had defective flowers, which is one reason why it produced only two fruits compared with the 30 he gets from his new variety.
He claims he is also able to maintain a comparable flavor and sugar profile even on productive plants.
The heirloom’s defects are, after all, just an accident of a narrow breeding strategy left over from the very beginning of genetic modification.

r3.title: The New Zealand writer Margaret Mahy

sentences.text: In a career spanning some fifty years, Margaret Mahy has come to occupy a unique place in New Zealand writing with innovative fiction and original characterisation.

In our solidly realist tradition, the linguistic fireworks of Mahy's children's fiction and the explorations of human behaviour at the heart of her supernatural teenage fiction stand gloriously alone.
Mahy's clearest heir, I have always thought, is Elizabeth Knox — and maybe the true inheritance there is sheer singularity.
Just as there is no one else like Knox in New Zealand writing, Mahy, too, has ventured into imaginative territory unknown to other local writers.
So it was with great pleasure that I visited Mahy recently at her Governor's Bay home to talk about her new book.

As with all journalists, she is generous to a fault with her time and attention; and, as always — despite her careful consideration of questions and thoughtful answers — I'm reminded she isn't truly comfortable making herself or her life the heart of any conversation.
Certainly, any consideration of the style of Mahy's novels and picture books throws up some irresistible theories.
As a writer committed to supporting herself through her art, she has seldom had the time for formal research.

Rather, it has been a matter of going out and finding inspiration from her immediate environment: the writing on the side of a bus; a spelling mistake in a note to herself; the similarity between a cat and a fur hat.

But despite these sometimes mundane origins, the settings for her stories are delightfully varied, as these books celebrate the dramatic plot twists and unpredictability of adventures on the high seas or in Antarctica, and also in quite unassuming places like the library or even down the back of a chair at home.
Mahy has a lifelong affection for characters who are agents of upheaval and disturbance.
Her junior and picture books are peppered with pirates, robbers and lions, though they appear alongside librarians, mothers and children, working against comfortable stereotype.
Her fictions often have at their heart a young adult burdened with special powers, such as the ability to cast spells in order to transform their world in supernatural and fantastical ways.

Another common feature is that, while the conclusions of her tales are usually predictable, they leave the reader feeling absolutely complete, the moral questions resulting from our hero's powers having been resolved.
Many of these themes can be found in her new novel, The Magician of Hoad.

The book was begun more than 15 years ago and envisioned as an 'entire' fantasy — one set in a fully imagined world with detailed history and complex tribal inter-relationships, a classical hero quest at its heart.
The story ballooned at one point to 800 pages and has been through at least two substantial rewrites.
Now half its original size, it is a fascinating read — an adventure, a romance, and a gold mine of Mahy literary preoccupations.
The other splendid Mahy publication this year is a re-issue of Bubble Trouble in a now-illustrated edition.
This tongue-twister tale first appeared in 1991, was included in 100 New Zealand Poems (1993) and has been recited by Mahy at countless private and public functions.

Perhaps more than any other work, Bubble Trouble is the Mahy that New Zealand children and their parents know so well, the rollicking story of a clown who serves up a joyous torrent of word-play and unexpected rhyme.
Those connections are four or five deep now.

I read The Lion in the Meadow in the School Journal in the late 1960s; my step-daughter listened to The Boy Who Was Followed Home over and over in the 1970s; my own children sat very still mouthing The Great White Man-Eating Shark in the 80s and 90s; now, in the 21st century, my grandchildren have heard Down the Dragon's Tongue, A Summery Saturday Morning and Dashing Dog many times.

Of course, readers are important to any working writer, but Mahy's espousal of the act of reading goes beyond that: a book is not properly finished, she has often said, until it has been read, because a reader brings something important to the book.

So, doubtless out of need to build a market — she's not ignorant of her popularity — but also out of genuine care for that other dynamic part of the author-reader relationship, Mahy has, until recently, kept up a punishing schedule of public appearances.
Private conversation with Mahy has always been a wild ride — marvellous, in the true sense of the word, the product of a hungry head and an infinite capacity to be astonished.
She races away at one stage to consult an encyclopaedia for L.
M.
Montgomery's date of death, and speculates about the 'real' Montgomery, creator of the ever-popular Anne of Green Gables.
Although I'd come to talk about her new book, I couldn't help but be captivated by her infectious curiosity.
A few years ago, the writer David Hill told a funny story.
Though his writing was, he conceded, very different from Mahy's, he had been affected by her peculiarly alert way of looking at the world, particularly the mad, slippery life of language.
Once, Hill said, in a motel room, a sign on a door caught his eye: 'This door is alarmed.'
Mahy would like that, thought Hill.

She would enjoy the comedy just below the surface of the formal warning; she would leap immediately to the possibilities for story and language play: 'Yes, and this window is concerned, this light fitting is irritated.'
His story was a wonderful comment on Mahy's vision.

questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “As with all journalists, she is generous to a fault with her time and attention...”

questions.prompt: Mahy is at ease speaking about her experiences.
questions.explanation: 题目说Mahy在谈论自己的经历时感到自在（at ease）。原文A段末尾说她“isn't truly comfortable making herself or her life the heart of any conversation（把话题中心放在自己或生活上让她感到不自在）”，直接矛盾，选 NO。

questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “...she isn't truly comfortable making herself or her life the heart of any conversation.”

groups.content:
Theories about Mahy's style
Mahy's determination to earn a living from writing has encouraged her to find the ideas for her work in {{32}} places. The stories themselves are set in locations that are {{33}} . In terms of characterisation, almost all of her books feature unruly people, and very often an adolescent who possesses {{34}} abilities. Finally, the endings of the stories tend to be {{35}} .

questions.explanation: 题目说她为了谋生，被迫从____地方寻找灵感。原文B段提到灵感来自“immediate environment（眼前环境）”，例如“writing on the side of a bus（公交车侧面的字）”等日常事物，对应选项 B (everyday)。
questions.tip: 公交车、拼写错误、猫等都属于“everyday places/things”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...finding inspiration from her immediate environment: the writing on the side of a bus...”

questions.explanation: 题目说故事背景设定在____的地点。原文B段提到地点既有“high seas or in Antarctica（公海或南极洲——exotic）”，也有“unassuming places like the library（图书馆——ordinary）”，对应选项 E。
questions.tip: 原文用了“delightfully varied（令人愉快的变化多端）”来连接这两类截然不同的地点。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...adventures on the high seas or in Antarctica, and also in quite unassuming places like the library...”

questions.explanation: 题目说青少年通常拥有____能力。原文B段提到年轻人拥有“special powers（特殊能力）”，例如“cast spells（施法）”来改变世界，对应选项 I (magical)。
questions.tip: “Cast spells / supernatural” 对应 “magical”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...burdened with special powers, such as the ability to cast spells...”

questions.explanation: 题目说故事结局往往是____。原文B段末尾说结局通常是“predictable（可预测的/unsurprising）”，但会让读者感到“absolutely complete（完全圆满/satisfying）”，对应选项 H。
questions.tip: 需同时匹配两个形容词的含义。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...conclusions... are usually predictable, they leave the reader feeling absolutely complete...”

questions.explanation: 当顾客询问残疾人通道时，Emily 回答所有三个选项（all three options）都具备此设施。

questions.quote: Customer: Now, are there handicapped accessible rooms? Emily: Yes, all three options have access for the physically disabled.

questions.prompt: Multiple meal options
questions.explanation: 原文指出另外两家只有简单的早餐，而 Royal Hotel 提供完整的餐厅和客房服务（full restaurant and room service）。
questions.tip: 题目问的是 "Multiple meal options"（多种餐饮选择），这直接对应原文的 "full restaurant"，排除了只提供 "limited menu" 的另外两家。
questions.quote: For a full restaurant and room service, the Royal Hotel is your best bet.

questions.prompt: Private dining
questions.explanation: Emily 介绍 Royal Hotel 的晚餐是在酒店高品质的**私人餐厅（private dining room）**提供的。
questions.tip: 这个信息点紧跟在 Royal Hotel 的午餐介绍之后，不要因为后面即将提到其他酒店就走神。
questions.quote: Dinners are in a nice low-key but high-quality setting in the hotel's private dining room...

questions.prompt: Group discount

questions.quote: Emily: No, sorry, not at the Royal Hotel... It looks like there is one at the Winchester, 15% off when you book eight or more rooms.

transcript.text: Part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a university tutor talking to two social science students about a project they are doing on the impact of technology on people's working lives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Kiara and Finn, can you tell me how your project is going?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Your general topic was the future of work, wasn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We read a lot of articles on it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Some were more interesting than others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There were a couple of writers that just made some strong statements without really backing them up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The problem is it's such a big topic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Some of the articles were aimed at graduates, and some of them were targeting people who've been in work for years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: We should have narrowed down our topic before we started searching.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: But anyway, the focus was always the changing nature of jobs, how it's all happening so quickly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Every single article said we can forget the way things used to happen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Like, you started out as an apprentice, and then you stayed in the same company for years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: That's over.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I see that you've highlighted job title in your notes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why is that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think for some people, a job title used to define them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: It was their identity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: They worked their way up from the bottom, and eventually, one day, they became manager or head of department.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: And even in their social circle, outside of work, they wanted other people to know how long they'd been in a job.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: And now?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It looks like we're moving away from the term job title.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: So, you know, instead, a lot of businesses are hiring people to work on a project done or lead a team, but the contracts are temporary.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Finn, do you think that's a big issue for young people?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Having to move on once a project's finished?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Not necessarily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It can be interesting to work in different places.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: People aren't always looking for a job that pays really well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's more about gaining experience and creating a network.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So money's not important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I haven't started work myself, but according to all the articles I read, it's more about the different rates of pay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If you have a good salary, you probably have enough to enjoy life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But if you're only earning the minimum wage, how do you get by?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's my biggest worry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I looked at that Richard Grieve survey on work-life balance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Oh, good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Only forty-eight percent of people believe that their work-life balance will improve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Is that a statistic that surprises you?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's hard to say.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I wonder what the survey actually asked.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Was it just, "Will your work-life balance improve," or did the interviewers break that down?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I mean, did they actually ask the people who took part, "Do you enjoy spending more time at work than home?"
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Good point.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: See if you can find out more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Um, Finn, what else have you been researching?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Learning new skills.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The general view is that employers are just going to want their workers to constantly upskill.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And apparently, employers will expect them to attend courses at weekends or after work, not as part of the working day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I don't think that's a bad thing, as long as the company pays for it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And think about it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If you were smart, you'd study things that would help you if you had to change companies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I hadn't thought about that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yes, good thinking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: What about mobile technology?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How might employees be affected now that phones and tablets make it possible to stay connected to work at all times?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's great.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You can use mobile technology, your device, to work where you like, on the way to class or the office.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The media often focuses on the negatives, but as far as I'm concerned, having a tablet I can carry with me means I can manage my studies and my family commitments more easily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I actually think that in the future, mobile technology will reduce employee stress.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So let's focus on the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To what extent do you think it'll help people in their professions or be a threat?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I was reading about architects using AI in the future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The writer was saying that one day, architects will use holograms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then their clients could see a three-dimensional house rather than just looking at a flat plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As soon as one architect starts to use AI, all the rival architects in the same area will have to use AI too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: That's the only way they'll manage to keep their clients.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: True.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: How about doctors?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Imagine if they had to give urgent medical attention to someone, but they weren't qualified to do it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: A hospital specialist could use AI and virtual reality to guide a doctor through, like, a complex procedure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, in an emergency situation, AI could really make the difference.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: And what about the law?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, the lawyers I know are always anxious about the amount of work they have to get through, but AI could help them with a whole lot of routine tasks, and that should make some of that anxiety go away.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yes, it probably could.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Also, if you're a sports referee, that could be a job that's affected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In what way?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Using AI would mean there were no mistakes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It would know for sure if a ball was out, for example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And you can't accuse AI of bias.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I can imagine that one day AI might do away with the need for human referees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I think so too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Let's move on to hu-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: That is the end of Part Three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to Part Three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

questions.prompt: Kiara and Finn agree that the articles they read on the future of work

She is curious about the kind of work the interviewees do.

questions.tip: Finn 提到了公司可能会让员工在业余时间学习，但他和 Kiara 都没有对此表示强烈反对（只要公司付钱就行），所以不选 B。

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture in a business class talking about a global petrol company, Telsa's expansion and its future development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Welcome, ladies and gentlemen, to the second lecture in our series on chain stores in the UK.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Today, I'll be focusing on a very successful global petrol company called Telsa, paying particular attention to their expansion and future development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There will be time for questions at the end, so please refrain from interrupting during the talk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: When it was founded, the company was a family-run organization with only one shop open in a small town in Southern England.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The family was able to compete with other local companies by offering special discounts for returning customers, which resulted in a massive expansion of their client base.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This strategy was so successful that they were able to open petrol stations across the country, subsequently increasing their market share in England.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Within a decade, Telsa was running establishments throughout the UK, including Wales and Scotland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: By comparing the sales income from all of their stores, they were able to collect data that highlighted which areas were the most profitable stations in the south of Scotland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They discovered that by closing the less useful stations in the south of Scotland, they could increase income from their other more profitable stations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This example demonstrates the importance of continually monitoring and maintaining a clear view of the finances of the company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Once the expertise required to run the company had exceeded the abilities of the family, they needed to hire professional consultants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: After assessing the company's financial statements, the consultants advised that Telsa close the head office of the convenience stores in Oxford.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They deemed the head office unnecessary and identified it as a financial drain on the company as the premises were expensive to run and generated no income.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To avoid firing any employees, they transferred over two hundred staff to other offices and retrained them to carry out their new roles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now that Telsa had conquered the petrol market in the UK, they were able to branch out into other niche areas that offered prospects for profits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They realized that they could establish a new environmentally friendly brand image by selling fresh food in their convenience stores that had been grown by local farmers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This strategy would not only broaden the scope of the company, but also help to strengthen its relationships with local communities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Every year, Telsa holds a meeting in London where all of the consultants and managers meet to discuss plans for development and improvement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: These meetings are essential to the evolution of the company as feedback is heard from all levels of the organization, from the sales staff to the CEOs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They did this by assigning every manager the task of holding staff discussions at which ideas and concerns would be passed on for evaluation at the meeting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Telsa decided to accommodate the individuality of each of their stores instead of forcing them to conform to one overriding company identity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They realized that by increasing the flexibility of the profit-making strategies of each of the retail stores, they subsequently became more commercially successful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The level of staff satisfaction also doubled as a result.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Individuals felt they were not being constrained to one way of thinking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To avoid misunderstandings and mistakes, any future changes were introduced in stages to familiarize the staff with the new regulations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, it's time to conclude the lecture for today, so I will leave you with some food for thought before you go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To run a successful business, one cannot underestimate the importance of maintaining open-mindedness when deciding on strategies for expansion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Sometimes it's necessary to employ an independent consultant who can offer an objective and unbiased view on the running of your company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Emotion will only ever cloud your ability to make business-related decisions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Research suitable case studies and look at how department stores, for example, were able to alter their organizational structure while minimizing costs and staff redundancies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Precedents are an essential resource when it comes to making decisions for your own business, so don't undervalue them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, that wraps up our lecture for today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If there are any questions...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.explanation: 录音中提到公司非常成功，因此能够开设遍布全国的 "petrol stations"（加油站），对应题目中的扩展方式。
questions.tip: 虽然前面提到了 "shop"，但那是过去式，题目问的是 "expanded by opening more..."（通过开设更多什么来扩张），注意捕捉 "open" 之后的核心名词。
questions.quote: This strategy was so successful that they were able to open petrol stations across the country, subsequently increasing their market share in England.

questions.explanation: 题目中的 "reducing the number"（减少数量）对应录音中的 "closing"（关闭），地点定位词 "southern" 后紧跟的 "Scotland" 即为答案。

questions.quote: They discovered that by closing the less profitable stations in the south of Scotland, they could increase the income from their other more profitable stations.

questions.explanation: 题目中的 "shut down"（关闭）对应录音中的 "closed"，紧接着提到的关闭对象就是 "head office"（总部）。

questions.explanation: 题目是被动语态 "A... was assigned"，录音中是主动语态 "assigning every manager"，主语转换后答案锁定 "manager"。

questions.explanation: 题目中的 "flexible in developing..." 对应录音中的 "increasing the flexibility of the..."，后面紧跟的名词 "strategies" 即为答案。

questions.quote: They realised that by increasing the flexibility of the profit-making strategies of each of the retail stores, they subsequently became more commercially successful.

questions.explanation: 题目中的 "introduced in..." 与录音完全一致，直接捕捉介词 "in" 后面的名词 "stages"（分阶段）。

questions.quote: To avoid misunderstandings and mistakes, any future changes were introduced in stages, in order to familiarise the staff with the new regulations.

questions.explanation: 录音提到在决定扩张计划时，保持（maintaining对应题干的Keep）“open-mindedness”（开放的心态）非常重要。

questions.tip: 这是一个拼写易错词，注意 "s" 和 "z" 的英美式拼写通用，但不要漏掉音节；不要填成 "department"（那是后面的词）。

sentences.text: The story of tea begins in China.
According to legend, in 2737 BC the Chinese emperor Shen Nung was sitting beneath a tree while his servant boiled drinking water, when some leaves from the tree blew into the water.
Shen Nung, a renowned herbalist, decided to try the infusion that his servant had accidentally created.
The tree was a Camellia sinensis, and the resulting drink was what we now call tea.
It is impossible to know whether there is any truth in this story, but tea-drinking certainly became established in China many centuries before it had even been heard of in the West.

Containers for tea have been found in tombs dating from the Han Dynasty (206 BC–220 AD), but it was under the Tang Dynasty (618–906 AD) that tea became firmly established as the national drink of China.
It became such a favourite that during the late eighth century a writer called Lu Yu wrote the first book entirely about tea, the Ch’a Ching, or Tea Classic.
It was shortly after this that tea was first introduced to Japan, by Japanese Buddhist monks who had travelled to China to study.
Tea received almost instant imperial sponsorship and spread rapidly from the royal court and monasteries to the other sections of Japanese society.
So at this stage in the history of tea, Europe was rather lagging behind.
In the latter half of the sixteenth century there are the first brief mentions of tea as a drink among Europeans, mostly from Portuguese who were living in the East as traders and missionaries.
But although some of these individuals may have brought back samples of tea to their native country, it was not the Portuguese who were the first to ship back tea as a commercial import.
This was done by the Dutch, who in the last years of the sixteenth century began to encroach on Portuguese trading routes in the East.
By the turn of the century they had established a trading post on the island of Java, and it was via Java that in 1606 the first consignment of tea was shipped from China to Holland.
Tea soon became a fashionable drink among the Dutch, and from there spread to other countries in continental western Europe, but because of its high price it remained a drink for the wealthy.
Britain, always a little suspicious of continental trends, had yet to become the nation of tea- drinkers that it is today.
Starting in 1600, the British East India Company had a monopoly on importing goods from outside Europe, and it is likely that sailors on these ships brought tea home as gifts.
The first coffee-house had been established in London in 1652, and tea was still somewhat unfamiliar to most readers, so it is fair to assume that the drink was still something of a curiosity.
Gradually, it became a popular drink in coffee-houses, which were as much locations for the transaction of business as they were for relaxation or pleasure.
They were, though, the preserve of middle- and upper-class men; women drank tea in their own homes, and as yet tea was still too expensive to be widespread among the working classes.
In part, its high price was due to a punitive system of taxation.
One unforeseen consequence of the taxation of tea was the growth of methods to avoid taxation—smuggling and adulteration.
By the eighteenth century many Britons wanted to drink tea but could not afford the high prices, and their enthusiasm for the drink was matched by the enthusiasm of criminal gangs to smuggle it in.

What began as a small-time illegal trade, selling a few pounds of tea to personal contacts, developed by the late eighteenth century into an astonishing organised-crime network, perhaps importing as much as seven million lb annually, compared to a legal import of five million lb!
Worse for the drinkers was that taxation also encouraged the adulteration of tea, particularly of smuggled tea which was not quality-controlled through customs and excise.
Leaves from other plants, or leaves which had already been brewed and then dried, were added to tea leaves.
By 1784, the government realised that enough was enough, and that heavy taxation was creating more problems than it was worth.
The new Prime Minister, William Pitt the Younger, slashed the tax from 119 per cent to 12.5 per cent.
Suddenly legal tea was affordable, and smuggling stopped virtually overnight.
Another great impetus to tea-drinking resulted from the end of the East India Company’s monopoly on trade with China, in 1834.

Before that date, China was the country of origin of the vast majority of the tea imported to Britain, but the end of its monopoly stimulated the East India Company to consider growing tea outside China.
India had always been the centre of the Company’s operations, which led to the increased cultivation of tea in India, beginning in Assam.

There were a few false starts, including the destruction by cattle of one of the earliest tea nurseries, but by 1888 British tea imports from India were for the first time greater than those from China.
The end of the East India Company’s monopoly on trade with China also had another result, which was more dramatic though less important in the long term: it ushered in the era of the tea clippers.
While the Company had had the monopoly on trade, there was no rush to bring the tea from China to Britain, but after 1834 the tea trade became a virtual free-for-all.
Individual merchants and sea-captains with their own ships raced to bring home the tea and make the most money, using fast new clippers which had sleek lines, tall masts and huge sails.
In particular, there was competition between British and American merchants, leading to the famous clipper races of the 1860s.
But these races soon came to an end with the opening of the Suez Canal, which made the trade routes to China viable for steamships for the first time.
