groups.content:
Malaria in 19th-century Italy
Up until the late nineteenth century, experts failed to make the connection between malaria and {{14}} . The most popular belief at the time was the {{15}} theory, which upheld the idea that diseases were carried by unclean air. Another common idea was that malaria was a {{16}} disease, and as a result people from certain parts of the country were often held responsible for the spread of epidemics. Malaria was particularly widespread in rural regions, where {{17}} could be extremely short.

questions.explanation: 题目说直到19世纪末，专家们未能建立疟疾与____之间的联系。原文B段提到有些人将沼泽、水和疟疾联系起来，但“did not make the further leap towards insects（没有进一步联想到昆虫）”，填 insects。
questions.tip: 虽然我们知道是蚊子（mosquitoes），但原文在此处特指未能跨越到“昆虫”这一概念，且蚊子也是昆虫的一种。
questions.quote: Everybody now knows that malaria is carried by mosquitoes. But in the 19th century most experts subscribed to the theory of 'miasma' or 'poisoning of the air'. Others made a link between swamps, water and malaria, but did not make the further leap towards insects. The consequence of these theories was that little was done to combat the disease before the end of that century.

questions.explanation: 题目说当时最流行的信念是____理论，该理论支持疾病由不洁空气传播。原文B段提到大多数专家认同“theory of 'miasma' or 'poisoning of the air'（瘴气理论或空气中毒）”，填 miasma。
questions.tip: “Unclean air” 对应 “poisoning of the air”，理论名称为 miasma。
questions.quote: But in the 19th century most experts subscribed to the theory of 'miasma' or 'poisoning of the air'.

questions.explanation: 题目说另一个普遍的想法是疟疾是一种____疾病。原文B段末尾提到流行病被归咎于来自意大利较热地区的人，鉴于广泛认为“malaria was hereditary（疟疾是遗传的）”，填 hereditary。
questions.tip: “Held responsible” 对应 “blamed on”，原因是认为它是 hereditary。
questions.quote: Epidemics were blamed on people who originated from the hotter parts of Italy, given the widespread belief that malaria was hereditary.

questions.explanation: 题目说疟疾在农村地区尤为普遍，在那里的____可能极短。原文B段提到在疟疾地区，土地工人的“life expectancy（预期寿命）”是可怕的22.5岁（即极短），填 life expectancy。
questions.tip: “Extremely short” 对应 “terrifying 22.5 years”。
questions.quote: In warm, damp, malarial zones, the life expectancy of land workers was a terrifying 22.5 years.

groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 2?
In boxes 18-20 on your answer sheet, write:

questions.prompt: The volunteers in Giovanni Battista Grassi's research came from all parts of Italy.
questions.explanation: 题目说Giovanni Battista Grassi研究中的志愿者来自意大利的所有地区（all parts）。原文C段只提到“healthy human volunteers（健康的人类志愿者）”，并未提及他们来自哪里，信息缺失，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.tip: 不要因为文章讲的是意大利就默认志愿者来自全国各地。
questions.quote: One of the first breakthroughs in the war against malaria came in 1898 when the zoologist Giovanni Battista Grassi demonstrated that the micro-organisms causing the disease were carried in the digestive tract of the mosquito. By releasing mosquitoes into rooms to drink the blood of healthy human volunteers, Grassi was able to make the direct link between the insects and the disease.

questions.prompt: Experiments in Italy proved that it was possible to remain healthy despite being in malarial zones.
questions.explanation: 题目说意大利的实验证明，即使在疟疾区，保持健康也是可能的。原文C段提到确凿证据来自于实验：健康人被带入疟疾区但“kept free of mosquito bites – and remained well（由于没被蚊子咬而保持了健康）”，选 TRUE。
questions.tip: “Remain healthy” 对应 “remained well”，“despite being in malarial zones” 对应 “introduced into malarial zones”。
questions.quote: Definitive proof of this theory was obtained after an extraordinary series of experiments in Italy, where healthy people were introduced into malarial zones but kept free of mosquito bites – and remained well.

questions.prompt: In the early twentieth century, quinine was successfully administered to all inhabitants of vulnerable regions.
questions.explanation: 题目说在20世纪初，奎宁被成功地给到了脆弱地区的所有居民（all inhabitants）。原文E段说虽然最初**决定（decided）**给所有人，但农民经常怀疑并“stubborn refusal to accept（顽固拒绝接受）”，所以并没有成功给到“所有”人，选 FALSE。
questions.tip: “Successfully administered to all” 与原文的 “refusal to accept” 矛盾。
questions.quote: It was originally decided to give quinine to all those in vulnerable regions – even healthy people. However, peasants were often suspicious of medicine being forced upon them, and doctors were frequently met with hostility and stubborn refusal to accept the treatment offered. But despite the refusals, the strategy as a whole was hugely successful.

groups.instructions:
Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A-H.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A-H, in boxes 21-26 on your answer sheet.

questions.prompt: a figure showing the dramatic results of an anti-malarial drug programme
questions.explanation: 题目提到显示抗疟疾药物计划显著结果的数据（figure）。原文E段提到在使用奎宁策略后，“Deaths from malaria fell by some 80%（疟疾死亡人数下降了约80%）”，80%即具体数据，选 E。
questions.tip: “Figure” 对应 “80%”，“Dramatic results” 对应 “fell by some 80% / hugely successful”。
questions.quote: But despite the refusals, the strategy as a whole was hugely successful. Deaths from malaria fell by some 80% in the first decade of the 20th century and some areas escaped altogether from the scourge of the disease.

questions.prompt: an important discovery about how malaria is spread
questions.explanation: 题目提到关于疟疾如何传播的重要发现。原文C段提到Grassi证明了微生物是“carried in the digestive tract of the mosquito（由蚊子消化道携带）”并直接联系了昆虫和疾病，这是关于传播方式的突破性发现，选 C。
questions.tip: “How malaria is spread” 对应 “carried in... mosquito... link between insects and the disease”。
questions.quote: One of the first breakthroughs in the war against malaria came in 1898 when the zoologist Giovanni Battista Grassi demonstrated that the micro-organisms causing the disease were carried in the digestive tract of the mosquito. By releasing mosquitoes into rooms to drink the blood of healthy human volunteers, Grassi was able to make the direct link between the insects and the disease.

questions.prompt: mention of an expert's decision not to halt the spread of the disease
questions.explanation: 题目提到一位专家决定不阻止疾病传播。原文F段提到主要疟疾学家Alberto Missiroli“refused to order the distribution of quinine, so allowing the epidemic to spread unchecked（拒绝下令分发奎宁，从而任由流行病肆虐）”，选 F。
questions.tip: “Decision not to halt” 对应 “refused to order... allowing... to spread”。
questions.quote: Yet the country's leading malariologist Alberto Missiroli refused to order the distribution of quinine, so allowing the epidemic to spread unchecked. According to Snowden, he did this in order to create the ideal conditions for a new strategy, supported by the US Rockefeller Foundation – a massive experiment involving the extermination of mosquitoes with the chemical DDT.

questions.prompt: the significance of the malaria story for today's readers
questions.explanation: 题目提到疟疾故事对当今读者的意义。原文H段开头说由于全球每年仍有超百万人死于疟疾，Snowden的书具有“contemporary relevance（当代相关性/现实意义）”，选 H。
questions.tip: “Significance for today” 对应 “contemporary relevance”。
questions.quote: As there are still more than 1m deaths every year from malaria worldwide, Snowden's book also has contemporary relevance. This is a disease that affects every level of the societies where it is rampant.

questions.prompt: examples of false assumptions which held back scientific understanding of malaria
questions.explanation: 题目提到阻碍科学理解疟疾的错误假设的例子。原文B段提到19世纪专家信奉“miasma（瘴气）”理论或认为疟疾是“hereditary（遗传的）”，这些导致了“little was done（无所作为）”，即阻碍了理解和防治，选 B。
questions.tip: “False assumptions” 对应 “theory of 'miasma' / belief that malaria was hereditary”。
questions.quote: But in the 19th century most experts subscribed to the theory of 'miasma' or 'poisoning of the air'. Others made a link between swamps, water and malaria, but did not make the further leap towards insects. The consequence of these theories was that little was done to combat the disease before the end of that century.

questions.prompt: a reference to legislation to support the fight against malaria
questions.explanation: 题目提到支持抗击疟疾斗争的立法参考。原文D段提到意大利在1904年引入了“quinine law（奎宁法）”，即立法，选 D。
questions.tip: “Legislation” 对应 “law”。
questions.quote: A complicated approach was adopted, which made use of quinine – a drug obtained from tree bark which had long been used to combat fever, but was now seen as a crucial part of the war on malaria. Italy introduced a quinine law and a quinine tax in 1904, and the drug was administered to large numbers of rural workers.

14.q: experts failed to make the connection between malaria and
14.s: did not make the further leap towards insects

14.q: Up until the late nineteenth century

15.q: The most popular belief at the time
15.s: most experts subscribed to the theory

15.q: diseases were carried by unclean air

16.q: people from certain parts of the country were often held responsible
16.s: Epidemics were blamed on people who originated from the hotter parts of Italy

17.q: Malaria was particularly widespread in rural regions

19.s: Definitive proof of this theory was obtained after an extraordinary series of experiments in Italy

19.q: remain healthy despite being in malarial zones
19.s: healthy people were introduced into malarial zones but kept free of mosquito bites – and remained well

20.s: all those in vulnerable regions – even healthy people

21.q: a figure showing the dramatic results
21.s: Deaths from malaria fell by some 80%

22.s: the micro-organisms causing the disease were carried in the digestive tract of the mosquito

23.s: the country's leading malariologist Alberto Missiroli refused to order

23.q: not to halt the spread of the disease
23.s: allowing the epidemic to spread unchecked

24.q: the significance of the malaria story for today's readers
24.s: Snowden's book also has contemporary relevance

25.s: the theory of 'miasma' or 'poisoning of the air'

25.q: held back scientific understanding of malaria
25.s: did not make the further leap towards insects

26.s: Italy introduced a quinine law and a quinine tax in 1904
a crucial part of the war on malaria

sentences.text: Theories on the origin and evolution of language have been a major area of my research for many years.
By 1859, when British scientist Charles Darwin published The Origin of Species, there was already a great deal of interest in this subject.
However, the debate became plagued by strange theories, so much so that in 1866 the influential Société de Linguistique de Paris banned all discussions about the origin of language.
The ban lasted for more than a century, before a surge of research began during the 1990s.
Linguists, psychologists, anthropologists and archaeologists now frequently debate the origin of language and have published many articles and books on this topic.
And yet, despite almost frenzied activity, limited progress has been made.
I believe there are four reasons for this.
The first is an insufficient concern with the archaeological and fossil proof of the brains and behaviour of our human ancestors.

Many theories to date rely on an assumed association between brain size and language abilities, without acknowledging the problem this creates: fossil evidence indicates that the Neanderthals had larger brains than modern humans, Homo sapiens, but archaeological evidence indicates that the Neanderthals lacked a capacity for language.
So something is seriously amiss with those theories.
That 'something' might relate to the second reason for limited progress: insufficient concern with the other major aural and vocal communication system of modern humans: music.

Even though the Société de Linguistique de Paris had nothing to say about studying the origin of music, academics appear to have had a self-imposed ban, with limited discussion of this issue during the 19th and 20th centuries.
However, there are notable exceptions that should be acknowledged.
One is the aforementioned Charles Darwin who, in his 1871 book on human evolution, The Descent of Man, devoted several pages to the development of music.
Another is the renowned ethnomusicologist John Blacking, whose 1973 book, How Musical is Man?, broached the idea that music is an inherent and universal human quality.
The origin of music deserves as much attention as that of language, as we cannot treat one without the other.
Those writers who had evidently annoyed the Société de Linguistique de Paris were quite aware of this.
For them, music and language were intimately linked; the French writer and philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau's On the Origin of Language (1781) was a reflection on both music and language.
In contrast, Morten Christiansen and Simon Kirby's book, Language Evolution (2000), which they conceived as 'a definitive book on the subject', failed to mention music in any of its 17 chapters.
Those authors have an important lesson to learn from Rousseau and other writers of his time who addressed the origin of language.
Music is a universal feature of human society and plays a significant role in the lives of all individuals.

Indeed, music is perhaps in even greater need of study than language: the latter has a self-evident function—the transmission of information—and can be readily accepted as a product of evolution, even if its specific evolutionary history remains unclear.
But what is the point of music?
That question leads directly to a third reason for our lack of progress in understanding how language evolved, and indeed the human mind in general: an insufficient concern with emotion.
If music is about anything, it is about expressing emotion.
But while archaeologists have put significant effort into examining the intellectual capacities of our ancestors, their emotional lives have been sorely neglected.
This has contributed to the neglect of music, which, in turn, has constrained our understanding of language.
There is one further reason why progress has been limited: those who have been most influential regarding the evolution of language have simply got it wrong, and misled everyone else.

Linguist Derek Bickerton has made an important contribution towards our understanding of the origin of language by bringing his profound knowledge of linguistics to the discussions that have occurred.
But Bickerton's idea that the precursor of modern language consisted of words strung together with limited, if any, grammar is, I believe, fundamentally mistaken.

Bickerton refers to this precursor as 'proto-language' and suggests that it was similar to the type of language spoken by young children today, and mastered by apes through the use of computer keyboards.
This idea has dominated the field of language origins for the last two decades, and is one that I once found persuasive.
But I now understand that it is not only flawed but has severely limited the progress that should have been made.
My book therefore provides an alternative view, one that draws on the ideas of a linguist who has, I believe, identified the true nature of proto-language.
Her name is Alison Wray.
She argues that proto-language was 'holistic' rather than compositional in character.

By this she means that the precursor to language was a communication system composed of 'messages' rather than words; each message was uniquely associated with an arbitrary meaning, as are the utterances of language today.
But in Wray's proto-language, they were not composed out of smaller units of meaning (i.e.
words) which could be combined together using a rule system (i.e.
grammar) to make more complex messages with emergent meanings.
For Wray, proto-language was semantically complex and agrammatical.
I believe this insight enables us to understand the origin of music as well as language, and to relate both to the emotional lives of our human ancestors.

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, what does the writer suggest about the origin of language?
questions.explanation: 第一段提到，尽管现在的研究活动几乎到了狂热的程度，但取得的进展却十分有限，这种强烈的反差表明缺乏进展是让人意外的 。
questions.tip: 你可能想选A（涉及的学科太多），但原文只是客观列举了多个学科在参与讨论，并没有说学科“太多”是导致进展缓慢的原因 。
questions.quote: Linguists, psychologists, anthropologists and archaeologists now frequently debate the origin of language and have published many articles and books on this topic. And yet, despite almost frenzied activity, limited progress has been made. (第1段)

options.text: Too many branches of science have been involved in its study.
The Société de Linguistique de Paris instigated research in this area.
The lack of progress is surprising given the amount of work being done.
Most progress in the study of language was made between 1859 and 1866.

questions.prompt: What is the ‘problem’ referred to in the second paragraph?
questions.explanation: 第二段指出的“问题”是，现有的理论假设大脑越大语言能力越强，但这与“化石证据（尼安德特人脑更大）”和“考古证据（尼安德特人没语言能力）”相互冲突打脸 。
questions.tip: 不要选B（化石证据不足），原文明确给出了实实在在的化石证据，问题出在这些证据与现有的理论假设完全矛盾 。
questions.quote: Many theories to date rely on an assumed association between brain size and language abilities, without acknowledging the problem this creates: fossil evidence indicates that the Neanderthals had larger brains than modern humans, Homo sapiens, but archaeological evidence indicates that the Neanderthals lacked a capacity for language. (第2段)

options.text: Some current theories are based on conflicting evidence.
There is insufficient fossil evidence to reach a conclusion.
Fossil evidence suggests that Homo sapiens had larger brains than Neanderthals.
Archaeological evidence shows that Neanderthals were able to talk.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s work in 1781?
questions.explanation: 作者认为现代的理论家（如写《语言进化》却没有提音乐的作者们）有一堂重要的课需要从卢梭那里学习，这意味着现代学者应该多关注卢梭将音乐与语言结合起来研究的方法 。
questions.tip: 别选C，后来的《Language Evolution》这本书在17个章节里完全没有提到音乐，和卢梭的观点截然相反，绝对不是“继承/反映（mirrored）”了卢梭的思想 。
questions.quote: In contrast, Morten Christiansen and Simon Kirby's book, Language Evolution (2000), which they conceived as 'a definitive book on the subject', failed to mention music in any of its 17 chapters. Those authors have an important lesson to learn from Rousseau and other writers of his time who addressed the origin of language. (第4段)

options.text: Modern theorists should pay more attention to his approach.
His ideas supported those of the Société de Linguistique de Paris.
His ideas were mirrored in a later book called Language Evolution.
His ideas are too outdated to be of any relevance today.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s current view of Derek Bickerton’s ideas?
questions.explanation: 作者直言不讳地说，Derek Bickerton 关于早期语言（proto-language）缺乏语法的假设，从根本上就是错误的（fundamentally mistaken） 。
questions.tip: 你可能看到原文说他的观点“主导了过去二十年”，就想当然以为这是被广泛接受的好事，但作者紧接着就说这个想法不仅有缺陷，还严重阻碍了研究进展 。
questions.quote: But Bickerton's idea that the precursor of modern language consisted of words strung together with limited, if any, grammar is, I believe, fundamentally mistaken... This idea has dominated the field of language origins for the last two decades, and is one that I once found persuasive. But I now understand that it is not only flawed but has severely limited the progress that should have been made. (第7段)

options.text: They have had little impact on the study of language.
They have helped the study of linguistics to progress.
They are not accepted by the majority of linguists.
The assumption behind them is wrong.

questions.prompt: In the final paragraph, the writer concludes that Alison Wray’s ideas will help establish a link between
questions.explanation: 作者在文章结尾明确总结，Alison Wray 的见解能让我们理解音乐和语言的起源，并将这两者都与人类祖先的情感（emotional lives）生活联系起来 。
questions.tip: 选项B只是 Alison Wray 理论内部的一个运作机制（语言由信息包构成），而不是作者认为该理论最终能帮助建立的宏大“联系（link）” 。
questions.quote: For Wray, proto-language was semantically complex and agrammatical. I believe this insight enables us to understand the origin of music as well as language, and to relate both to the emotional lives of our human ancestors. (第8段)

groups.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-H, below.

options.text: suggested music was an essential part of every individual.
made no link between music and language in a comprehensive study.
believes that early language was very musical.
felt that the origin of language should not be debated.
states that early language was made up of basic words used in an unsystematic way.
devoted 17 chapters of a book to music.
believes that proto-language had no individual words.
referred to music in part of a book about the development of human beings.

questions.prompt: The Société de Linguistique de Paris
questions.explanation: 1866年，巴黎语言学会直接“禁止（banned）”了所有关于语言起源的讨论，这完美对应选项D“认为不应该被讨论” 。
questions.tip: 不要想得太复杂，这里的“banned all discussions”是非常直白的字面替换，没有任何深层引申意思 。
questions.quote: However, the debate became plagued by strange theories, so much so that in 1866 the influential Société de Linguistique de Paris banned all discussions about the origin of language. (第1段)

questions.prompt: Charles Darwin
questions.explanation: 达尔文在他关于“人类进化（human evolution）”的书中，花了数页篇幅专门讨论音乐的发展，这对应选项H“在一本关于人类发展的书中提到了音乐” 。
questions.tip: 选项F“花了17章写音乐”是张冠李戴，写了17章却只字没提音乐的是后来的 Christiansen and Kirby 。
questions.quote: One is the aforementioned Charles Darwin who, in his 1871 book on human evolution, The Descent of Man, devoted several pages to the development of music. (第3段)

questions.prompt: John Blacking
questions.explanation: John Blacking 提出，音乐是人类“与生俱来且普遍的特质（inherent and universal human quality）”，这直接对应选项A“音乐是每个个体的核心部分” 。
questions.tip: 只要抓住“universal（普遍的）”和“every individual（每个个体）”这两个词的同义替换，这道题就能瞬间锁定 。
questions.quote: Another is the renowned ethnomusicologist John Blacking, whose 1973 book, How Musical is Man?, broached the idea that music is an inherent and universal human quality. (第3段)

questions.prompt: Christiansen and Kirby
questions.explanation: Christiansen 和 Kirby 写了一本关于语言进化的“权威著作（definitive book）”，但在17个章节中却对音乐只字未提，这对应选项B“在全面研究中没有将音乐与语言建立联系” 。
questions.tip: 你可能只看到了“17 chapters”就急着选F，但原文白纸黑字写的是“failed to mention music（没有提到音乐）”，一定要把句子看完 。
questions.quote: In contrast, Morten Christiansen and Simon Kirby's book, Language Evolution (2000), which they conceived as 'a definitive book on the subject', failed to mention music in any of its 17 chapters. (第4段)

questions.prompt: Derek Bickerton
questions.explanation: Derek Bickerton 认为语言的前身是由缺乏语法的“词（words）”串在一起组成的，这对应选项E“早期语言由基本词汇组成，使用方式不系统（无语法）” 。
questions.tip: 虽然他在讲早期语言，但他认为这种语言依然是由一个个“词（words）”构成的，千万不要和后来 Alison Wray 认为“没有单个词（no individual words）”的观点搞混淆了 。
questions.quote: But Bickerton's idea that the precursor of modern language consisted of words strung together with limited, if any, grammar is, I believe, fundamentally mistaken. (第7段)

questions.prompt: Alison Wray
questions.explanation: Alison Wray 认为早期语言是由“信息（messages）”构成的整体，而“不是由更小的意义单位（即词汇）组合而成的”，这对应选项G“早期语言没有单个词汇” 。
questions.tip: 这里的“not composed out of smaller units of meaning (i.e. words)”是解题的绝对核心，明确否定了单个词汇的存在 。
questions.quote: By this she means that the precursor to language was a communication system composed of 'messages' rather than words... But in Wray's proto-language, they were not composed out of smaller units of meaning (i.e. words) which could be combined together using a rule system (i.e. grammar)... (第8段)

groups.instructions: Choose THREE letters, A-G.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, which THREE of the following areas have not been studied enough in order to understand the origin of language?
questions.explanation:
作者列举的第一个研究不足的原因是，对我们人类祖先的“考古学和化石证据（archaeological and fossil proof）”关注不够，这精准对应选项A的史前时代证据 。
作者列出的第二个导致进展有限的原因，是对现代人类另一个主要的交流系统——“音乐（music）”——的关注严重不足 。
作者指出的第三个缺乏进展的原因是，对“情感（emotion）”的关注不够，研究者过于关注智力而忽视了祖先的情感生活 。
questions.tip:
选项F“human intellect（人类智力）”是已经被广泛研究过的领域（put significant effort into examining the intellectual capacities），作者指出的是缺乏对智力背后的实物化石证据的关注 。
文章明确列出了几条“insufficient concern with...”的内容，这里的定位非常直接，不需要去过度推敲其他干扰项 。
原文直接写了“an insufficient concern with emotion”，这道多选题其实就是送分题，只要顺着文章结构找到作者列出的几个原因就能一一对应拿分 。
questions.quote:

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Let's have an international celebration and get people to show off things about their home country."
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And we all agreed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The first year, the celebration lasted just one day, and it featured three countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It was a great success and was written about in our local newspaper.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And so the next year, even though it cost more, the organizers expanded it to an International Week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: On each of the first six days of the week, one country is designated to star.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Everyone has a ball.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Of course, we move it to the school gym if it rains like last year, but nobody minds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To apply to have a day for their country, people don't need to belong to a particular country association.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They can just be a group who identify themselves with a particular country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They don't need to worry at this stage about funding, but some grants are available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The organizing committee has to select the ones with the best ideas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Unfortunately, for large outdoor activities, we aren't allowed to use the local stadium because they've got other commitments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But the community center lets us use its parking lot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The hall is kind of small, but it has been kind enough to permit us to make use of its classrooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Local people have been very generous.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: A lot of business people let us have things like tables and amplifiers for the week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The organizing committee handles all the administration, and the town library has been great about featuring books about the countries.

transcript.text: Section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Following instructions from their tutor, you will hear two economic students called James and Anna discussing a recent survey about the cost of buying a house in New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five on page six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, for this week's assignment, you're going to assess the value survey on house prices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What were the survey's findings?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Was it a reliable survey?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Work in pairs, discuss what you've read, and generate some ideas for the assignment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Shall we work together, Anna?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Sure, James.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, um, first, how did the value survey actually measure the cost of houses?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because there are lots of ways of calculating it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it looked at all houses, didn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: New and old.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So it started with average incomes across the whole workforce and then worked out house prices in relation to that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I mean, to what people were earning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So it's about affordability, what people pay in real terms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's no information about the size of a house a typical family can buy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No, that's a limitation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay, then in the assignment, we should give some background.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I mean, what's different about the value survey?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, there's lots of these surveys every year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Value is actually one of the newer ones, but it stands out because it gives figures for a range of the largest urban centers, which none of the others do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, good point.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then one finding was that New Zealand houses are relatively expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Why is that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Because most of them are built of wood, and that's quite cheap.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, it is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the problem is there are too many regulations and restrictions about where you can build.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if more building sites were created for housing, the costs would come down.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's it, isn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Because there are plenty of contractors ready to do the work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, um, what else?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, what about transport?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I mean, it's all very well to talk about new housing, but how are people going to get there?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Is the survey proposing new roads, new rail networks?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It should be a coordinated approach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, but the survey didn't mention it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a missed opportunity because a commitment to funding public transport from the outset would improve air quality in our cities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: True.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay then, the next survey, what can we expect?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It'll look at all the same places, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Exactly the same.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the next one will give an idea of the way prices are moving.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The government may have to think about how house prices are affecting society.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Then in the assignment, we need to evaluate how reliable the survey was.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we should look at some of the criticism made by commentators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So there's the economist Andrew Coleman.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He actually questioned whether the survey was money well spent because it only looked at a single year in isolation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A year when it was difficult to borrow money to buy a house, pushing up costs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So he thought the survey should consider a longer timeframe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Did you get that article by Professor Massey?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Because he's the leading authority on this topic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, interesting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He realized the method used to calculate how much money people had didn't take savings into account.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So actually, people looking for a house were richer than the survey shows, making houses cheaper in real terms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then Richard Bernard, his criticism was original.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He found out they were using quite outdated software to process all the information they gathered, which was crazy because they actually had the money available for an upgrade.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So even though it was a highly regarded team of people, the way the statistics were interpreted was open to question.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then Professor Lowndes, he thought the report was just badly written.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: After all the work that went into gathering valid information, the finished report was just too long and weakly structured, and there was too much unnecessary detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And the last one, Maria Darling, she made a point about the properties that were evaluated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There weren't enough of them, you mean?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: No, it wasn't that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But they were never identified for privacy reasons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But she thought the actual properties used should have been revealed, you know.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The process should have been transparent if the people are going to have full confidence in the survey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So a lot of criticism.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, but this sort of research is often controversial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about how different building materials are chosen for flooring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to thirty-seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to thirty-seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We’ve been talking about choosing building materials in the last week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, a great many factors influence the choice of building materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can’t make a house of cards, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And people who live in glass houses and all that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyhow, today I’d like to say a few words about flooring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some artificial materials can be used, like plastic for instance, which offer mixed blessings when used as a flooring surface.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the one hand, plastic is cheaper than nearly any other alternative, short of bare ground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Plastic also does not warp like wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the other hand, the best that can be said about plastic is that it looks like wood or stone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it cannot replace the real materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As I have mentioned, I’m fixing up a new house.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The decorator my wife hired told me plastic does a great job of looking exactly like plastic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Besides, it scratches easily, fades or discolors, and starts cracking within a year or two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if you’re fitting out a sleazy hotel or plan to live in a trailer park, go with the plastic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Really though, for all intents and purposes, this leaves us with wood or stone as choices for flooring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Stone and wood are alike in at least one respect: both go through processing before they can be put to use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since few of us cut our own lumber or quarry our own stone, this is not perhaps a pressing concern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Still, do-it-yourselfers would do well to remember to buy only properly seasoned wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unseasoned wood warps, and a warped floor quickly becomes firewood, and its owner quickly becomes poorer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Likewise, except for dull-hued materials like slate or sandstone, most stone floors are polished before installation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The choice goes well beyond just wood or stone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Each type requires many further considerations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A few special remarks are called for when considering wood, for example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As always, aesthetics, personal taste, and layout all play roles, as well as the type of house or room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, and certainly don’t forget the cost.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When it comes to cost, a rule of thumb is that the softer and less exotic the wood, the lower the cost.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the US, for instance, pine is both ubiquitous and cheap.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mahogany is imported and exorbitantly expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you’re on any kind of budget when remodeling, it’s really helpful to remember to go for the softer woods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Aside from cost, there are still lots of different factors that are important in choosing the best flooring for the job.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Continuing with the example of wood, one must consider the effects of each type of wood on the mood of the room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When selecting the best wood to use, particular attention needs to be paid to its grain patterns, texture, and color.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In rooms where relaxation or deep thought is the aim, say bedrooms or the study, dark, strong-grained woods are the rule.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here, the grain ought to match the furniture for a feeling of homogeneity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In rooms where activity and motion are typical, the dining room or living room, lighter, finer-grained lumber is more suitable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In such a setting, the wood grain might be useful in offering a contrast to the furniture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This leads to a feel of subconscious excitement in keeping with the room’s function.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In either case, though, consult a decorator.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is a decorator’s job to know what materials to use to fit the function of the room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though some things about putting together a room are subjective and based on one’s individual taste, materials appropriate to a room’s function are much more straightforward.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A decorator takes the needs of the customer and uses a mathematical formula rather than subjective words.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since feelings vary from person to person, verbal descriptions of wood types tend to be ambiguous.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You want the wood you select, not something approximate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And if you do decide to do it yourself, remember that all wood must be treated with preservatives to enhance its appearance and preserve its natural beauty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the lecture, you have some time to look at questions thirty-eight to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions thirty-eight to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In the case of stone, or quarry tile as flat-cut flooring stone is properly called, a new set of considerations must be weighed up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Simple color aside, the degree of reflection must be kept in mind.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is called the reflectance rate, which is expressed in a number between zero point zero and one point zero, depending on the amount of light it reflects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At one end of the scale is polished silver.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At a rating of one point zero, this shiny surface reflects nearly all of the light directed at it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Numbers closer to zero describe materials that absorb more light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving down the scale a bit, we see that plastic that has been painted white has a rate of zero point eight, which makes sense.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know that the color white reflects all other color, while black absorbs all color, and plastic itself is a relatively reflective material.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Materials that are denser and darker have reflectance rates much closer to zero.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The quarry tile I mentioned a while ago has a rate of zero point one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you may know, quarry tile is generally dark brown and made from clay, so it is quite dense.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, there is considerable variation among types of quarry tile because of the hue or treatment of the clay during its creation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Does anyone have any guesses as to what material may have a rate of almost zero point zero?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We can guess most of these materials are black in color, but plastic, wood, and even stone reflect some light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One material with a rate of almost zero point zero is black velvet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The texture produces almost no shine at all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Carrera marble, despite its white hue, is actually lower in reflectivity than black onyx.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In any case, the fact that tiles vary somewhat should not be forgotten.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A highly reflective floor would not be suitable in a library.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It would be indispensable in a ballroom, should your home be large enough to feature one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Again, a rule of thumb is that light means lively.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since form and material follow function, one should only use the more reflective materials in rooms where the cultivation and expression of energy is important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bear in mind, too, that most types of stone cost more than all but the rarest of wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, there is no reason why some rooms of a house should not feature wood floors or other stone tiles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can even mix the two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A room with wood panels on the walls can have a beautiful stone floor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My bedroom has white birch walls and a light blue slate floor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The place looks like a Russian hunting lodge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember, though, go with what feels right for you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Good taste and the laws of interior design are the homeowner's servants, not his master.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's only beautiful when you decide it is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I mean, you're the one who lives there, not the decorator, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, are there any questions?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have 45 seconds to check your answers to Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

sentences.text: The potato was first cultivated in South America between three and seven thousand years ago, though scientists believe they may have grown wild in the region as long as 13,000 years ago.
The genetic patterns of potato distribution indicate that the potato probably originated in the mountainous west-central region of the continent.
Early Spanish chroniclers who misused the Indian word batata (sweet potato) as the name for the potato noted the importance of the tuber to the Incan Empire.

The Incas had learned to preserve the potato for storage by dehydrating and mashing potatoes into a substance called chuño, which could be stored in a room for up to 10 years, providing excellent insurance against possible crop failures.
As well as using the food as a staple crop, the Incas thought potatoes made childbirth easier and used them to treat injuries.
The Spanish conquistadors first encountered the potato when they arrived in Peru in 1532 in search of gold, and noted Inca miners eating chuño.

At the time the Spaniards failed to realize that the potato represented a far more important treasure than either silver or gold, but they did gradually begin to use potatoes as basic rations aboard their ships.
After the arrival of the potato in Spain in 1570, a few Spanish farmers began to cultivate them on a small scale, mostly as food for livestock.
Throughout Europe, potatoes were regarded with suspicion, distaste and fear.
Generally considered to be unfit for human consumption, they were used only as animal fodder and sustenance for the starving.
In northern Europe, potatoes were primarily grown in botanical gardens as an exotic novelty.
Even peasants refused to eat from a plant that produced ugly, misshapen tubers and that had come from a heathen civilization.
Some felt that the potato plant’s resemblance to plants in the nightshade family hinted that it was the creation of witches or devils.
In meat-loving England, farmers and urban workers regarded potatoes with extreme distaste.
In 1662, the Royal Society recommended the cultivation of the tuber to the English government and the nation, but this recommendation had little impact.
Potatoes did not become a staple until, during the food shortages associated with the Revolutionary Wars, the English government began to officially encourage potato cultivation.
In 1795, the Board of Agriculture issued a pamphlet entitled “Hints Respecting the Culture and Use of Potatoes”; this was followed shortly by pro-potato editorials and potato recipes in The Times.
Gradually, the lower classes began to follow the lead of the upper classes.
A similar pattern emerged across the English Channel in the Netherlands, Belgium and France.

While the potato slowly gained ground in eastern France (where it was often the only crop remaining after marauding soldiers plundered wheat fields and vineyards), it did not achieve widespread acceptance until the late 1700s.
The peasants remained suspicious, in spite of a 1771 paper from the Faculté de Paris testifying that the potato was not harmful but beneficial.

The people began to overcome their distaste when the plant received the royal seal of approval: Louis XVI began to sport a potato flower in his buttonhole, and Marie-Antoinette wore a purple potato blossom in her hair.
Frederick the Great of Prussia saw the potato’s potential to help feed his nation and lower the price of bread, but faced the challenge of overcoming the people’s prejudice against the plant.

When he issued a 1774 order for his subjects to grow potatoes as protection against famine, the town of Kolberg replied: “The things have neither smell nor taste, not even the dogs will eat them, so what use are they to us?”

Trying a less direct approach to encourage his subjects to begin planting potatoes, Frederick used a bit of reverse psychology: he planted a royal field of potato plants and stationed a heavy guard to protect this field from thieves.
Nearby peasants naturally assumed that anything worth guarding was worth stealing, and so sneaked into the field and snatched the plants for their home gardens.
Of course, this was entirely in line with Frederick’s wishes.
Historians debate whether the potato was primarily a cause or an effect of the huge population boom in industrial-era England and Wales.
Prior to 1800, the English diet had consisted primarily of meat, supplemented by bread, butter and cheese.
Few vegetables were consumed, most vegetables being regarded as nutritionally worthless and potentially harmful.
This view began to change gradually in the late 1700s.

The Industrial Revolution was drawing an ever-increasing percentage of the populace into crowded cities, where only the richest could afford homes with ovens or coal storage rooms, and people were working 12–16-hour days which left them with little time or energy to prepare food.
High-yielding, easily prepared potato crops were the obvious solution to England’s food problems.

Whereas most of their neighbours regarded the potato with suspicion and had to be persuaded to use it by the upper classes, the Irish peasantry embraced the tuber more passionately than anyone since the Incas.
The potato was well suited to the Irish soil and climate, and its high yield suited the most important concern of most Irish farmers: to feed their families.
The most dramatic example of the potato’s potential to alter population patterns occurred in Ireland, where the potato had become a staple by 1800.

The Irish population doubled to eight million between 1780 and 1841, this without any significant expansion of industry or reform of agricultural techniques beyond the widespread cultivation of the potato.

Though Irish landholding practices were primitive in comparison with those of England, the potato’s high yields allowed even the poorest farmers to produce more healthy food than they needed with scarcely any investment or hard labour.
Even children could easily plant, harvest and cook potatoes, which of course required no threshing, curing or grinding.
The abundance provided by potatoes greatly decreased infant mortality and encouraged early marriage.

r2.title: The origin and development of applause

sentences.text: A Scholars aren’t quite sure about the origins of applause, but the form that is still most common, clapping the hands together, was formalized in Western culture during and after performances.
During the time of the Roman Republic (509 BC – 27 BC) the common way to end a play was for the chief actor to yell ‘Valete et plaudite!’
(‘Goodbye and applause!’)
thus signaling to the audience that it was time for them to give praise by striking hands and making explosive noise.
It’s no surprise, then, that this became a means of crowd manipulation.
Rome saw the rise of a professional class of applauders, or ‘people who clapped for their dinner’, hired to infiltrate crowds and manipulate their reaction to performances.
Actors would hire a dozen or so people to spread out among their audiences and prolong the applause, or, if they were feeling especially bold, to start ‘spontaneous’ chants and shouts of praise.
B The Roman Republic came to an end and was replaced by the Roman Empire (27 BC – 476 AD) where applause became a way for leaders to interact directly with their citizens.
One of the chief methods they used to estimate their standing with the people was gauging the greetings they got when they entered the arena.
Leaders became astute at reading the volume, the rhythm, and the length of the crowd’s claps for clues about how well they were doing as officials and lawmakers.
‘We should think of it as an ancient type of opinion poll,’ says Greg Aldrete, a professor of history.
‘This is how you gauge the people.’
Roman leaders were gathering data about people by listening to applause.
C Clever leaders of the ancient world researched their rivals, too.

Cicero, the Roman lawyer, would send friends to stand around outside the arena, taking notes to see what kind of greeting each official got when he entered, the better to see who was beloved by the people, and who was not.
They had a lot of information to assess.
‘Ancient crowds were more interactive than they are today,’ Aldrete points out.
‘There was a lot of back and forth between speakers and crowds.
And particularly in the Greco-Roman world, crowds, especially in cities, were really good at communicating messages through rhythmic clapping, sometimes coupled with shouts.’
The coding was, he says, invaluable when assessing an orator’s fortunes.
D Around the first century AD, those systems of applause became more and more elaborate.
Applause no longer meant, simply, ‘claps’.
While Greco-Roman audiences certainly smacked their palms together the same way we do today, their overall strategies of applause were much more varied than clapping alone.
Crowds expressed degrees of approval of the person or persons before them, ranging from claps, to snaps (of the finger and thumb), to waves (of the edge of the toga).

The emperor Aurelian decided to replace this gesture by waving a special handkerchief instead, a prop which he then distributed to all Roman citizens, so they would never be without a way to praise him.
E Although style of applause may have changed over the centuries, the need to manipulate remained.
16th-century French poet Jean Daurat is credited with bringing back the Roman practice of hiring professional applauders.
In France, this group became known as a ‘claque’.
Daurat handed out tickets to his own performances to people who promised to applaud at the end.
By the early 1820s, claques had become institutionalized, with an agency in Paris specializing in the distribution of the claqueurs’ services.
The historian William B.
Cohen describes the intricate price lists agencies of this kind would hand out to potential patrons: polite clapping would cost this many francs, enthusiastic applause would cost this many.

The claque also underwent a kind of classification: the rieurs (laughers) would laugh loudly at the jokes; the pleureurs (criers) would feign tears in reaction to performances; the commissaires (officers) would learn a play or a piece of music by heart and then call attention to its best parts.
This practice spread to Milan, to Vienna, and to London before falling out of fashion.
The claque lost its power once people became aware of its tricks.
F And clapping itself evolved.
In the 18th century, symphonies and concerts became more serious, aligning themselves with the reverence and spirituality associated with religious ceremonies.
Knowing when to maintain silence, as well as when to clap, became a mark of sophistication, a kind of code for audiences to learn.
Applause became a matter of ‘do’ or ‘don’t’, so losing many old shades of meaning.
Those changes changed performers, too.
Applause became much less of a true dialogue with an audience, especially so with opera, where the singers saw it as part of a basic transaction with the crowd.
So by the time the 19th century arrived, applause had become standardized and institutionalized, and had become an expectation rather than the reward it used to be.
G In the 21st century we’re reinventing applause, to make it what it used to be: a coded form of communication.
More and more the digital world allows us to link and like and share through our devices.
By connecting with others in this way, we become part of the performance by participating in it, demonstrating our appreciation by amplifying and extending the show through commenting and praising.
Our kind of applause matters more now, in many ways, because it is no longer momentary and short-lived, but is far more permanent instead.

questions.explanation:

原文说“claque”经历了一种分类，被分成了大笑的人、假哭的人等不同类型，完美对应D选项的“被分成了不同类别”。

questions.quote:
16th-century French poet Jean Daurat is credited with bringing back the Roman practice of hiring professional applauders. In France, this group became known as a ‘claque’.
The claque also underwent a kind of classification: the rieurs (laughers) would laugh loudly at the jokes; the pleureurs (criers) would feign tears in reaction to performances; the commissaires (officers) would learn a play or a piece of music by heart and then call attention to its best parts. This practice spread to Milan, to Vienna, and to London before falling out of fashion.

sentences.text: The New Zealand species of lizard, the tuatara, is firmly embedded in the national psyche: an icon for today which dates from the age of dinosaurs; an ancient reptile commemorated on the back of the five-cent coin.
New Zealanders feel an affinity with the tuatara, and accept that active conservation management is required to ensure it will be among the legacies left to future generations.
When European explorers reached New Zealand in 1769 they found two large islands, which together they called the mainland, and many tiny offshore islands around the coast.
The naturalists who came with the explorers disregarded the tuatara, though it is improbable none were seen.
Only several decades later did a tuatara specimen reach the British Museum, where it was eventually classified as just another type of lizard.
One of the first scientists who realised that aspects of tuatara anatomy were odd—unchanged for tens of thousands of years—was Albert Gunther in 1876.
Gunther believed the tuatara was one of the most valuable objects in zoological anatomical collections, and also noted, in passing, the reptile was likely to become extinct.
From today's perspective, it is striking that Gunther expressed no concern about the probable demise of the tuatara.
He and his contemporaries were products of their age, strongly influenced by Charles Darwin's theory, which had only recently been published.
Their views were something like this: 'Extinction is a natural process.
It is sad that species disappear, but that is part of nature.'
There is a second important aspect of Gunther's work.
He recorded, correctly, that some of the mammals introduced by Europeans were predators of the tuatara—particularly rats.

But what he did not realise was that New Zealand has two species of rat, both introduced, both with an appetite for tuatara: the ship's rat came with European explorers and settlers; but the kiore rat had already been in the country for hundreds of years, brought by Polynesians from the Pacific Islands.
Gunther failed to recognise the distinction, believing all rats to be a relatively recent introduction.
Little further research was conducted until Ian Crook of the NZ Wildlife Service published his findings in 1973, which can be summarised as follows.
Tuatara thrive on offshore islands with no rats.
Tuatara never survived on islands with ship's rats.
On a few islands, small and declining populations of tuatara occur with the kiore.
This should not be seen, however, as evidence that tuatara and kiore can coexist.
Rather, Crook proposed, kiore probably only arrived recently on such islands, and thus the small populations represent extinctions in progress.

Throughout the 1990s, Richard Holdaway and his colleagues at Victoria University in Wellington documented the surprising discovery that kiore probably arrived about 1,800 years ago, although the human population of New Zealand is thought to be no older than 800 years.
How is this possible?
Presumably, Holdaway argued, the kiore were brought by Polynesian explorers who visited the country but did not settle.
Thereafter, the rats were agents of ecological warfare, exterminating perhaps 1,000–3,000 species.
Thus, tuatara and many other species were already rare or extinct when permanent human inhabitants—the Maori—arrived around 1300.
This hypothesis is still being debated, but the evidence continues to accumulate in its favour.
Conservation practice has changed dramatically since Crook's findings were published in 1973.
Eradication of rats from any given environment was believed to be virtually impossible until about 1980, but since then has become routine.
Enormous conservation benefits are accruing as newly rat-free offshore islands are providing sanctuaries for the country's rarest species.
In 1995, for example, Nicola Nelson of the Department of Conservation established 68 tuatara on Titi Island.
Since then, four more populations of tuatara have been established elsewhere under similar conditions.
Today, numbers of tuatara are still a fraction of what they once were, but for the first time in 1,800 years the decline has been reversed.
While the recovery of rare species is itself a good thing, the truly significant outcome of this research is that it liberates the imagination.
If we can remove predatory introduced mammals from islands, why not from the mainland too?
Perhaps the questions we ask should demonstrate even more visionary ambition.
Can non-mammalian pests also be removed from the mainland?
Our rivers, for example, are full of surrogate rats, in the form of introduced species of fish called trout.
Some day more people will understand that trout have replaced a whole native fauna in our waterways, just as rats replaced tuatara on the mainland.
Will such knowledge lead to the creation of mainland 'aquatic islands' where we can once again establish those species of indigenous fish that used to live in our rivers?
Similarly, can bellbirds and tuis replace birds like starlings and mynahs?
The answers to such questions are uncertain, and opposing sides will doubtless be fiercely debated.
But the role of scientific knowledge in illuminating the past will be crucial.
Just as we no longer tolerate extinction, in the future we may no longer accept a mainland devoid of the biological wonders of our past such as tuatara.
Conservation is thus not primarily about the past but about imagining and then creating the future we wish for our children and ourselves.
For 80 million years until humans arrived, tuatara occurred throughout New Zealand—might they do so again?

Rats and tuatara cannot live together.

The first Polynesian explorers formed permanent settlements.
Ship's rats are the oldest rat species in the country.
Rats caused extinctions before any humans settled.

questions.tip: 你可能会因为听到男生后面说“can play piano”（弹钢琴）而填错，但那是男生的提问，且被女生明确否定了。
questions.quote: They've also got a few vacancies in what is called the guest liaison department. They are involved with the entertainment in the resort, especially the daily music shows and parades. They definitely need people who can sing.

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到这个职位需要有与儿童（children）一起工作的经验。
questions.tip: 你可能会被前面的 volleyball, surfing, cricket 等运动名称干扰，但这些是工作内容，题目问的是需要和“谁”相处的经验。
questions.quote: Among the most popular things for guests are the games and water sports activities, which take place on the beach that belongs to the resort. They are always looking for fit young people to help out with things like volleyball, surfing, and cricket. But they definitely need people who have worked with children for that vacancy.

questions.explanation: 录音中明确指出前台行李员这个职位的要求（requirement）是你得会开车（drive）。
questions.tip: 如果没抓到答案词，你可能会被后面解释为什么要开车的“golf buggies”（高尔夫球车）干扰，但卷面需要的是一个动词技能。
questions.quote: Finally, there are vacancies in the reception area. You'd work as part of the concierge department, carrying bags to and from rooms. A requirement for this role is that you can drive.

questions.explanation: 录音中说员工不需要为往返岛屿的交通（transport）付费，完美对应题目的“free（免费）”。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到男生提问的“accommodation”（住宿），但录音接着澄清了免费住宿仅限正式员工，所以不能填它。
questions.quote: Do they provide free accommodation for staff? It looks like they only provide it to permanent employees. But staff don't have to pay for transport to and from the island.

questions.explanation: 男生提问餐食（meals）如何，女生给予肯定回答，说值班时会提供（provided）。
questions.tip: 你可能会被后面的 groceries（食品杂货）干扰，但那是说提供餐食所以能“省下买杂货的钱”，实际提供的东西是 meals。
questions.quote: What about meals? Yes, they're provided when you're on duty, so you would save money on groceries.

questions.explanation: 录音中给出了三个可选日子，男生最终提出了星期四（Thursday），并得到了女生的确认（Fine）。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到 Wednesday, Thursday, Friday 三个词，如果没有听完男生最终敲定的日子就下笔，很容易把前面的 Wednesday 当成答案。
questions.quote: I know the resort personnel manager wants interviews on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday here at the college. Which day would suit you? Can we do it on Thursday, as I work on Wednesdays? Fine. Is two o'clock okay?

questions.explanation: 录音明确说到除了带简历（CV），还需要提供一张照片（photo）。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到 work experience（工作经验）或 qualifications（资质），但这些是简历包含的内容，题目问的是除了 CV 还需要带什么附加的独立物品。
questions.quote: Is there anything I need to take to the interview? Let me see. Yes, you need to bring a CV giving details of your work experience and qualifications. And because they are planning on interviewing a lot of people, they've asked everyone to provide a photo as well, so they can remember who is who.

transcript.text: Section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear the manager of a new sports center talking to potential customers about the facilities there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to sixteen on page four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to sixteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good evening and welcome to Carrara's brand new sports and leisure center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Um, first I'll tell you about our facilities, then feel free to wander around the center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, as you can see from the map I've given you, we're sitting in our cafe, which we hope will be a favorite place to visit after exercising.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To one side of us, and right in front of you as you enter the complex, is the shop.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Be sure to have a look in there later as we've got some great opening specials on footwear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the other side of the cafe, and ideally situated between the cafe and the child-minding facilities, we have the playground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can sit and relax there while your kids have a great time on the equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And our childcare facilities are available to anyone using the center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's talk a little bit about our heated swimming pool, which is also near the entrance on the other side from the cafe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has a five-meter water slide, which will be very popular with kids of all ages, and in the corner nearest the changing rooms, we have a high-tech hot spa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The water is heated to thirty-eight degrees centigrade, which is the ideal temperature to relax tired muscles after a workout.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So where can you do these workouts?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, we have a large weights room located at the cafe end of the administration block.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the weights room, you'll find all the latest equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We also have trainers there who can put a program together for you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another place to get a good workout is in the gym, which is shown on the map to the right of the changing rooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There will be all sorts of classes offered there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our aim is to provide all your exercise and recovery needs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So as well as the spa to help aching bodies, we also have a special area for massage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's in the funny-shaped room close to the administration area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Its distinctive shape has already led to the nickname of the Bullet Room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll be offering Swedish and Chinese massage there, and we'll offer physiotherapy in the future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty on page five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, let me tell you something about our different memberships.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, we offer different types of membership to cater for different needs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you are a fitness freak, then choose our all-in membership.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This gives you access to everything in the center, all the classes and sports.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's usually our most expensive option, but for a short time, we're offering twelve months for the price of nine, which is a huge saving.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you prefer just the gym classes, you may want to consider the gym and weights package.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It works out at ten dollars a week, which is good value.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you just want to swim, then we recommend getting a Swim Plus membership.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With this, you have unlimited use of the pool and spa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The other package we've reduced for this month only is the Off Peak.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is aimed at people who are happy to come at less busy times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, we have the family pack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We believe in keeping the whole family fit and healthy, so this package works out cheaper than buying it separately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Your flyer has details of all the prices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So anyone who signs up for a new membership tonight will receive two fantastic presents from us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We wanted to make these rewards something different from the norm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We could have just chosen a towel for you to use in the gym or some clothing from the shop, but we wanted to show our appreciation by giving you something special.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So not only are we going to give you a voucher for a session in our massage center, a great way to unwind after your workout, but you'll also get this great device that measures your heart rate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, just for turning up tonight, we'd like to give everyone here a drink bottle to take away with them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's all I wanted to say.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.tip: 做地图题首先要明确起点“cafe（咖啡馆）”，一旦开头的参照点跟丢，后续的相对位置就会全部错位。
questions.quote: Now, as you can see from the map I've given you, we're sitting in our cafe, which we hope will be a favorite place to visit after exercising. To one side of us and right in front of you as you enter the complex is the shop.

questions.tip: 你可能会因为没听懂“child-minding facilities（托儿设施）”而找不到参照物，平时要注意积累同类场景的同义替换词汇。

questions.prompt: Spa

questions.quote: Let's talk a little bit about our heated swimming pool, which is also near the entrance on the other side from the cafe. It has a five-meter water slide, which will be very popular with kids of all ages, and in the corner nearest the changing rooms, we have a high-tech hot spa.

questions.prompt: Weights room
questions.explanation: 录音说明力量训练室（weights room）位于行政楼（administration block）靠近咖啡馆的那一端（cafe end），完全对应图上的D。
questions.tip: 注意听清关键定位修饰语“cafe end（咖啡馆那一端）”，如果只听到了行政楼，可能会在相邻的几个选项（如C和D）中纠结。
questions.quote: So where can you do these workouts? Well, we have a large weights room located at the cafe end of the administration block.

questions.prompt: Gym
questions.explanation: 录音直接点明健身房（gym）在更衣室（changing rooms）的右边（to the right of），一看地图就是B点。
questions.tip: 这道题非常直接，关键是目光要迅速回到“更衣室”这个新的核心参照物上，不要在之前的区域停留。
questions.quote: Another place to get a good workout is in the gym, which is shown on the map to the right of the changing rooms.

questions.prompt: Massage room
questions.explanation: 录音指出按摩室靠近行政区，是一个形状奇怪（funny shaped）的房间，对应的只有E。
questions.tip: 哪怕你跟丢了“administration area”这个方位词，只要听到后面对于形状的描述“funny shaped/distinctive shape”，也能帮你果断锁定全图唯一非方正形状的房间E。
questions.quote: Our aim is to provide all your exercise and recovery needs, so as well as the spa to help aching bodies, we also have a special area for massage. It's in the funny shaped room close to the administration area. Its distinctive shape has already led to the nickname of the Bullet Room.

你可能会漏听具体的月份买赠细节，这种情况下要迅速抓住“huge saving（巨省钱）”这个强烈的态度信号词，从而锁定D选项。
