r2.title: Coins: The First Form of Money

sentences.text: A Few people pay much attention to coins; we take them for granted.

Since the advent of paper currency and the abandonment of a monetary system based on intrinsic or actual value, they have been demoted to the status of change: what is left when you have paid for something with “paper” money.

There is even a belief that they will one day be obsolete, as will paper or plastic notes, and money will at last have achieved the pure status of a mathematical formulation, a system of electronic credits and debits.

B In the modern media environment, the sheer number of visual images is overwhelming, but it makes one stop to think that coins are among the most durable of our artefacts, and future archaeologists will scrutinise coins in order to learn about their distant ancestors.
This is exactly the way ancient coins have informed us for over four millennia.

There are thousands of different coins, each designed to carry meaning as well as value, tiny but rich sources of documentary evidence about events and cultural attitudes, frequently produced with exquisite craftsmanship.
C Coins in Europe date from 2,500 to 2,700 years ago, and seem to have originated in the ancient kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey.
Before coins, trade was based on barter: the direct trade of commodities.
Barter required the physical presence of both commodities that were being traded.
Metal coins were far more portable, and not subject to the same spoilage on long sea journeys as a commodity like grain might be if it became wet.
However, they could also be accumulated, and these hoards could be stolen.
Coins were therefore a temptation to criminals.
The Greeks, however, were the first to realise the full potential of the new invention.
They were a trading people of seafarers.
Their civilisation, which was composed of dozens of city-states, was highly decentralised.
Despite the potential for theft, the Greeks realised that they could benefit enormously from a system that used coins, because it meant that they no longer had to carry goods with them to barter.
D The value of coins was generally based on the intrinsic value of the metal they were made of.
At first this was mostly silver, and this meant that the discovery of silver mines on Greek territory actually increased the quantity of money they could produce.

Had the Greek mining been on a larger scale, it could have caused problems similar to those faced by the Spanish centuries later, when so much gold from the New World was brought into their economy that it resulted in serious inflation.

One advantage of intrinsic value was that coins could be weighed to determine the amount of metal they contained, so that the only thing an issuing state had to guarantee was the purity of the metal to prevent accusations of fraud and cheating, which could cause fighting and unrest.

This was quite difficult to do, especially with coins made of gold, until Archimedes realised that different metals have different weight-volume ratios, and that by measuring the amount of displacement when coins were immersed in water, it was possible to establish whether gold was alloyed with silver.
E All ancient coins were made by hand using engraved metal moulds.
Many hundreds of coins were made, and as a result the moulds often cracked and new ones had to be engraved.
This explains the endless variety encountered in coins with the same designs because the moulds had to be remade repeatedly, by many different artisans.
One of the distinctive features of coins, in fact, is that they are the work of anonymous craftsmen, and yet each coin is an intimate reflection of the character of its city of origin.
It was the Greeks who realised that coins could have a double function, as a unit of value and as a symbol of the identity of the city that issued them.
The Greek view of life was deeply motivated by a spirit of competition, and coins, which circulated around the trading world, were a way of advertising the qualities of each particular city-state.

F Interestingly, Greek coins from the city of Athens, which was the home of the greatest sculptors of the classical period, seem to have been completely disconnected from the high sculptural tradition.
The beautiful features of the city’s patron, Athena (with her owl on the reverse of the coin), seem to have been repeated virtually unaltered for many years.
Perhaps this was because the Athenian currency had grown increasingly to be the international standard and, like the US dollar today, a uniform design implied integrity.

G One side of a coin was always occupied by the head of a divinity, so it was a relatively small step, at around 323 BC, for Greek coins to replace that head with the portrait of the reigning monarch, a tradition that has continued in monarchies to the present day.
Republics may have either symbolic heads – going back to the older tradition of divinities – or the features of a distinguished past head of state.

The Romans adopted the Greek practice of coin design and as a result, the features of many great Romans have survived and are known to modern generations, despite the fact that the art of portrait painting was completely lost for more than a millennium following the fall of the Roman Empire.

r3.title: Looking at daily life in ancient Rome

sentences.text: A If our ideas on Roman life are not to become lost in confusion, we must study it within a strictly defined time.
Nothing changes more rapidly than human customs.

Looking at our own more familiar world, apart from the great scientific discoveries of recent centuries which have turned it upside down—steam, electricity, railways, motor cars and aeroplanes, for example—it is clear that the elementary forms of everyday life have been subject to increasing change.

Potatoes, for example, were not introduced into Europe until the sixteenth century, coffee was first drunk there in the late sixteenth or early seventeenth, and the banana was used in desserts in Europe at the beginning of the twentieth.
The law of change was not less operative in antiquity.
It was a commonplace of Roman rhetoric to contrast the crude simplicity of the Republic (509BC–27BC) with the luxury and refinement of the imperial times which followed.
There is no common measure, whether of home, or house, or furniture, between ages which are so different.

B Since a choice of time must necessarily be made, this history will confine itself to studying the generation which was born about the middle of the first century AD, toward the end of the reign of Claudius (41–54AD) or the beginning of the reign of Nero (54–68AD), and which lived on into the reign of Trajan (98–117AD) or of Hadrian (117–138AD).
This generation saw the Roman Empire at its most powerful and prosperous.

It was witness to the last conquests of the Caesars: the conquest of Dacia, in modern-day eastern Europe, which brought vast mineral wealth into the Empire, and the conquest of Arabia, which helped to bring the riches of India and East Asia flooding into Rome.
In the material domain, this generation attained the pinnacle of ancient civilisation.

C By a fortunate coincidence—all the more fortunate in that Latin literature was soon to run nearly dry—this generation is the one whose records combine to offer us the most complete picture of Roman life that we possess.
We have a profusion of vivid and picturesque descriptions, precise and colourful, in such works as the Epigrams of Martial, the Satires of Juvenal and the Letters of Pliny.

In addition, the Forum of Trajan in Rome itself and the ruins of Herculaneum and Pompeii, the two prosperous resorts buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79AD, supply an immense fund of archaeological evidence.

Later excavations have also restored to us the ruins of the city of Ostia, which date in the main from the time when the Emperor Hadrian created this great commercial city as a realisation of his town planning ideas.
Fortune has favoured the historian of this time.
D It is not enough to focus our study of Roman life only on a fixed time.
It would lack foundation and consistency if we did not also focus it in space—in the country or in the town.

Even today when the facilities for communication bring something of the city into the smallest and most isolated country cottage, there remains a significant difference between rural existence and the excitement of city life: a much greater gulf separated the peasant from the townsman of antiquity.

So large was the inequality between them that, according to the historian Rostovtzeff, it pitted one against the other in a fierce and silent struggle which pierced the wall protecting the Roman privileged classes from the barbarian flood from the north.
When the barbarian forces began to invade Roman territory, the peasants decided to fight alongside them.
E The townsman, in fact, enjoyed all the goods and resources of the earth.

The peasant knew nothing but unending labour without profit, and was unable to enjoy the activities available in even the poorest of cities: the liveliness of the sports field, the warmth of the public baths and the magnificence of public spectacles.
In a work on the history of everyday life, we must give up any attempt to blend two such dissimilar pictures into one, and must choose between them.

The time which we have chosen to describe day by day is that of those Roman subjects who spent their time exclusively in the town, or rather in The City, Rome, which they regarded as the hub and centre of the universe, proud and wealthy ruler of a world which seemed at that time to have been pacified for ever.

F To perform our task well, we must first try to form an adequate picture of the surroundings in which our subjects lived, and by which their lives were coloured, freeing ourselves from any misconceptions concerning it.
We must seek to reconstruct the physical nature of the great city and the social milieu of the various classes of the hierarchy by which it was governed.
We must also investigate the moral background of thought and sentiment which can help explain both its strength and its weaknesses.

The way in which the Romans of Rome employed their time can only be studied satisfactorily after we have plotted out the main lines of the framework within which they lived and outside of which the routine of their daily life would be more or less unintelligible.

questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “...this generation is the one whose records combine to offer us the most complete picture of Roman life that we possess.”

works on this period are popular among the reading public.

questions.prompt: In comparing urban and rural life in the Roman Empire, the writer states that
questions.explanation: 题目问在比较罗马帝国的城乡生活时，作者指出了什么？原文D段提到在古代，农民与市民之间隔着“much greater gulf（更大的鸿沟）”，且这种不平等导致了激烈的斗争，说明两者几乎没有共同点，选 B (rural life and urban life had little in common)。
questions.tip: A（文盲）未提及；C（信息少）未提及；D（读者兴趣）未提及。重点在于强调巨大的“gulf（鸿沟）”和“inequality（不平等）”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph D) “...a much greater gulf separated the peasant from the townsman of antiquity.”

options.text: rural life and urban life had little in common.
little information is available concerning rural life.
most readers of history are more interested in city life.

groups.instructions:

questions.prompt: Rome's conquest of Arabia resulted in large‑scale immigration from the east into Rome.
questions.explanation: 题目说罗马征服阿拉伯导致了来自东方的大规模移民（large-scale immigration）进入罗马。原文B段只说征服阿拉伯帮助带来了“riches of India and East Asia flooding into Rome（印度和东亚的财富涌入罗马）”，是财富而非人口，文中未提及移民，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.tip: “Riches flooding in” 不等于 “Immigration”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...conquest of Arabia, which helped to bring the riches of India and East Asia flooding into Rome.”

questions.prompt: More can be learned about Roman life from the literature of the period studied in this book than from later Latin literature.
questions.explanation: 题目说从本书研究时期的文学中能学到的罗马生活比从**后期的拉丁文学（later Latin literature）**中更多。原文C段提到拉丁文学“was soon to run nearly dry（很快就要枯竭了）”，暗示后期文学资源贫乏，而该时期提供了最完整的画面，选 YES。
questions.tip: “Run nearly dry” 对应后期文学更少，支持了题目中的比较。
questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “...all the more fortunate in that Latin literature was soon to run nearly dry...”

questions.prompt: Discoveries at Herculaneum and Pompeii showed that certain beliefs about Roman life were wrong.
questions.explanation: 题目说赫库兰尼姆和庞贝的发现表明关于罗马生活的某些信仰是错误的（beliefs... were wrong）。原文C段只说它们提供了“immense fund of archaeological evidence（巨大的考古证据）”，并未提及是否纠正了错误的信仰，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.tip: 原文只提到了证据的丰富性，没提对错。
questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “...supply an immense fund of archaeological evidence.”

questions.prompt: Roman peasants provided assistance to the Empire when it was attacked.
questions.explanation: 题目说当帝国受到攻击时，罗马农民提供了帮助（provided assistance）。原文D段末尾说当野蛮人入侵时，农民决定“fight alongside them（与他们[野蛮人]并肩作战）”，即帮助入侵者而非帝国，选 NO。
questions.tip: “Fight alongside them” 中的 them 指代 “barbarian forces”，意味着背叛了帝国。
questions.quote: (Paragraph D) “When the barbarian forces began to invade Roman territory, the peasants decided to fight alongside them.”

questions.prompt: Rural inhabitants of the Roman Empire had a difficult life.
questions.explanation: 题目说罗马帝国的农村居民生活艰难（difficult life）。原文E段提到农民除了“unending labour without profit（无休止的劳动且没有利润）”外一无所知，这显然是艰难的生活，选 YES。
questions.tip: “Unending labour without profit” 对应 “difficult life”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph E) “The peasant knew nothing but unending labour without profit...”

questions.prompt: Entertainment facilities were limited to the city of Rome itself.
questions.explanation: 题目说娱乐设施**仅限于（limited to）**罗马城本身。原文E段提到农民甚至无法享受“available in even the poorest of cities（即使在最贫穷的城市也有的）”活动，说明娱乐设施在其他城市也有，不限于罗马，选 NO。
questions.tip: “Available in even the poorest of cities” 否定了 “Limited to the city of Rome”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph E) “...unable to enjoy the activities available in even the poorest of cities...”

The scope of the writer's study
It was important for the writer to limit several aspects of his {{37}} . He decided to focus on a limited {{38}} in Roman history, and to concentrate on the section of the population who were {{39}} . The writer was interested in the physical environment, the people that ruled the country and the {{40}} that contributed both to Rome's strength and to its weaknesses.

questions.explanation: 题目说限制他的____的几个方面很重要。原文F段开头提到为了“perform our task well... investigate（执行好我们的任务……调查）”，且全文都在界定研究（study）的范围。选项中 investigation（调查/研究）最符合语境，对应study/task。
questions.tip: 题目标题是 “The scope of the writer's study”，文中多处用 “study/investigate”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “we must study it...”; (Paragraph F) “To perform our task well... investigate...”

questions.explanation: 题目说他决定专注于罗马历史上一个有限的____。原文B段开头提到“Since a choice of time must necessarily be made... confine itself to studying the generation（既然必须做出时间的选择……限制于研究这一代人）”，对应有限的时期，选 H (period)。
questions.tip: “Time / generation” 对应 “period”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “Since a choice of time must necessarily be made...”

questions.explanation: 题目说专注于____的那部分人口。原文E段提到作者选择了那些“spent their time exclusively in the town（时间完全花在城镇里）”的罗马臣民，即市民，选 E (city-dwellers)。
questions.tip: “Spent time in town” 对应 “city-dwellers”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph E) “...Roman subjects who spent their time exclusively in the town...”

questions.explanation: 题目说作者对物理环境、统治者以及导致罗马强弱的____感兴趣。原文F段提到必须调查“moral background of thought and sentiment（思想和情感的道德背景）”，这可以解释其优势和劣势。道德背景、思想情感对应价值观，选 C (values)。
questions.tip: “Moral background of thought and sentiment” 概括为 “values”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “We must also investigate the moral background of thought and sentiment which can help explain both its strength and its weaknesses.”

questions.explanation: 工作人员询问全名，顾客逐个字母拼写了自己的姓氏：C-A-R-L-T-O-N。
questions.tip: 注意首字母大写，听到 "It's..." 后面的字母拼读要立刻记录。
questions.quote: Agent: First, could I have your full name please? Customer: Sure, it’s Emily Carlton, C-A-R-L-T-O-N.

questions.explanation: 顾客先报了一个号码（...41938），被工作人员确认时发现口误，立刻纠正为 41968。
questions.tip: 典型的“自我纠正”陷阱，必须听到 "Oh no, I misspoke" 后面的数字才是最终答案。
questions.quote: Customer: Oh, it’s 07-235 55 41938. Agent: Sorry, did you say 41938 at the end? Customer: Oh no, I misspoke. It’s 41968.

questions.explanation: 顾客说 5 月底结束工作，想在接下来的那个月（following month）旅行，即 June（六月）。
questions.tip: 需要进行简单的月份推算，不要听到 May 就填，要听后面的 "following month"。
questions.quote: Customer: Well, I’m planning to finish my work by the end of May, so I want to travel the following month. Agent: Great. So June then? Customer: Yes, that’s correct.

questions.explanation: 工作人员问有没有特定想去的地方，顾客明确说想住在 the coast（海岸）附近。
questions.tip: 注意介词搭配 "near the..."，答案直接填名词 coast 即可。
questions.quote: Agent: Do you have a specific area in mind? Customer: Yes, I’d love to stay near the coast.

questions.explanation: 顾客解释选择海岸的原因是想要欣赏 ocean（海洋） 上的日出日落美景（views）。
questions.tip: 题目问的是 Type of View（景观），必须填顾客想看的 ocean；不要被后面中介提到的 garden（花园）干扰，那是房产自带设施。
questions.quote: Agent: Why do you choose it? Customer: Well, I love the idea of enjoying beautiful views of both sunrise and sunset over the ocean.

questions.explanation: 顾客说虽然泳池（pool）和露台（patio）都不错，但她真正想要的是一个 barbecue area（烧烤区）。
questions.tip: 原文出现了 pool 和 patio 作为干扰项，注意转折词 "but if I’m honest, what I really want is..." 引导正确答案。
questions.quote: Agent: Would you like any additional features, like a pool or a patio...? Customer: Hmm, let me think. A pool sounds nice... A patio would be great... but if I’m honest, what I really want is a barbecue area.

questions.explanation: 顾客说虽然读过悬崖（cliffs）和森林（forests）的介绍，但真正让她着迷的是那里的 caves（洞穴）。
questions.tip: "cliffs and forests" 是干扰项，注意转折词 "but what really fascinates me is..." 才是重点。
questions.quote: Agent: Are you interested in exploring any natural attractions? Customer: Definitely. I’ve read about some amazing cliffs and forests, but what really fascinates me is the number of caves there.

questions.explanation: 顾客说她不怎么跑步（jogging）或骑行（cycling），但真的很喜欢打 golf（高尔夫）。
questions.tip: "jogging or cycling" 是否定信息（don't do much），正确答案在 "but I really enjoy..." 后面。
questions.quote: Agent: And what about sports? Customer: Hmm. I don’t do much jogging or cycling, but I really enjoy playing golf.

questions.explanation: 顾客说偶尔游泳（swimming），但真正想尝试的是 surfing（冲浪）。
questions.tip: 同样是转折逻辑，swimming 是干扰项，"what I really want to try is..." 引导答案。
questions.quote: Agent: How about water activities? Customer: Well, I like swimming occasionally, but what I really want to try is surfing.

questions.explanation: 顾客希望去体验当地文化，特别提到了有传统 Irish music（爱尔兰音乐）的酒吧。
questions.tip: 题目已经有了 "Evening Entertainment"，填 music 或者 Irish music 均可。
questions.quote: Agent: Lastly, for evening entertainment, do you have any preferences? Customer: I’d love to experience the local culture, maybe a pub with traditional Irish music.

6.s: what I really want is a barbecue area

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a hotel manager talking to some new staff.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, all of you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I do apologize for being a little late starting our meeting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of our guests has been taken ill.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Susie, who's our assistant manager, has driven him to the hospital, but she was in the middle of compiling our weekly report for head office, which is urgent, and I had to finish writing it for her.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, this is the first day of work at the Ocean Edge Hotel for all of you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me say something that might surprise you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You've all got a qualification in hospitality, and some of you have got very high grades.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But to me, what counts most is that you enjoy the contact with guests and really want to make a career in the hospitality industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll be getting some very valuable experience here, so make the most of it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A few words about the history of the Ocean Edge Hotel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There have been buildings on this site for about two hundred and fifty years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know that in the eighteenth century there was a bakery here when the town was very new.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The building was destroyed by fire in the early nineteenth century and houses were constructed on the site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These, in their turn, were demolished in the middle of the twentieth century and replaced by the hotel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think it's fair to say that this is a popular place to work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're always getting job applications from local people, even when we haven't any vacancies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And whereas in many hotels, staff tend to stay for a year or even less, here five is pretty standard.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And in fact, several of our staff have been here for ten years or more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You're the first people we've appointed in the last three years, and we only needed to do that because we're currently constructing twenty-five new bedrooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Depending on their location, hotels usually have mostly business guests or mostly tourists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We attract a large number of tourists who come to spend a few days beside the ocean.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We also have quite a lot of people who are here on business and perhaps stay for one or two nights.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What we've noticed recently, though, is that we're getting more and more regulars, people staying here for four nights every week because they have jobs in this locality but live somewhere else in the country, so they go home for the weekend.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, let me give you an idea of the layout of the hotel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All the bedrooms are along walkways in the gardens, and the main building, which we're in now, has most of the other rooms that guests use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Obviously, when they arrive, the first place they find themselves in is the reception area, where we're sitting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The desk is over on the right of the entrance, and the office is immediately behind it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a connecting door from the desk itself and another entrance from the corridor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A lot of local residents hire the function room for parties and other events.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is right at the front of the hotel, on the left of the reception area opposite the desk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This room is booked several evenings a week and most weekends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a major source of income.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Companies are very important customers for us, and a large number of local firms hold conferences here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To reach the main conference room, you go past the fountain as far as you can and the door is directly in front of you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The meeting room is often hired by companies and other local organizations for small gatherings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For this room, you turn into the corridor at the side of the reception desk, and you'll see the room facing you at the end of the corridor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our restaurant is open to the public as well as to hotel residents, and I'm pleased to say it has a very good reputation locally.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You turn left just before the fountain as though you're heading for the guests' rooms, and it's the large room on your right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, I should mention that there-

questions.prompt: Why has the manager arrived late at this meeting?
questions.explanation: 经理迟到是因为副经理 Susie 送客人去医院了，他不得不帮 Susie 写完那份紧急报告（finish writing it）。
questions.tip: 你可能听到“hospital”就想选 C，但送客人去医院的是 Susie，而不是经理本人。
questions.quote: Susie, who is our assistant manager, has driven him to the hospital. She was in the middle of compiling our weekly report for head office, which is urgent, and I had to finish writing it for her.

options.text: He had to complete a report.
He had to speak to head office.
He had to take a guest to hospital.

questions.prompt: What is the main thing the manager is looking for in his staff?
questions.explanation: 经理说对他而言最重要的是你享受与客人接触（enjoy the contact），这对应选项 B 的“热情（Enthusiasm）”。
questions.tip: 虽然录音提到了 qualifications（资格证书），但经理紧接着用了转折词 "but to me"，说明证书不是他最看重的。
questions.quote: you've all got a qualification in hospitality, and some of you have got very high grades, but to me, what counts most is that you enjoy the contact with guests and really want to make a career in the hospitality industry.

questions.prompt: When did the Ocean Edge Hotel first open?
questions.explanation: 录音明确提到原有的房屋在 20 世纪中期被拆除，并被这家酒店“取代（replaced）”，说明酒店是在 20 世纪开业的。
questions.tip: 要分清时间线：18 世纪是面包房，19 世纪是房子，只有 20 世纪才变成酒店。
questions.quote: These, in their turn, were demolished in the middle of the 20th century and replaced by the hotel.

questions.prompt: How long do staff generally remain at the hotel?
questions.explanation: 经理说在这家酒店，员工待“五年（five years）”是非常标准的（pretty standard），即普遍情况。
questions.tip: 你可能听到 ten years，但那是针对“几位（several）”老员工的特例，不是普遍现象。
questions.quote: And whereas in many hotels staff tend to stay for a year or even less, here five years is pretty standard. In fact, several of our staff have been here for ten years or more.

questions.prompt: Which group of guests is growing fastest?
questions.explanation: 录音说最近注意到越来越多（more and more）的回头客是在当地工作但家在外地、周末回家的人。
questions.tip: 你可能听到 tourists（游客）很多，但题目问的是 "growing fastest"（增长最快），对应录音中的 "more and more"。
questions.quote: What we’ve noticed recently though is that we’re getting more and more regulars—people staying here for four nights every week because they have jobs in this locality, but live somewhere else in the country, so they go home for the weekend.

options.text: people staying for one or two nights on business
people working locally who go home at weekends

questions.prompt: Office
questions.explanation: 录音说前台桌子在右边，而办公室就在桌子的“正后方（immediately behind it）”。
questions.tip: 注意方位介词 behind，不要被后面的 corridor（走廊）干扰，办公室是紧挨着前台桌子的。

questions.quote: You turn left just before the fountain, as though you're heading for the guest's rooms, and it’s the large room on your right.

transcript.text: Section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a discussion between a student called Helen and her tutor about an assignment that Helen is working on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-four on page five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Come in, Helen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How can I help you?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I'm doing research for the anthropology assignment, and I was hoping to check a few details.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You chose the topic of Pacific Island tapa cloth, didn't you?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What have you found out so far?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I was going to introduce my assignment by saying that the tapa cloth is a fabric made from bark, just the outer layer of the trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's particularly common in the Pacific Islands, but not exclusive to them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In fact, many other peoples around the world have made high-quality cloth from bark.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But what sets Pacific tapa apart is the incredible variety of roles it's played in this region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nice introduction, though I think you could be more specific regarding dates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so what about the raw materials used?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, tapa cloth is made from several species of tree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In the Pacific, the paper mulberry tree is most common, but it doesn't thrive in all conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In fact, it wasn't originally found in the islands, but was carried in their canoes by the first migrants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Tapa is also made from the breadfruit tree, which is convenient because its fruit is a staple food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The paper mulberry tree is only grown for tapa making, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, what about the Maori people here in New Zealand?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the Maori don't make tapa now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's right, and you need to account for it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know that when Maori migrated here from the other Pacific Islands, they were prepared to make tapa because they brought the paper mulberry tree with them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The thing was, after they'd been in New Zealand a bit, they found the flax plant, which is superior to tapa because it makes a stronger fabric.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the time Europeans arrived in the eighteenth century, Maori were making all their fabric from flax and had been for some time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So with the production process itself, first, the inner bark is beaten with wooden hammers to soften the fibers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then the different pieces are glued together using an adhesive paste made from the arrowroot tuber.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This is the only way to fabricate large pieces of cloth because bark strands are too fine to be woven together and stitching isn't strong enough.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-five to thirty on page six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-five to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So now you need details about different countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Where would you start?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I think Samoa is the obvious place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's famous for its very fine cloth called siapo, which is hand-painted with representations of the ancestors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Still today, at the most profound events in life, such as births, funerals, weddings, and the investiture of chiefs, Samoans wear siapo robes to add significance and meaning to the ceremony.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then I could talk about Tonga.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It seems to me that the great innovation in Tonga has been developing a simple, coarse cloth, which is quick and easy to make.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This is suitable for all sorts of everyday functions around the house like bed covers, mosquito nets, and curtains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good point.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, what about Cook Islands tapa?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the soil there is poor quality, so the breadfruit tree is often used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: One type of thick cloth called tikoru was wrapped around the poles and used to mark the entrances to places of worship, so it was highly regarded in local culture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You might mention Fiji as well, which is interesting because tapa was actually used as a currency there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fijians used to sail between the islands and exchange tapa for other commodities like canoes or pigs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I know that in Tahiti, the tapa cloth is different because the patterns are in color, which is considered more valuable than the usual brown patterns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You're right about the Tahitians using colored pigments, but they aren't more valuable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The colors are only a decoration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People enjoy wearing bright robes, especially for dancing and competitive games, and do it just for fun.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, I'll make a note of it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, the last place I was going to mention was Tikopia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Even today, it's commonplace to see people wearing clothes made of tapa cloth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In many of the other islands, the tapa only comes out on special occasions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But here, you see people working in the gardens wearing tapa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Sounds promising, Helen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll look forward to reading your assignment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Pacific tapa cloth is different from other types of tapa cloth because it is
questions.explanation: 录音明确提到，让太平洋地区的tapa布与众不同的是它在这一地区扮演着难以置信的多样化角色（incredible variety of roles），这完美对应了选项C的“更广泛的用途”。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到世界上其他民族也制作高质量的布就误想选B，但录音并没有说太平洋的布质量更好，也没说它是当今唯一在制作的布，所以果断排除A和B。
questions.quote: Well, I was going to introduce my assignment by saying that the tapa cloth is a fabric made from bark, just the outer layer of the trees. It's particularly common in the Pacific Islands, but not exclusive to them. In fact, many other peoples around the world have made high-quality cloth from bark. But what sets Pacific tapa apart is the incredible variety of roles it's played in this region.

options.text: put to a wider range of uses

questions.prompt: What does Helen say about the paper mulberry tree?
questions.explanation: 录音指出构树（paper mulberry tree）最初并不生长在这些岛屿上，而是被第一批移民带着过海的，这说明它并非太平洋地区的本土原产植物。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到“食物（food）”就想选A，或者听到“所有环境（all conditions）”就想选C，但录音说的是面包树结的果子是食物，且构树并不能在所有环境下茁壮生长。
questions.quote: In the Pacific, the paper mulberry tree is most common, but it doesn't thrive in all conditions. In fact, it wasn't originally found in the islands, but was carried in their canoes by the first migrants. Tapa is also made from the breadfruit tree, which is convenient because its fruit is a staple food. The paper mulberry tree is only grown for tapa making, though.

options.text: It is also a source of food
It is not native to the Pacific
It can grow in any environment

questions.prompt: Why did the Maori people of New Zealand stop making tapa?
questions.explanation: 毛利人停止制作tapa布，是因为他们后来发现了一种更优良的亚麻植物，用它做出来的布料要结实得多。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为听到“欧洲人（Europeans）”就脑补他们引进了其他面料而误选B，但录音明确说在欧洲人到来之前，毛利人就已经在使用亚麻做布了。
questions.quote: Now, what about the Maori people here in New Zealand? But the Maori don't make tapa now. That's right, and you need to account for it. We know that when Maori migrated here from the other Pacific Islands, they were prepared to make tapa because they brought the paper mulberry tree with them. The thing was, after they'd been in New Zealand a bit, they found the flax plant, which is superior to tapa because it makes a stronger fabric. By the time Europeans arrived in the eighteenth century, Maori were making all their fabric from flax and had been for some time.

options.text: They could not find the right trees in New Zealand
They were introduced to other fabrics by the Europeans
They found a better material for making fabric

questions.prompt: Large pieces of tapa are made from smaller pieces which are
questions.explanation: 录音中提到大块的布是用一种糊状黏合剂把不同的小块“粘（glued）”在一起的，完美替换了选项A的“stuck together”。
questions.tip: 录音里确实抛出了“编织（woven）”和“缝合（stitching）”这两个干扰词，但紧接着就否定了它们，说树皮太细不能编织，缝合也不够结实，千万别听到选项原词就急着选。
questions.quote: So with the production process itself, first the inner bark is beaten with wooden hammers to soften the fibers. Then the different pieces are glued together using an adhesive paste made from the arrowroot tuber. This is the only way to fabricate large pieces of cloth because bark strands are too fine to be woven together, and stitching isn't strong enough.

groups.instructions:
According to the speakers, what function has tapa cloth played in the following countries?
Write the correct letter, A, B, C or D, next to questions 25 - 30.
NB You may use any letter more than once.

questions.prompt: Samoa
questions.explanation: 萨摩亚人会在人生中最深远的事件（如出生、葬礼、婚礼）上穿这种布，为仪式增添非凡的意义，这对应了精神（spiritual）层面的诉求。
questions.tip: 不要因为听到“人生事件”就只当成是普通实用的习俗，要抓住“ceremony（仪式）”和“significance（意义）”背后代表的信仰与精神高度。
questions.quote: I think Samoa is the obvious place. It's famous for its very fine cloth called siapo, which is hand-painted with representations of the ancestors. Still today, at the most profound events in life, such as births, funerals, weddings, and the investiture of chiefs, Samoans wear siapo robes to add significance and meaning to the ceremony.

questions.prompt: Tonga
questions.explanation: 汤加的布做起来又快又简单，主要用于做床罩、蚊帐和窗帘等各种家庭日常功能，非常注重实际应用（practical）。
questions.tip: 这道题很直接，但如果你没有跟上录音从萨摩亚转换到汤加的节奏，可能就会错过这些代表日常实用的家具词汇。
questions.quote: Okay. Then I could talk about Tonga. It seems to me that the great innovation in Tonga has been developing a simple, coarse cloth which is quick and easy to make. This is suitable for all sorts of everyday functions around the house, like bed covers, mosquito nets, and curtains.

questions.prompt: Cook Islands
questions.explanation: 库克群岛的布被用来标记礼拜场所（places of worship）的入口，在当地文化中备受尊崇，同样属于宗教和精神（spiritual）层面的用途。
questions.tip: 你可能听到“poles（柱子）”或者“soil（土壤）”想选实用，但这里的核心词是“worship（礼拜）”，直接锁死了它的精神属性。
questions.quote: Good point. Now, what about Cook Islands tapa? Well, the soil there is poor quality, so the breadfruit tree is often used. One type of thick cloth called tikoru was wrapped around the poles and used to mark the entrances to places of worship, so it was highly regarded in local culture.

questions.prompt: Fiji
questions.explanation: 斐济人曾经把tapa布当成货币（currency）来使用，用来交换其他商品，这是最典型的商业（commercial）功能。
questions.tip: 听到“独木舟”或“猪”千万别脑补成休闲或者单纯的实用，前面的“货币（currency）”和“交换（exchange）”才是判定商业用途的题眼。
questions.quote: You might mention Fiji as well, which is interesting because tapa was actually used as a currency there. Fijians used to sail between the islands and exchange tapa for other commodities like canoes or pigs.

questions.prompt: Tahiti
questions.explanation: 塔希提人喜欢穿颜色鲜艳的长袍去跳舞和参加比赛，做这些完全是为了好玩（just for fun），直接对应休闲娱乐（recreational）。
questions.tip: 你可能在前面听到“valuable（有价值的）”想往商业上选，但随后老师纠正说那只是装饰，其真正的目的就是为了“fun（好玩）”。
questions.quote: I know that in Tahiti, the tapa cloth is different because the patterns are in color, which is considered more valuable than the usual brown patterns. You're right about the Tahitians using colored pigments, but they aren't more valuable. The colors are only a decoration. People enjoy wearing bright robes, especially for dancing and competitive games, and do it just for fun.

questions.prompt: Tikopia
questions.explanation: 在蒂科皮亚岛，你会看到人们穿着tapa布在花园里干活（working），说明它就是一种适合日常劳作的实用（practical）服装。
questions.tip: 录音前面用“特殊场合（special occasions）”做了对比，如果你没听出这是一个转折（But here...），就很容易被前面的信息误导。
questions.quote: Oh, I'll make a note of it. Well, the last place I was going to mention was Tikopia. Even today, it's commonplace to see people wearing clothes made of tapa cloth. In many of the other islands, the tapa only comes out on special occasions. But here, you see people working in the gardens wearing tapa.

21.q: different from other types of tapa cloth
put to a wider range of uses

22.q: It is not native to the Pacific
22.s: it wasn't originally found in the islands

23.s: they found the flax plant, which is superior to tapa

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about how the discovery of gold in the 1860s transformed New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, today we're focusing on New Zealand in the 1860s, and in particular, how the discovery of gold transformed the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At that time, gold had created great wealth in North America and Australia, and naturally, New Zealand was hoping for the same success.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People knew there was gold in New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some had been found in 1852, leading to a brief gold rush in which people had come from all parts of the world to see if they could dig up any for themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But now New Zealand needed experienced gold prospectors, people who knew where to look for the stuff to find it in other areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what the local government started doing in the late 1850s was promising a reward if these prospectors discovered gold anywhere in their province.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The man who eventually answered the call was an Australian miner called Gabriel Read, who came to Otago in May 1861.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The story goes that he was walking outside his tent at night when he saw gold shining like stars in a nearby river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It didn't take long for word of his find to spread, and soon thousands were coming to Otago to take part in the gold rush.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Who were these people?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the men that came were predominantly laborers and tradesmen, and often very young, although some were married and left their families back in the countries they came from.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But women did come too, to the towns that suddenly sprang up by the gold fields.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They made a living by starting up hotels, simple ones, of course, where new arrivals would often stay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And then there were businessmen who knew there was money to be made by setting up services like hardware stores that sold mining and camping equipment, and of course, banks where gold could be deposited.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, the businessmen often did better than the miners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So as I mentioned before, where there was a gold field, a town began to grow too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At first, the buildings were constructed in a temporary fashion, just made out of materials such as canvas and timber.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But later, once supplies started arriving, it was concrete, so the structures became more permanent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the fact was, the gold fields were often in very isolated areas, so life was very difficult for these people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The miners were often working at the bottom of deep gorges, so they had to cope with freezing temperatures and also sudden flooding when winter ice melted in the mountains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If this wasn't bad enough, the miners also had to deal with another problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because they had to carry everything with them, they had a very poor diet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They mostly drank tea, and the main thing they had to eat was flour, which they cooked in different ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's all that was available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, some miners were lucky, others not.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the gold that was found certainly brought many benefits to the Otago region, and also a couple of problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, the town of Dunedin was suddenly transformed into the biggest city in New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of the original residents complained about how the value of land was increasing and about the inadequate sanitation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can imagine how crowded it might have felt with the sudden influx of thousands of immigrants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But overall, the gold brought many positive changes to the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There was immense investment and growth in the shipping industry, just what the region needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another unexpected benefit of this wealth was that it provided the funds for the first university in the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As well as this, as the industry developed, there was a great demand for workers of all sorts, but most of all, there was a demand for experienced and skilled engineers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They often started their own companies, and many of these companies are still operating today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What we will discover next week is that these companies are still-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

• 1852: there was a brief gold rush.
• Late 1850s: local governments offered a {{31}} to experienced gold prospectors.
• May 1861: miner Gabriel Read found gold in a {{32}} .
Who took part in the gold rush?
• Mainly young single men or men leaving families at home.
• Women opened {{33}} for the miners.
• Businessmen offered services, e.g. hardware stores and {{34}} .
What were early mining towns like?
• At first, the buildings were made of canvas and timber, and later {{35}} .
What difficulties did miners face at the gold fields？
• The freezing temperatures and unexpected {{36}} .
• A poor diet of tea and {{37}} .
What benefits and problems did gold bring to the Otago region?
Growth of the Otago town of Dunedin led to complaints about:
• The increasing price of {{38}} .
• Problems with sanitation.
The gold also resulted in:
• Investment in shipping.

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到政府承诺如果能发现黄金就会给予 prospectors 一笔 reward。
questions.tip: 不要因为听到 promise 就去寻找类似词汇，注意听后文“reward”这个核心词。
questions.quote: So what the local government started doing in the late 1850s was promising a reward if these prospectors discovered gold anywhere in their province.

questions.explanation: 录音中提到 Gabriel Read 是在附近的河流里看到了像星星一样闪烁的黄金。
questions.tip: 注意不要漏听“in a nearby river”这个具体的发现地点。
questions.quote: The story goes that he was walking outside his tent at night when he saw gold shining like stars in a nearby river. It didn't take long for word of his fine to spread, and soon thousands were coming to Otago to take part in the gold rush.

questions.explanation: 录音中说女性来到矿区后通过开设简易的旅馆（hotels）来维持生计。
questions.tip: 注意听到“starting up hotels”时不要犹豫，这就是答案。
questions.quote: But women did come, too, to the towns that suddenly sprang up by the gold fields. They made a living by starting up hotels, simple ones, of course, where new arrivals would often stay.

questions.explanation: 录音中列举了商人提供的服务，其中明确提到了人们可以存金子的银行（banks）。
questions.tip: 不要只盯着前面的 hardware stores，注意听并列的另一个服务。
questions.quote: And then there were businessmen who knew there was money to be made by setting up services like hardware stores that sold mining and camping equipment. And of course, banks where gold could be deposited.

questions.explanation: 录音中对比了建筑材料的变化，起初是帆布和木材，后来随着供应充足，变成了混凝土（concrete）。
questions.tip: 注意区分建筑材料的演变过程，不要错填成起初的材料。
questions.quote: At first, the buildings were constructed in a temporary fashion, just made out of material such as canvas and timber. But later, once supply started arriving, it was concrete. So the structures became more permanent.

questions.explanation: 录音提到矿工在深谷工作时，除了要应对严寒，还要面对冰雪融化引发的突然洪水（flooding）。
questions.tip: 注意“unexpected”对应录音中的“sudden”，确认填入洪水这个灾害。
questions.quote: The miners were often working at the bottom of deep gorges, so they had to cope with freezing temperatures and also sudden flooding when winter ice melted in the mountains.

questions.explanation: 录音中说矿工饮食很差，除了喝茶，主要的食物就是面粉（flour）。
questions.tip: 注意题目中的“flower”是发音干扰项，录音说的是“flour”，千万别拼错了。
questions.quote: If this wasn't bad enough, the miners also had to deal with another problem, because they had to carry everything with them, they had a very poor diet. They mostly drank tea. And the main thing they had to eat was flour, which they cooked in different ways.

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到当地居民抱怨土地（land）价值上涨的问题。
questions.tip: 注意听 complaints 后面的具体内容，不要遗漏“value of land”中的核心词。
questions.quote: Some of the original residents complained about how the value of land was increasing and about the inadequate sanitation.

questions.explanation: 录音中提到黄金带来的意想不到的好处之一是资助了该国的第一所大学（university）。
questions.tip: 注意“funds for the first university”这个结构，不要把资金来源（funds）误当成建设的目标。
questions.quote: Another unexpected benefit of this wealth was that it provided the funds for the first university in the country.

questions.explanation: 录音中提到随着行业发展，对于各类工人需求很大，尤其是经验丰富的工程师
questions.tip: 注意听“in particular”之后的强调内容，这就是题目对应的核心答案。
questions.quote: As well as this, as the industry developed. There was a great demand for workers of all sorts, but most of all, there was a demand for experienced and skilled engineers.

33.s: where new arrivals would often stay

37.q: A poor diet of tea and
37.s: They mostly drank tea, and the main thing they had to eat was flour

39.s: the first university in the country

r1.title: How to find your way out of a food desert

sentences.text: Over the last few months, a survey has been carried out of over 200 greengrocers and convenience stores in Crown Heights, a neighborhood in Brooklyn, New York.

As researchers from the Brooklyn Food Association enter the details, colorful dots appear on their online map, which display the specific location of each of the food stores in a handful of central Brooklyn neighborhoods.
Clicking on a dot will show you the store’s name and whether it carries fresh fruit and vegetables, wholegrain bread, low-fat dairy and other healthy options.
The researchers plan eventually to survey the entire borough of Brooklyn.
‘We want to get to a more specific and detailed description of what that looks like,’ says Jeffrey Heehs, who leads the project.
He hopes it will help residents find fresh food in urban areas where the stores sell mostly packaged snacks or fast food, areas otherwise known as food deserts.
The aim of the project is also to assist government officials in assessing food availability, and in forming future policies about what kind of food should be sold and where.
In fact, the Brooklyn project represents the intersection of two growing trends: mapping fresh food markets in US cities, and private citizens creating online maps of local neighborhood features.

According to Michael Goodchild, a geographer at the University of California at Santa Barbara, citizen map makers may make maps because there is no good government map, or to record problems such as burned-out traffic lights.
According to recent studies, people at higher risk of chronic disease and who receive minimal incomes for the work they do frequently live in neighborhoods located in food deserts.
But how did these food deserts arise?
Linda Alwitt and Thomas Donley, marketing researchers at DePaul University in Chicago, found that supermarkets often can’t afford the amount of land required for their stores in cities.
City planning researcher Cliff Guy and colleagues at the University of Leeds in the UK found in 2004 that smaller urban groceries tend to close due to competition from suburban supermarkets.
As fresh food stores leave a neighborhood, residents find it harder to eat well and stay healthy.
Food deserts are linked with lower local health outcomes, and they may be a driving force in the health disparities between lower-income and affluent people in the US.
Until recently, the issue attracted little national attention, and received no ongoing funding for research.
Now, more US cities are becoming aware of their food landscapes.
Last year, the United States Department of Agriculture launched a map of where food stores are located in all the US counties.

Mari Gallagher, who runs a private consulting firm, says her researchers have mapped food stores and related them to health statistics for the cities of Detroit, Chicago, Cincinnati and Washington, DC.
These maps help cities identify where food deserts are and, occasionally, have documented that people living in food deserts have higher rates of diet-related diseases.
The Brooklyn project differs in that it’s run by a local core of five volunteers who have worked on the project for the past year, rather than trained, academic researchers.

To gather data, they simply go to individual stores with pre-printed surveys in hand, and once the storekeeper’s permission has been obtained, check off boxes on their list against the products for sale in the store.

Their approach to data collection and research has been made possible by technologies such as mapping software and GPS-related smart phones, Google Maps and OpenStreetMap, an open-source online map with a history of involvement in social issues.
Like Brooklyn Food Association volunteers, many citizen online map makers use maps to bring local problems to official attention, Goodchild says.

Heehs, the mapping project leader, says that after his group gathers more data, it will compare neighborhoods, come up with solutions to address local needs, and then present them to New York City officials.
Their website hasn’t caught them much local or official attention yet, however.
It was launched only recently, but its creators haven’t yet set up systems to see who’s looking at it.
Experts who visited the Brooklyn group’s site were optimistic but cautious.
‘This kind of detailed information could be very useful,’ says Michele Ver Ploeg, an economist for the Department of Agriculture.
To make the map more helpful to both residents and policy makers, she would like to see price data for healthy products, too.
Karen Ansel, a registered dietician and a spokesperson for the American Dietetic Association, found the site confusing to navigate.
‘That said, with this information in place the group has the tools to build a more user-friendly site that could be …
very helpful to consumers,’ she says.
‘The group also should ensure their map is available to those who don’t have internet access at home,’ she adds.

In fact, a significant proportion of Brooklyn residents don’t have internet access at home and 8 percent rely on dial-up service, instead of high-speed internet access, according to Gretchen Maneval, director of Brooklyn College’s Center for the Study of Brooklyn.
‘It’s still very much a work in progress,’ Heehs says of the online map.
They’ll start advertising it online and by email to other community groups, such as urban food garden associations, next month.
He also hopes warmer days in the spring will draw out fresh volunteers to spread awareness and to finish surveying, as they have about two-thirds of Brooklyn left to cover.

sentences.text: A An excellent definition was developed in the 1980s by Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland and used by the World Business Council for Sustainable Development: “Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.”
Nowadays, governments and companies need to account for the social consequences of their actions.
As a result, corporate social responsibility (CSR) has become a priority for business leaders around the world.
When a well-run business applies its vast resources and expertise to social problems that it understands and in which it has a stake, it can have a greater impact than any other organisation.

The notion of licence to operate derives from the fact that every company needs tacit or explicit permission from governments, communities, and numerous other stakeholders to justify CSR initiatives to improve a company’s image, strengthen its brand, enliven morale and even raise the value of its stock.
B To advance CSR, we must root it in a broad understanding of the interrelationship between a corporation and society.
Successful corporations need a healthy society.
Education, health care, and equal opportunity are essential to a productive workforce.
Safe products and working conditions not only attract customers but lower the internal costs of accidents.
Efficient utilisation of land, water, energy, and other natural resources makes business more productive.
Good government, the rule of law, and property rights are essential for efficiency and innovation.
Strong regulatory standards protect both consumers and competitive companies from exploitation.
Ultimately, a healthy society creates expanding demand for business, as more human needs are met and aspirations grow.
Any business that pursues its ends at the expense of the society in which it operates will find its success to be illusory and ultimately temporary.
At the same time, a healthy society needs successful companies.
No social programme can rival the business sector when it comes to creating the jobs, wealth, and innovation that improve standards of living and social conditions over time.
C A company’s impact on society also changes over time, as social standards evolve and science progresses.
Asbestos, now understood as a serious health risk, was thought to be safe in the early 1900s, given the scientific knowledge then available.
Evidence of its risks gradually mounted for more than 50 years before any company was held liable for the harms it can cause.
Many firms that failed to anticipate the consequences of this evolving body of research have been bankrupted by the results.
No longer can companies be content to monitor only the obvious social impacts of today.
Without a careful process for identifying evolving social effects of tomorrow, firms may risk their very survival.
D No business can solve all of society’s problems or bear the cost of doing so.
Instead, each company must select issues that intersect with its particular business.
Other social agendas are best left to those companies in other industries, NGOs, or government institutions that are better positioned to address them.

The essential test that should guide CSR is not whether a cause is worthy but whether it presents an opportunity to create shared value – that is, a meaningful benefit for society that is also valuable to the business.
Each company can identify the particular set of societal problems that it is best equipped to help resolve and from which it can gain the greatest competitive benefit.
E The best corporate citizenship initiatives involve far more than writing a cheque: they specify clear, measurable goals and track results over time.
A good example is General Electric’s programme to adopt underperforming public high schools near several of its major U.S. facilities.
The company contributes between $250,000 and $1 million over a five-year period to each school and makes in-kind donations as well.
GE managers and employees take an active role by working with school administrators to assess needs and mentor or tutor students.

In an independent study of ten schools in the programme between 1989 and 1999, nearly all showed significant improvement, while the graduation rate in four of the five worst-performing schools doubled from an average of 30 % to 60 %.
Effective corporate citizenship initiatives such as this one create goodwill and improve relations with local governments and other important constituencies.
What’s more, GE’s employees feel great pride in their participation.
Their effect is inherently limited, however.
No matter how beneficial the programme is, it remains incidental to the company’s business, and the direct effect on GE’s recruiting and retention is modest.
F Microsoft’s Working Connections partnership with the American Association of Community Colleges (AACC) is a good example of a shared-value opportunity arising from investments in context.
The shortage of information-technology workers is a significant constraint on Microsoft’s growth; currently, there are more than 450,000 unfilled IT positions in the United States alone.
Community colleges, with an enrolment of 11.6 million students, representing 45 % of all U.S. undergraduates, could be a major solution.

Microsoft recognises, however, that community colleges face special challenges: IT curricula are not standardised, technology used in classrooms is often outdated, and there are no systematic professional development programmes to keep faculty up to date.
Microsoft’s $50 million five-year initiative was aimed at all three problems.
In addition to contributing money and products, Microsoft sent employee volunteers to colleges to assess needs, contribute to curriculum development, and create faculty-development institutes.
Microsoft has achieved results that have benefited many communities while having a direct and potentially significant impact on the company.
G At the heart of any strategy is a unique value proposition: a set of needs a company can meet for its chosen customers that its competitors cannot.
The most strategic CSR occurs when a company adds a social dimension to its value proposition, making social impact integral to the overall strategy.
Consider Whole Foods Market, whose value proposition is to sell organic, natural, and healthy food products to customers who are passionate about food and the environment.
The company’s sourcing emphasises purchases from local farmers through each store’s procurement process.
Buyers screen out foods containing any of nearly 100 common ingredients that the company considers unhealthy or environmentally damaging.
The same standards apply to products made internally.
Whole Foods’ commitment to natural and environmentally friendly operating practices extends well beyond sourcing.
Stores are constructed using a minimum of virgin raw materials.

Recently, the company purchased renewable wind-energy credits equal to 100 % of its electricity use in all of its stores and facilities, the only Fortune 500 company to offset its electricity consumption entirely.
Spoiled produce and biodegradable waste are trucked to regional centres for composting.
Whole Foods’ vehicles are being converted to run on biofuels.
Even the cleaning products used in its stores are environmentally friendly.
And through its philanthropy, the company has created the Animal Compassion Foundation to develop more natural and humane ways of raising farm animals.
In short, nearly every aspect of the company’s value chain reinforces the social dimensions of its value proposition, distinguishing Whole Foods from its competitors.

groups.instructions: The text has seven paragraphs, A–G. Choose the correct heading for each paragraph and move it into the gap.

options.text: How CSR may help one business to expand
CSR in many aspects of a company’s business
A CSR initiative without a financial gain
Lack of action by the state on social issues
Drivers or pressures motivate companies to address CSR
The past illustrates businesses are responsible for future outcomes
Companies applying CSR should be selective
Reasons that business and society benefit each other

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.explanation: A段末尾提到的“经营许可（licence to operate）”以及来自政府、社区和其他利益相关者的许可，正是推动企业进行CSR的“驱动力或压力（Drivers or pressures）”。
questions.tip: 不要只看第一句的“定义”，段落重心在于解释为什么企业现在必须（priority, need to）关注CSR，即外部压力。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) The notion of licence to operate derives from the fact that every company needs tacit or explicit permission from governments, communities, and numerous other stakeholders...

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.explanation: B段详细论述了“成功的公司需要健康的社会（need a healthy society）”以及“健康的社会需要成功的公司（needs successful companies）”，体现了商业与社会的互惠互利。
questions.tip: 看到段落中列举了教育、医疗等细节时，不要迷失，要抓住段落首尾的逻辑框架——相互依存（interrelationship）。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) Successful corporations need a healthy society... At the same time, a healthy society needs successful companies.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C

questions.prompt: Paragraph F

sentences.text: A For the early practitioners of marketing in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the business of selling was simply a matter of continually finding new customers.
By contrast, marketing managers in the current era recognise the importance of gathering information about the market and about potential customers.

They recognise that if companies are to be profitable, customers must gain and retain their perceptions of value from the brands they buy over a long time frame, rather than from a single transaction.
This also means that customers must see value in returning continually to the stores where they shop, as well as to the service providers they deal with.
B Marketing practitioners and marketing scientists have never worked more closely than they currently do.

There are many reasons for this, including the fact that this is the information age where convergence in telecommunications, media and technology is causing old ways to be challenged, and new methods and tools to be tested.
Customer expectations have risen as new technologies allow new approaches.

For instance, the subscriber-TV music channel Channel [V] encourages its viewers to sign up for text messages and email alerts that tell them when their favourite artists and songs are about to be broadcast.

Competitive advantage lies in being able to recognise which customers can be given greater attention, not just because they demand it but because it makes commercial sense to provide high levels of product quality and service.
C Modern marketing information systems rely on information technology to enable marketing intelligence to be gathered and to store and analyse marketing research information.

While some of the information used is gathered by government bodies such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics and Statistics New Zealand, most of it is purposefully gathered by marketing organisations for client companies.

In the process, computer technology is used to manipulate the data and then to present the information in such a way that executives can readily identify any problems or issues, and quickly arrive at solutions.
D In order to produce superior value and satisfaction for customers, marketing managers need information at almost every turn.
They need information about customers – end-users and resellers – as well as competitors and governmental and other forces in the marketplace.
One marketing executive put it this way: 'To manage a business well is to manage its future; and to manage the future is to manage information.'
Increasingly, marketers are viewing information not just as an input for making better decisions but also as an important strategic asset and marketing tool.
As household incomes increase, choice widens and buyers become better at discriminating, so sellers need information about how buyers respond to different products and advertising campaigns.
E The supply of information has also increased greatly.

It has been suggested by the futurist and best-selling author John Naisbitt that the United States and, by observation, developed countries such as Australia, New Zealand and Singapore are moving from industrial to information-based economies.

These post-industrial economies earn 70–80% of their Gross Domestic Product from services, and have entered what some commentators have termed the 'Information Age' or the 'Information Technology Era'.
F One study found that with all the information now available through supermarket scanners, a packaged-goods product controller is bombarded with one million to one billion new numbers each week.
As Naisbitt points out: 'Running out of information is not a problem, but drowning in it is.'

Yet marketers frequently complain that they lack information of the right kind but have plenty of the wrong kind, or they claim that marketing information is so widely spread throughout the organisation that it takes great effort to locate even simple facts.

In addition, subordinates may withhold information they believe will reflect badly on their performance and important information often arrives too late to be useful, or on-time information is not accurate.
So marketing managers need better information.
Although marketing organisations have greater capacity to provide managers with information, they often do not use it well.
As a result, many marketing organisations are now studying their managers' information needs and designing information systems specifically to meet those needs.
G One solution is to use a Marketing Information System (MIS).
This consists of people, equipment and procedures which, when put together, are able to gather, analyse, evaluate and distribute needed, timely and accurate information to marketing decision-makers.
The MIS begins and ends with marketing managers.
First, it interacts with these managers to assess the information needs they have.
Next, it develops the needed information from internal records, marketing intelligence activities and the research process.
The analysis unit processes the data to make it more useful and, finally, the MIS distributes it to managers in the right form and at the right time to help them make better marketing decisions.
H However, the costs of obtaining, processing, storing and delivering information can mount quickly.
In some cases additional information will do little to change or improve a manager's decision, or the costs of the information will exceed the returns from the improved decision.

For example, if an organisation estimates that launching a new product without any further information will yield a profit of $500,000, then it would be foolish to spend $30,000 for additional information that would increase the profit to only $525,000.
By itself, information is valueless – its value comes from its use.

questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “This also means that customers must see value in returning continually to the stores where they shop...”

questions.tip: “Not be advisable” 对应 “foolish / costs... exceed the returns”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph H) “...then it would be foolish to spend $30,000 for additional information that would increase the profit to only $525,000.”

questions.explanation: 题目说从工业经济向信息经济的转变在新西兰比在澳大利亚发生得更快（more quickly）。原文E段只是将澳大利亚、新西兰和新加坡列为正在转型的发达国家（moving from industrial to information-based），并没有比较它们之间的速度快慢，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.quote: (Paragraph E) “...developed countries such as Australia, New Zealand and Singapore are moving from industrial to information-based economies.”

questions.prompt: Employees sometimes hide information that gives a poor impression of them.
questions.explanation: 题目说员工有时会**隐藏（hide）**给他们带来不良印象的信息。原文F段提到：“subordinates may withhold information they believe will reflect badly on their performance（下属可能会隐瞒他们认为会给表现带来负面影响的信息）”，选 YES。
questions.tip: “Hide” 对应 “withhold”，“Poor impression” 对应 “reflect badly”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “In addition, subordinates may withhold information they believe will reflect badly on their performance...”

questions.prompt: Managers frequently fail to make good use of the information they receive.
questions.explanation: 题目说经理们经常**未能（fail to）**利用好他们收到的信息。原文F段末尾提到：“they often do not use it well（他们经常没用好它）”，选 YES。
questions.tip: “Fail to make good use” 对应 “do not use it well”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “Although marketing organisations have greater capacity to provide managers with information, they often do not use it well.”

questions.prompt: Marketing information has to be used to be valuable.
questions.explanation: 题目说营销信息必须**被使用（be used）**才有价值。原文H段最后一句：“By itself, information is valueless – its value comes from its use（信息本身是无价值的——它的价值来自于它的使用）”，选 YES。
questions.tip: “Has to be used to be valuable” 对应 “value comes from its use”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph H) “By itself, information is valueless – its value comes from its use.”
