sentences.text: Although it's hard to imagine in this age of urban sprawl and automobiles, North America once belonged to huge, elephant-like mammoths, camels, bear-sized beavers and other giant beasts, collectively known as 'megafauna'.
Some 11,000 years ago, however, these large-bodied mammals—about 70 species in all—disappeared.
Their demise coincided roughly with the arrival of humans on the continent and dramatic climate change—factors that have inspired several theories about the die-off.
Yet despite decades of scientific investigation, the exact cause remains a mystery.
Now new findings offer support to one of these controversial hypotheses: that human hunting drove these huge megafauna species to extinction.
This belief resulted in the overkill model which emerged in the 1960s, when it was put forth by Paul S.
Martin of the University of Arizona.

Since then, critics have charged that no archaeological remains exist to support the idea that the first Americans hunted to the extent necessary to cause these extinctions, but at the annual meeting of the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology in Mexico City in October 1999, specialist John Alroy of the University of California at Santa Barbara argued that, in fact, hunting-driven extinction is not only plausible, it was unavoidable.
He has determined, using a computer simulation, that even a very modest amount of hunting would have wiped out these animals.

Assuming an initial human population of 100 people that grew no more than two per cent annually, Alroy determined that, if each band of, say, 50 people killed 15 to 20 large animals a year, humans could have eliminated the animal populations within 1,000 years.
Large mammals in particular would have been vulnerable to the pressure because they have longer gestation periods than smaller mammals and their young require extended care.
However, not everyone agrees with Alroy's assessment.
For one thing, the results depend on population-size estimates for the extinct animals—estimates that are not necessarily reliable.
But a more specific criticism comes from mammal expert Ross D.
E.

MacPhee of the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, who points out that the relevant archaeological record contains barely a dozen examples of stone points embedded in mammoth bones (and none, it should be noted, are known from other megafaunal remains)—hardly what one might expect if hunting drove these animals to extinction.

Furthermore, some of these species had a vast range, covering the whole continent—the Jefferson's ground sloth, for example, lived as far north as the Yukon and as far south as Mexico—which would have made hunting them in numbers sufficient to cause their extinction rather unlikely, he says.
MacPhee agrees that humans most likely brought about these extinctions (as well as others around the world that coincided with human arrival), but not directly.

Rather than through hunting, he suggests that people may have introduced a deadly disease, perhaps through their dogs or accompanying vermin, which then spread wildly among the native species because of their low resistance to the new introductions.
Repeated outbreaks of a deadly disease could thus quickly drive them to the point of no return.
So far, MacPhee does not have empirical evidence for this theory, and it will not be easy to come by: such disease would kill far too quickly to leave its signature on the bones themselves.
But he hopes that analyses of tissue and DNA from the most recent animal remains will eventually reveal the microbes responsible.
The third explanation for what brought on this North American extinction does not involve human beings.
Instead, its proponents blame the loss on the climate.
The Pleistocene epoch in question witnessed considerable climate instability, explains Russell W.
Graham of the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.
As a result, their regular habitats disappeared, and species that had once formed communities split apart.
For some animals, this brought opportunity.
For much of the megafauna, however, the increasingly uniform terrain left them with shrinking geographical ranges—a death sentence for large animals, which need correspondingly large ranges.
Although these creatures managed to maintain viable populations through most of the Pleistocene period, the final major climate fluctuation pushed them over the edge, Graham says.
For his part, Alroy is still convinced that human hunters were the destroyers of the giant animals.
The overkill model explains everything the disease and climate scenarios explain, he asserts, and in addition makes accurate predictions about which species would eventually become extinct.

The second theory suggests that humans introduced a {{17}} which wiped out the large mammals. However, so far this theory also lacks any {{18}} .
The final theory suggests that this period experienced significant {{19}} , which eventually led to the loss of habitat and to the division of the {{20}} that some of the large mammals had organized.

sentences.text: A Beneath the flat, impassive surface of Australia lie hidden mountains, valleys and gorges – ancient traps and channels for the deadly salt that is stealthily killing so much of the Australian landscape.
The war on salt is calling forth new weapons.

A suite of high technologies used by geologists to see underground and prospect for gold and minerals is now being used to pinpoint the presence of salt beneath the landscape, and to predict where it might move.

B Unless this process is clearly understood, warns Chief of Exploration and Mining Dr Neil Phillips, the hard work now underway of planning and tree-planting on the surface may be rendered ineffective: salt can still sneak past and erupt, following one of the ancient river channels formed millions of years ago.

The use of airborne electromagnetics to detect salt hidden beneath the landscape has been around for a decade, but the past two years have seen a major development in its precision and powers of detection.
Like the use of radar in battles, it has the potential to turn the tide of the struggle in favour of the defence by helping to pinpoint, plot and predict the movements of the foe.
C Angus Howell, who farms near Warrenbayne, in Southeast Australia, saw his first outbreak of salt in 1948.
Over the ensuing decades the patches spread and multiplied until they consumed almost 100 hectares.
By the late 1970s, Howell and his fellow farmers had decided it was time for action and established a government-funded “Landcare” group in a bid to save Australia's farmland.
But despite a mounting effort by scientists, farmers and governments, the “white death” continued to encroach.
Small successes were eclipsed by larger defeats and fresh outbreaks.
D “The technical solutions just aren't there yet for dealing with broadacre salinity, nor are the social and economic solutions.
How do you introduce the land-use changes that are needed when people still need to make a living?”
Howell asks.
There is no satisfactory solution yet.
Part of the problem has lain in salt's ability to mount ambushes, emerging somewhere new, sometimes unexpected and unexplained, beating plans to intercept it.
Only now are scientists starting to really disclose its secret subterranean stores and passages.
E The need for such knowledge is pressing.
Salt has already afflicted six million hectares of once-productive country.

At present rates, it is predicted that, by 2050, it will have sterilised a total of 17 million hectares and the waters of Australia's Murray River will regularly exceed the World Health Organisation's salt limits for drinking water.
Defeating this assault may take centuries, not decades.

F Electromagnetic surveys measure the electrical conductivity of soil to reveal the distribution of salt and the nature and variability of the regolith – the weathered rock and sediment that may lie above the bedrock.

Magnetic surveys measure small differences in the Earth's magnetic field, enabling scientists to probe the deep past and reconstruct ancient landscapes – rivers, basins and faults now buried under tens of metres of sediment.
These features help to reveal where groundwater is stored, dictate the direction of groundwater movement, and are critical to predicting or ruling out salinity hot-spots.
G Radiometric analysis is based on the detection of radiation emitted by elements contained in rocks and soils, allowing scientists to delineate landforms.
These factors influence the mobility of salt through the soil profile and help determine where to plant particular crop species to tackle the problem.
Using data from the Murray River region, scientists have revealed a network of ancient drainage systems that channelled water beneath the current land-surface.
These buried channels may carry salt and sometimes run at right angles to channels on the surface.
This implies that the salt could move underground in quite a different direction to what one would expect by looking at surface slope and drainage.

H One of the biggest advances in detection, says Professor Neil Phillips, has come with the integration of different techniques such as magnetics, electromagnetics and radiometrics, and ground mapping.
Individually, these technologies only gave clues to what was going on underground.
Together they provide a far more revealing picture of the subsurface landscape, several hundred metres deep.

Advanced airborne electromagnetics, in particular, enables scientists to take “slices” of the landscape at depths of five metres, ten metres, fifteen metres and so on, to determine where salt may be stored at depth.
This is building up a four-dimensional picture of the subsurface landscape, enabling researchers to understand movements of salt in length, breadth, depth and time.

From such technologies it will be possible to locate salt stores, identify how saline they are, look at man-made and natural changes to the landscape that may cause it to mobilise, and then predict where it will head to and over what time span.
This in turn will give the salt warriors time to model various ways of containing or curbing the menace, see what works best and then try it out on the ground.

questions.tip: 重点是“technologies... used for gold... now being used to pinpoint salt”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “A suite of high technologies used... for gold... is now being used to pinpoint the presence of salt...”

options.text: They can both be found in the same locations.
Both have been found to have an impact on the landscape.
The same techniques can be used to find both.
Neither is present in mountainous areas.

questions.prompt: What is the 'process' referred to in Section B?
questions.explanation: 题目问Section B中提到的“process”指的是什么？Section B开头说“Unless this process is clearly understood... salt can still sneak past and erupt, following one of the ancient river channels（除非这个过程被清楚理解……盐仍然可以潜行并爆发，沿着古河道……）”。这里的process指代的就是盐在地下潜行移动的过程，对应选项 B。
questions.tip: 上下文语境中，process指代的是导致“ineffective”的原因，即盐的隐秘活动。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...salt can still sneak past and erupt, following one of the ancient river channels...”

options.text: the killing of vegetation by salt
salt's ability to travel below ground
the ability of trees to decrease salt levels
the detection of salt by tracing other minerals

questions.prompt: According to Angus Howell, one problem in the fight against salinity is that

questions.quote: (Paragraph D) “How do you introduce the land-use changes... when people still need to make a living?”

farmers' requests for help have been ignored.
some possible measures may cause farmers to lose income.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the writer's view of the salinity problem in Australia?

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a woman asking a tourist representative about walks in the local area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions one to six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: G'day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What can I do for you?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'd like to do a day's walk in the area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Do you have any suggestions?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, the most popular day walks around here are the Village Walk, the McGrady Falls Trail, and the Coal Mine Walk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you just want a short walk, you can do the Village Walk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's just six kilometers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The McGrady Falls is twelve kilometers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Coal Mine Walk's a bit longer again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's thirteen point five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So are those two more difficult as well as longer?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, the Village Walk's classified as easy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: McGrady Falls has some climbing, which is a bit difficult, but overall it's moderate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the Coal Mine Walk's mostly on flat ground, and the paths are very good, so that's down as easy in spite of the length.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And, um, what's special about each of the walks?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I mean, what interesting things could I see?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, with the Village Walk, you start off in the village.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's really nice, and right in the middle there's the museum.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's very popular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It tells you a bit about the background to the region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then at the edge of the village, there's a park where you can have a rest and look at the view before you set off on the walk back.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's pretty impressive on a clear day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You get a fantastic view of the mountains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I wouldn't mind a chance to go swimming.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Can I do that at the McGrady Falls?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, just under the falls there's a great pool.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At this time of year it's quite chilly, but it's a good way of cooling off after the climb up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And if you're interested in flowers, it's a really good walk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll see lots of them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And the Coal Mine Walk?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Do you actually go down a mine?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: No, it's closed down now, but there are signs along the path telling you all about the mine's history.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's very popular with school parties, but it's not just aimed at children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's interesting for anyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it sounds good, but I think I'll go for the McGrady Falls Trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Is there anything else I should know about it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Things to take and so on?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, I should tell you there's an entrance fee for the trail, for maintenance, et cetera.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's, uh, ten dollars for adults, and you'll need a map because the walk's not guided, but they'll give you one when you pay your entry fee.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And I'd like to take a picnic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The best thing is to get that from the café at the beginning of the trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They'll pack it all up for you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Great.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And can you tell me how to get there?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The start of the trail is about nine kilometers from here, so it's best to get a bus.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Will the bus that stops at the front of the hotel take me there?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's the number two-six-eight bus.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It wouldn't take you there directly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's best if you walk down to the market, and then you can catch the number two-seven-nine there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It'll take you directly to the start of the trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And will it be easy to tell when to get off?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You need to ask the bus driver to stop at the lake.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mm-hmm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The start of the walk is just beyond that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And the trail is a round trip?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, so you can get the same bus back.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But mind that you're not too late.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The last bus leaves at five-thirty on weekdays and six-thirty on Saturdays and six o'clock on Sundays.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, thanks for all that information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: No problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Have a good walk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a radio program giving some advice about saving energy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you'll have some time to look at questions eleven to sixteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to sixteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, ladies and gentlemen, and thanks for tuning in to Action Radio, where we discuss current affairs and global issues.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My name is Jill, and today I'll be discussing the very relevant issue of the importance of saving water and how you can do this at home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most common type of wasted energy in the domestic environment is heat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, since the walls of my home are very well insulated, I am lucky to have no issue with this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've discovered, however, that I waste a lot of water as a result of my lifestyle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've researched ways to minimize my water usage online and have been pleasantly surprised to find that there are specialists in the area who can make some changes to my home immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The only downside is that the works are quite expensive and there are no means of getting financial assistance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, if any of you listeners are interested in reducing your energy usage, here are a couple of easy and positive changes you can make immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A lot of the magazines will recommend that you change your bulbs for those with energy-saving capabilities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, I have found that these make little difference to your electricity bills, and they also severely reduce the light levels in your home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, simply switch off all plug sockets and appliances to make an immediate saving on your electricity consumption.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If this doesn't make enough of a saving for you, you could later try turning down the thermostat as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite the discount that my energy provider gave me for prompt payment, my monthly bills were very expensive for the amount of energy that I was using, so I decided to change providers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Not only did I make a huge monthly saving, but the company also offered me other perks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I am now able to pay my monthly bills online, for example, which I am thrilled about because it means that I no longer have to drive to the bank.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once I have been a customer with them for a year, they will also offer a deduction for all of the energy-saving appliances I use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, many of you will have an electricity meter at home, so I'm sure you'll all understand the issues associated with them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They occupy a lot of space in your home and can be unsightly if you're unable to tuck them away in a cupboard.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mine is quite large as it measures both my gas and electricity, but I was luckily able to hide it in the coat cupboard where I can keep it hidden but also access it easily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Having said that, whenever I have to take a meter reading, I have to use a torch because the screen is too dark to read the numbers correctly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I have recently had an extension built on my house to make room for a new bathroom complete with a low-energy boiler so I can take long showers guilt-free.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The walls are nice and thick and well-insulated, but unfortunately, the window is a little drafty, so I'm going to have to invest in upgrading it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Speaking of renewable energy, I initially considered installing solar panels on the roof instead of using a low-energy boiler, which was the less expensive option.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the end, I decided that the panels would look too ugly on my house despite that they were technically easy to operate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, if you're a fan of taking long showers like I am, then switching from baths to showers will not help to reduce your water usage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, here are some small but effective changes you can make.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When making a cup of tea, for example, measure out the amount of water that you need before boiling it, and when brushing your teeth, use a cup of water instead of a running tap.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I tried filling up my washing machine before switching it on, but I found that the clothes were not thoroughly cleaned, so I would not recommend this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If your tap drips when it is turned off, then you should call a plumber to fix it as this can result in a lot of water being wasted.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before finishing today's show, I'd like to address two questions that we often get asked by listeners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We had some great feedback about our answer to last week's question on how to calculate the price involved in powering domestic appliances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's see how we do this week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of our most commonly asked questions this week was which device is the lowest energy option for watching films?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The simplest answer is that the smaller the screen, the lower the energy used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of our listeners wrote in with a question that made me chuckle, and the answer is yes, solar panels only work when the sun is out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, on a more serious note, a number of you wanted to know what the most efficient temperature is to set the thermostat to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The answer is that the closer you set it to room temperature, the lower the energy used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before I say goodbye until next week, I'll leave you with one last tip: Turn off the lights when you leave the room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A,B or C.

questions.prompt: What was Jill surprised to find?
questions.explanation: Jill 很惊喜地发现，该领域的专家可以**立即（immediately）**对她的家做出一些改变。
questions.tip: "Make some changes... immediately" 对应选项 A "work... could be done soon"。B 选项（隔热差）被否定，原文说 "walls... are very well insulated"；C 选项（财政援助）被否定，原文说 "no means of getting financial assistance"。
questions.quote: Jill: ...pleasantly surprised to find that there are specialists in the area who can make some changes to my home immediately.

options.text: Some work to reduce the water usage to her house could be done soon.

questions.prompt: What does Jill say every family can do straight away?
questions.explanation: Jill 建议大家可以简单地**关掉（switch off）**所有的插座和电器，以立即节省电力消耗。
questions.tip: "Switch off all... appliances" 对应选项 C。A 选项（节能灯泡）被她说成 "make little difference"；B 选项（调低恒温器）是如果你觉得省得不够多，**以后（later）**可以尝试的，不是 "straight away"。
questions.quote: Jill: Instead, simply switch off all plug sockets and appliances to make an immediate saving on your electricity consumption.

questions.prompt: What pleased Jill about the energy provider?
questions.explanation: Jill 对能够在**网上支付账单（pay my monthly bills online）**感到非常兴奋（thrilled）。
questions.tip: "Pay my monthly bills online" 对应选项 B。A 选项（及时付款折扣）是前一家供应商给的，且账单依然很贵；C 选项（节能设备折扣）是**一年后（Once I have been a customer... for a year）**才有的福利。
questions.quote: Jill: I am now able to pay my monthly bills online, for example, which I am thrilled about...

options.text: reduction in price for prompt payment
having a reduction in price of the energy-saving sources

questions.prompt: What difficulty does Jill have with the energy meters?
questions.explanation: 每当 Jill 读取电表时，她必须使用手电筒，因为屏幕太暗（too dark），无法正确读取数字。
questions.tip: "Screen is too dark to read the numbers" 对应选项 B。A 选项（难以接触）被否定，原文说 "access it easily"；C 选项（分不清气电）未提及，且原文说该表同时测量两者。
questions.quote: Jill: ...whenever I have to take a meter reading, I have to use a torch because the screen is too dark to read the numbers correctly.

options.text: The figures are hard to read accurately.
She can’t tell whether they’re for electricity or for gas.

questions.prompt: What kind of energy-saving method is Jill going to take next?
questions.explanation: Jill 提到窗户有点透风（drafty），所以她打算投资**升级（upgrading）**它（在雅思语境中，升级透风窗户通常指安装双层玻璃）。

transcript.text: Part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear two students, called Josh and Emily, discussing an assignment on applying scientific techniques to art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hi, Emily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hi, Josh.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Are you ready to work on the assignment?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, we need to describe how modern scientific techniques are being used in the field of art history.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And Dr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Abbott suggested that we choose some famous cases to illustrate the argument.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what have you found?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, there's a Canadian forensic scientist called Biro.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, I think I've heard of him.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What do you know about him?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, I'm a big fan of Jackson Pollock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The modern American artist?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Didn't he paint those really huge abstract paintings?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's him.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I guess it would be pretty easy to fake one of those paintings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: No way, Emily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I know a lot of people think that even a child could paint one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To the untrained eye, they might look simple, but they're incredibly intricate works of art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, sorry, but I really can't agree with you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Anyway, what did Biro find out?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, Biro worked on a case where a client asked him to prove that a painting she bought for only five dollars was an authentic Jackson Pollock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So was it a fake?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, Biro found evidence to show it was a genuine Pollock, but the art world didn't accept his findings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, one critic said that compared to other Pollocks, the white and yellow lines on the painting were too straight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Come on, Josh.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That doesn't seem that convincing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: No, you're right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is a bit weak.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the strongest argument was that there were no records of previous owners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For the painting to be authentic, you really should be able to trace the painting all the way back to the artist's studio.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, that's true, I suppose.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Did they consult with anyone else?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Mm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The International Foundation for Art Research got involved.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And what was their verdict?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, they saw a definite similarity in the painting techniques used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You mean the way Pollock dripped the oils on the canvas?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And they noted the dirt and paint marks on the back, which all of Pollock's paintings have.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why is that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He used to lie his canvases down on the ground when he painted them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the foundation were worried about the acrylic paint that was used on the painting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's quite common now, but it was very unusual back in Pollock's day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it was probably painted much later.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So whose side are we on in this argument?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: When it comes to art, you can see the art critic's point.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If their knowledge and expertise tells them that it definitely isn't a Pollock painting, shouldn't we believe them?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I mean, that is usually how it works in the art world, isn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Art historians have always judged paintings, but things are changing now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If we have modern scientific techniques like fingerprint analysis, why not use them?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Mm, that's true.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, maybe we need a combination.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think you're right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-five to thirty on page six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-five to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So did you find out anything else, Josh?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, have you ever heard of a painting called The Battle of Anghiari?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I have, actually.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's the lost masterpiece by Leonardo da Vinci, the famous Italian artist.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: What about it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, an Italian art analyst called Seracini thinks he knows where it is, and he's using scientific techniques to help locate it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, art historians knew where the painting was last seen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's right, in the Hall of the 500 in Florence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, Seracini had a theory that the painting was still there, and he set out to prove it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He used a lot of different technology, like radar and thermographic cameras.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But initially, he scanned every inch of the hall with a laser in order to make a really accurate three-D model of the building's design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Did he think the painting was hidden in the building somewhere?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, to find out what the hall looked like in Leonardo's time, he took pictures of it with a thermographic camera.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Couldn't he have used ultrasound to do that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Not really.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Different types of building materials produce different amounts of radiation, and you can really see those differences in a thermal image.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So brick would look different from wood or glass, for example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes Seracini worked out what the building looked like when it was first built and what renovations took place after that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He found that two large glass windows on the east wall had been removed and filled in by the time da Vinci started work on his painting, leaving a space big enough for it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But why hasn't the painting been seen for four hundred years?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Mm-hmm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To answer that question, Seracini needed to study that wall even more closely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Did he use the thermographic camera again?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This time he used another kind of technology, radar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And what did that show?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It showed there were in fact two walls there, an older one and a newer one built in front of it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So does Seracini believe that da Vinci's painting is on the concealed wall?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, on a stone wall concealed by the newer brick wall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what's the next stage in the investigation?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, he isn't allowed to remove any plaster or bricks, so he's now experimenting with a gamma ray camera to try and verify his theory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I think we've got some really strong examples there of how science can help art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Let's see if we can type up an outline.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a zoology lecturer talking about a group of primitive animals called gastropods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this module, we've been looking at various field survey methods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And now I'm going to give you a brief introduction to the specific organism that we'll be focusing on during our first field trip.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And that's the gastropod.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Gastropods are invertebrates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're organisms without a backbone, and they're more commonly known as snails, or if they haven't got a shell, slugs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, in terms of their evolution, gastropods go back a long way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As with other primitive animals, the minerals in their body fluids are very similar to the mineral composition of the sea, indicating that they began life there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And their fossilized remains have been found in rocks dating back at least five hundred million years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Looking at the physical features of the gastropods, well, they all have one muscular foot for swimming or walking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This foot is lubricated with mucus, and it's this that leaves the sticky trail that you see behind snails and slugs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also have an organ called a radula, which they use for feeding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, of course, the snails, though not the slugs, have a shell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In terms of their dimensions, snail shells in Britain range from the dwarf snail, which is one point five millimeters long, to the Roman snail, whose shell can be as big as fifty millimeters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As well as size variations, you get a lot of differences in the form of snail shells.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, the majority coil to the right, but there are a few that coil to the left.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then some shells, for instance, the plated snail, have regularly spaced ribs, while the prickly snail has prominent spines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are even a number of species with hair on their shells.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Colors on the shells also vary, as do patterns, so appearances are really varied.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, let's turn now to feeding habits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of you who are gardeners will know to your cost that some gastropods eat healthy plants, but you may not realize that these are the minority.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most species feed on rotting plants, or they eat fungi and algae.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some species eat dead animals, and there are some that are actually carnivorous.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They prey on live animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, the shield slug feeds on worms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And apart from their own feeding habits, I should point out that gastropods themselves have plenty of predators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Birds and frogs are the main ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But there's even an entire family of flies that have specialized in preying on gastropods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And of course, last but not least, I should mention human predators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was the Romans who probably first introduced edible snails into Britain during the first century, and they are still eaten today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, the collection of wild snails for cooking has caused local extinctions of one species, which is also under threat internationally.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So there are lots of predators, but to protect themselves, gastropods have often developed special defenses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll just give you one example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The glutinous snail avoids predators by folding its mantle over its shell and turning itself into a very slippery blob of jelly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, turning now to gastropod habitats, most species like dampness and shade.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In general, both very hot and very cold weather is bad for gastropods, but dry conditions are the least favorable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Snails cope with this by withdrawing into their shells, and often they form a thick film of mucus over the mouth of their shell to minimize loss of water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Habitats with a long, stable history tend to support the biggest range of gastropod species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for instance, long established forests usually support more species than newer plantations of trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And old natural meadowland is much better than land which has recently been farmed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And there is a small number of highly specialized species that live in unusual habitats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, the blind snail spends its whole life buried under the ground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

r1.title: The Rise And Fall Of Detective Stories

sentences.text: The detective story is normally said to have begun in the fertile brain of the great American writer Edgar Allan Poe (1809–49), especially in his stories featuring the detective C.
Auguste Dupin.
From 1859, Dupin had a counterpart in Monsieur Lecoq, created by the French author Emile Gaboriau.
Despite these American and French origins, it was to Britain that detective fiction migrated, where it took root and flourished, becoming a characteristically British genre.
This transition occurred because of one author and his great detective.

The most famous of all fictional detectives, Sherlock Holmes, was introduced by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in A Study in Scarlet, first published in 1887, and later became the subject of four novels and 56 short stories.
Nearly all of the Holmes stories are narrated by his friend Dr Watson.
Watson is constantly amazed and stupefied by Holmes’s genius, but despite years of working with him, Watson is never able to produce these brilliant insights himself.
Holmes is memorably eccentric, with a range of endearing and less endearing habits.
He is a brilliant private detective, categorically better than the plodding and mediocre officials of Scotland Yard, who constantly turn to him when they are baffled.

This in itself is pure fiction: in real life there were never any brilliant private detectives to whom Scotland Yard turned when they failed, and the Yard’s Criminal Investigation Department (CID) had a remarkable clear-up rate and was highly competent.

Most of the Holmes stories are set among the higher levels of 19th-century British society, a world inhabited by professional men, retired army officers and country gentlemen, as well as members of royalty and cabinet ministers.
Few take place among the working classes or the very poor, whereas in fact much crime was a product of the poverty and gangs in London’s underworld.
In the 20th century detective stories became increasingly popular.
Reading these stories was one of the characteristic aspects of the British middle classes in the ‘golden age’ of British detective fiction—the 1920s and 30s.
Their emphasis on rationality, the inevitable triumph of justice, and the existence of an unofficial super-detective tells us much about the society of the time.

So, too, do the stock characters and unstated prejudices in these works: country folk and domestic servants were almost always depicted as unintelligent, and women were often depicted in a simplistic, two-dimensional way, although a few female detective writers would present female characters in a more realistic manner.
Most of the well-known British authors of ‘golden age’ detective stories were drawn from the middle classes, like their audience.

Conan Doyle was a doctor who turned to writing fiction while he awaited his patients; Freeman Wills Crofts was a railway engineer in Northern Ireland; Gilbert Keith Chesterton and Anthony Berkeley were journalists; Cecil Street a career army officer.
Apart from a few superstars such as Agatha Christie, financial rewards for these interwar authors were rather meagre; a few hundred pounds per book—a useful income, but nothing princely.
US writers such as Rex Stout and Ellery Queen attempted to recreate the ‘golden age’ of British detective fiction.
For the most part their books were mere imitations of the British models, although they were seldom wholly successful.
But in the 1920s and 1930s, America also saw the rise of the ‘hard-boiled’ genre and its detective type: the tough private cop who appeared in the works of Dashiell Hammett and Raymond Chandler.

Apart from the violence that appeared throughout their works, Hammett’s and Chandler’s novels were often marked by a political agenda that sought to expose the inequality they saw at the heart of American life.

Britain had no real parallel either to their outlook on the world or (until much later) to their violence, but upheld the belief that the authorities should punish criminals regardless of their circumstances.
By around 1960, the classic British detective story was in serious decline.
It seemed that writers had simply run out of ingenious plots and puzzles for their detectives to solve.
The best-known crime fiction writers, such as P.
D.
James, eschewed private detectives for police inspectors, and straightforward puzzles for stories that were full of unexpected twists.
Today the detective story no longer exists in Britain, at least in its old form.
Arguably this mirrors the transformation of that society as a whole.

The belief that scientific developments were invariably beneficial possibly reached its height during the period when the classic detective story flourished, as did the belief in putting rationality at the heart of Britain’s education system.

And finally, the central belief that evil-doers would inevitably get their just deserts through the incorruptibility of the judicial system was replaced by a questioning of some of the procedures and decisions associated with that system.

r2.title: Nanotechnology the science of the very small

sentences.text: A Nanoscience and nanotechnology have become very fashionable in recent times.
Their prominence has inspired science fiction and raised a lot of hope and hype about the possibilities.
But what exactly is nanotechnology?
Most definitions agree that it is the manufacture of structures that measure up to 100 nanometres (nm).
The diameter of an atom is typically only two or three tenths of a nanometre while that of the human hair is around 1,000,000 nm.
Essentially, we are now able to build new structures from atoms and molecules as if we were using the bricks of a children’s construction toy.
B Most of the electronic consumer goods that we use today contain components that measure less than 100 nm.
The lasers in our CD and DVD players make use of the properties of semiconductor layers that are just a few atoms in thickness, so we clearly are in the nanotechnology age.
There are many other everyday items that we take for granted that have nanoparticles in them.
One of these is sunscreen.
In the 1990s there were safety issues with many of the sunscreen products available, so scientists at Oxford University set about finding a solution.
The product they developed uses nanoparticles of titanium dioxide that are doped with the element manganese.
This product is almost transparent to the eye when spread on the skin, and it is effective for much longer than many of the traditional preparations.
In this case, we see an example of nanotechnology providing a solution to an existing problem rather than opening up new product areas.
C The technique of using nanotechnology to adapt existing products can also be applied to garments, upholstery, paint, and plastics to improve their longevity.
Bearing this in mind, it is interesting to ask whether nanotechnology can help with some of the world’s major current issues.
The recent growth in climate change awareness calls a range of things into question.
Can we use energy more effectively?
Can we reduce the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
Can we use and purify water more effectively?
Can health care be improved?
Nanotechnology may very well provide the solutions.
There are few times in history when the application of science to improving the human condition has been so apparent.
D We are already making new types of solar cells and batteries by using our newfound ability to manipulate matter at the atomic and molecular scale.
If we can capture some of the huge quantities of energy that arrive at the Earth’s surface from the Sun, and store it effectively, we can reduce the need for fossil fuel-based power stations.
We are already using nanoparticles and nanoporous materials to capture harmful greenhouse gases, and we may possibly convert some of them back into fuel.
There are, however, many technical problems involved, and it will be another decade or so before some of these ideas are deployed.
E Water purification is increasingly challenging and many believe that water, which we take for granted, is going to become more valuable than oil.
Currently we do not use water efficiently, and many industrial and food processes leave contamination in water that is potentially toxic and difficult to remove.
Nanofiltration may provide the solution to these problems, and may also offer new routes to the desalination of brackish water and groundwater in some parts of the world.
F Food production and processing are becoming more important as the world’s population increases.
There are concerns that potentially harmful nano-products might enter the body via the gut.

Such concerns are being addressed, but it is even more important to ask questions about how nanotechnology might increase the nutritious yield of food and be adapted to help preserve and package food.

There is already evidence to show that it might also be helpful in the primary production of raw food materials, by way of better delivery of pesticides in the field and better extraction of protein and carbohydrates.
G Healthcare is an area where the application of nanotechnology is already exceeding the expectations of ten years ago.

It is happening across several fronts: better appreciation of what the ‘natural’ nanoparticles circulating in body fluid do; better methods of delivering drugs to the body via nanoparticles that target the diseased body part; improvements to the diagnostic imaging techniques of ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging and X-ray computerised tomography.

We are now at the threshold of a new subject, ‘theranostics’, whereby nanoparticles will first deliver the diagnostic information to the clinician and then, using the same particle, deliver a form of therapy.

H Nanotechnology is a life-changing technology, making the quality of life better, enabling us to make use of our resources more effectively, thereby protecting our environment, and creating new business opportunities.
There are many other examples in the world of ‘new materials’ that also make use of nanotechnology.
The possibilities may well be limitless.

sentences.text: A One widely held assumption about talent is that it is a reasonably fixed characteristic and it is therefore the job of organisations to identify, recruit and retain star performers.
This belief affects the way people are managed in the workplace.
Most recruitment decisions are influenced by the skills and abilities of an individual rather than their aptitude and attitude.
In terms of career development, organisations invest in staff who have been selected to reach higher-level positions, while ignoring front-line employees and people with less perceived potential.
This idea, that talent is a fixed, identifiable characteristic – and that those firms with the best people do the best – is both flawed and harmful to people and organisations.
There is a lot of evidence on this point, and it is useful to highlight some of the most pertinent arguments.
B First, are there stars?
There is no question that in every field, from sports to computer programming to music, there are people who are better than the rest.
As psychologist Dean Keith Simonton, who has spent his career studying greatness, has said, 'Wherever you look, the same story can be told.
Identify the ten per cent who have achieved the most in a certain endeavour.
Count the accomplishments they have to their credit.
Now tally the accomplishments of the remaining 90 per cent.
The first tally will equal or surpass the second.'

For instance, in music, 16 individuals have produced about 50 per cent of the Western classical music that is performed and recorded today, while another 235 composers have produced the remaining half.

The more interesting questions concern not the existence of stars, but whether these stars can be reliably identified and, even more importantly, whether their talent is a fixed aspect or can be altered.
C Identifying the best people is tricky.
Quality of performance changes over time and this is true whether we are talking about professors or footballers.
If performance naturally varies, any measurement taken at a single point in time, such as when someone is being hired, will have error and imprecision.
Therefore, single assessments of talent are likely to contain mistakes in their categorisation of people.
Also, judgements about performance and ability depend on the standards used to judge what is good and bad.
It should surprise no-one that for Bach to be considered a great musician, standards of music needed to change to embrace the qualities that his compositions possessed.
Similarly, artists and art come in and out of fashion, which means that what is genius depends not only on a person's ability, but on the prevailing standards used to evaluate output.
D Finally, it is difficult to evaluate people and their abilities with precision.
In the domain of work, research shows that the best predictors of job performance tend to be measures of intelligence.
But even these measures correlate only loosely with performance, which means that more than 80 per cent of the variation in performance is unexplained by even the best predictors.
Even in the sports arena, where one would think natural ability would be readily assessed because sports teams spend lots of resources on identifying talent, mistakes get made.

Basketball star Michael Jordan was dropped by his high school basketball coach and a number of top American football quarterbacks were available early in their careers because they were not considered good enough by various teams.
E This leads on to the next question: is talent born or made?

Should organisations assume that almost anyone can become a star performer, which implies that there ought to be a greater emphasis on motivation and development, or do they just figure out who is good and who isn't?

Here the evidence is clear: talent is at least as much 'created' as inherent and, more importantly, the customary way companies think about identifying talent almost certainly works to destroy a lot of untapped potential.
Decades of research by K.

Anders Ericsson, professor of psychology at Florida State University, show that exceptional performance doesn't happen without around ten years of nearly daily, deliberate practice for about four hours a day, by people who, with the assistance of their coaches, have access to the best techniques.
Once achieved, exceptional performance can't be maintained without relentless effort.
So performance may be as much a consequence of training as it is of innate ability, which suggests that performance can be altered by how people are managed.

F Further research by Stanford psychology professor Carol Dweck shows that the tendency of organisations to see performance results as an opportunity for an 'assessment' of ability, results in lower performance and poor motivation.

Dweck identified two sets of goals that people bring to a performance context: 'performance goals, where the purpose is to validate one's ability or avoid demonstrating a lack of ability, and learning goals, where the aim is to acquire new knowledge and skills'.
People with performance goals have been shown to be more prone to helpless behaviour and debilitation after a setback, while people with learning goals strive for higher performance.
The implications for managing people and talent are clear.
Seeing talent as fixed and job performance as a way of classifying people creates a self-fulfilling prophecy in which ability and intelligence do become fixed.
By contrast, seeing ability as malleable leads to a different sort of self-fulfilling prophecy, in which individuals and their employers may invest in ways to enhance performance.

groups.instructions:

Which paragraph contains the following information?

questions.prompt: disagreement with the view that employing talented people enables companies to achieve top performance
questions.explanation: 题目提到反对“雇佣有才华的人能让公司获得最佳表现”这一观点。原文A段末尾指出：“this idea, that talent is a fixed, identifiable characteristic – and that those firms with the best people do the best – is both flawed and harmful（那种认为'拥有最优秀人才的公司表现最好'的观点既有缺陷又有害）”，明确表达了反对/不同意（disagreement）。
questions.tip: “Disagreement with the view” 对应 “is both flawed and harmful”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “...and that those firms with the best people do the best – is both flawed and harmful...”

questions.prompt: a description of what individuals have to do on a regular basis to improve their performance
questions.explanation: 题目提到描述个人为了提升表现必须定期做的事情。原文E段中部提到K. Anders Ericsson的研究表明，卓越的表现离不开“around ten years of nearly daily, deliberate practice（大约十年的几乎每天的刻意练习）”，这是对定期行为（regular basis）的具体描述。
questions.tip: “What individuals have to do on a regular basis” 对应 “nearly daily, deliberate practice”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph E) “...exceptional performance doesn't happen without around ten years of nearly daily, deliberate practice...”

questions.prompt: the evidence that exceptional talent exists in all areas of life
questions.explanation: 题目提到卓越才华存在于生活各领域的证据。原文B段开头提到：“in every field, from sports to computer programming to music, there are people who are better than the rest（在每个领域，从体育到编程到音乐，都有比其他人更优秀的人）”，并引用Simonton的话作为佐证。
questions.tip: “All areas of life” 对应 “every field, from sports to...”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “There is no question that in every field... there are people who are better than the rest.”

questions.prompt: how different ways of evaluating achievement at work can cause different reactions in employees
questions.explanation: 题目提到工作中评估成就的不同方式如何引起员工的不同反应。原文F段详细区分了“performance goals（表现目标）”和“learning goals（学习目标）”两种评估框架，并指出前者导致无助行为（helpless behaviour），后者导致追求更高表现（strive for higher performance），即不同的反应。
questions.tip: “Different ways of evaluating” 对应 “performance goals vs learning goals”，“Different reactions” 对应 “prone to helpless behaviour vs strive for higher performance”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph F) “People with performance goals have been shown to be more prone to helpless behaviour... while people with learning goals strive for higher performance.”

questions.prompt: the belief that the time when an assessment is carried out affects its accuracy
questions.explanation: 题目提到认为评估进行的时间点会影响其准确性的信念。原文C段前半部分指出：“any measurement taken at a single point in time... will have error and imprecision（任何在单一时间点进行的测量……都会有误差和不精确）”，直接对应题干。
questions.tip: “Time when an assessment is carried out” 对应 “taken at a single point in time”，“Affects its accuracy” 对应 “have error and imprecision”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “...any measurement taken at a single point in time... will have error and imprecision.”

questions.prompt: the extent to which different talented individuals have contributed to their particular area of achievement
questions.explanation: 题目提到不同有才华的个人对其特定成就领域的贡献程度。原文B段通过音乐界的例子（16 individuals produced 50%... another 235 produced the remaining half）量化了不同人才的贡献程度（extent of contribution）。
questions.tip: “Extent to which... contributed” 对应具体的百分比数据（50 per cent）。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...16 individuals have produced about 50 per cent of the Western classical music...”

groups.instructions:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 33–35 on your answer sheet.

questions.explanation: 题目问有多少位西方古典作曲家被认定为特别有才华？原文B段提到“16 individuals have produced about 50 per cent（16个人创作了约50%的作品）”，这些就是指代那些“better than the rest”的卓越人才，填 16。
questions.tip: 题目问数量（How many），定位B段的数字统计。
questions.quote: (Paragraph B) “...16 individuals have produced about 50 per cent of the Western classical music...”

questions.explanation: 题目问哪位作曲家最初对其作品获得的认可很少？原文C段提到对于“Bach（巴赫）”被认为是伟大的音乐家，音乐标准需要改变（implies initially standards didn't fit him/recognition was low），填 Bach。
questions.tip: “Little recognition” 对应原文 “standards... needed to change to embrace the qualities”。意思是当时的标准不认可他，后来改了标准才认可。
questions.quote: (Paragraph C) “...for Bach to be considered a great musician, standards of music needed to change...”

questions.explanation: 题目问谁可以帮助每天练习的人提高表现？原文E段提到那些每天刻意练习的人是“with the assistance of their coaches（在教练的帮助下）”，填 coaches。
questions.tip: “Who can help” 对应 “with the assistance of”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph E) “...with the assistance of their coaches, have access to the best techniques.”

groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 36–40 on your answer sheet, write:

questions.prompt: Companies usually hire people on the basis of their character.
questions.explanation: 题目说公司通常根据**性格（character）**招聘人。原文A段明确说：“Most recruitment decisions are influenced by the skills and abilities... rather than their aptitude and attitude（大多数招聘决定受技能和能力影响，而不是天赋和态度/性格）”，题目与原文直接矛盾，选 FALSE。
questions.tip: “Skills and abilities” 是实际依据，而非题目说的 “character（对应 attitude）”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph A) “Most recruitment decisions are influenced by the skills and abilities... rather than their aptitude and attitude.”

questions.prompt: There are some areas of sport that have a greater proportion of talent than others.
questions.explanation: 题目说某些体育领域比其他领域拥有更高比例的天赋人才。原文B段只说“in every field... there are people who are better（在每个领域都有更优秀的人）”，并没有比较不同体育领域之间人才比例的高低，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.tip: 原文说了每个领域都有人才，但没做跨领域的比例比较。

questions.prompt: Measures of intelligence accurately predict performance at work.
questions.explanation: 题目说智力测量能**准确预测（accurately predict）**工作表现。原文D段指出智力测量是最好的预测指标，但即使这些测量也“correlate only loosely（仅有松散的相关性）”，且超过80%的变异是“unexplained（无法解释的）”，即并不准确，选 FALSE。
questions.tip: “Accurately” 与 “correlate only loosely / unexplained” 矛盾。
questions.quote: (Paragraph D) “But even these measures correlate only loosely with performance... more than 80 per cent... unexplained...”

questions.prompt: There are cases in which talented sportspeople have been overlooked.
questions.explanation: 题目说有一些**有天赋的运动员被忽视（overlooked）**的案例。原文D段列举了篮球明星迈克尔·乔丹（Michael Jordan）被高中教练放弃，以及顶级橄榄球四分卫早期被认为“not considered good enough（不够好）”，这些都是被忽视的例子，选 TRUE。
questions.tip: “Overlooked” 对应 “dropped / not considered good enough”。
questions.quote: (Paragraph D) “Basketball star Michael Jordan was dropped... and a number of top American football quarterbacks were... not considered good enough...”

questions.prompt: Newly formed organisations have the most highly motivated staff.
questions.explanation: 题目说**新成立的组织（newly formed organisations）**拥有积极性最高的员工。原文F段讨论了Dweck的两种目标对动机的影响，并未提及“新成立的组织”这一特定类型的公司及其员工动机水平，选 NOT GIVEN。
questions.tip: 原文讨论的是管理方式对动机的影响，与公司成立时间无关。

27.s: those firms with the best people

30.s: performance results as an opportunity for an 'assessment' of ability
more prone to helpless behaviour and debilitation after a setback, while people with learning goals strive for higher performance

31.s: taken at a single point in time

35.s: with the assistance of their coaches

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You're going to travel up the James Bay Road through a region that is very remote and uninhabited, yet very beautiful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The highway is six hundred and twenty kilometers long, but it's fully paved for the entire length.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Where the highway begins, there is a roadside office where you must stop.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The road is remote, so your registration is very important in case of an emergency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The office is staffed twenty-four hours per day, seven days per week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You have to sign in to go up the road and sign out upon your return.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For additional safety, at different places along the highway, telephones have been installed which connect with staff in the office.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember, there is no mobile service in this remote area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first work of your field trip is at the end of the James Bay Road in Radisson, a small town of only three hundred inhabitants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will stay at Radisson Research Center, which works with various universities and Hydro-Quebec to carry out studies into the ecology of the region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because the research center and the road exist as a result of the development of hydroelectricity complexes in northern Quebec, Hydro-Quebec is responsible for all emergency assistance and security of all visitors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Your first few days at the center will be spent attending lectures about their past research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will hear that they have paid particular attention to any disturbance to the land caused by insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After that, you will visit the various outpost stations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are three of them, and when you visit them, you'll be able to observe how data on the varying patterns of the climate is collected and published for scientific research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The second part of your field trip is back down the James Bay Road to the Trans-Taiga Road, which is the northernmost continuous unpaved road in eastern North America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, it's very uneven gravel, so drivers have to be very careful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hydro-Quebec cautions that driving over rocks on the rough road may cause severe damage to the car.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Any breakdown is serious as repairs are costly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Along the way, you will be stopping at two hydroelectric generating stations, each on a different river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There you will meet with engineers who will explain and demonstrate how rainfall has an impact on producing electric energy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Your last two days of the trip will be spent camping out in the taiga on the Canadian Shield.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Taiga is the Russian term for a type of forest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will find the region is relatively poor in the number of plant species, yet there is a great variety of wildlife that can be seen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll go to an area that once had forest fires, and you'll see how the landscape has naturally small rocky hills which confine the lower wetlands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These low-lying areas are called muskeg, which is made up of slowly decomposing plants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is not safe to walk on it as it has pools that are not easily seen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So keep to the rocks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The muskeg is home to many small birds and waterfowl.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, there are at least sixty varieties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So keep your waterproof digital cameras handy so you can take plenty of pictures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then we will have documentation of the existing waterfowl as some are becoming extinct.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Water is a problem in this area, so you'll also be collecting test tubes of water to bring back to our research lab for analysis.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It needs to be monitored for pollution that may be caused by rainfall coming from the south.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

r1.title: The extinction of the cave bear

sentences.text: Hervé Bocherens, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Tübingen, Germany, says his colleagues find his research methods a little 'crude'.

He dissolves 30,000-year-old animal bones in hydrochloric acid, which is strong enough to burn through metal, soaks the bone solution in lye, cooks it at about 200 degrees Fahrenheit and freeze-dries it, until what's left is a speck of powder weighing less than one one-hundredth of an ounce.
The method may be harsh, but the yield is precious – the biography of a cave bear as told through its chemical components.
Bocherens is at the forefront of research on the bear, a European species that died out 25,000 years ago.

People have been excavating cave bear remains for hundreds of years— in the Middle Ages, the massive skulls were attributed to dragons — but the past decade has seen a burst of discoveries about how the bears lived and why they became extinct.
An abundance of bones has been found from Spain to Romania in caves where the animals once hibernated.
'Caves are good places to preserve bones, and cave bears had the good sense to die there,' Bocherens says.
Along with mammoths, lions and woolly rhinos, cave bears (Ursus spelaeus) were once among Europe's most impressive creatures.
Males weighed up to 1,500 pounds, 50 per cent more than the largest modern grizzly bears.
Cave bears had wider heads than today's bears, and powerful shoulders and forelimbs.
But the relationship between humans and cave bears has been mysterious.
Were humans prey for the bears, or predators?
Were bears the object of worship or fear?
Initially cave bears shared the continent of Europe, more than 100,000 years ago, with Neanderthals, a primitive species of humans.
Modern humans arrived in Europe about 40,000 years ago, and were soon aware of the bears.
They painted images of the animals on cave walls, and carved their likeness in fragments of mammoth tusk.
The walls of France's Chauvet cave are painted with lions, hyenas and bears; dating back 32,000 years, these are perhaps the oldest paintings in the world.
The painters weren't the cave's only occupants: the floor is covered with 150 cave bear skeletons, and its soft clay still holds paw prints.
Most dramatically, a cave bear skull was perched on a stone slab in the center of one chamber, placed deliberately by some long-gone cave inhabitant.
'There's no way to tell if it was just curiosity that made someone put a skull on the rock, or if it had religious significance,' says Bocherens.
Another discovery, hundreds of miles to the east of Chauvet, would shed light on the relationship between cave bears and humans.
The Swabian Jura is a limestone plateau in southwestern Germany that is riddled with caves.
A steel gate guards the Hohle Fels cave from vandals and curiosity-seekers.
Floodlights in the cave's main chamber illuminate the ceiling, vaulted like a cathedral above 5,000 square feet of floor space.
Long ago, as shown by the bones and tools that archaeologists have found, cave bears and human beings sought shelter here from winter weather.
In 2000, University of Tübingen paleobiologist Susanne Münzel unearthed a bear vertebra with a tiny triangular piece of flint embedded in it.
The flint was likely a broken spear point, hard evidence of a successful bear hunt 29,000 years ago.
Münzel also found bear bones that had clearly been scraped by stone tools.
Evidence for bears being a food source for early humans was shown by cut marks on skulls and leg bones where the flesh had been cut away.
Many of the bones were from baby bears, perhaps caught while hibernating.
Cave bears disappeared not long after humans spread throughout Europe, and one theory is that hunting led to the bears' extinction.
Hervé Bocherens' test tubes may hold the clues.

Running his white powder through a mass spectrometer, he identifies different isotopes, or chemical forms, of elements such as carbon and nitrogen that reflect what the bears were eating and how quickly they grew.
After studying hundreds of bones from dozens of sites in Europe, Bocherens has found that cave bears ate mainly plants.
This would have made bears particularly vulnerable to the last Ice Age, which began around 30,000 years ago.
This Ice Age shortened or eliminated growing seasons, and altered the distributions of plant species across Europe.
Cave bears began to move from their old territories, according to a DNA analysis of teeth found near the Danube River.
The cave bear population there was relatively stable, with the same genetic patterns showing up generation after generation.
But about 28,000 years ago, newcomers with different DNA patterns arrived — a possible sign of hungry bears suddenly on the move.
But changes in the climate can't be solely to blame for the bears' extinction.

According to the latest study, by Erik Trinkaus and his colleagues at the Max Planck Institute, cave bear populations began a long, slow decline 50,000 years ago — well before the climate began to change.
The new study supports a different explanation for the cave bears' demise.
As Neanderthals, and then a growing population of modern humans moved into the caves of Europe, cave bears had fewer safe places to hibernate.
An acute housing shortage may have been the final blow for these magnificent beasts.

Research into the existence and disappearance of cave bears
Evidence from the Chauvet cave in France

Evidence from the Hohle Fels cave in the Swabian Jura, Germany
• Bones and tools found in the cave indicate it provided {{9}} for both bears and humans.
Susanne Münzel's findings
• A spear point in the vertebra of a bear indicates that a hunt had taken place.
• Marks on the bones of bears indicate the removal of flesh.
Hervé Bocherens' findings
• Isotopes from the bones indicate that {{10}} were the cave bears' preferred food.
Factors leading to the disappearance of the cave bear
• Climate change
– The Ice Age changed vegetation growth in {{11}}

• Human population expansion
– Competition from Neanderthals and modern humans for caves may have reduced opportunities for cave bears to {{13}} .
