r1.title: A Brief History Of Canned Food

sentences.text: In 1795, the French government had a problem: they faced the fact that it is not easy to win battles abroad when your soldiers are hungry and malnourished.
That year they established a 12,000-franc prize for whoever could find a way to preserve food – from milk and meat to fruits and vegetables.
French chef Nicolas Appert took more than a decade to develop a process that involved cooking food in glass jars and then using seals made of cork to make them airtight.
In 1810, he published a book whose title translates as “The art of preserving all animal and vegetable substances for several years”, and collected his prize money.
Appert’s achievement didn’t escape the notice of British merchant and inventor Peter Durand, who applied for a British patent later that year.
Durand used techniques similar to Appert’s, although he adapted the model to include the use of tin vessels as well as glass jars.
Following these discoveries, canned food was initially produced for soldiers and explorers.
But even after people became aware of the existence of bacteria in the late 19th century, canning companies couldn’t work out exactly why some of their tins turned bad.
And even into the 20th century, newspapers were full of accounts not only of food poisoning but also of cases of the fatal disease botulism resulting from people eating canned food.
For that reason, many continued to look upon canned food with suspicion and fear.
The US food manufacturer, The Heinz Company, realized bad cans were bad for business.
From the 1890s to 1920s, the company insisted on weekly manicures for its canning-factory workers to ensure that any bacteria beneath employees’ fingernails stayed out of the food.
Heinz employees were required to shower and change their clothing regularly.
In an era when food-factory hygiene was not universally adopted, what might have been considered a nuisance by workers was at least good for consumers.
Some canning companies killed bacteria with chemical additives such as sodium benzoate, which is still used today in canned food, and formaldehydes, which are now known to cause cancer.
Some of the larger canning companies, such as Heinz, Libby, and Campbell’s, installed expensive steam-retort technology developed in the 1870s.
Steam retorts worked like steam engines, using pressure to raise canning temperatures high enough to make food safe.
Yet some batches of cans, even when made with this advanced technique, would explode after months on the shelf, while the contents of other cans might mysteriously sour.
Smaller canning manufacturers relied on the open kettle method* and they had even less consistent results.
US canning companies eventually banded together to discover the scientific principles affecting the canning process.
In 1913, they launched the Research Laboratory of the National Canners Association in order to look into the elusive bacteriology responsible for all manner of spoiled canned food.
The research done by the laboratory in the decades that followed helped resolve the problem of spoiled food and led to improved flavor, color, nutritional value, and texture.

Before this time, canning companies had discovered through trial and error that the best way to avoid bad cans was to cook food at high temperatures for long periods, an approach that sacrificed flavor.
“Food safety and palatability were often at cross-purposes,” remarks food historian Gabriella Petrick.
For string beans, for instance, long cooking times in hot water leach out the green color, creating an unattractive grayish-toned bean.
The addition of salt was one technique employed in the early 20th century to prevent this happening, thereby maintaining the visual appeal of the product and restoring a certain amount of taste.
One of the major canning innovations of the 20th century was the development of aseptic processing.

This technique, which involves sterilizing the container separately from the food, was invented in Switzerland in the 1960s for processing milk, but is now used widely for canned tomatoes and many juices.

Small volumes of food are heated to a precise temperature and for a precise time in order to avoid overcooking and preserve color and nutrients, explains food scientist Philip Nelson, who won the 2007 World Food Prize in recognition of his research on making aseptic processing workable on a large industrial scale.
Today, despite all the modern alternatives, Appert’s technology still reigns supreme for long-term storage.
More than two centuries on, the simple can is still the best solution for the safe and effective preservation of a wide range of foodstuffs worldwide.
*open kettle method: food is cooked in a covered container and then poured while hot into sterile jars.

sentences.text: A The development of robots that interact socially with people and assist them in everyday life has been an elusive goal of modern science.
Despite impressive advances in the mechanical aspects of this problem, producing robots that bond and socialize with people for sustained periods of time has proven difficult.

The most successful robots so far have been storytellers, but they have only been able to maintain human interest for a limited time and typically rely on the robot telling stories that change over time.
In practice, commercially available robots seldom cross the 10-hour barrier (i.e., individual users tend to spend less than a combined total of 10 hours with the robots before losing interest).
This observation is in sharp contrast to the long-term interactions and bonding that commonly develop between humans and their pets.

B In a recent study, researchers from the Institute for Neural Computation in California introduced a state-of-the-art social robot into a classroom of 18-to-24-month-olds for five months as a way of studying human/robot interactions.
The researchers, including Fumihide Tanaka and Javier R.
Movellan, introduced a toddler-sized humanoid robot into a classroom at a childhood education center.
One of the QRIO series of robots, the 58 cm machine, was originally developed by Sony.
‘Children of toddler age were chosen because they have no preconceived notions of robots,’ according to Tanaka.
One of the goals of the study was to establish whether it was possible for social robots to maintain the interest of children beyond the 10-hour barrier.
C The researchers sent instructions to the robot about every two minutes to do things like giggle, dance, sit down, fall down, or walk in a certain direction.
The 45 sessions were videotaped, and interactions between toddlers and the robot were later analyzed.
The results showed that the quality of those interactions improved steadily over 27 sessions.
The interactions deteriorated quickly over the next 15 sessions, when the robot was ordered to behave in a more limited, predictable manner.
Finally, the human/robot relations improved in the last three sessions, after the robot had been instructed to display its full range of behaviors.
D ‘Initially, the children treated the robot very differently from the way they treated each other,’ Tanaka said.
‘Early in the study, some children cried when QRIO fell.
But a month into the study, the toddlers helped QRIO stand up by pushing its back or pulling its hands.’
‘The most important aspect of interaction was touch,’ Tanaka said.
‘At first, the toddlers would touch the robot on its face, but later on they would touch it only on its hands and arms, like they would with other humans.
Another robot-like toy named Robby, which resembled QRIO but did not move, was used as a control in the study.
While hugging of QRIO increased, hugging of Robby decreased throughout the study.
Furthermore, when QRIO laid down on the floor, caretaking behaviors were frequently observed toward QRIO but seldom toward Robby.’

E The study concluded that after 45 days of immersion in a childcare center over a period of five months, long-term bonding and socialization occurred between toddlers and a state-of-the-art social robot.
Overall, the interaction between children and the robot improved over time and the children progressively treated it more as a peer than a plaything.
‘To my knowledge, this is the first long-term study of this sort,’ said Ronald Arkin, a roboticist at the Georgia Institute of Technology in the US.
F Tanaka and Movellan are now developing autonomous robots for the toddler classroom.
‘It could have great potential in educational settings, assisting teachers and enriching the classroom environment,’ Tanaka said.
The researchers hope that more advanced versions of robots like QRIO could become personalized tutors to assist teachers in classrooms.
A robotic tutor could react on the spot to social cues and approximate social skills like facial expression and eye gaze, they said.
‘It is becoming clear that, to achieve this goal, we are going to endow machines with something similar to emotion, not just traditional forms of intelligence,’ said Movellan.

G Associate Professor David Powers, an expert in artificial intelligence and cognitive science at Flinders University in South Australia, commented, ‘In this study, it is clearly demonstrated that a limited range of robot behaviors, however impressive, is nowhere near as important to human/robot interaction as being able to make appropriate responses from a broad repertoire of behaviors.’
Ronald Arkin was not surprised by the affection demonstrated by the toddlers toward the robot.
‘Humans have a tremendous propensity to bond with artifacts, whether it be a car, a doll, or a robot,’ he said.
But he also cautioned that researchers do not yet understand the consequences of increased human/robot interaction.
‘Studying how robots and humans work together can give us insight into whether this is a good thing or a bad thing for society,’ Arkin said.
‘We need to find out what the consequences are of introducing a robot into a cadre of children.
How will that enhance, or potentially interfere with, their social development?
Do we really understand the long-term impact of having a robot as a childhood friend?’

r3.title: A New Voyage Round The World

sentences.text: Part travelogue, part historical record of the Caribbean pirates, part scientific treatise, A New Voyage Round the World was William Dampier’s account of his twelve-year series of journeys around the globe from 1679 to 1691.

The wealth and novelty of Dampier’s descriptions, combined with the highly counts of his comrades’, escapades, proved so popular with a public hungry for tales of discovery and adventure that A New Voyage went into its third reprint within a year of publication.
So groundbreaking was Dampier’s account that the writers Swift and Defoe were inspired to create two of the most famous books in the English language, Gulliver’s Travels and Robinson Crusoe.
Dampier’s commentators have portrayed him as an unusual, not to say peculiar, man.
Notwithstanding his undoubted qualities as an observer, he has been variously characterised as aloof, arrogant, hot-tempered and a weak leader of men.
When he arrived on the western coast of Australia, he promptly elected to leave and head north out of dislike for the cold of more southerly latitudes.

This physical sensitivity has often been seized on by his detractors, who point out that, as a result, Dampier missed out on becoming the name forever associated with the European discovery of Australia, that honour instead going to Captain James Cook some 80 years later.
Yet it should be remembered that he was able to endure a never-ending plague of discomforts and ailments in the tropics.
And once, wrecked off Ascension Island in the South Atlantic Ocean, he managed with his crew to survive for five weeks without help, living entirely on turtles and goats.
What of his early life, then?
Dampier was born in 1651 in Somerset, England, the son of a tenant farmer, George, and his wife Ann.
His birthplace, Hymerford House, stands to this day.
His parents died before he reached seniority and his guardians apprenticed the young William to a ship’s captain, the boy having shown very early inclinations to see the world’.
There was nothing in his childhood to set Dampier apart from the numerous other young boys who were sent to sea at this time.
Having made brief passages to France and Newfoundland, he completed a more extended voyage to Java, where he began to learn the art of navigation.

Returning briefly to Somerset, a neighbour offered Dampier a position overseeing his plantation in Jamaica, which he took up for a time, but he soon returned to sea on a trading voyage among the Caribbean islands.
From the viewpoint of posterity, the most significant aspect of this time was that, as plantation manager, Dampier first started to keep a journal.
Although Dampier wrote several books, A New Voyage Round the World is the most important and it is worth considering just why this text met with such success.
Certainly, the book would not have done so well purely on the merits of Dampier’s findings regarding meteorology and natural history, even though they broke new ground at the time.
What appealed more to book buyers of this era was his narrative of life among the pirates of the Caribbean islands, whom he joined for several years after leaving Jamaica.
These tales of adventure among rogues and villains who had no regard for the law sparked widespread interest among his countrymen back home.
More important even than this, however, it is the superb nature of Dampier’s prose, and his ability to communicate so vividly that raised the book above the common lot.
Dampier himself admits in the book’s preface that he received help with the writing of the book, and other evidence exists to suggest that he was assisted by an unknown source.
But whatever outside assistance he may have had, the book still has certain problems.

In particular, his observations about nature are sometimes roughly dropped into the narrative at very odd junctures and these asides can sometimes interrupt the flow of the story Dampier himself kept his observations about nature entirely separate from the main body of his travels, and we should therefore hold James Knapton responsible, as he was in charge of checking and revising Dampier’s text, and his publishing company brought the finished book to a wider audience.

Dampier’s life has been chronicled in full by numerous biographers, and I refer the reader in particular to Clennell Wilkinson’s excellent (and sadly out-of- print) 1929 biography, as well as the recent portrait by Anton Gill.

In short, despite wide acclaim for his writing, Dampier was not blessed in the art of wealth accumulation Travelling with the pirates, while providing subsistence and adventure, never netted him the treasure chest that a more astute financial operative might have acquired.
He died in 1715, aged sixty-three, in Colerman Street, London.
We have then a man of myriad and colourful parts, and perhaps not always the easiest of sailors to get along with because of his arrogance and hot temper.
But to dwell on these aspects today is to miss the point: it is A New Voyage Round the World that should provide the most illuminating and entertaining of Dampier’s legacies.
Above all, the text is studded with some wonderfully colourful expressions, and readers will enjoy some of the finest descriptions of storms in the English language, and the liberal wit throughout.

questions.quote: Dampier himself kept his observations about nature entirely separate from the main body of his travels, and we should therefore hold James Knapton responsible, as he was in charge of checking and revising Dampier’s text, and his publishing company brought the finished book to a wider audience.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's well signposted, so you can see exactly where to go, and it's an easy route with no steep hills.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's thirty-five kilometers long from Amsden to Lowington and consists partly of cycle paths and partly roads.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me outline the route briefly starting at Amsden Railway Station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first part is a cycle path running eastwards, roughly parallel to the rail track.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Almost immediately, the railway curves away and goes around the southern side of a little lake.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the cycle path takes the northern route around the lake.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Keep your eyes open for the swans that nest there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The path then joins the road, and the next landmark is a group of massive rocks which tower over the countryside.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will see them to the east of the road just before the road goes under the railway.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're very impressive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Soon, you'll come to a fork in the road where you're going to leave the road and head off toward the river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But if you want to make a detour to Colleen Nature Reserve, go straight on instead of leaving the road here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Continuing along the cycle path, you'll reach the River Cleave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The cycle path follows the river southwards.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After a bit, you'll see the Ashington China Factory, which closed in nineteen sixty-two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When you get there, there's a bridge over the river, and you carry on with Langton Forest to the south and farmland to the north.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The route ends at Langton Village, where you'll find a railway station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So you can either catch the train here or cycle back to Amsden.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the program, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: One point to remember when you're cycling on the Amsden Way is that you should keep your eyes open for sheep which occasionally stray onto the cycle path from adjoining fields.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So be careful to avoid accidents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The path is well constructed, so it's not affected by wet or muddy conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There might be the odd car or tractor when you're cycling on roads, but most traffic has been diverted to the main road that bypasses the whole area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, a bit more about some of the places you'll see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The starting point, Amsden Station, was quite busy in the early twentieth century with services to several major cities, but it was closed in the nineteen fifties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And actually, a small company was set up to turn it into a sort of railway museum, maintaining it in the style of the nineteen fifties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And the station was ready for trains to start using it again earlier this year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's only used by a few local trains, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a visitor center at the station which has a small exhibition about the history of railway transport all over the world and a facility for hiring bikes if you don't have one of your own.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's also a small shop just across the road from the station that sells refreshments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As I said, you can cycle to Langton and return to Amsden by train or the other way around because you can take your cycle on the train.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's no need to book.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's plenty of room and no extra charge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the service is very limited, and the trains between these two places don't run on weekdays.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you want to see the River Elm, there's a footpath from Amsden Station, and you can safely leave your bike in the car park there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Leave yourself plenty of time, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Going down's easy, but the climb up is very steep, so the walk back up to the top can take quite a while.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But it's worth the effort.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The scenery is wonderful, and the footpath runs right next to the river, down to a waterfall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, if you'd like to do some more cycling in the area, there are lots of other cycle paths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll be talking on the radio about them, and you'll be able to get full details in the Saturday edition of the local paper.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The National Cycle Network also has some details on their website, although I have to say they don't have many local ones yet, but that may change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we'll be telling you more about...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.

transcript.text: Now, the topic was the just-in-time, or JIT, supply system used by a lot of manufacturers, 1st in Japan and then in the West, I think.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But actually, one thing I should have made clearer and talked about was the fact that the Americans actually pioneered the idea of just-in-time, though it wasn't called that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Henry Ford and his cars, in fact, at the turn of the 20th century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And later, a big US supermarket chain used it, and this was where Toyota in Japan got the idea for its car making.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, that would have been a good addition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Uh, now, before we go any further, I think I would suggest that you should have stopped and clearly defined just-in-time for your seminar colleagues.

transcript.text: You said its aim was to reduce waste, and you mentioned that classic business theory assumes that stock or inventory of parts are counted as assets, but just-in-time sees them as unnecessary waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But you never told us that JIT simply means waiting until the last moment to order new supplies as you need them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, you're right.

transcript.text: I should have done that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, you talked a bit about standardizing parts as a way of streamlining JIT.

transcript.text: Where did you get your data from?

transcript.text: Mm-hmm.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll get a copy for you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Great.

transcript.text: I look forward to reading through it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And while you're at it, you might want to find out about cases where JIT might not be suitable, and that's in service industries like tourism or healthcare, where customers are paying for something that they can't actually see or count.

transcript.text: Mm-hmm.

transcript.text: [chuckles]

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I was on edge, I guess.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was all just too abrupt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, I'll try to improve that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we'll take a closer look at the crucial role honeybees have played in human history and their relevance in modern times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These remarkable insects are not only essential for our ecosystem but have also left their mark on various aspects of human culture and science.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's begin by tracing their historical significance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The earliest indications of human interaction with bees date back thousands of years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Archaeological evidence shows that ancient humans harvested honey from natural hives found within a hollow structure deep underground, such as a cave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These findings suggest that early societies valued honey as a prized resource.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Later, in ancient civilizations, honey gained spiritual importance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, it was common to offer honey in sacred spaces, such as a place of worship, including a temple, as a gesture of devotion and reverence for the gods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on, early societies recognized the versatile uses of honey and beeswax in daily life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Beeswax, for example, was often applied to preserve or weatherproof materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Objects crafted from wood were frequently coated with this substance to enhance their durability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Meanwhile, honey itself became an essential part of traditional healing practices, valued for its ability to treat infections and accelerate recovery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was regarded as a natural form of medicine and held in high regard for its antibacterial properties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, let's consider the agricultural and environmental roles of honeybees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Farmers and observers have long noticed that bee behavior is intricately linked to shifts in atmospheric conditions, making them reliable indicators of changing weather patterns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Interestingly, in some parts of the world, bees adapt their hive-building techniques to suit their surroundings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In regions with harsher climates, they may incorporate clay-like substances, such as mud, into their hive structures to provide extra insulation and protection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This adaptive behavior is a testament to their resilience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, the physical structure of bees has fascinated scientists for centuries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their ability to collect and transport pollen is made possible by the specialized hairs on their appendages, commonly referred to as legs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This unique feature allows them to play an indispensable role in pollinating crops and supporting ecosystems worldwide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lastly, let's discuss the modern applications of honeybee products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In agriculture, bees directly contribute to the cultivation of crops, including various fruits and leafy plants, as well as staple foods like greens and other vegetables.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Additionally, byproducts like propolis, a resinous material produced by bees, are now used in treating issues affecting human skin, thanks to their antimicrobial properties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Beeswax, on the other hand, has gained popularity in the culinary world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is often employed in food preparation, especially in cooking, where its heat-resistant qualities make it ideal for creating natural coatings for certain dishes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

r1.title: A River Reveals Its Roman Past

sentences.text: 2,000 years ago, the town of Arles, in what is now south-western France, was a busy gateway to the area of the Roman Empire known as Gaul.
Goods from all over the Mediterranean were transferred there to barges – long, shallow riverboats – then pulled up the Rhône river to supply the northern half of the great empire.
Today, Arles is a small, quiet place, and the Rhône is polluted and mostly ignored.
Archaeologist Luc Long is a native of Arles.
He had already worked on sunken ships all over the Mediterranean when, in 1986, a friend persuaded him to dive for the first time in his home river.
Long reluctantly agreed.
The two men entered the river on a chilly November morning, when the water was around 8°C, thick, cloudy and foul-smelling.
They could see no more than a metre ahead through the murky water.
At a depth of about six metres, Long saw a sunken truck.
To his surprise, he discovered an ancient Roman jar – known as an amphora – on the driver’s seat.
These containers were used throughout the Roman Empire to transport olive oil, fish sauce, and other products.
When empty, they would simply be discarded.
Within a short time the divers found themselves swimming over a vast field of amphorae.
Long had never seen so many intact ones, and he has been mapping this Roman rubbish dump ever since.
For the first 20 years or so, no one paid much attention to what Long was doing.
When, in 2004, one of his colleagues came across a 34-metre-long Roman barge, Long doubted that there would ever be enough money available to raise it.
In 2007, Long handed over the study of this wreck – which he named Arles-Rhône 3 – to three younger archaeologists, and continued his survey of the rest of the dump, around 50 metres upstream.
This was where he started finding pieces of the Roman town of Arles, including statues.
Word began to leak out.
The French customs police warned Long that antiquities thieves might be watching his operation.
So when his divers found a two-metre statue of the god Neptune, they brought it to the surface at night.
Before the diving season was over, divers had discovered a rare marble bust of the Roman emperor Julius Caesar.
An exhibition was built around the statue, and news of it spread around the world.
‘The exhibition’s success was astonishing,’ said Claude Sintes, director of Arles’ local antiquities museum, where the exhibition was held.
‘When a modest town like ours gets 400,000 visitors, the politicians understood that the economic return was strong.’

By the autumn of 2010, the Caesar exhibition was nearing its end, and some politicians were looking for more culture to invest in, because the European Union had designated the region around Arles a 2013 European Capital of Culture.
Suddenly nine million euros became available to build a new wing on the museum and put a Roman barge into it.
There was just one small problem.
The project would need to be completed by 2013.
That meant the barge needed to be extracted by the end of the diving season in 2011.
This was because although the wood of the boat had suffered no microbial decay, water had filled its cells, leaving the whole structure soft and spongy.
If that were to evaporate, the boat would collapse.
The solution was to bathe the wood for months in a polymer called polyethylene glycol, then freeze-dry it in small sections – gradually infusing it with the polymer before extracting the water.
The process would take nearly two years.
So there was only one diving season to extract the boat from the Rhône.
‘We thought the project was doomed to fail,’ said Benoît Poinard, a professional diver and the site foreman.
Normally, Poinard explained, the Rhône is safe for diving only from late June to October; otherwise the current is too strong.
Only three or four months would not be enough to excavate Arles-Rhône 3.
Then 2011 arrived.
It hardly snowed in the Alps that winter and that spring it barely rained.
The Rhône’s current was so gentle that the team got in the water by early May.
The team worked straight into November, losing only a single week to bad weather – and completed the job.
‘Two hours after we finished,’ Poinard said, ‘the Rhône became undiveable for the whole winter.’
When Arles-Rhône 3 sank, it was carrying 33 tons of stone for building work.
It had come from a quarry just north of Arles, and was probably heading towards a construction site further down the river.
The boat was pointed upstream, though, rather than downstream, indicating it had been moored at the quay when it sank.
A flash flood had probably swamped it.
As soon as the flood subsided, the barge would have been covered in a coating of fine clay no more than 20 cm thick.
This was where the archaeologists discovered the personal effects that the crew had left on the boat, including cooking utensils and plates.
When the restorers were taking the boat apart, they also found a silver coin sealed between two planks of wood; it had been put there to bring good luck.
And it did – 2,000 years later.
Arles-Rhône 3 was able to take its place in the new wing of the museum, on schedule, just over two years after re-emerging from the cloudy depths of the Rhône.

sentences.text: A.
In 1977 Irene Pepperberg, a recent graduate of Harvard University, didsomething very bold.
At a time when animals still were considered automatons, she set out to find what was on another creature’s mind by talking to it.
She brought a one-year-old African gray parrot she named Alex into her lab to teach him to reproduce the sounds of the English language.
“I thought if he learned to communicate, I could ask him questions about how he sees the world.”
B.
When Pepperberg began her dialogue with Alex, who died last September at the age of 31, many scientists believed animals were incapable of any thought.
They were simply machines, robots programmed to react to stimuli but lacking the ability to think or feel.
Any pet owner would disagree.
We see the love in our dogs’ eyes and know that, of course, they has thoughts and emotions.
But such claims remain highly controversial.
Gut instinct is not science, and it is all too easy to project human thoughts and feelings onto another creature.
How, then, does a scientist prove that an animal is capable of thinking—that it is able to acquire information about the world and act on it?
“That’s why I started my studies with Aex,” Pepperberg said.
They were seated—she at her desk, he on top of his cage—in her lab, a windowless room about the size of a boxcar, at Brandeis University.
Newspapers lined the floor; baskets of bright toys were stacked on the shelves.
They were clearly a team—and because of their work, the notion that animals can think is no longer so fanciful.
C.
Certain skills are considered key signs of higher mental abilities: good memory, a grasp of grammar and symbols, self-awareness, understanding others’ motives, imitating others, and being creative.

Bit by bit, in ingenious experiments, researchers have documented these talents in other species, gradually chipping away at what we thought made human beings distinctive while offering a glimpse of where our own abilities came from.

Scrub jays know that other jays are thieves and that stashed food can spoil; sheep can recognize faces; chimpanzees use a variety of tools to probe termite mounds and even use weapons to hunt small mammals; dolphins can imitate human postures; the archerfish, which stuns insects with a sudden blast of water, can learn how to aim its squirt simply by watching an experienced fish perform the task.
And Alex the parrot turned out to be a surprisingly good talker.
D.
Thirty years after the Alex studies began; Pepperberg and a changing collection of assistants were still giving him English lessons.
The humans, along with two younger parrots, also served as Alex’s flock, providing the social input all parrots crave.
Like any flock, this one —as small as it was—had its share of drama.
Alex dominated his fellow parrots, acted huffy at times around Pepperberg, tolerated the other female humans, and fell to pieces over a male assistant who dropped by for a visit.

Pepperberg bought Alex in a Chicago pet store where she let the store’s assistant pick him out because she didn’t want other scientists saying later that she’d particularly chosen an especially smart bird for her work.
Given that Alex’s brain was the size of a shelled walnut, most researchers thought Pepperberg’s interspecies communication study would be futile.
E.
“Some people actually called me crazy for trying this,” she said.
“Scientists thought that chimpanzees were better subjects, although, of course, chimps can’t speak.”
Chimpanzees, bonobos, and gorillas have been taught to use sign language and symbols to communicate with US, often with impressive results.
The bonobo Kanzi, for instance, carries his symbol-communication board with him so he can “talk” to his human researchers, and he has invented combinations of symbols to express his thoughts.
Nevertheless, this is not the same thing as having an animal look up at you, open his mouth, and speak.

Under Pepperberg’s patient tutelage, Alex learned how to use his vocal tract to imitate almost one hundred English words, including the sounds for various foods, although he calls an apple a “banerry.”
“Apples taste a little bit like bananas to him, and they look a little bit like cherries, so Alex made up that word for them,” Pepperberg said.
F.
It sounded a bit mad, the idea of having lessons to practice, and willingly doing it.
But after listening to and observing Alex, it was difficult to argue with Pepperberg’s explanation for his behaviors.
She wasn’t handing him treats for the repetitious work or rapping him on the claws to make him say the sounds.
“He has to hear the words over and over before he can correctly imitate them,” Pepperberg said, after pronouncing “seven” for Alex a good dozen times in a row.
“I’m not trying to see if Alex can learn a human language,” she added.
“That’s never been the point.
My plan always was to use his imitative skills to get a better understanding of avian cognition.”
G.
In other words, because Alex was able to produce a close approximation of the sounds of some English words, Pepperberg could ask him questions about a bird’s basic understanding of the world.
She couldn’t ask him what he was thinking about, but she could ask him about his knowledge of numbers, shapes, and colors.
To demonstrate, Pepperberg carried Alex on her arm to a tall wooden perch in the middle of the room.
She then retrieved a green key and a small green cup from a basket on a shelf.
She held up the two items to Alex’s eye.
“What’s same?”
she asked.
Without hesitation, Alex’s beak opened: “Color.”
“What’s different?”
Pepperberg asked.
“Shape,” Alex said.
His voice had the digitized sound of a cartoon character.
Since parrots lack lips (another reason it was difficult for Alex to pronounce some sounds, such as ba), the words seemed to come from the air around him, as if a ventriloquist were speaking.
But the words—and what can only be called the thoughts—were entirely his.
H.
For the next 20 minutes, Alex ran through his tests, distinguishing colors, shapes, sizes, and materials (wool versus wood versus metal).
He did some simple arithmetic, such as counting the yellow toy blocks among a pile of mixed hues.
And, then, as if to offer final proof of the mind inside his bird’s brain, Alex spoke up.
“Talk clearly!”
he commanded, when one of the younger birds Pepperberg was also teaching talked with wrong pronunciation.
“Talk clearly!”
“Don’t be a smart aleck,” Pepperberg said, shaking her head at him.
“He knows all this, and he gets bored, so he interrupts the others, or he gives the wrong answer just to be obstinate.
At this stage, he’s like a teenager; he’s moody, and I’m never sure what he’ll do.”

sentences.text: From ancient times to the present, historians have asked the question: How and why did an ordinary little town in central Italy grow so much bigger than any other in the ancient Mediterranean and come to control such a huge empire?
During the first century BCE, Roman writers themselves began systematically to study the earlier centuries of their city and their empire.

Yet these historians had little more direct evidence of the earliest phases of Rome's history than modern writers have, and in some ways perhaps not as much, as there were no surviving documents or archives.
Their 'histories' about the foundation of ancient Rome tell us a good deal about how the Romans saw their city, their values, and their failings.
However, they tell us very little indeed about what they claim to inform us about: that is, what earliest Rome was actually like.
One fact is obvious.
Rome was already a very old city by 63 BCE, the birth date of its first emperor.
But how exactly are we to access reliable information about the origins of Rome?

One way of doing this is by turning away from the histories of Roman writers and seeking out clues in the Latin language, or in later Roman institutions that might point back to features of earliest Rome.
Much more tangible, however, is the evidence of archaeology.
Dig down deep in the city of Rome, below the visible ancient monuments, and a few traces of a much earlier settlement or settlements remain.

Beneath the Forum itself (an ancient marketplace at the centre of the city) lie the remains of an early cemetery, which caused tremendous excitement when they were first unearthed at the start of the 20th century.

Cemeteries imply the existence of a community, and traces of that are presumably to be found in the groups of huts whose faint outlines have been detected under various parts of the later city, including on the Palatine (the centremost of the seven hills on which Rome is built).
We have little idea of the nature of these huts beyond their construction in wood, clay, and thatch, and still less of the lifestyle they supported.
But we can fill in some of the gaps if we look just outside Rome.
One of the best preserved and most carefully excavated of these early structures was found at Fidenae, a few miles north of the city, in the 1980s.

It is a rectangular building, some six by five metres, made of wood and rammed earth - a construction method still utilised up to the present day - with a simple porch around it, formed by the overhanging roof.
Inside was a central hearth, some large pottery storage jars, and traces of predictable foodstuffs and domestic animals.
There are vivid glimpses of human and other life here; the question is, what do those glimpses add up to?
The archaeological remains certainly demonstrate that there is a long and rich prehistory behind the ancient Rome we can still see, but quite how long that prehistory is is another matter.
Part of the problem is the conditions of excavation in the city itself.
The site of Rome has been so intensively built on for centuries that we find these traces of early occupation only in spots that happen not to have been disturbed.

The foundations dug in the first and second centuries CE for the vast marble temples of the forum obliterated much of what then lay beneath the surface; the cellars of grand Renaissance houses cut through even more ancient remains in other parts of the city.
So we have tiny snapshots, never the big picture.
This is archaeology at its most difficult, and - although new fragments of evidence emerge all the time - its interpretation, and reinterpretation is almost always contested and often controversial.

For example, there is an ongoing debate about whether the small pieces of wattle and daub found in excavations in the Forum in the mid-20th century indicate that there was an early hut settlement there too, or whether they were inadvertently introduced as part of the rubble used a few centuries later to provide a new raised surface for the area.
It has to be said that this place, though fine for a cemetery, would have been rather damp and marshy for a village.
Precise dating is even more contentious.

It cannot be stressed enough that there is no certain independent date for any of the archaeological material from earliest Rome or the area around, and that arguments still rage about the age of almost every major find.

It has taken decades of work over the past century or so - using such diagnostics as the existence of wheel-made pottery (assumed to be later than handmade), the occasional presence on graves of Greek ceramics (whose dating is better, but still not perfectly understood) and careful comparison from site to site - to produce a rough chronological scheme covering the period from around 1000 to 600 BCE.
On that basis, the earliest burials in Rome would have been around 1000 BCE, and the earliest known settlements around 750-700 BCE.
But even these dates are far from certain.
Recent scientific methods - including radiocarbon dating, which calculates the age of any organic material - have suggested that they are all too 'young', by as much as a hundred years.

The building at Fidenae, for example, was dated around the middle of the eighth century BCE according to traditional archaeological criteria, but that is pushed back to around the end of the ninth century BCE if we follow radiocarbon analysis.
If anything, Rome appears to be getting older.

questions.quote: And what time would you like the room for? Oh, I'm not sure. 7.45? Not too late. Okay. And people will probably be leaving about 11. Fine. We're open until 11.30.

questions.tip: 注意听价格对应关系，standard menu 是 25，gold menu 是 50，不要张冠李戴。
questions.quote: Or the celebration menu which is three courses is very popular. That's 35 pounds. Okay. I think I'd rather go with that. And there's also our gold menu that's a five-course menu at 50 pounds.

questions.quote: Now, not all the guests eat meat. Will there be something for them? Of course. We'll make sure there's a vegetarian option for each course.

questions.quote: And do you know if any of the guests have food allergies? Anything like shellfish, for example? I'll need to check, but I do know that one of my daughter's friends is very allergic to strawberries.

questions.explanation: 女士询问除了甜点（desserts）之外，能否也提供 cheese（芝士/奶酪），服务员表示没问题。
questions.tip: 你可能听到 "I'd like a choice" 想填 choice，但 choice 是抽象概念，题目问的是具体食物名称。
questions.quote: Do you have any other requests for desserts? Well, I'd like a choice if possible. And could we have cheese as well? Of course, no problem.

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a short talk given to a group of retired people about a club called Connect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've been asked to talk to you today about Connect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Connect is a club for people who have retired from full-time work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first Connect club began back in nineteen sixty in Brisbane, Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'll concentrate on Frankston Connect, the club where I'm a member.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It services the communities around the suburb of Frankston here in Melbourne.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so what are our club aims?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're not a fitness club or anything like that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some Connect branches do charity work, but that's not for us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our objective is to provide social contact with others who have similar interests and ideas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, meetings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have monthly club meetings where the usual club business is discussed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, at the last meeting, we talked about how much money was spent that month.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, at that meeting, someone had just returned from an overseas trip, and he spoke about that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then we looked at entries for our photography competition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The winner will be announced soon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Up until now, we've used the school hall for our meetings, but that's about to be renovated, so we needed to find an alternative.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's been a great venue because of its size, and it's so easy to get to, but I'm sure historical Frankston Hall will suit us just fine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our social committee plans and organizes club trips from time to time, and they're always looking for suggestions from members for new places to go to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you join, you should check the activities list that's posted on our website each month and attend anything that interests you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Come and make friends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're just one big happy family.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So how do you join, and what about membership fees?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Just fill in the form and give it to me before you leave this morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are a few payment options.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some members prefer to make an annual payment, which is a slightly cheaper option, or you can pay monthly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why don't you get a group together?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It makes the activities more fun.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If you still haven't decided whether to join or not, let me try to tempt you with some of our upcoming events.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our Moonlight Wildlife Walk was previously available to members' immediate families as well, but this wonderful activity has become so popular that it's now limited to just members.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although it's free, we do ask our members to pay something to the wildlife fund so it can continue its good work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Everyone makes their way to the wildlife park independently, arriving at dusk, where a guide walks with the group and tells us about all the animals we encounter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, Theater in the Park.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We see a different play every month.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The park's on the train line and easy to access, so we don't organize buses or anything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Come along and recline on a blanket on the grass.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although some members prefer to take along their own seat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No need to make a reservation, there's plenty of space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After the play, we all walk to a local cafe where you can purchase coffee and cake.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a really fun night out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bird watching is a regular activity, and it's organized by the keen bird watchers in the club.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This activity consists mainly of early morning and late afternoon walking trips to spot the birds when they're most active.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bird watching attracts only small numbers, so one of our ardent bird watchers drives members in the club van to the best spots.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The City Botanical Gardens walk is a popular activity that occurs a couple of times a year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Members make their own way there and usually meet up outside the gates at eight forty-five AM, setting off for the hour's walk with the volunteer guide by nine AM.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many members bring a friend or relative, and this is fine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the State Library.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our visits here in the past have always been great because there's something for everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can easily spend a whole day in there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a lovely restaurant, and you can take food into the small cinema there, where we'll be watching a short film about the history of our local area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what else can I tell you?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: The main aim of Frankston Connect is to
questions.explanation: 录音明确说明俱乐部的目标是为有相似兴趣和想法的人提供社交接触，这对应了选项A的“结交志同道合的人”。
questions.tip: 录音中虽然提到了“健身（fitness）”和“慈善（charity）”，但前面都有明显的否定词，你在听题时千万不要只抓取原词，而忽略了前后的否定语境。
questions.quote: Okay, so what are our club aims? We're not a fitness club or anything like that. Some Connect branches do charity work, but that's not for us. Our objective is to provide social contact with others who have similar interests and ideas.

options.text: encourage members to stay physically active.
raise money through activities and events.

questions.prompt: What happened at last month's meeting?
questions.explanation: 录音提到上个月的会议讨论了那个月花了多少钱，完美对应选项A的“讨论俱乐部财务”。
questions.tip: 录音虽然提到有人刚从海外旅行回来，以及摄影比赛的获胜者很快会公布，但这些要么是个别成员的分享，要么是未来发生的事，你可能会因为听到零星干扰词而选错，一定要注意听清动作时态和会议的核心议题。
questions.quote: Now, meetings. We have monthly club meetings where the usual club business is discussed. For example, at the last meeting, we talked about how much money was spent that month. Also, at that meeting, someone had just returned from an overseas trip, and he spoke about that. Then we looked at entries for our photography competition. The winner will be announced soon.

options.text: The members planned a trip to a foreign country.

questions.prompt: The venue for the monthly meetings will change because the school hall is
questions.explanation: 录音中提到学校大厅即将被翻新，所以需要找个替代地点，这说明大厅现在不能用了，对应选项C。
questions.tip: 录音提到过去的大厅尺寸很大且很容易到达，这恰好直接排除了选项A和B，你千万不要把场地过去的优点当成了现在需要更换的原因。
questions.quote: Up until now, we've used the school hall for our meetings, but that's about to be renovated, so we needed to find an alternative. It's been a great venue because of its size, and it's so easy to get to, but I'm sure historical Frankston Hall will suit us just fine.

questions.prompt: The Social Committee would like members to
questions.explanation: 录音指出社交委员会一直在寻找成员关于新去处的建议，这直接对应选项C的“提供未来活动的点子”。
questions.tip: 录音明确说是委员会自己计划和组织活动，并没有要求成员帮忙组织，你在听的时候要准确抓取委员会对成员的期待其实是给出“建议（suggestions）”。
questions.quote: Our social committee plans and organizes club trips from time to time, and they're always looking for suggestions from members for new places to go to.

options.text: invite their friends and family to join.

questions.prompt: How can you save money on members' fees?
questions.explanation: 录音明确说到年度付款（annual payment）是一个稍微便宜一点的选择，这对应了选项B的“付一年的钱”。
questions.tip: 录音前面提到了今天上午填表交钱，后面提到了也可以按月付款，你可能会将今天交表或普通的付款方式跟“省钱”混淆，做题时必须精准锁定“更便宜（cheaper）”所对应的具体条件。
questions.quote: So how do you join, and what about membership fees? It's simple. Just fill in the form and give it to me before you leave this morning. There are a few payment options. Some members prefer to make an annual payment, which is a slightly cheaper option, or you can pay monthly.

options.text: pay for two people or more.

groups.instructions:
What information does the speaker give about each of the following future club events?

questions.explanation: 录音提到虽然活动免费，但要求成员向野生动物基金支付一点钱，这对应了选项E的“要求捐助资金”。
questions.tip: 听到“免费（free）”时你可能会觉得完全不需要花钱，但紧跟着的“支付一点钱（pay something）”才是真实的考点，做题时不要被前半句的让步状语迷惑。
questions.quote: If you still haven't decided whether to join or not, let me try to tempt you with some of our upcoming events. questions.tip: 录音说不需要预订，直接排除了选项A，你听到“预订（reservation）”这个词时一定要注意前面的否定表达“没必要（no need）”。
questions.quote: Okay, Theater in the Park. We see a different play every month. The park's on the train line and easy to access, so we don't organize buses or anything. Come along and recline on a blanket on the grass. Although some members prefer to take along their own seat. No need to make a reservation, there's plenty of space.

questions.explanation: 录音提到会有热心成员开着俱乐部的面包车（club van）载大家去最好的地点，这对应了选项H的“俱乐部提供交通工具”。
questions.tip: 这道题干扰信息较少，你容易犯的错误是没有第一时间把录音里的“在俱乐部面包车里载成员”和选项里的“提供交通工具”迅速联系起来。
questions.quote: Bird watching is a regular activity, and it's organized by the keen bird watchers in the club. This activity consists mainly of early morning and late afternoon walking trips to spot the birds when they're most active. transcript.text: Section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear two students talking about the Moa with the lecturer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Thank you all for coming here today to hear about the Moa, a kind of animal which has been extinct for a long time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, first of all, we look at what the Moa are.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Moa are nine species of flightless birds endemic to New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were the dominant herbivores in New Zealand's forest, shrubland, and subalpine ecosystems for thousands of years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But around five hundred years ago, they all went extinct.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When I mention extinct animals during ancient times, you may immediately think of dinosaurs, which disappeared around sixty-six million years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fossils of dinosaurs, which we use to study, are large in number, but not many of those of Moa remain, though both animals appeal to people today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So the Moa sound more mysterious now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But Sir, I've got a question about these flightless birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: How can we distinguish them from other birds?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's a good question.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Birds are commonly characterized by being warm-blooded, having feathers and wings, usually capable of flight, and laying eggs, while the flightless Moa, until their extinction, were the largest birds in the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their heads are relatively small in relation to their bodies, and they are the only wingless birds lacking even the vestigial wings and substantial tailbones in their family.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's impressive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: But were they born to be like that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I mean, when they were chicks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yes, absolutely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's move on to the chicks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The eggs of Moa were laid in nests and incubated for about two months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The chicks would be well-developed upon hatching and probably would be able to leave the nests to feed on their own almost immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've heard that the male Moa are thought to have incubated the eggs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Is that true?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I think there is a possibility for that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've read somewhere that the sex-specific DNA recovered from the outer surfaces of eggshells suggested that these eggs were likely to have been hatched by the male, but we still need to consult more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But I have a question.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There has been some occasional speculation that the Moa were still alive because someone said they had caught sight of them in New Zealand in the late nineteenth century or even the twentieth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Do you think it's possible?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm not amazed by that, since that kind of thing has been claimed several times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: But I find it funny because no reliable evidence of Moa tracks has ever been found, and experts still contend that Moa survival is extremely unlikely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: So what was the reason for the Moa's extinction?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I wonder if it was global warming or some other factors related to their living environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, before the arrival of human settlers in New Zealand, the Moa's only predator was the massive Haas eagle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then the Maori arrived sometime before CE thirteen hundred, and all Moa genera were soon driven to extinction by hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What a horrible thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's look at the features of some species of Moa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The South Island giant Moa may have been the tallest birds ever known, and the second tallest of the nine Moa species is the North Island giant Moa, with the females being markedly larger than males, both in weight and height.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And I've heard that the smallest of the Moa birds are the coastal Moa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Is that right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yes, you are right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And have you heard about any other kind of Moa before?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I know the crested Moa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The eggs they laid may be larger than others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As they mainly lived in the remote interior of the Southern Island, their fossils are rare or absent in archaeological sites, and no egg remains have yet been identified.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Are there any species of Moa that have got more fossils?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, of course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A considerable amount of remains of the stout-legged Moa exist due to the well-preserved properties of their habitat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their skulls reveal relatively bad vision, a good sense of smell, and a very short bill.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then there is the eastern Moa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were remarkable in having very long and narrow windpipes, which probably enabled them to make louder, more resonant calls than those of other Moa and had the greatest vocal abilities, so they could communicate when they could not see each other in the forest or at night.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They used a range of senses apart from sound in their search for food, such as their sense of smell and vision.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of human memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In today's psychology lecture, I'll be talking about human memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And what I want to do first is establish the historical context.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So I'll outline various ideas about human memory and how they've changed over time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So first, early cultures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, in the earliest times, let's say before three thousand years BC, people were dependent on being able to remember things, perhaps even more than we are today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's because humans could not write.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The skill hadn't been developed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So a good memory was important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For one thing, it helped people navigate in the area around their homes, and it was the only way to access family history and ancestry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What's more, a good memory might be the difference between life and death.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most people were hunters and gatherers, so it was essential to understand which foods were poisonous and which were not.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was particularly true of plants because they sometimes looked very similar, and the only way to store this information and pass it on to the next generation was to remember it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, because it was so long ago, there's limited information about what techniques were used to assist memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so moving on now to the ancient Greeks, and the Greek poet named Simonides, who lived around five hundred BC, was the man sometimes described as the father of memory training.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Simonides' most important idea was that it's much easier to remember information if we connect it with one particular place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, over hundreds of years, other Greek scholars developed his ideas about memory, and a lot of this information has survived.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we know that by the first century, the Greeks believed that people could use their human senses to improve their memory, and this was particularly true when it came to sight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There was a strong connection there, they believed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, next I should talk about the ancient Romans, who, like the Greeks, believed memory training was extremely important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They used memory in many different ways, obviously, but most of all, in ancient Rome, people thought that one of the greatest skills was the ability to give an impressive speech in public, and memory was one of the keys to doing that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So this was why, from about one hundred BC, the Romans wanted to develop techniques to improve memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And an important figure here was Cicero, a Roman political leader.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of Cicero's ideas was that humans actually have two types of memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a memory that can be developed, which he called the artificial memory, and there's another type of memory which he called natural.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And the point is that you can learn techniques to help improve your artificial memory, an idea that's interested some academics ever since.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So moving next to later European history, and the first thing to note is that during the Middle Ages, a group of academics called the Scholastics were also interested in memory techniques.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Scholastics used these techniques when they were instructing pupils about religion, and this raised the profile of memory techniques.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But later, attitudes towards memory began to change, and this started in the seventeenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People began to see memory training as an art form, and that didn't interest them so much anymore because they thought that science had the answers to most human questions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This attitude really continued into the nineteenth century as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Children weren't taught memory techniques, but were expected to learn lots of facts, and to do this by constantly repeating things like dates and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so then we come to modern times, and in the nineteen forties, a remarkable series of studies was conducted with a man known simply as S.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Psychologists found that S never made notes about anything, although he was a journalist and never forgot facts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The researchers concluded that S had an unusual medical condition, which meant he developed incredible memory skills.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was important as it seemed to support the ideas of the ancient Greeks and other much earlier scholars.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in the later part of the twentieth century, the focus switched to computers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, well, that's the historical context.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's now turn to-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0
