sentences.text: A During your childhood, there will have been some kind of craze which affected all the people in your school.
It may have been to do with a particular toy or possibly a must-have item of clothing.
It may have been something as simple as a type of pen or as expensive as an electronic games console.
Fashion designers, toy manufacturers and anyone else involved in the retail trade love conformity.
Set up a craze, especially in the young, and everyone will go for it.
In fact, it's an ideal way to sell huge quantities of merchandise.
The levels of conformity in consumerism are phenomenal.
When you actually stand back and consider how easily we are persuaded that having certain items is the only way we can ensure peace of mind, you see what an important concept conformity is.
B Conformity has been described as “yielding to group pressure” (Crutchfield, 1962).
However, this implies that other people put pressure on us to make us conform and this is not always the case.
A better definition is given by Aronson (1976) who said it was a “change in a person's behaviour or opinions as a result of real or imagined pressure from a person or group of people”.
This would make more sense, as often the pressure we feel is imagined.
The person or group he refers to would have to be important to us at the time, regardless of their status.
C There has been considerable research on conformity.
One of the first studies looked at the answers people gave when asked to estimate the number of beans in a bottle (Jenness, 1932).
If you have ever entered a “guess the number” competition, you probably looked at the previous estimates made and based your judgment on what other people had guessed.
This is more or less what happened in the Jenness study.
First of all, he asked the respondents to give their own estimates, and then he asked them to decide a group estimate.
Finally, he asked them alone again and discovered that they had stayed with the group answer.

D Probably the most famous study on conformity was undertaken by Asch (1951) when he created a situation where many of his subjects gave answers which were blatantly untrue, rather than contradict the people they were with.
He did this by getting his subject to sit round a table with six stooges (colleagues of the experimenter) so that the subject was second to last.
He showed them all a large card which had three lines of different lengths drawn on it, labelled A, B and C.
He then gave them a card with a single line and asked them to match this in terms of length to one of the lines A, B or C.

E The stooges gave untrue responses in a number of the trials and the subjects were left in the situation where they either reported what they saw with their own eyes or conformed to the norm of the group.
When the results were assessed, Asch found that in one out of every three trials where the wrong answer was given, the subject gave the same wrong answer as the stooges.
This led to an average level of conformity of 32 per cent.
Asch interviewed his subjects after the trials to try to find out why they conformed to an answer which was so obviously wrong.
Most of them said that they did not want to cause problems within the group, although they also stated that when they did give wrong answers it made them anxious.

(Asch found that when there was just one other person present who did not go along with the majority, no matter how many others there were, it was sufficient to make the subject give the right answer.)
F Kelman (1953) outlined three processes which can explain social conformity.
The first is compliance, where subjects go along with the crowd to prevent any in-group hostility or bad feeling and to maintain group harmony.
However, they do not change their own private belief.
If we look back to the Asch study, we can see that the subjects were simply complying with the demands of the experimental situation but hadn't actually internalized the group's norms.
They agreed in public, but dissented in private.
In a process known as internalization, however, subjects do actually see the view of the group as the more valid one.
They may be able to do this, for example, by convincing themselves that their eyesight is poor.
Sometimes, however, subjects actually seem to change their beliefs because they want to become more like their heroes.
If they really want to become part of an in-group, they will start to identify with that group and take on the group's values and beliefs, even if they are different to their own.
Kelman calls this identification.
It frequently happens with teenagers who want to become more like a peer group in order to be accepted, and suddenly seem to go against all the values and beliefs of their parents.
G So why is it that we have to conform?
Some people feel confident most of the time, have high self-esteem and do not have to go along with the majority.
For most of us, though, how confident we feel varies from day to day, depending on the situation we are in, and this can influence behaviour.

Studies on conformity

questions.explanation: 录音明确说家庭套票（deal for families）的价格是 65 美元。
questions.tip: 你可能听到 35 就想填，但录音说那是“节省了（saving of）”35 美元，不是票价。
questions.quote: A standard adult ticket is normally $30, but there's a special deal for families of $65, which is a saving of $35.

questions.explanation: 录音说 385 路车大约需要 40 分钟（approximately 40 minutes）到达那里。
questions.tip: 另一辆 388 路车要“多花 20 分钟（20 minutes longer）”，也就是 60 分钟，不要听到 20 就填。
questions.quote: The 385 will get you there in approximately 40 minutes depending on traffic.

questions.explanation: 录音提到游客喜欢抱动物并“拍照（get your photo taken）”，但这需要支付小额费用。
questions.tip: 题目是 "have a ..."，对应录音中的 "get your photo taken"，需提取名词 photo。
questions.quote: They've stopped that, but most tourists love the fact that you're allowed to hold some of the animals and get your photo taken.

questions.explanation: 这是一道拼写题，录音特意纠正了拼写，是 ROSIE。
questions.tip: 注意听男士说的 "No"，他否定了女生拼的 ROZY，一定要写纠正后的版本。
questions.quote: Is it ROZY? No, it's ROSIE.

questions.explanation: 录音说因为需求火爆，演出已经“延长到了周六（extended to Saturday）”。
questions.tip: 不要填 Tuesday（开始时间）或 Wednesday（特场时间），题目问的是 "run to..."（持续到...）。
questions.quote: Next week, it says it starts on Tuesday... but because of the demand it's been extended to Saturday.

questions.explanation: 录音说周一晚上的预演秀提供门票“折扣（discount）”。
questions.tip: 听到 "Monday" 和 "tickets" 时要竖起耳朵，答案就在紧随其后的 "offering a..." 后面。
questions.quote: Ah, it says there's a special preview show on the Monday and they're offering a discount on tickets that night.

questions.explanation: 录音中提到市中心的“博物馆（museum）”现在有一个通过实践操作的展览（exhibition）。
questions.tip: 题目问去哪里看展览，录音虽然先问了 "What's the museum like?"，但答案就是这个地点。
questions.quote: What's the museum like? It's very popular with children and there's a very hands-on exhibition on at the moment.

questions.explanation: 录音建议孩子们带一个“盒子（box）”把做好的折纸带回家，而且只要一个小的（little one）。
questions.tip: Scissors（剪刀）和 paper（纸）是提供的（provided），不需要带，别填错了。
questions.quote: They just advise children to bring a box to carry the completed origami home in. Just a little one will do.

questions.explanation: 录音明确说咸水湖是在“海洋一侧（ocean side）”。
questions.tip: 不要听到 centre 或 mountain 就填，录音对此进行了明确的否定 "No"。
questions.quote: Is that in the centre of the island near the mountain? No, it's on the ocean side.

questions.explanation: 生问能不能“露营（camp）”，男士回答 "I'm afraid..." 表示否定，即不允许露营。
questions.tip: 题目是 "not allowed to"，对应录音中被委婉否定的动作 camp。
questions.quote: Are you allowed to camp there? That would be lovely, but I'm afraid the land is all...

3.s: you're allowed to hold some of the animals

7.s: spend a day in the city center

transcript.text: Section 2.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You'll hear a talk about tourism in the mining community.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm delighted to welcome you to our mining community and very pleased that you're interested in the ores and pits of this area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think you'll be pleasantly surprised with your special experience here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let me start by giving you some warnings on safety rules and regulations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Rule number one: always wear safety equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is a litany of safety equipment that mining workers use for their protection, from helmets to safety glasses and gloves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is essential that all workers wear the necessary safety equipment at all times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There have been countless stories of workers being saved by helmets, which are the hard hats that you can see on the shelf beside you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, visitors wearing helmets is mandatory in the mining area, although you are free to take them off when you're in the mining museum and picnic area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You won't need to pay any deposit, though you should return them to the counter once you finish the visit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The helmets are offered in all sizes, so choose a suitable one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our mining community is currently being refurbished for some of the main area, so please make a note of that, and you'll know what to look out for.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, when you go in or out of the mine, please pay attention to the road, for it has just been repaired because of the rough surface and can be really slippery since it's still wet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The history and process of tin mining are complicated and involve a lot of special words, but here you will see how it was and still is done.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After a short 5 to 10-minute walk, visitors can track round a numbered route with clear explanations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of the tour is in the open air, so nice weather helps.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All areas are clearly posted with signs, but if you have problems traveling around or climbing up and down, you can turn to the staff here, and we are happy to help.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you are interested, Blue Hills Tin Stream is a working water-powered tin streaming mill that gives visitors a very clear idea of how difficult it is to get tin out of rock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I hope you'll enjoy the informative indoor presentation and this self-guided tour, but you have to bear one thing in mind, that smoking is forbidden throughout the whole community.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though you can take phones and, of course, use them, you'll also be surprised that there will be more than just one place to go in the mine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The underground tunnel is now being refurbished and only relevant workers can access it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But it will soon be all finished, and I believe it's a lovely place for you to explore around.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Don't forget to wear protective clothing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's mandatory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, let's start by seeing where you can go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you can see on our map in the brochure I've given you, we are here at the reception block.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have a famous mill which is used for making and processing materials such as steel and coal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To visit it, just go straight ahead, north along the path in front of you, and you'll find it at the end of the path.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, towards the east, go along the path from our starting point.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Turn left to the corner and then turn right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is a car park at the east end of the lane.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To the west, there is a museum.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Pass the shop around the crossroads, and it is just located at the west end of the road.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And by the way, the shop is specialized in selling a variety of ore-related souvenirs, including key rings, postcards, tin-made Lewis chessmen, and even Roman soldiers which are made from beautiful pyrite.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you are interested in the laboratory where scientific experiments, analyses, and research are carried out, it is situated at the southern part of the park, opposite the shop.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I bet you'll be happy to hear that this laboratory is also used for gold and crystal refinement, so don't miss this one for the sake of it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I assume by this time you'll all need some rest and refreshment, so we have an excellent café which caters for delicious food and beverages at the other side of the road next to the shop.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, if you want to spend some time in the fresh air, we have a perfect picnic area which is just right and northeast of the reception block.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Further east, there is a path leading to the northern part of the park, and at the end of it is the toilet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, most of the visitors would choose to use the mailbox and send the beautiful postcards to their friends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To reach it, just...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 2.

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about hard hats?
questions.explanation: 录音明确说明安全帽提供所有的尺寸（offered in all sizes），直接对应选项C。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到前半部分说安全帽强制佩戴（mandatory）或者听到无需押金（won't need to pay any deposit）而没有看清选项细节，导致错选A（所有区域都要戴，实际博物馆可摘下）或B（需要押金）。
questions.quote: There have been countless stories of workers being saved by helmets, which are the hard hats that you can see on the shelf beside you. So, visitors wearing helmets is mandatory in the mining area, although you are free to take them off when you're in the mining museum and picnic area. You won't need to pay any deposit, though you should return them to the counter once you finish the visit. The helmets are offered in all sizes, so choose a suitable one.

options.text: They must be worn in all areas.
A deposit is needed to borrow the hats.
They are available in all sizes.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about the outside area of the mine?
questions.explanation: 录音提醒大家注意外面的道路，因为地面还是湿的（still wet）会很滑，对应选项A。
questions.tip: 你听到“repaired”或“rough surface”时容易被选项带偏，但录音说的是道路刚才“已经”修好了，且是因为以前不平整才修的，B和C都是利用原词设置的陷阱。
questions.quote: Our mining community is currently being refurbished for some of the main area, so please make a note of that, and you'll know what to look out for. So, when you go in or out of the mine, please pay attention to the road, for it has just been repaired because of the rough surface and can be really slippery since it's still wet.

options.text: The ground is uneven in some area.

questions.prompt: Visitors who have difficulty in going up and down
questions.explanation: 录音提到如果上下攀爬有困难，可以向这里的工作人员求助（turn to the staff here），直接对应选项A。
questions.tip: 句子比较长时，你可能会因为没听懂完整意思而根据前面的“signs”或“all areas”乱选，甚至脑补出残障通道（ramp），一定要等转折词but后面的核心信息出现。
questions.quote: All areas are clearly posted with signs, but if you have problems traveling around or climbing up and down, you can turn to the staff here, and we are happy to help.

questions.prompt: What is prohibited everywhere?
questions.explanation: 录音直截了当地说明整个区域绝对禁止吸烟（smoking is forbidden throughout the whole community），对应选项A。
questions.tip: 你可能会在听到“phones”时因为注意力不集中以为是不让用，但紧接着录音明确说手机当然是可以使用的（of course, use them），直接排除了干扰项C。
questions.quote: I hope you'll enjoy the informative indoor presentation and this self-guided tour, but you have to bear one thing in mind, that smoking is forbidden throughout the whole community. Though you can take phones and, of course, use them, you'll also be surprised that there will be more than just one place to go in the mine.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about underground tunnels?
questions.explanation: 录音指出目前地下隧道只有相关工人才可以进入（only relevant workers can access it），说明目前进入受限，对应选项B。
questions.tip: 你在听到结尾的“protective clothing”和“mandatory”时，可能因为没看清选项的否定前缀而错选C，要特别留意unnecessary这种反向考查的干扰词。
questions.quote: The underground tunnel is now being refurbished and only relevant workers can access it. But it will soon be all finished, and I believe it's a lovely place for you to explore around. Don't forget to wear protective clothing. It's mandatory.

questions.quote: If you are interested in the laboratory where scientific experiments, analyses, and research are carried out, it is situated at the southern part of the park, opposite the shop. I bet you'll be happy to hear that this laboratory is also used for gold and crystal refinement, so don't miss this one for the sake of it.

questions.tip: 这句话前面铺垫了很长的美食描述，你很容易走神，导致错过了最后最关键的参照物“shop”和紧接其后的相对方位“next to”。
questions.quote: I assume by this time you'll all need some rest and refreshment, so we have an excellent café which caters for delicious food and beverages at the other side of the road next to the shop.

questions.prompt: Toilet
questions.explanation: 从野餐区继续往东走，有一条向北部延伸的道路（leading to the northern part），这条路的尽头就是厕所，对应字母E。

questions.quote: Of course, if you want to spend some time in the fresh air, we have a perfect picnic area which is just right and northeast of the reception block. Further east, there is a path leading to the northern part of the park, and at the end of it is the toilet.

questions.explanation: 录音明确指出专利申请非常复杂，没有专业人士的帮助（without professional help）是做不到的，直接对应选项D需要专家协助。
questions.tip: 录音中确实提到了“very costly”（非常昂贵），这就直接排除了选项G（申请便宜）。
questions.quote: Hmm, I did some research on patents. Right. A patent means no one else can financially benefit from your invention. Right. It seems to be very costly to apply for, so you really need to know what you've invented is worth going through all the rigmarole for. Well, I don't think it's something you can do without professional help.

questions.prompt: trademarks
questions.explanation: 录音中提到商标能为公司的价值增加数百万美元（add millions of dollars to how much a company's worth），这与选项F的“增加公司价值”是直接的同义替换。
questions.tip: 虽然接着提到了注册成本不高（doesn't seem to cost much），但这里讨论的最核心商业特征是品牌增值，切勿因为听到一点否定搭配就草率选G，导致主次不分。
questions.quote: Let's have a look at trademarks next. We are both quite familiar with these. I mean, just think how well-known the logos of some companies are. They seem to really instill trust in a brand, and so they add millions of dollars to how much a company's worth. And from what I've discovered, it doesn't seem to cost much to register trademarks either.

questions.prompt: design
questions.explanation: 录音里说大公司注册手机的外观设计是为了保持其独特性（remain quite distinctive），“distinctive”完美同义替换选项H的“unique”。
questions.tip: 读题要仔细，不要一听到“big corporations”就自行脑补这会增加公司价值（选项F），这里明确强调的是让产品外观（how something looks）与众不同。
questions.quote: Ah, design. This has quite a specific meaning as it relates to how something looks and not how it works. I read it's standard for the big corporations that make mobile phones to register the design of their handsets, so they remain quite distinctive.

questions.prompt: circuit
questions.explanation: 录音指出电路保护非常局限，只能在这个国家内执行（can only be enforced in this country），可以直接推导对应选项E“在海外不适用（not applicable overseas）”。
questions.tip: 录音中干扰信息多，你可能会听到“computer chips”这种生僻方向而发懵，但只要抓紧“only...in this country”这个地点限制条件，就能排除其他干扰。
questions.quote: You mean circuit? Well, circuits are a type of protection that safeguards original layout design for things like computer chips, so it's fairly narrow in its meaning, and it is quite limited as it can only be enforced in this country.

questions.prompt: trade secret
questions.explanation: 录音提到为了保守商业机密，必须确保所有员工都签署一份协议（sign an agreement），这直接命中选项A的“需要签署额外合同（sign an additional contract）”。
questions.tip: 录音前面特意提到了他们故意没有申请专利（not patented），所以不要因为听到专利相关背景就去错选需要专家协助（D）。
questions.quote: When I think of trade secrets, I immediately think of Granny May's Cookies. They've deliberately not patented their special recipe so that the other manufacturers don't know what the ingredients are. Hard for them to discover. Yeah, but it must be difficult to maintain a trade secret because you have to make sure that all staff sign an agreement and stick to it if they leave.

groups.instructions:
Complete the flow chart below.
Choose FOUR letters from A-H, next to question 27-30.
groups.content:
The process of intellectual property management
• Quarterly research report is written up by the {{27}} .
• Identify whether it is patentable.
• Deliver the report to {{28}} to make amendments.
• In the review meeting, {{29}} will check all the amendments.
• The final decision will be sent to {{30}} to analyze the cost of the whole process.

questions.explanation: 录音中清晰说到“quarterly research report”（季度研究报告）是由“The project leader”（项目负责人）制作的，直接得出对应选项F。
questions.tip: 此处有一个“Let me look at my notes”的小停顿干扰，你可能会在这个间隙断层导致没跟上录音，务必要稳住听到最后点出的核心身份。
questions.quote: Well, it all gets initiated by the quarterly research report. This is produced by the... Let me look at my notes. The project leader. They have to write up the report with details of how they are meeting their research deadlines.

questions.explanation: 录音提到把报告发给“commercialization committee”（商业化委员会），且他们会审查修改意见（amendments），稳准狠对应选项A。
questions.tip: 录音接着解释了该委员会由“program leader”和“industry representative”组成，你如果没看全选项、只抓到了后半截的补充说明，极容易踩坑错选E或G。
questions.quote: They send it on to the commercialization committee, which consists of the program leader and an industry representative. They review the report bearing amendments to the intellectual property.

questions.explanation: 录音提到在审查会议上，所有的修改意见都会被“delivery officer”（交付主管）汇总并过一遍（gone through），此处的officer与选项H的manager是职位头衔的同义替换。
questions.tip: 由于这里的选项词是delivery manager，而录音说的是delivery officer，你可能因为找不出一模一样的词而犹豫不敢选，记住雅思流程图经常出现类似身份名词的小替换。
questions.quote: Right. Then from that review meeting, all the amendments are brought together and gone through by the delivery officer, who works out the most beneficial way to register the intellectual property.

questions.explanation: 录音表明他们随后会让“business manager”（业务经理）知道决定的内容，并且指出这和随后的财务问题（financial issues）挂钩，完美对应选项B。
questions.tip: 录音在提到财务和商业问题（financial or commercial issues）时，实际上是在对流程图题干中的“analyze the cost”（分析成本）进行同义转换，一旦忽略了流程整体语义的对应，就会错失答案。
questions.quote: If I've got this right, they then let the business manager know what has been decided, and it's at this point that the intellectual property gets taken out of the control of the research area, and it becomes more to do with the financial or commercial issues of registration.

30.s: financial or commercial issues of registration

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of an environmental studies lecture about the possibility of using insects as a source of food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page eight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over the last few weeks, we've been talking about the challenges of producing food for the global population.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And, uh, there's been a lot of interest recently in new sources of food, and one of the most interesting is insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, why should insects be considered as a food source?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, for a start, a number of them are full of protein, and many also have certain vitamins, which may surprise you, more so than a typical farm animal, in fact.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And compared to farm animals, whose waste products contain a great deal of ammonia, the waste products of insects are far less acidic and would therefore do very little damage to the soil or to any of the rivers that run through farmland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, when it comes to the production of insects, the expense would be very low.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No trees need be chopped down or forest turned to pasture, so the space that they would occupy would be radically smaller than for, say, cows or sheep.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But even if some consumers decided that they'd rather not put insects in their shopping basket, we could also consider how insects might be added to animal feed, the food given to farm animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's already known that some insects, if they were part of the animal feed, would act as a sort of natural antibiotic within a cow or sheep's digestive system, thus removing the need for human intervention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This would be a cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative for farmers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, if consumers do decide that insects are a potential superfood, a way of feeding the world,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: then the next question is where do we source them from?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The wild, perhaps?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Or should they be bred on insect farms?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, if we take from the wild, one potential consequence of this is that too many will be taken, and in turn, a species could become endangered or extinct.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, for insects which are harvested from the wild, we have no way of knowing where they have been or what they have come in contact with, and this could have harmful consequences for human health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Imagine the scenario if food producers or retailers were supplied with insects that were carrying bacteria.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is not something we want to add to the food chain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If insects are bred on farms, the problems I've just outlined could be avoided.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And in many countries, it's already the case that demand for insects is growing, really growing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And it's not in rural areas where you'd expect, but, in fact, in the cities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Thailand, for example, where the demand has really shot up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, people in countries where insects are traditionally what people eat, they'll tell you that when insects are intensively farmed, their taste is simply not the same.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ironically, this is the same accusation that people have when it comes to the way that cows and sheep are raised.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Insect farmers also face a series of challenges, and researchers are keen to assist.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, when it comes to breeding, different insects have different requirements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For a start, it's essential to maintain a suitable temperature for many species to reproduce.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If this isn't right, nothing's going to happen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another problem is something that often happens when any species is bred in a confined space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And so far, researchers and farmers have not come up with any clear or long-term effective solution to it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're talking about the problem of disease.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You don't want a whole colony wiped out in one go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's also the question of where insects need to be kept.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If insects are to be bred as a superfood, then the tanks used to house them have to be better designed, and this has to happen so that cleaning takes up less time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If we're talking about mass production, we don't want this to be a time-consuming activity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, like I said before, insects have long been part of the diet in some countries, but not so in others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If farmers want to encourage people in, say, England or France or Germany to eat insects, then they're gonna have to develop a strategy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And I'm not talking about production, but marketing, something that'll persuade potential customers to try something different.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I've given you a general overview of the situation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let's look at some specific examples.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

sentences.text: Coffee originated around the Red Sea, most probably in Ethiopia in Africa, and there are records of coffee cultivation in Yemen as early as the 6th century.
By the 13th century, the growing, roasting and grinding of coffee to make a strong-flavoured infusion was widespread throughout the Arab world.
News of the drink was brought to Europe by traders, but people there were at first wary of the new drink.
However, Pope Clement the Eighth gave the drink his seal of approval after trying a cup for himself, and the trend quickly caught on.
The 17th century saw the spread of coffee drinking throughout Europe.
Coffee houses opened in Vienna, Paris and London, and they soon became the favourite meeting places of politicians, and were also known to attract artists of all kinds.
By the 18th century, coffee production was well established in Java in Indonesia and also throughout the Caribbean.
Coffee drinking continued to grow in popularity; one of the repercussions of the famous Boston Tea Party of 1773 was that the USA adopted coffee as its national beverage.
Today, coffee is drunk around the world, though each nation has its own ways of preparing and serving it.
Coffee is now grown in more than 50 countries, although production is not at all straightforward.
Because it is vulnerable to frost, coffee can only be grown successfully between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.
In addition, crop maintenance is labour intensive.
The plants require constant care and attention, and in most areas the picking is carried out by hand.
The ripe berry-like fruits which are harvested are called ‘cherries’.
These ripen over a period of six to eight months and turn a deep red when ripe, which explains their name.
Inside there are two green beans that have to be separated from the pulp and the skin, and dried.
This process is known as curing, and it can be done by one of two methods.
For the traditional ‘dry method’ of curing, the cherries are laid out in the sun until completely dry, and then the dried skins and pulp are removed from the beans.
The ‘wet method’ is a more recent development and it is employed for high-quality hand-picked cherries.
The outer, fleshy layer is removed, then the cherries are soaked and fermented, followed by washing and drying.
Finally, the skins are removed by a machine, revealing the green beans.
In both cases, the green beans are sorted, graded and packed for export.
Roasting tends to be done in the country of import.
The roasting process is necessary to reduce the acidity of the beans and to develop the aromatic oils, which give the coffee its aroma and flavour.
Finally, grinding exposes a larger surface area to the water, ensuring optimum contact between the ground beans and the water, resulting in a more satisfying cup of coffee.
The flavour, character and quality of coffee varies tremendously – not only between countries, but also between estates within the same country.
The soil, altitude and climate are all factors that contribute to the character of the bean, thereby affecting the final taste.
There are four varieties of coffee plant, but only two are sold on any commercial scale.
The most important of these is coffea arabica, which grows on steep mountain slopes at high altitudes.
The arabica bean produces coffee that is rich, aromatic and full of flavour, and it accounts for 70% of world coffee production.
Coffee experts agree that the arabica bean is far superior in flavour to other types.
The other main variety, coffea canephora, produces the coffee bean known as robusta.
Grown on the lower slopes, where cultivation is easier, robusta beans have a higher caffeine content than arabica beans, and a rougher, almost earthy flavour that lacks delicacy and subtlety.
It costs about half the price of arabica and is used in the cheaper blends of both fresh and instant coffee.
There are three types of instant coffee.
The cheapest is made from robusta beans that have been brewed into a concentrate.
This is sprayed into a stream of hot air that instantly evaporates all moisture, leaving a fine powder.
Some of the spray-dried powders undergo further heating to produce granular coffees; the better ones include some arabica beans.
The best instant coffees are freeze-dried.
For these, an arabica coffee concentrate is frozen and processed in a vacuum to produce crisp, dry particles of coffee.
Caffeine is a stimulant that is present in coffee.
It makes the nervous system more active, which is usually the desired effect.
However, it can cause sleeplessness and therefore some consumers prefer to buy coffee without caffeine.
Decaffeinated coffee is available in all the regular coffee forms: whole beans, ground or instant.
Caffeine is removed by soaking the beans in water, or by the use of solvents or carbon dioxide.
The latter is thought to be the best method as it does not affect the flavour and there is no residue.
To qualify as decaffeinated, coffee must contain less than 0.9% caffeine.

questions.prompt: Ripe coffee fruits are called cherries because of their colour.
questions.explanation: 题目说咖啡果因为颜色被称为cherries，原文明确提到它们成熟时变成深红色，这就解释了名字的由来。

questions.quote: The roasting process is necessary to reduce the acidity of the beans and to develop the aromatic oils, which give the coffee its aroma and flavour.

questions.prompt: Arabica coffee is harder to grow than robusta coffee.

questions.quote: The other main variety, coffea canephora, produces the coffee bean known as robusta. Grown on the lower slopes, where cultivation is easier, robusta beans have a higher caffeine content than arabica beans, and a rougher, almost earthy flavour that lacks delicacy and subtlety.

sentences.text: A Dark chocolate is gaining a reputation as a heart-healthy food, and research suggests that there might be some substance behind those claims.

Ginger Hultin, owner of Champagne Nutrition in Seattle and a spokesperson for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics says, "Cocoa contains antioxidants in addition to magnesium, potassium, zinc, and iron.
Plus, studies have shown that there could be some benefit to consuming chocolate or cocoa for the cardiovascular system, including potentially lowering blood pressure."
B Dark chocolate's health benefits come from its cocoa – specifically its cocoa flavanols.
Flavanols are a type of polyphenol, and polyphenols are one group of phytochemicals.
Many fruits and vegetables contain flavanols, but they are especially rich in tea, wine, and cocoa.
During digestion, cocoa is broken down into smaller chemical compounds.
Some research suggests that these compounds have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties and may help protect against cardiovascular disease, which affects both the heart and brain.

For example, research has found that even two weeks of eating dark chocolate or other flavanol-rich cocoa products is better than a placebo for lowering blood pressure in people who already have high blood pressure.
C Not all chocolate is created equal, however.
Milk chocolate and white chocolate undergo more processing and contain far less cocoa solids, meaning they have fewer flavanols.
Additionally, dairy products added to milk chocolate may interfere with the absorption of antioxidants.
To obtain meaningful health benefits, consumers should look for dark chocolate with at least 70% cocoa content.
Even then, the exact flavanol content is rarely listed on packaging, as manufacturers have no legal obligation to provide this information.
Some specialist brands now produce high-flavanol chocolate, but these products tend to be significantly more expensive than regular dark chocolate.
D The quantity of chocolate needed to produce health benefits has been a matter of debate.
Several studies have suggested that consuming 20 to 30 grams of dark chocolate per day – roughly two to three small squares – is associated with the greatest cardiovascular benefits.
Consuming more than this amount may add extra calories, sugar, and saturated fat without providing additional protective effects.
One large observational study involving over 20,000 participants found that those who ate modest amounts of dark chocolate had a 12% lower risk of developing heart disease compared to non-consumers.

However, the same study noted that people who ate chocolate daily also tended to have higher overall calorie intakes and were more likely to be sedentary, suggesting that correlation does not necessarily equal causation.
E Researchers have also investigated dark chocolate's potential effects on cognitive function and mood.
A small randomised trial conducted in Italy gave healthy adults either high-flavanol chocolate or low-flavanol chocolate for five days.
Those receiving high-flavanol chocolate performed better on visual memory tests and reported feeling less mental fatigue.

Similarly, a study from Australia found that regular consumption of dark chocolate was associated with lower odds of clinical depression, though the authors cautioned that people with depression might simply turn to chocolate as a form of self-comfort.
Further research with larger sample sizes is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.
F Despite the promising evidence, experts urge caution against overconsumption.
Dark chocolate remains a calorie-dense food, typically containing around 600 calories per 100 grams.
Excessive intake can contribute to weight gain, which in turn raises the risk of diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease – the very conditions that moderate consumption may help prevent.
Furthermore, some dark chocolate products contain high levels of heavy metals such as lead and cadmium, which accumulate in the body over time and can damage the kidneys and nervous system.
Consumer advocacy groups have called for stricter regulation and mandatory testing of heavy metal levels in cocoa products.

G In conclusion, while dark chocolate cannot be considered a medicine, incorporating a small amount into a balanced diet appears to offer genuine health benefits, particularly for cardiovascular health.
The key is moderation, attention to cocoa percentage, and awareness of potential contaminants.
As Ginger Hultin notes, "Dark chocolate is not a magic bullet, but it can be a pleasant and potentially beneficial part of an overall healthy eating pattern."

sentences.text: According to game theory, our chances of success in negotiations are based on the choices of others.
Computer models have been developed to work out how events will unfold as people and organisations act in what they perceive to be their own best interests.
Numerical values are placed on the goals, motivations and influence of players, and likely options are considered.
Game-theory software then evaluates the ability of each of those players to influence others, and hence predicts the course of events.
Although many individuals would feel uncomfortable having a computer make decisions for them, many organisations run such computer simulations for law firms, companies and governments.
But feeding software with accurate data on all the players involved is especially tricky for political matters.

Reinier van Oosten of Decide, a Dutch firm that models political negotiations, notes that predictions may become unreliable when people unexpectedly give in to ‘non-rational emotions’, such as hatred, rather than pursuing what is apparently in their best interests.
However, sorting out people’s motivations is much easier when making money is the main object.
Accordingly, modelling behaviour using game theory is proving especially useful when applied to economics.
Using game-theory software to model auctions can be very lucrative.
Consulting firms are entering the market to help clients design profitable auctions, or to win them less expensively.

In 2006, in the run-up to an online auction of radio-spectrum licences by America’s Federal Communications Commission, Dr Paul Milgrom, a consultant and Stanford University professor in the United States, customised his game-theory software to assist a consortium of bidders.
He was apprehensive at first, but the result was a triumph.
When the auction began, Milgrom’s software tracked competitors’ bids to estimate their budgets for the 1,132 licences on offer.
Crucially, the software estimated the secret values bidders placed on specific licences, and determined that certain big licences were being over-valued.
Milgrom’s clients were then directed to obtain a collection of smaller, less-expensive licences instead.
Two of his clients paid about a third less than their competitors for an equivalent amount of spectrum, saving almost $1.2 billion.
Such a saving makes one wonder why everyone isn’t using game-theory software.
And, if they were, how would that affect the game?
PA Consulting, a British firm, designs models for software based on game theory to help its clients solve specific problems in areas from pharmaceuticals to the production of television shows.
British government agencies have asked PA Consulting to build models to test zoning rules that govern how many of a certain type of business should be allowed to operate in one area.
To give a simple example: if two competing ice-cream sellers share a long beach, they will set up stalls back-to-back in the middle and stay put, explains Dr Stephen Black, a modeller for PA.
Unfortunately for potential customers at the far ends of the beach, each seller prevents the other from relocating—no other spot would be closer to more people.
Introduce a third seller, however, and the stifling equilibrium is broken as relocations and pricing changes energise the market.
By studying a chain of events such as this, software designers can assess the effect of change and see the patterns in possible outcomes that may occur.
As a result, the use of modelling makes clients more inclined to look at future repercussions when making business decisions, Black says.
Where is all this heading?
Alongside the increasingly elaborate modelling software, there are also efforts to develop software that can assist in negotiation and mediation.
Two decades ago, Dr Clara Ponsatí, a Spanish academic, came up with a clever idea.
She accepted that, as negotiators everywhere know, the first side to disclose the maximum amount that it is willing to pay loses considerable bargaining power.
Without leverage, it can be pushed backward in the bargaining process by a clever opponent.
But if neither side reveals the concessions it is prepared to make, negotiations can become very slow or collapse.
However, difficult negotiations can often be pushed along by neutral mediators, especially if they are entrusted with the secret bottom lines of all parties.
Ponsatí’s idea was that if a human mediator was not trusted, affordable or available, a computer could do the job instead.
Negotiating parties would update the software with the confidential information on their bargaining positions after each round of talks.
Once positions on both sides were no longer mutually exclusive, the software would be used to split the difference and propose an agreement.

Ponsatí, now head of the Institute of Economic Analysis at the Autonomous University of Barcelona in Spain, says such ‘mediation machines’ could be employed to push negotiations forward by unlocking information that would otherwise be withheld from an opponent.
Could mediation which has been achieved using software based on game theory spread from auction bids and utility pricing to resolving political and military disputes?
Today’s game-theory software is not yet sufficiently advanced to mediate between warring countries.
But one day opponents on the brink of war might be tempted to use it to exchange information without having to engage in conflict.
According to some game theorists, opponents could learn how a war would turn out, skip the fighting and strike a deal.
Over-optimistic, perhaps—but game theorists do have rather an impressive track record when it comes to predicting the future.

questions.quote: Ponsatí, now head of the Institute of Economic Analysis at the Autonomous University of Barcelona in Spain, says such ‘mediation machines’ could be employed to push negotiations forward by unlocking information that would otherwise be withheld from an opponent.

transcript.text: Part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a discussion between Fiona, who is the head of a college drama department, and a new tutor called Ed, who is preparing to run a voice coaching workshop for drama students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ed, well, I'm delighted that you've joined the drama department.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, part of my job is to support you during your probationary year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's ensure that you're clear about what you'll be doing in the first voice coaching workshop you run next week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'll be observing you working with the students as you show them how to project their voices on stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll be evaluating how you cope with the practical activities as well as the theory, and if all goes well, you'll then have finished the final stage of your voice coach diploma.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That'd be great, Fiona.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Anyway, I've thought through the workshop, and I've done a plan to highlight the key areas I intend to cover.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's look at your plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so let's see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm glad you've thought about seating patterns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You say you want to begin with the students sitting in star-shaped patterns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's fine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are various seating patterns you can use at this stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I like trainees sitting cross-legged in a circle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other people like students in rows.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But actually, all these can be represented diagrammatically, which would be clearer than going into lots of detailed explanations like you've done here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But it doesn't matter which one I use at the beginning of a workshop?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's whatever you feel comfortable with.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So in the initial phase, I explain the objectives of the session.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then in the first activity, you say they should quickly rise, walk briskly around the room, weaving in and out to avoid each other.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I think it's important that they don't get in each other's way and that they learn to move within a confined space, aware of other people, but primarily concentrating on their own thoughts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Absolutely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in your plan, you've omitted to mention that in the second activity, you will get the students to pair off.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So you need to rethink that section and include reasons why it's essential for them to listen to each other talking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It doesn't matter what they actually say, and at the same time, get them to think about their posture because that governs their lung capacity and most crucially, their breathing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Will do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, a common issue in the UK is that we rehearse in small rooms, then transfer to a larger stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So bearing in mind that voice projection is not shouting, later in the course, you'll need to work in a much bigger space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Does it have to be an enclosed space?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I, I suppose it does because ultimately they're going to work in a theater.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Ideally, an enclosed space, but there's no reason why you couldn't go somewhere outdoors, although I'd avoid a very public space like a park.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, your next activity on how to convey emotion on stage is fine, but your selection of texts for the students to experience emotional depth leaves a little to be desired.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's not enough to include a few extracts that you find enjoyable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You need to consider the different kind of emotion that each extract should present, from sorrow through to ecstasy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Classical stuff is all well and good, but include many more contemporary sources.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I understand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, out of the twenty books you list, some are more useful than others, and I think you should flag up the disadvantages so that people don't waste money buying them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Take Vocal Instruction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I know I recommended it for you to read for its historical perspective, but bear in mind it was written thirty years ago, and it shows.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yeah, agreed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I thought Improve Your Accent was interesting, but it's very narrow in its outlook, don't you think?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, I'm not sure it's interesting [chuckles] .
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And another one you need to warn people about is The Actor's Handbook.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's an expensive book, very useful, but according to the publishers, they're going to reissue it with new color photos, and at the moment, it's out of print.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There aren't any second-hand copies out there, so tell them not to waste time looking for it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I didn't know that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There's one more that I want to mention, and that's Confident Voice Delivery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It exaggerates its claims on how to be successful to such an extent that I think it is positively misleading.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But maybe I'm biased.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: [chuckles] Okay, I'll make a note of that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So the others...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part three.

groups.instructions:
What disadvantage do the speakers identify for each of the following textbooks?
Choose FOUR correct answers, A-G, next to questions 27–30.

questions.prompt: Vocal Instruction
questions.explanation: Fiona 评价这本书是三十年前写的，“并且能明显看出来（and it shows）”，这说明它的内容已经过时了。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为听到“historical perspective”觉得它有历史价值是个优点，但这道匹配题要选的是缺点（disadvantages），后半句的“三十年前写的”才是对其缺点的最终定性。
questions.quote: Take Vocal Instruction. I know I recommended it for you to read for its historical perspective, but bear in mind it was written thirty years ago, and it shows.

questions.prompt: Improve Your Accent
questions.explanation: Ed 直接评价这本书的视野“非常狭窄（very narrow in its outlook）”，直接等同于选项中的 too limited。
questions.tip: 听到前半句的“interesting”时不要急着下定论，紧跟在转折词 but 后面的内容才是这段话要表达的核心缺点。
questions.quote: I thought Improve Your Accent was interesting, but it's very narrow in its outlook, don't you think?

questions.prompt: Actors' Handbook
questions.explanation: Fiona 提到这本书目前绝版了（out of print），且外面没有二手书（aren't any secondhand copies），所以目前是买不到的（unavailable）。
questions.tip: 你一开始听到“expensive”很容易秒选 A，但接着听会发现他们马上要出新版了，现在市面上根本买不到，所以对于学生来说核心缺点已经变成了“买不到”，不能再去浪费时间找。
questions.quote: And another one you need to warn people about is The Actor's Handbook. It's an expensive book, very useful, but according to the publishers, they're going to reissue it with new color photos, and at the moment it's out of print. There aren't any secondhand copies out there, so tell them not to waste time looking for it.

questions.prompt: Confident Voice Delivery
questions.explanation: Fiona 认为这本书在宣传如何成功时夸大了说辞（exaggerates its claims），简直起到了误导的作用，对应选项中的“不切实际的（unrealistic）”。
questions.tip: 夸大其词（exaggerates）是这道题唯一的同义替换关键，这里没有太多干扰项，核心就是要准确抓取并理解这个词的情感色彩。

transcript.text: I'd like to begin this course with a few remarks about good insects and bad ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Bugs are all around us, and that's both a benefit and an annoyance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Sometimes maybe even serious harm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, let's talk about the good things that insects do for us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Probably the most important insect for humans, and maybe for all other life, is the bee.

transcript.text: Bees help plants in the process of pollination, and thus are necessary to most flowering plants and fruit trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is, they carry pollen from male flowers to female.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In fact, there would be no we.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: No lesser thinker than Albert Einstein pointed out that without bees, humanity would be dead within a year or less.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We'd starve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's that simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That should maybe make us just a little humble.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A little less dramatic is the fact that bees also make the honey we eat, and they produce beeswax, which is useful in candles and is also used as a first-rate polish for furniture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

sentences.text: Roald Amundsen, the Norwegian explorer celebrated for navigating the Arctic’s Northwest Passage in 1906, turned his sights southward in 1911 to claim the ultimate exploratory prize--the South Pole.
Although meticulously planned, his expedition pivoted on chance when he learned of Robert Peary’s disputed claim to the North Pole.
To secure fame and funding, Amundsen secretly redirected his goal.
Competing against Captain Robert Falcon Scott’s British team in a race to the Pole, he endured extreme cold, frostbite, and setbacks but demonstrated calm leadership and precise planning.
On December 14, 1911, Amundsen and his team reached the South Pole, leaving behind letters for King Haakon VII and Scott.
His success, founded on dog-pulled sleds, discipline, and scientific precision, contrasted with Scott’s tragic failure.
Amundsen’s triumph symbolised a new era in exploration--where mastery of detail, efficiency, and foresight replaced romantic endurance as the mark of true achievement.
Amundsen’s preparations were exhaustive.
He meticulously studied the methods of indigenous Arctic peoples and polar veterans, choosing dog sleds over ponies and motor sledges, which Scott relied on.
Amundsen’s team consisted of experienced skiers and dog handlers, and his route was carefully mapped using previous expeditions’ data.
He established a series of supply depots along the route to the Pole, marked by tall black flags to ensure safe return.
This logistical foresight proved crucial, as it allowed his team to travel lighter and faster on the final push.
In contrast, Scott’s expedition, though brave and well-intentioned, was plagued by poor planning and misfortune.
Scott’s reliance on motorised sledges, which broke down, and ponies, which could not withstand the extreme cold, slowed his progress.
His team man-hauled their sledges for much of the journey, exhausting themselves.
Despite reaching the Pole on January 17, 1912, they discovered Amundsen’s tent and Norwegian flag already planted there.
Disheartened and weakened, Scott and his four companions perished on the return journey, just 11 miles from a supply depot.
The legacy of the two expeditions highlights a shift in exploration philosophy.
Amundsen approached the challenge as a technical problem to be solved with careful preparation and respect for the environment.
Scott, in the tradition of British heroic exploration, emphasized perseverance and moral courage but underestimated the Antarctic’s harsh realities.
Amundsen’s success was not merely a geographical conquest but a demonstration of modern, systematic exploration.
His methods influenced future polar and scientific expeditions, embedding the principle that survival and success depend as much on planning and adaptability as on bravery.

sentences.text: A The world's great deserts were formed by natural processes interacting over long intervals of time.
During most of these times, deserts have grown and shrunk independent of human activities.
Paleodeserts, large sand seas now inactive because they are stabilized by vegetation, extend well beyond the present margins of core deserts, such as the Sahara.
In some regions, deserts are separated sharply from surrounding, less arid areas by mountains and other contrasting landforms that reflect basic structural differences in the regional geology.
In other areas, desert fringes form a gradual transition from a dry to a more humid environment, making it more difficult to define the desert border.
B These transition zones have very fragile, delicately balanced ecosystems.
Desert fringes often are a mosaic of microclimates.
Small hollows support vegetation that picks up heat from the hot winds and protects the land from the prevailing winds.
After rainfall, the vegetated areas are distinctly cooler than the surroundings.
In these marginal areas, human activity may stress the ecosystem beyond its tolerance limit, resulting in degradation of the land.

By ponding the soil with their hooves, livestock compact the substrate, increase the proportion of fine material, and reduce the percolation rate of the soil, thus encouraging erosion by wind and water.
Grazing and the collection of firewood reduce or eliminate plants that help to bind the soil.
C This degradation of formerly productive land—desertification—is a complex process.
It involves multiple causes, and it proceeds at varying rates in different climates.
Desertification may intensify a general climatic trend toward greater aridity, or it may initiate a change in local climate.
D Desertification does not occur in linear, easily mappable patterns.
Deserts advance erratically, forming patches on their borders.
Areas far from natural deserts can degrade quickly to barren soil, rock, or sand through poor land management.
The presence of a nearby desert has no direct relationship to desertification.
Unfortunately, an area undergoing desertification is brought to public attention only after the process is well underway.
Often little or no data are available to indicate the previous state of the ecosystem or the rate of degradation.
Scientists still question whether desertification, as a process of global change, is permanent or how and when it can be halted or reversed.

E Desertification became well known in the 1930s when part of the Great Plains in the United States turned into the "Dust Bowl" as a result of drought and poor practices in farming, although the term itself was not used until almost 1950.
During the Dust Bowl period, millions of people were forced to abandon their farms and livelihoods.

Greatly improved methods of agriculture and land and water management in the Great Plains have prevented that disaster from recurring, but desertification presently affects millions of people on almost every continent.
Increased population and livestock pressure on marginal lands have accelerated desertification.
In some areas, nomads moving to less arid areas disrupt the local ecosystem and increase the rate of erosion of the land.
Nomads are trying to escape the desert, but because of their land-use practices, they are bringing the desert with them.
F It is a misconception that drought causes desertification.
Droughts are common in arid and semiarid lands.
Well-managed lands can recover from drought when the rains return.
Continued land abuse during droughts, however, increases land degradation.

By 1973, the drought that began in 1968 in the Sahel of West Africa and the land-use practices there had caused the deaths of more than 100,000 people and 12 million cattle, as well as the disruption of social organizations from villages to the national level.
G At the local level, individuals and governments can help to reclaim and protect their lands.
In areas of sand dunes, covering the dunes with large boulders or petroleum will interrupt the wind regime near the face of the dunes and prevent the sand from moving.
Sand fences are used throughout the Middle East and the United States, in the same way snow fences are used in the north.
Placement of straw grids, each up to a square meter in area, will also decrease the surface wind velocity.
Shrubs and trees planted within the grids are protected by the straw until they take root.

Sand that manages to pass through the grass belts can be caught in strips of trees planted as windbreaks 50 to 100 meters apart adjacent to the belts.
Small plots of trees may also be scattered inside oases to stabilize the area.

sentences.text: A Photography gained the interest of many scientists and artists from its inception.
Scientists have used photography to record and study movements, such as Eadweard Muybridge’s study of human and animal locomotion in 1887.
Artists are equally interested by these aspects but also try to explore avenues other than the photo-mechanical representation of reality, such as the pictorialist movement.
Military, police, and security forces use photography for surveillance, recognition and data storage.
Photography is used by amateurs to preserve memories, to capture special moments, to tell stories, to send messages, and as a source of entertainment.
Various technological improvements and techniques have even allowed for visualising events that are too fast or too slow for the human eye.
B One of such techniques is called fast motion or professionally known as time-lapse.
Time-lapse photography is the perfect technique for capturing events and movements in the natural world that occur over a timescale too slow for human perception to follow.
The life cycle of a mushroom, for example, is incredibly subtle to the human eye.

To present its growth in front of audiences, the principle applied is a simple one: a series of photographs are taken and used in sequence to make a moving-image film, but since each frame is taken with a lapse at a time interval between each shot, when played back at normal speed, a continuous action is produced and it appears to speed up.
Put simply: we are shrinking time.
Objects and events that would normally take several minutes, days or even months can be viewed to completion in seconds having been sped up by factors of tens to millions.
C Another commonly used technique is high-speed photography, the science of taking pictures of very fast phenomena.
High-speed photography can be considered to be the opposite of time-lapse photography.
One of the many applications is found in biology studies to study birds, bats and even spider silk.
Imagine a hummingbird hovering almost completely still in the air, feeding on nectar.
With every flap, its wings bend, flex and change shape.
These subtle movements precisely control the lift its wings generate, making it an excellent hoverer.
But a hummingbird flaps its wings up to 80 times every second.
The only way to truly capture this motion is with cameras that will, in effect, slow down time.
To do this, a greater length of film is taken at a high sampling frequency or frame rate, which is much faster than it will be projected on screen.
When replayed at normal speed, time appears to be slowed down proportionately.
That is why high-speed cameras have become such a mainstay of biology.

D In common usage, high-speed photography can also refer to the use of high-speed cameras that the photograph itself may be taken in a way as to appear to freeze the motion, especially to reduce motion blur.
It requires a sensor with good sensitivity and either a very good shuttering system or a very fast strobe light.
The recent National Geographic footage—captured last summer during an intensive three-day shoot at the Cincinnati Zoo—is unprecedented in its clarity and detail.
“I’ve watched cheetahs run for 30 years,” said Cathryn Hilker, founder of the zoo’s Cat Ambassador Program.
“But I saw things in that super slow-motion video that I’ve never seen before.”
The slow-motion video is entrancing.
Every part of the sprinting cat’s anatomy—supple limbs, rippling muscles, hyperflexible spine—works together in a symphony of speed, revealing the fluid grace of the world’s fastest land animal.
E But things can’t get any more complicated in the case of filming a frog catching its prey.
Frogs can snatch up prey in a few thousandths of a second—striking out with elastic tongues.
Biologists would love to see how a frog’s tongue roll out, adhere to prey, and roll back into the frog’s mouth.
But this all happened too fast, 50 times faster than an eye blink.
So naturally people thought of using high-speed camera to capture this fantastic movement in slow motion.
Yet one problem still remains—viewers would be bored if they watch the frog swim in slow motion for too long.
So how to skip this?
The solution is a simple one—adjust the playback speed, which is also called by some the film speed adjustment.

The film will originally be shot at a high frame (often 300 frames per second, because it can be converted to much lower frame rates without major issues), but at later editing stage this high frame rate will only be preserved for the prey catching part, while the swimming part will be converted to the normal speed at 24 frames per second.
Voila, the scientists can now sit back and enjoy watching without having to go through the pain of waiting.
F Sometimes taking a good picture or shooting a good film is not all about technology, but patience, like in the case of bat.
Bats are small, dark-colored; they fly fast and are active only at night.
To capture bats on film, one must use some type of camera-tripping device.
Photographers or film-makers often place camera near the bat cave, on the path of the flying bats.

The camera must be hard-wired with a tripping device so that every time a bat breaks the tripping beam the camera fires and it will keep doing so through the night until the camera’s battery runs out.
Though highly-advanced tripping device can now allow for unmanned shooting, it still may take several nights lo get a truly high quality film.
G Is it science?
Is it art?
Since the technique was first pioneered around two hundred years ago, photography has developed to a state where it is almost unrecognisable.
Some people would even say the future of photography will be nothing like how we imagine it.
No matter what future it may hold, photography will continue to develop as it has been repeatedly demonstrated in many aspects of our life that “a picture is worth a thousand words.”

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear an engineering student giving a presentation about a research project on design features of the International Space Station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For my presentation, I'm going to summarize the findings of a research project on life aboard the International Space Station in the early days of its operation, its teething problems as it were.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'll start by giving a little background information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The space station crew were essentially a constantly changing team of scientists from different countries who lived on the space station for several months at a time, and they conducted a number of experiments, including some studies of living conditions in space, which is what I'm going to be looking at now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So what was life like on board in the very confined conditions of the space station?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, the early impressions recorded by the astronauts were very different from what people had expected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They'd expected that the air would smell stale or artificial, but the astronauts found that it was fresh.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So that was one very positive finding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And although they were in such a confined space and people worried that it would get very hot, in fact, they found that it was very easy to turn the temperature up or down in order to keep it within a comfortable range.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The feedback on the food was also positive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Astronauts on previous space stations had described the meals as boring, but the International Space Station meals were praised for their variety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So that was another good piece of feedback.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And something which is taken for granted today, but was a key morale booster in those days, was communication between the space station and Earth, which the astronauts said was clear and reliable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So in the early days, it seems that the mood was overall very positive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: However, after a few days, the difficulties and frustrations became clearer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Above all, the crew complained about the constant noise caused by the air filters, which used to rattle and buzz twenty-four hours a day, interrupting their sleep.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As well as that, the astronauts complained that the Velcro fasteners, which were positioned all over the station, didn't work well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And so a lot of the time, objects weren't secure in the cabin, but floated about.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: A particularly serious problem was that the systems used on the space station had been developed in a number of different countries, and they didn't always work well together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: For example, it was impossible to mix the water produced from different systems because it contained different sorts of preservatives, and these reacted together and blocked the pipes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Another problem was connected to repairs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: At the best of times, these took up an inordinate amount of time on the station, and the crew complained that many of the tools that they'd been provided with weren't suitable for the jobs they had to do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So they had to improvise, which meant that jobs took a lot longer than they needed to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Another related problem was to do with access to equipment that needed maintaining.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Because the instructions on the equipment were often located in places where they were difficult to read, like on the back of equipment, it was often difficult or impossible to read them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So having identified these problems, the researchers came up with a number of suggestions about how conditions could be improved on subsequent missions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: First, it became clear that although there had been a great deal of consultation with the crews, the systems and equipment on the space station needed much more wide-ranging testing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then the whole issue of language training came under review.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Astronauts from different countries had to be able to talk to the controllers on Earth and to understand them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, although they'd had extensive language training, the astronauts sometimes had problems comprehending what was said because they weren't familiar with the accent of the speaker, and this sometimes led to quite dangerous misunderstandings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Finally, and this is the point I found most surprising, the researchers felt that the designers of the space station were paying too much attention to safety rather than considering operating issues.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is, how the station could be run comfortably and smoothly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And the recommendation was to make changes here at quite a fundamental level.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So those were the main points I covered in the...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0
