questions.explanation: 录音提到人们本来预期空气味道会不好，但宇航员发现空气其实很“fresh”（清新），直接填入即可。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了stale（污浊的）或者artificial（人造的），但那是人们“预期的（expected）”错误情况，要注意听后面的转折词but，它引出的才是真实的答案。
questions.quote: Well, the early impressions recorded by the astronauts were very different from what people had expected. They'd expected that the air would smell stale or artificial, but the astronauts found that it was fresh. So that was one very positive finding.

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到国际空间站的餐食因为其“variety”（多样性）而受到赞扬，这和题目里“有足够的……”完美对应。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了boring，但录音明确说那是“之前的空间站（previous space stations）”的食物，做题时千万不要张冠李戴。
questions.quote: The feedback on the food was also positive. Astronauts on previous space stations had described the meals as boring, but the International Space Station meals were praised for their variety. So that was another good piece of feedback.

questions.explanation: 录音提到空间站和地球之间的“communication”（通讯）非常清晰可靠（clear and reliable），也就是题目所说的efficient（高效）。
questions.tip: 你可能会在录音里死等efficient这个词，但雅思最喜欢用同义替换（比如用clear and reliable来替换），做填空题一定要理解整体语义。
questions.quote: And something which is taken for granted today, but was a key morale booster in those days, was communication between the space station and Earth, which the astronauts said was clear and reliable. So in the early days, it seems that the mood was overall very positive.

questions.explanation: 录音明确说到空气过滤器会24小时发出噪音，“interrupting their sleep”（打断他们的睡眠），也就是题目里问的导致了lack of sleep（缺乏睡眠）。
questions.tip: 你可能会想填noise，但题干前面已经有caused（导致）了，空气过滤器的问题导致的结果是“缺乏睡眠”，一定要看清题目的因果关系。
questions.quote: However, after a few days, the difficulties and frustrations became clearer. Above all, the crew complained about the constant noise caused by the air filters, which used to rattle and buzz twenty-four hours a day, interrupting their sleep.

questions.explanation: 录音举例说没法混合不同系统产生的“water”（水），因为里面含有不同的防腐剂（preservatives），对应题目“混合……时遇到问题”。
questions.tip: 这个答案其实给得很直接，容易错是因为你可能会被后面紧跟着出现的一大串复杂生词（如preservatives）分散注意力，导致大脑空白忘了写答案。
questions.quote: A particularly serious problem was that the systems used on the space station had been developed in a number of different countries, and they didn't always work well together. For example, it was impossible to mix the water produced from different systems because it contained different sorts of preservatives, and these reacted together and blocked the pipes.

questions.explanation: 录音提到宇航员抱怨提供给他们的很多“tools”（工具）不适合他们要干的活（weren't suitable），完美对应题目“提供的……不总是适合其目的”。
questions.tip: 你可能会填repairs或jobs，但题目缺的是一个能够“被提供、被使用（available）且不适合”的具体物品名词，要精准捕捉“tools... weren't suitable”这个搭配。
questions.quote: Another problem was connected to repairs. At the best of times, these took up an inordinate amount of time on the station, and the crew complained that many of the tools that they'd been provided with weren't suitable for the jobs they had to do. So they had to improvise, which meant that jobs took a lot longer than they needed to.

questions.explanation: 录音里说设备上的“instructions”（说明书）经常贴在设备背面等难读的地方，对应题目“难以获取设备的……”。
questions.tip: 你可能光顾着听equipment（设备）去了，但题目问的是“难以获取设备的什么”，录音明确说难读到的是instructions，一定要抓准句子的核心主语。
questions.quote: Another related problem was to do with access to equipment that needed maintaining. Because the instructions on the equipment were often located in places where they were difficult to read, like on the back of equipment, it was often difficult or impossible to read them.

questions.explanation: 录音提到系统和设备需要更多广泛的（wide-ranging）“testing”（测试），这里的wide-ranging直接同义替换了题目中的extensive（广泛的）。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了consultation（咨询），但这出现在although（尽管）引导的让步状语从句里，是已经做过的事，真正的建议和重点永远在主句里。
questions.quote: So having identified these problems, the researchers came up with a number of suggestions about how conditions could be improved on subsequent missions. First, it became clear that although there had been a great deal of consultation with the crews, the systems and equipment on the space station needed much more wide-ranging testing.

questions.explanation: 录音指出宇航员有时候理解困难，是因为对说话人的“accent”（口音）不熟悉，对应题目“需要练习听懂控制员的……”。
questions.tip: 你可能一听到language training就想填language，但这只是引入的大话题，往下听具体导致“听不懂（comprehending）”的原因其实是对accent不熟。
questions.quote: Then the whole issue of language training came under review. Astronauts from different countries had to be able to talk to the controllers on Earth and to understand them. Now, although they'd had extensive language training, the astronauts sometimes had problems comprehending what was said because they weren't familiar with the accent of the speaker, and this sometimes led to quite dangerous misunderstandings.

questions.explanation: 录音里提到设计师在“safety”（安全）上放了太多注意力（paying too much attention to），这也就是建议中应该减少强调（less emphasis on）的部分。
questions.tip: 你可能听到operating issues就想当答案填进去，但录音里说的是应该多考虑（rather than considering）操作问题，而对安全关注太多，理清这层对比关系才不会填反。
questions.quote: Finally, and this is the point I found most surprising, the researchers felt that the designers of the space station were paying too much attention to safety rather than considering operating issues. That is, how the station could be run comfortably and smoothly. And the recommendation was to make changes here at quite a fundamental level.

sentences.text: A FIRE and flood are two of humanity's worst nightmares.
People have, therefore, always sought to control them.
Forest fires are snuffed out quickly.
The flow of rivers is regulated by weirs and dams.
At least, that is how it used to be.
But foresters have learned that forests need fires to clear out the brush and even to get seeds to germinate.
And a similar revelation is now dawning on hydrologists.
Rivers – and the ecosystems they support – need floods.
That is why a man-made torrent has been surging down the Grand Canyon.
By Thursday, March 6th it was running at full throttle, which was expected to be sustained for 60 hours.
B Floods once raged through the canyon every year.
Spring Snow from as far away as Wyoming would melt and swell the Colorado river to a flow that averaged around 1,500 cubic metres (50,000 cubic feet) a second.
Every eight years or so, that figure rose to almost 3,000 cubic metres.
These floods infused the river with sediment, carved its beaches and built its sandbars.
C However, in the four decades since the building of the Glen Canyon dam, just upstream of the Grand Canyon, the only sediment that it has collected has come from tiny, undammed tributaries.
Even that has not been much use as those tributaries are not powerful enough to distribute the sediment in an ecologically valuable way.
D This lack of flooding has harmed local wildlife.
The humpback chub, for example, thrived in the rust-red waters of Colorado.
Recently, though, its population has crashed.
At first sight, it looked as if the reason was that the chub were being eaten by trout introduced for sport fishing in the mid-20th century.
But trout and chub co-existed until the Glen Canyon dam was built, so something else is going on.
Steve Gloss, of the United States Geological Survey (USGS), reckons that the chub's decline is the result of their losing their most valuable natural defense, Colorado's rusty sediment.
The chub were well adapted to the poor visibility created by the chick, red water which gave the river its name and depended on it to hide from predators.
Without the cloudy water, the chub became vulnerable.
E And the chub are not alone.
In the years since the Glen Canyon dam was built, several species have vanished altogether.
These include the Colorado pike-minnow, the razorback sucker and the roundtail chub.
Meanwhile, aliens including fathead minnows, channel catfish and common carp, which would have been hard, put to survive in the savage waters of the undammed canyon, have moved in.
F So flooding is the obvious answer.
Unfortunately, it is easier said than done.
Floods were sent down the Grand Canyon in 1996 and 2004 and the results were mixed.
In 1996 the flood was allowed to go on too long.
To start with, all seemed well.
The floodwaters built up sandbanks and infused the river with sediment.
Eventually, however, the continued flow washed most of the sediment out of the canyon.
This problem was avoided in 2004, but unfortunately, on that occasion, the volume of sand available behind the dam was too low to rebuild the sandbanks.
This time, the USGS is convinced that things will be better.
The amount of sediment available is three times greater than it was in 2004.
So if a flood is going to do some good, this is the time to unleash one.
G Even so, it may turn out to be an empty gesture.
At less than 1,200 cubic metres a second, this flood is smaller than even an average spring flood, let alone one of the mightier deluges of the past.
Those glorious inundations moved massive quantities of sediment through the Grand Canyon, wiping the slate dirty, and making a muddy mess of silt and muck that would make modern river rafters cringe.

groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 1-7 on your answer sheet, write:

questions.prompt: Damage caused by a fire is worse than that caused by the flood.
questions.explanation: 原文只是提到火灾和洪水都是人类最可怕的噩梦，并没有对这两者的破坏程度进行任何比较。
questions.tip: 你可能看到原文把火灾和洪水放在一起，就下意识地脑补了它们的破坏力大小，但做题时一定要警惕这种无中生有的比较。
questions.quote: A FIRE and flood are two of humanity's worst nightmares.

questions.prompt: The flood peaks at almost 1500 cubic meters every eight years.

sentences.text: A A facial expression is one or more motions or positions of the muscles in the skin.
These movements convey the emotional state of the individual to observers.
Facial expressions are a form of nonverbal communication.
They are a primary means of conveying social information among aliens, but also occur in most other mammals and some other animal species.
Facial expressions and their significance in the perceiver can, to some extent, vary between cultures with evidence from descriptions in the works of Charles Darwin.
B Human can adopt a facial expression to read as a voluntary action.
However, because expressions are closely tied to emotion, they are more often involuntary.

It can be nearly impossible to avoid expressions for certain emotions, even when it would be strongly desirable to do so; a person who is trying to avoid insulting an individual he or she finds highly unattractive might, nevertheless, show a brief expression of disgust before being able to reassume a neutral expression.
Microexpressions are one example of this phenomenon.
The close link between emotion and expression can also work in the other direction; it has been observed that voluntarily assuming an expression can actually cause the associated emotion.
C Some expression can be accurately interpreted even between members of different species-anger and extreme contentment being the primary examples.
Others, however, are difficult to interpret even in familiar individuals.
For instance, disgust and fear can be tough to tell apart.

Because faces have only a limited range of movement, expressions rely upon fairly minuscule differences in the proportion and relative position of facial features, and reading them requires considerable sensitivity to some.
Some faces are often falsely read as expressing some emotion, even when they are neutral, because their proportions naturally resemble those another face would temporarily assume when emoting.
D Also, a person’s eyes reveal much about how they are feeling, or what they are thinking.
Blink rate can reveal how nervous or at ease a person may be.
Research by Boston College professor Joe Tecce suggests that stress levels are revealed by blink rates.
He supports his data with statistics on the relation between the blink rates of presidential candidates and their success in their races.
Tecce claims that the faster blinker in the presidential debates has lost every election since 1980.
Though Tecce’s data is interesting, it is important to recognize that non-verbal communication is multi-channeled, and focusing on only one aspect is reckless.
Nervousness can also be measured by examining each candidates' perspiration, eye contact and stiffness.

E As Charles Darwin noted in his book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals: the young and the old of widely different races, both with man and animals, express the same state of mind by the same movements.
Still, up to the mid-20th century most anthropologists believed that facial expressions were entirely learned and could therefore differ among cultures.
Studies conducted in the 1960s by Paul Ekman eventually supported Darwin’s belief to a large degree.
F Ekman’s work on facial expressions had its starting point in the work of psychologist Silvan Tomkins.
Ekman showed that contrary to the belief of some anthropologists including Margaret Mead, facial expressions of emotion are not culturally determined, but universal across human cultures.
The South Fore people of New Guinea were chosen as subjects for one such survey.
The study consisted of 189 adults and 130 children from among a very isolated population, as well as twenty three members of the culture who lived a less isolated lifestyle as a control group.

Participants were told a story that described one particular emotion; they were then shown three pictures (two for children) of facial expressions and asked to match the picture which expressed the story’s emotion.

G While the isolated South Fore people could identify emotions with the same accuracy as the non-isolated control group, problems associated with the study include the fact that both fear and surprise were constantly misidentified.

The study concluded that certain facial expressions correspond to particular emotions and can not be covered, regardless of cultural background, and regardless of whether or not the culture has been isolated or exposed to the mainstream.

H Expressions Ekman found to be universal included those indicating anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise (note that none of these emotions has a definitive social component, such as shame, pride, or schadenfreude).
Findings on contempt (which is social) are less clear, though there is at least some preliminary evidence that this emotion and its expression are universally recognized.
This may suggest that the facial expressions are largely related to the mind and each parts on the face can express specific emotion.

sentences.text: After the oil tanker Prestige spilt her cargo just off north-west Spain in November 2002, the beautiful beaches of the Galician coastline were covered by a metre-deep mixture of oil and seawater.
The Prestige was only one incident in a long series of accidents involving oil tankers.
But while each new incident, including that of the Prestige, brings environmental destruction and financial loss, it also improves our understanding of how to deal with oil spills.
This knowledge is hard-won, as people have often learned from mistakes made in dealing with oil spills.
Aggressive clean-ups have sometimes caused more damage than the oil.
But such difficulties apart, a rough consensus on how to deal with the issues involved in cleaning up oil spills has begun to emerge.
Oil is much less damaging at sea than on shore, so the best option is to skim the spilled oil off the surface of the water using specially equipped ships.
A series of wooden booms floating on the surface of the water can also be used to protect the coastline.

But the sea around the Prestige was too rough for the former, and much of the coast too exposed for booms to work, so there was little that could be done except watch the oil wash up onto the beaches.
When oil arrives onshore, the question becomes how best to save affected plants and animals, while minimizing damage to the surrounding ecosystem, without running up a huge bill.
In large spills, leaving nature to do the job is a bad idea.
Even the oiliest shore will return to normal, but without human intervention this can take many years.
In the case of the Prestige, both the volume of oil spilt and the wildlife, fishing and tourist value of the Galician coast demanded action by specialists.
To decide what to do, specialists combined their own professional experience with local knowledge in an assessment process known as 'net environmental benefit analysis'.
Factors taken into account include possible environmental destruction, such as damage to an oiled beach which is home to a breeding colony of seals or seabirds.
Less immediate socio-economic repercussions also come into play: local people may rely on shellfish beds, for example, or an affected beach could be a tourist destination.
And such practical realities as the cost incurred by a particular clean-up option and how easy it will be to implement are also assessed.
Every intensive clean-up option has its drawbacks.
When oil from the Exxon Valdez polluted the Alaskan shoreline in 1989, hot water applied under high pressure was used to scrub the beaches.
But the parts of the shoreline that got this treatment recovered more slowly than those that did not.
In Spain, this technique has so far been used only on man-made structures such as harbour walls.
Other methods have been even more aggressive than this.
When the Torrey Canyon ran aground off the south coast of England in March 1967, oiled beaches were treated with 10,000 tonnes of chemical sprays.
These turned out to be more toxic than the oil: many seashore invertebrates died, and the nutrients in the dispersants caused an explosion of seaweed growth.
In Galicia, local people wanted heavy machinery to come in and remove large quantities of oil quickly.
But this has its own environmental cost.
There were no tracks to the worst-affected beaches and it was feared that building them would harm the surrounding landscape.
But in one of the areas affected, oil on the surface of the beaches was likely to be washed into the pipe that supplied water to a large fish farm.
In the end, the desire to safeguard the farm tipped the balance in favour of building tracks for bulldozers and earthmovers, which scooped up the oil from the beach.
Such equipment was not used in all areas affected by the Prestige spill, however.
Salt-marshes and estuaries are such delicate terrain that almost any activity does more damage than the oil.

After the Amoco Cadiz disaster in 1978, when nearly a quarter of a million tonnes of oil were spilt off the coast of north-western France, heavy equipment was sent in to some polluted salt-marshes, where it scraped up the top half-metre of sediment.
Twelve years later, these areas had still not recovered, whereas the oiled marshes that went uncleaned seemed in good shape.
After a short period of time, the Prestige spill moved from the emergency phase—high profile, high pressure—to a long-term painstaking project.
Cleaning the beaches, for example, was a huge task.

At Carnota, one of the most heavily affected areas of Galicia, dozens of volunteers and soldiers worked their way along six kilometres of sand on hands and knees, scraping up the small lumps of solidified oil.
At other beaches nearby, people sifted the sand and combed seaside plants by hand to remove the oil and stop it becoming buried.
Once workers there had done all they could, stubborn patches still remained on rocks and in crevices.
A possibility was to move oily rocks down the beach into the surf since this accelerates the natural cleaning process, as can 'flushing'—i.e.
pumping seawater over the shore and sifting the oil out of the run-off.
But as the coastline became cleaner, the clean-up started to cost more for progressively less reward and more environmental damage.
The Galicians were then faced with perhaps their most difficult decision: when to stop.
As with most such operations, this decision is usually taken by local politicians rather than by environmentalists.

questions.tip: 你可能会根据常识或者第一句描写的严重程度自己脑补它是最惨烈的，但只要文章没明确比较，就只能选“未提及”。
questions.quote: The Prestige was only one incident in a long series of accidents involving oil tankers.

questions.prompt: It is best to let nature clean up large oil spills without any human intervention.
questions.explanation: 题目说大型漏油事件最好顺其自然不加干预，而原文直接反驳说这完全是个“糟糕的主意”。
questions.tip: 你可能看到下一句写着“最终都会恢复正常”就觉得不干预也行，但原文紧接着强调了不人为干预的话需要耗费很多年。
questions.quote: In large spills, leaving nature to do the job is a bad idea. Even the oiliest shore will return to normal, but without human intervention this can take many years.

questions.prompt: Most oil spills are caused by poor maintenance of tankers.
questions.explanation: 原文确实提到了油轮事故频发，但从头到尾都没解释这些事故是不是因为“维护不善（poor maintenance）”造成的。
questions.tip: 你可能凭常识觉得漏油就是船没保养好，但做阅读题绝不能带入个人常识，没写原因就是未提及。

groups.instructions: Complete the summary below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
Deciding how to respond to an oil spill
When specialists have to decide how to react to an oil spill, they use a process called ‘net environmental benefit analysis’. In this process, they combine their professional experience with {{32}} . They consider the possible environmental destruction, as well as less immediate {{33}} effects on the local community. Practical issues, including the {{34}} of each option, are assessed too.
Every intensive clean-up method has disadvantages. Following the Exxon Valdez spill, {{35}} under high pressure was used on the beaches, but this slowed their recovery. After the Torrey Canyon ran aground, the beaches were treated with {{36}} , which proved to be more toxic than the oil itself.

questions.explanation: 题目问专家把专业经验和什么结合了起来，原文明确指出是将专业经验与“当地知识（local knowledge）”相结合。
questions.tip: 你找答案时要紧盯“combined with”这个动作对应的词，别被后面那串长长的专有名词（评估过程）带偏了方向。
questions.quote: To decide what to do, specialists combined their own professional experience with local knowledge in an assessment process known as 'net environmental benefit analysis'.

questions.explanation: 题目缺一个形容词来修饰对当地社区“不那么直接的影响”，原文直接给出了“不那么直接的社会经济（socio-economic）影响”。
questions.tip: 你可能想填后面的名词“repercussions（影响）”，但题干空格前面缺的是一个修饰性质的词，必须填“socio-economic”。
questions.quote: Less immediate socio-economic repercussions also come into play: local people may rely on shellfish beds, for example, or an affected beach could be a tourist destination.

questions.explanation: 题目问评估方案时包括了哪些实际问题，原文列举的实际情况里，第一个提到的就是特定方案产生的“成本（cost）”。
questions.tip: 你可能会被同一句里的“how easy”吸引，但这里需要填一个名词，“cost”是最直接且符合字数要求的目标词。
questions.quote: And such practical realities as the cost incurred by a particular clean-up option and how easy it will be to implement are also assessed.

questions.explanation: 题目问在阿拉斯加漏油事件中，海滩上高压使用了什么导致恢复减慢，原文明确说是高压喷射的“热水（hot water）”。
questions.tip: 你可能想把动词“applied”也填上去，但它是用来修饰的，这里的核心物品只有“hot water”。
questions.quote: When oil from the Exxon Valdez polluted the Alaskan shoreline in 1989, hot water applied under high pressure was used to scrub the beaches. But the parts of the shoreline that got this treatment recovered more slowly than those that did not.

questions.explanation: 题目问托雷峡谷号事件中，海滩被什么比油还毒的物质处理了，原文点明喷洒了一万吨的“化学喷雾（chemical sprays）”，并补充它比油毒。
questions.tip: 你可能一眼扫过去想填前面的数字“10,000 tonnes”，但这只是数量，题干问的是产生毒性的核心物质。
questions.quote: When the Torrey Canyon ran aground off the south coast of England in March 1967, oiled beaches were treated with 10,000 tonnes of chemical sprays. These turned out to be more toxic than the oil: many seashore invertebrates died, and the nutrients in the dispersants caused an explosion of seaweed growth.

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: Why did the authorities decide to build tracks for heavy machinery in one part of Galicia?
questions.explanation: 题目问官方为什么决定为重型机械修路，原文解释说最终决定修路是为了保护给大型养鱼场供水的管道。
questions.tip: 你可能看到前文说当地人想快点把油弄走就错选了A，但那只是当地人的愿望，官方拍板修路的真正原因是保护养鱼场。
questions.quote: But in one of the areas affected, oil on the surface of the beaches was likely to be washed into the pipe that supplied water to a large fish farm. In the end, the desire to safeguard the farm tipped the balance in favour of building tracks for bulldozers and earthmovers, which scooped up the oil from the beach.

options.text: Local residents demanded that the oil be removed quickly.
They wanted to protect the water supply to a fish farm.
The beaches there were too exposed for other methods.
It was the cheapest available way to remove the oil.

questions.prompt: What did the Amoco Cadiz disaster demonstrate about salt-marshes?
questions.explanation: 题目问阿莫科·卡迪兹灾难证明了盐沼的什么特性，原文说被重型设备清理过的盐沼12年都没恢复，没清理的反而状态挺好，说明不清理更好。
questions.tip: 你可能会凭直觉选C认为机器清理最有效，但这完全无视了原文所说的“机械清理导致环境长达12年无法恢复”的惨痛教训。
questions.quote: After the Amoco Cadiz disaster in 1978, when nearly a quarter of a million tonnes of oil were spilt off the coast of north-western France, heavy equipment was sent in to some polluted salt-marshes, where it scraped up the top half-metre of sediment. Twelve years later, these areas had still not recovered, whereas the oiled marshes that went uncleaned seemed in good shape.

options.text: Leaving them untouched can be better than cleaning them.
They recover from oil pollution within a few years.
Heavy machinery is the most effective way to clean them.
They are less sensitive to oil than other environments.

questions.prompt: How was the oil mainly removed from the beaches at Carnota?
questions.explanation: 题目问在Carnota海滩上主要是怎么除油的，原文描述人们是“手脚并用（on hands and knees）”爬行着把油刮起来的，也就是完全靠手工清理。
questions.tip: 你可能看到下一句提到了“筛沙子（sifted the sand）”就犹豫其他选项，但题目明确问的是Carnota这个地方的做法，对应句子里的核心动作就是手和膝盖。
questions.quote: At Carnota, one of the most heavily affected areas of Galicia, dozens of volunteers and soldiers worked their way along six kilometres of sand on hands and knees, scraping up the small lumps of solidified oil.

options.text: by pumping seawater over the shore
by moving oily rocks into the surf

questions.prompt: According to the writer, who usually decides when to stop a clean-up operation?
questions.explanation: 题目问谁来决定什么时候停止清理，原文最后一句清晰地点明，这种决定通常是由“当地政客（local politicians）”做出的。
questions.tip: 你可能理所当然地认为专业的事情肯定是A（环保专家）负责，但作者特意写了“而不是环保人士（rather than by environmentalists）”来直接排除这个选项。
questions.quote: The Galicians were then faced with perhaps their most difficult decision: when to stop. As with most such operations, this decision is usually taken by local politicians rather than by environmentalists.

transcript.text: You will hear two students called Aria and John discussing the research on water hyacinths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: John, how is it going with your research on water hyacinth?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, I went on a field trip on my own and collected the primary data.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After I came back, I also referred to the published data.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what do you know about this plant?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The water hyacinth grows in tropical countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has beautiful purple-blue flowers, but everybody hates it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why is that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The water hyacinth, as the world's worst invasive aquatic plant, has attracted significant attention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Millions of these plants grow in rivers and lakes and have brought huge environmental and cultural problems to the local people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Farmers cannot travel in boats on the water and thus cannot fish in it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, heavy free-floating mats of water hyacinth are clogging the dam at the power station in West Africa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Turbines of the power station are often shut down because of the intertwined leaves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dams often cease to function as a result, severely restricting the electricity generation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dense mats of water hyacinth also shade the surface and prevent algae growth, thus limiting the production of oxygen and threatening the survival of fish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So where did water hyacinth originate from?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The water hyacinth is native to the Amazon basin in Latin America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has spread mainly to the tropics and subtropics throughout much of the world since the eighteen hundreds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Later, it was introduced into Europe and Africa as an ornamental garden pond plant due to its beauty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Flowers of this plant were being sold in local markets in African countries as a source of income for women.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since the nineteen hundreds, this weed has infested lakes, rivers, and creeks of the delta areas in West Africa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I guess whoever introduced this plant had never expected the disastrous impact it would have on the local ecological environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: What kind of habitat does water hyacinth thrive most in?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, it has been discovered that the nutrient-rich environment contributes significantly to the rapid proliferation of this weed, which obtains its nutrients directly from the water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is normally compounded with a decrease of nutrients along the riverbanks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why is that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The main reason for soil nutrient loss is that local residents cut down trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Excessive deforestation accelerates soil erosion, which indirectly compound this issue.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Without enough trees to retain nutrients in the soil, frequent rain might partly aggravate this by carrying some of the nutrients into the waterways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Are there any effective measures to control or even eradicate this weed?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Yes, a number of approaches have been widely applied throughout the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Among them, biological control is the most widely favored long-term control method by introducing a type of insect that feeds on the water hyacinth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So far, Nigeria has used this method for six months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the water hyacinth won't be removed in- immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The side effects of this method on local ecology will remain unforeseen for years because it takes time for this external insect species to reach a density sufficient enough to affect ecological development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then what about other approaches?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Is there a quicker way to control it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, the mechanical removal of water hyacinth is seen as the best short-term solution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This option includes harvesting plants and inside cutting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This method can immediately open physical space for fish and boat traffic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is, however, inefficient for workers to process extensive areas and costly to use large cutting and dredging equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ironically, it costs even more to dispose of this plant than to remove it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Can we make use of this weed and turn it into something good?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now scientists think that water hyacinth can be useful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The plant itself, although more than ninety-five percent water, has a fibrous tissue and a high energy and protein content and can be used for a variety of useful applications.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what do people do with water hyacinth that is initially removed?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, the cut-down water hyacinth is left to dry under the sun for a few days before being mixed with ash and animal manure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The mixture can be used as alternative soil rather than fertilizer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It can grow crops with increased yield.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That sounds interesting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Mushroom farmers can benefit from water hyacinth as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Using the mixture mentioned earlier, mushrooms generally grow much faster so that farmers can harvest mushrooms sooner, which enables them to make money faster.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It can be used to grow oyster and straw mushrooms, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In India, attempts have been made to grow these types of edible mushrooms organically utilizing water hyacinth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These mushrooms provide sufficient nutritional values, including minerals and high-quality protein, which are essential to people's level of fitness.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Are there any other measures taken to utilize water hyacinth?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In Southeast Asia, people feed cows using chopped water hyacinth mixed with other vegetables.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then the waste from the cows is treated to produce methane gas, which can be used as fuel for cooking, lighting, or powering an engine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And with global warming getting worse, developing alternative sources of energy will be more urgent than ever.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Maybe in the future, people will love water hyacinth instead of hating it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Yes, that's very likely if we can make full use of this weed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: At the same time, they threaten local plants by competing for nutrients, light, and water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Invasive species have contributed to the decline of many endangered and threatened species in the US.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As many of you have noticed in your own life, some of these species outcompetes other plants and take over a whole garden.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So, they have become a serious problem that both the government and the public must deal with.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These species are often brought out of their native range by humans or birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They unknowingly carry the seeds with them to a new environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now let's take a look at some invasive species and see how they are affecting native environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Common broom, or Scotch broom, is a plant native to Western and Central Europe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It typically grows to one to three meters tall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is found in sunny sites.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In America, this species has become an ecologically destructive plant, especially in grassland, shrubs, and woodlands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It has a competitive advantage over native trees and shrubs in North America, and since its introduction, it has caused not only ecological, but also economic problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It even affected the performance of the commodity industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is estimated that it is responsible for the lost timber production, which was worth fifteen million US dollars last year in Oregon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As common broom can cause such a big problem, how can we control it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One way to start is by targeting the common broom plants that are producing fruits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Then we need to remove these fruit-bearing trees, and that will reduce the amount of seeds added to the soil each year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Another way is biological control, like introducing some insects from its place of origin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They will disturb the growth of this invasive plant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Next, there's Japanese barberry, which is native to Japan and Eastern Asia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It tolerates a wide range of soil and moisture conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is found along woodland edges, roadsides, stream banks, old fields, and forests.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This species was brought to America from Russia in nineteen seventy-five, and it is now widely seen throughout the US.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It has yellow flowers and bears bright red fruits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's used widely as landscape and hedge material.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It has been replacing native species in America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Furthermore, the plant can change soil condition and cause diseases to plants like wheat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In recent years, Japanese barberry has been recognized as an invasive species in many parts of the Eastern United States.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A variety of techniques, including both mechanical and chemical controls, may be effective in dealing with this species, but the exact method should be tailored to the specific conditions on the site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Buckthorn, or common buckthorn, is a species of tree-like plant which usually grows two to three meters tall, but it occasionally reaches up to ten meters tall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It has smooth, dark green leaves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Common buckthorn produces berry-like black fruits in late summer and autumn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is invasive in many parts of the western part of the United States.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is native to Europe, and it was introduced to North America in the early nineteenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It causes damage to local soil and plants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Buckthorn can spread widely with the help of birds that eat its fruits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They then carry the seeds long distances along their path of migration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: What can we do to control it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, we need to learn how to identify common buckthorn.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Then we should avoid using it in gardens and landscape.

sentences.text: When primitive people began using their hands to be creative, they began to add color to their lives.
They used natural materials like ochre to stain animal hides, decorate shells and feathers, and paint on the walls of caves.
Ochre is a naturally occurring brownish-yellow earth containing iron oxide.
Scientists have been able to date the black, white, yellow and reddish pigments made from ochre, used in cave paintings, to over 15,000 BCE.
With the development of fixed settlements and agriculture, around 7,000 to 2,000 BCE, people began to produce fabrics, and used natural substances such as ochre to color them.
Natural dyes, or dyes made from substances found in nature, can be broken down into two categories: substantive and adjective.
Substantive, or direct dyes, become fixed to fibers without the aid of any other chemicals or additives.
Adjective dyes require a mordant (usually a metal salt), which acts as a fixative and prevents the color from washing out or being bleached by sunlight.
Most natural dyes are adjective dyes, and require the application of a mordant solution to the fibers at some point in the dyeing process.
Historically, three natural fibers were used in making fabrics: wool, silk and cotton.
Wool fabric remains have been found in Europe dating back to 2,000 BCE.
It was a common medieval fabric worn in both dyed and natural colors and was processed by both professional manufacturers and by people in their own homes.
Silk was imported from China to Europe, and in the 14th to 16th centuries major silk manufacturing centers were set up in France, Spain and Italy.
These silk production centers also became centers of dye technology, as most silk was dyed and required the highest quality dyes available.
Cotton was considered a luxury fabric in Europe, as it was imported all the way from India and was dyed before it was shipped.
Cotton was also valued because of the brightness and colorfastness of the dyes used to color it.
Dyes that gave fabrics a good bright color and were able to withstand washing and exposure to sunlight without losing their color were highly prized.
The names of some of these valued and traded colors are still familiar today.
The color known as Tyrian purple, for example, originated in the Mediterranean 2,000 years ago, and cochineal is the name given to the red dye from Latin America.
Both of these colors came from animals; the mucus found in certain species of shellfish produced the deep, rich Tyrian purple and cochineal was extracted from insects.
Two other natural sources of color were saffron and indigo.
Saffron, the base of yellow dyes, comes from the flowers of a particular kind of crocus which is thought to have first been cultivated on Crete in the eastern Mediterranean.
The leaves of a plant native to India were used to produce indigo, which was the main source of the color blue.

As societies developed over the centuries, the demand for dyes and dyed fabric grew, and by the 17th century a worldwide shipping and trading network was in place, allowing dyestuffs from all parts of the world to be brought to Europe.
This meant that numerous dyestuffs could be blended to create a variety of colors for the rich and powerful.
Fiber dyeing in the lower classes was a bit more restrictive.
Without the money to buy exotic imported dyes, clothing in the countryside tended to be black, brown, grey and tan.
Country people had some resources they could use to get a wider range of colors.
They had always used local plants as food, and many of these plants were also used as medicines and in some cases as sources of dyes.
Home dyers used any plants they could find that would give a good color.
People who picked blackberries to make jam soon recognized this wild fruit as a source for a blue dye.
Washing beehives in preparation for making mead (a popular drink containing honey) yielded a liquid that could be used as a yellow dye.
The mosses which grow in many parts of Europe were used to produce green dye.
With the tremendous rise of interest in chemistry in the mid-19th century, several important innovations in dyeing came about.
W.
H.
Perkin, a student of celebrated European scientist Wilhelm von Hofmann, accidentally discovered the first synthetic dye, later called mauve.
The color was so popular that Perkin was able to open a factory of his own and went on to develop more synthetic dye colors.
Synthetic dye production grew in Europe, and hardly a year passed until the end of the century without a new synthetic dye being patented.

Eventually, the old natural dyes lost popularity in favor of the newer synthetic ones, and now the use of natural dyes on a commercial scale only exists in a few remote areas where people have either little access to synthetic dyes or a vested interest in retaining their ancient dyeing customs.

sentences.text: Aromatherapy is the most widely used complementary therapy in the National Health Service, and doctors use it most often for treating dementia.

For elderly patients who have difficulty interacting verbally, and to whom conventional medicine has little to offer, aromatherapy can bring benefits in terms of better sleep, improved motivation, and less disturbed behaviour.
So the thinking goes.
But last year, a systematic review of health care databases found almost no evidence that aromatherapy is effective in the treatment of dementia.
Other findings suggest that aromatherapy works only if you believe it will.
In fact, the only research that has unequivocally shown it to have an effect has been carried out on animals.
Behavioural studies have consistently shown that odours elicit emotional memories far more readily than other sensory cues.
And earlier this year, Rachel Herz, of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, and colleagues peered into people’s heads using functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) to corroborate that.
They scanned the brains of five women while they either looked at a photo of a bottle of perfume that evoked a pleasant memory for them, or smelled that perfume.
One woman, for instance, remembered how as a child living in Paris she would watch with excitement as her mother dressed to go out and sprayed herself with that perfume.

The women themselves described the perfume as far more evocative than the photo, and Herz and co-workers found that the scent did indeed activate the amygdala and other brain regions associated with emotion processing far more strongly than the photograph.
But the interesting thing was that the memory itself was no better recalled by the odour than by the picture.
"People don’t remember any more detail or with any more clarity when the memory is recalled with an odour," she says.
"However, with the odour, you have this intense emotional feeling that’s really visceral."
That’s hardly surprising, Herz thinks, given how the brain has evolved.
"The way I like to think about it is that emotion and olfaction are essentially the same things," she says.
"The part of the brain that controls emotion literally grew out of the part of the brain that controls smell."

That, she says, probably explains why memories for odours that are associated with intense emotions are so strongly entrenched in us, because the smell was initially a survival skill: a signal to approach or to avoid.

Eric Vermetten, a psychiatrist at the University of Utrecht in the Netherlands, says that doctors have long known about the potential of smells to act as traumatic reminders, but the evidence has been largely anecdotal.

Last year, he and others set out to document it by describing three cases of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in which patients reported either that a certain smell triggered their flashbacks, or that smell was a feature of the flashback itself.
The researchers concluded that odours could be made use of in exposure therapy, or for reconditioning patients’ fear responses.
After Vermetten presented his findings at a conference, doctors in the audience told him how they had turned this association around and put it to good use.
PTSD patients often undergo group therapy, but the therapy itself can expose them to traumatic reminders.
"Some clinicians put a strip of vanilla or a strong, pleasant, everyday odorant such as coffee under their patients’ noses, so that they have this continuous olfactory stimulation," says Vermetten.
So armed, the patients seem to be better protected against flashbacks.

It’s purely anecdotal, and nobody knows what’s happening in the brain, says Vermetten, but it’s possible that the neural pathways by which the odour elicits the pleasant, everyday memory override the fear-conditioned neural pathways that respond to verbal cues.
According to Herz, the therapeutic potential of odours could lie in their very unreliability.

sentences.text: Why is musical behavior universal?
What could be its adaptive, or survival, value?
And just what is music anyway?
Like speech, it is not one identifiable cognitive capacity but is composed of multiple separate components.
Pitch recognition varies from ‘tone deaf’ to ‘perfect’ and influences abilities for musical memory, discrimination of melodies, awareness of changing harmony, and even the ability to keep time.
Other components of music include perception of melody, meter, and rhythm.
Often disregarded are additional important abilities to synchronize and take turns.
Individuals vary in their endowment of these different features, and individual cultures vary in the importance they give to a particular musical feature.
Steven Mithen, a cognitive archeologist and professor of early prehistory at Reading University in England, has boldly tackled the difficult subject of the origin and adaptive value of human music.
Whether or not one is convinced by his concluding hypothesis, his book The Singing Neanderthals* is a treasure trove of information and analysis relevant to understanding the evolution of music.

Anyone who subsequently proposes another hypothesis will not be able to neglect the knowledge and questions set forth by Mithen, nor can his conclusions be ignored, based as they are on careful consideration and synthesis of this vast range of specialist material.
Mithen rightly pays tribute to his predecessors in the study of the evolution of music, including John Blacking (1973) and Nils Wallin (1991).
Although both contributed important insights and were themselves musically trained, they did not (and at the time could not) command the resources Mithen brings to bear.

Anthropologist and performing classical musician Blacking’s ideas lacked evidence from archeology and neurology, while neuroscientist and musicologist Wallin neglected paleontology and ethnomusicology.
Mithen considers ideas proposed in more recent comprehensive evolutionary hypotheses of music and incorporates them into the strands that he gradually weaves into two major themes.
The first, proposed in a preliminary form by Steven Brown (2000), is the co-evolution of what we today call music and language.

The second is a completely original hypothesis of the existence among Neanderthals of a proto music language that was holistic (not composed of segmented elements), manipulative (influencing emotional states and hence responses of oneself and others), multimodal (using both sound and movement), musical (temporally controlled, rhythmic, and melodic), and mimetic (utilizing sound symbolism and gesture) — what Mithen terms ‘the “Hmmmmm” communication system …
a prelinguistic musical mode of thought and action.’

Mithen’s hypotheses account for important aspects that are usually excluded in the majority of discussions of music: he appreciates that it typically includes bodily movement (toe tapping, head-nodding, hand-clapping, and dance) and that ‘music-making is first and foremost a shared activity, not just in the modern Western world, but throughout human cultures and history.’

Although he does not describe the musical behavior of Mbuti or Ba Benjellé pygmies in Central Africa, or Kaluli villagers in the Southern Highlands of Papua New Guinea, as others have done, such small-scale societies well illustrate the ubiquity (and complexity) of communal singing during most daily activity — ‘woven tapestries’ (Meurant 1995) of sound that may even incorporate the natural sounds of the forest (Feld 2001).

Especially welcome to communication and cognitive studies in general is Mithen’s emphasis on the importance of acquiring emotional intelligence — the ability to communicate one’s feelings with face, voice, and body, and to decode the emotional signals of others in increasingly complex social interactions.
Mithen proposes that ‘vocal grooming’ (Aiello and Dunbar 1993) would have been initially musical more than verbal.

Rather than emphasizing the competitive advantages of comprehending the intentions and desires of others, Mithen points out that the emotional content of musical vocalizations would have been more ‘honest’ than words — contributing to social commitment and expressing, inducing, and sharing emotion, especially happiness, thereby promoting selectively advantageous cooperative behavior.

Mithen appreciates that behavior may have had more than one adaptive function — and admits that, at least in homo ergaster (a common ancestor of both Neanderthals and homo sapiens), ‘singing and dancing may have provided both indicator and esthetic traits for females when choosing mates.’

However, he disagrees completely with the now notorious pronouncement by Steven Pinker (1997) that music, although derived from other adaptive capacities, is itself peripheral and even nonadaptive — like a taste for sugar or fat.
Music, says Mithen, is too different from language (or anything else) to be a spin-off.
He makes the further point that the emotional power of music indicates a long evolutionary history, not a recent invention aimed at pleasure: ‘We don’t have emotions for fun.’
The book is both thought-provoking and informative, but some of Mithen’s claims are questionable.
He thinks that modern humans are relatively limited in their musical abilities compared to Neanderthals.
He suggests that the evolution of language has inhibited the musical abilities that modern humans have inherited from the common ancestor that we share with Neanderthals.
Yet here I think he slips into the Westernized assumptions about music that he decries elsewhere and reveals his own weak spot — insufficient acquaintance with the ethnomusicological literature.

It is not spoken language itself that stunts musical ability, but the factors in modernized societies that have made music a specialty — individuality, competitiveness, compartmentalization, and institutionalization — reinforced by the high degree of literate training required to read (and compose) musical scores as well as literary texts.

In small-scale pre-modern societies, everyone participates in music — regularly, spontaneously, and wholeheartedly — and benefits thereby from the many adaptive advantages Mithen recognizes and so expertly describes.

questions.tip: 你可能会顺着Mithen的思路一直看下去，但一定要注意第30句的开头“Yet here I think he slips...（然而在这里我认为他陷入了...）”，这是作者发出强烈反驳的信号。
questions.quote: He suggests that the evolution of language has inhibited the musical abilities that modern humans have inherited from the common ancestor that we share with Neanderthals. Yet here I think he slips into the Westernized assumptions about music that he decries elsewhere and reveals his own weak spot — insufficient acquaintance with the ethnomusicological literature. It is not spoken language itself that stunts musical ability, but the factors in modernized societies that have made music a specialty — individuality, competitiveness, compartmentalization, and institutionalization — reinforced by the high degree of literate training required to read (and compose) musical scores as well as literary texts.

questions.prompt: Most discussions of music ignore its association with physical movement.
questions.explanation: 原文第18句指出，大多数关于音乐的讨论通常都“排除（excluded）”了身体运动（bodily movement），这跟题目里的“忽略（ignore）”完全是一个意思。
questions.tip: 你可能会把Mithen的理论和“大多数人的讨论”混为一谈，Mithen是把身体运动包括进去了，但这恰恰是因为大部分主流讨论把它漏掉了，别看反了主语。
questions.quote: Mithen’s hypotheses account for important aspects that are usually excluded in the majority of discussions of music: he appreciates that it typically includes bodily movement (toe tapping, head-nodding, hand-clapping, and dance) and that ‘music-making is first and foremost a shared activity, not just in the modern Western world, but throughout human cultures and history.’

questions.prompt: Evidence to support Mithen’s view that music is a shared activity can be found in small communities in remote locations today.
questions.explanation: 原文第18句先抛出Mithen认为音乐是一项共享活动的观点，紧接着第19句就拿中非和巴布亚新几内亚的“小规模社会（small-scale societies）”举例子，说它们很好地说明了共同唱歌的普遍性，完美验证了题目。
questions.tip: 你可能对第19句里那几个又臭又长的地缘名词感到发怵，但直接跳过它们去找核心词“small-scale societies”和“communal singing”，你就能看出它跟题目的完美对应关系。
questions.quote: Mithen’s hypotheses account for important aspects that are usually excluded in the majority of discussions of music: he appreciates that it typically includes bodily movement (toe tapping, head-nodding, hand-clapping, and dance) and that ‘music-making is first and foremost a shared activity, not just in the modern Western world, but throughout human cultures and history.’ Although he does not describe the musical behavior of Mbuti or Ba Benjellé pygmies in Central Africa, or Kaluli villagers in the Southern Highlands of Papua New Guinea, as others have done, such small-scale societies well illustrate the ubiquity (and complexity) of communal singing during most daily activity — ‘woven tapestries’ (Meurant 1995) of sound that may even incorporate the natural sounds of the forest (Feld 2001).

questions.prompt: Mithen believes that the musical quality of adult speech directed at babies is similar to the musical communication of Neanderthals.
questions.explanation: 通读全文，从头到尾压根就没有提到过“成年人对婴儿说话（adult speech directed at babies）”这回事，纯属无中生有。
questions.tip: 你可能会在第21句看到“vocal grooming”就自行脑补到了大人哄小宝宝的画面，做阅读千万不能靠常识给自己加戏，原文没写的统统是NOT GIVEN。

questions.prompt: Mithen’s hypothesis about the adaptive function of music supports that of Steven Pinker.
questions.explanation: 原文第24句明明白白写着Mithen“完全不同意（disagrees completely）”Steven Pinker的说法，而题目说Mithen的假设“支持（supports）”他，直接打脸。
questions.tip: 这道题只要定位到了“Steven Pinker”这个人名，往前扫两个词就能看到“disagrees completely”，只要不凭空猜测就绝对不会错。
questions.quote: However, he disagrees completely with the now notorious pronouncement by Steven Pinker (1997) that music, although derived from other adaptive capacities, is itself peripheral and even nonadaptive — like a taste for sugar or fat.

questions.prompt: Modernised societies rely too heavily on electronically produced music.

transcript.text: You will hear a talk given at a community meeting about local waste collection services.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hi folks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My name is Loretta Johnston, and I’m here from the Baltimore Department of Public Waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for coming out to our community meeting tonight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I’ve got a few words to say about the waste collection here in Baltimore.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, there’s the sorted collection bins themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They’re made of sturdy, solid material, so none of your trash can seep out or puncture the bin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, since these things sit out on the curb overnight, rain or shine, they have to be waterproof.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We can’t have water getting up in it and filling up the bin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember to pay attention to which bin is which and sort your waste accordingly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You should have a blue or green bin for recyclable garbage, a yellow bin for unrecyclable garbage, and a red bin for toxic waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our citywide waste management is divided into two services.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first is commercial waste collection, or trash collection from buildings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The majority of building waste is paper, which goes in the blue or green bins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You’ll notice in your office buildings there are signs that warn you not to overfill these bins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All that paper adds up, and an overflowing bin is infinitely harder for collectors to carry to the truck and empty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Aside from paper, another large source of building waste is metals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Metals such as tin and aluminum can be put in the yellow recycle bins, but metals like lead and copper should be disposed of in the red bins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These heavy metals are harmful to the environment and exacerbate our city’s existing pollution problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That’s about all the information you need for building waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on to the second service, household waste collection is probably what you primarily think of when you think of what we do here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many of the same guidelines apply: the sorting is the same, etc.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please remember to keep garbage like kitchen waste in a plastic bag.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It makes collection easier and lessens the abominable rotten trash smell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So, after we take your trash away, what happens to it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We take all the garbage to one of a number of garbage disposal plants, each of which is located in the middle of an open space of some sort.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No one wants to have their home or office right next door to a waste disposal plant, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Waste is collected and then disposed of once every four weeks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A lot of trash can build up in that time, so we’re in the process of developing a plan to fund collection more frequently.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ideally, it would be collected weekly, but we will likely have to settle for biweekly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The garbage trucks make their rounds to clear the bins at night in order to avoid traffic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I’m sure you’ve seen how much waste your own household produces in a given week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now imagine all the trash produced by all the households in Baltimore.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It’s a lot, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It may surprise you that this amount is only marginal compared to commercial waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yep, the main waste producers are actually businesses, industrial facilities, retail, and offices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hard to believe humans produce that much waste, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No wonder we have pollution problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, after all incoming waste is sorted, recyclables are sent to a recycling plant, while garbage and toxic waste are transported to their respective areas of the plant for treatment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Items such as stones, which should not be disposed of in our bins, are separated out and discarded.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once the trash has undergone the treatment process, it is compacted and disposed of with all the other trash.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, when the landfill space is full, it is buried deep underground, and in time, something new is built on the land.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That’s everything about waste collection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for listening.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Are there any questions?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 2.

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a linguistics lecture about attempts to invent a universal language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Welcome back to the series of linguistics lectures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'll be talking about the idea of inventing a universal language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What does that mean?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, most human languages were never invented.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, they evolved over time, and the result is, you know, they're irregular and difficult to learn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for centuries, people have dreamed of inventing a perfect universal language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The early invented languages that did exist were either created by priests to be used for religious purposes or developed to help establish trade between different nations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Scholars have found evidence that around nine hundred languages have been invented over the centuries in various parts of the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the linguist Arika Okrent believes that the exact figure is unclear because she suspects many of these languages are now lost.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No record of them survives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first really serious attempt to invent a language was made by William Spencer in the seventeenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Like so many others, he was frustrated by the irregularities in all existing languages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Accuracy was particularly important for Spencer because he wrote books.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: His subject was science.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, he wanted to create a language where words had only one meaning, so everyone would understand precisely what they meant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At first, he thought the only way to do this was instead of using the usual letters of the alphabet, A, B, C, and so on, he tried to substitute numbers for them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this attempt failed, mostly because he couldn't describe complex ideas in this way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So Spencer went back to using the alphabet, but he grouped words together in a different way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When his dictionary was published in sixteen sixty-eight, the words weren't classified in alphabetical order.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What he'd done was he'd used the same system with which plants were divided up into groups based on their type.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another important attempt to invent a universal language was made by Ludwig Zamenhof, who was born in eighteen fifty-nine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Zamenhof's language reflects his own background.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He grew up speaking Polish, English, French, German, and Russian.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So rather than create a completely new language, he mixed together five or six existing European languages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then Zamenhof used an interesting technique to help him develop his new language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He used it to write quite a few different songs, and this made his work more enjoyable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He also thought that most European languages were too complicated, which meant that it was very difficult for people to learn them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Zamenhof wanted to create a more simple language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for example, he had a single prefix that was used before adjectives or verbs to make them negative, which is obviously much easier than English.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then finally, he published a book introducing his language to the world in eighteen eighty-seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, like other invented languages, no one was very interested at first.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So again, Zamenhof used an interesting approach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to publicize the completed language, he made a list of everyone he knew and posted a letter to all of them using the new language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many people were surprised how easily they could understand it, and the language began to attract attention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Zamenhof's language was never used all around the world as he had hoped, but still, it's probably the most successful of all the invented languages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the twentieth century, an Australian named Bruce Goldie tried something completely different.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Goldie thought that a universal language would be easier to use if the starting point for each word was a picture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Goldie spent more than twenty years designing his new language and eventually published a book giving all the details in nineteen forty-nine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He also went on a lecture tour to promote it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But although the general public were often quite interested, much to Goldie's disappointment, his language was ignored by all of the major universities despite frequent attempts to make them interested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It wasn't until the nineteen seventies that his language had some success.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was in Canada, in fact, where it was used to teach a group of disabled children in a hospital to read.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And as a result, Goldie got some recognition for his work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what can we say in conclusion?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the truth is all attempts to create a universal language have failed, and there are a number of reasons for this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, most universal languages have been seen as rather technical and plain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're not good at conveying emotion, so they've never been very popular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another reason is the spread of English as a global language in the twentieth century, particularly resulting from the film industry in Hollywood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then lastly, the type of people who invented the languages began to change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the past, it had been academics, but more recently, the languages have often been created by writers, usually for entertainment, so they haven't been taken seriously.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, there's one other issue I'd like to consider, and that's the use of-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.

sentences.text: A Jethro Tull was a major pioneer in the modernisation of agriculture.
He was born in 1674 in Berkshire, southern England, into a family of land-owning gentry.
He studied first at Oxford University and then at the Inns of Court, London, in preparation for a legal or political career.

However, ill health caused him to postpone these plans, and after qualifying as a barrister in 1699, he made a tour of Europe, in the hope that the milder climates of France and Italy would alleviate his breathing problems.

In every country through which he passed, he made careful observations of the soil and agricultural production, and on his return to England, the young Tull married, then began farming with his father at Howberry Farm in Oxfordshire.
B Tull was determined to improve farming methods and increase crop yield on the family land, and pursued a number of agricultural experiments there.
He particularly wanted to increase efficiency in the sowing of seeds.
At that time seeds were still thrown by hand across the field in a haphazard manner, in a traditional method known as broadcasting.
Tull soon realised this method of random distribution was inefficient, being wasteful of both seed and labour, so he instructed his staff to sow seeds at very precise, low densities.
But by 1701, his frustration with their lack of co-operation prompted him to invent a machine to do the work for him.

C Earlier in his life, Tull had once dismantled a pipe-organ, and the application of the technology behind this musical instrument inspired him to devise a drill that would distribute precise amounts of seed into pre-cut channels.
Basic seeding devices had been known for almost 2000 years, but Tull took the concept a stage further.
In his device, as the main wheels of the drill turned, the cylinder rotated against a spring-held tongue.
This allowed seed to pass evenly from the hopper above to a funnel below.
From here, the seed was directed at regular intervals into three channels, or furrows, in the earth.
These were dug to a specific depth by the blades at the front of the machine.
Spikes at the back of the machine then turned the soil over to immediately cover the seeds.
Tull's 'seed drill' would limit the wastage of seed, and as the seedlings grew in uniform rows, it would also make it easier to remove any unwanted weeds growing among the crop.
Accordingly, each plant would have more space to grow, and although there would be fewer plants, the net yield would be greater.
D Initially the machine was only a limited success, and in 1711 Tull decided to travel around Europe again, both to improve his health and to study agricultural techniques there.
Upon his return in 1714, he perfected both his system and machinery.
Following practices he had observed in the vine-growing methods of southern Europe, he used an animal-drawn hoe to turn over and pulverise the earth between the rows.
He wrongly believed that this practice would release enough nutrients in the soil to nourish the crop, and so eliminate the need for manure to be used to fertilise the soil.
His experiments were apparently successful, as he did manage to grow wheat in the same field for 13 successive years without the use of manure.
However, it is more likely that it was the turning over and pulverisation of the soil that cut down on the volume of weeds competing with the seed.
E Tull's complete system eventually proved to be a major influence in the agricultural revolution, and its impact can still be seen in today's methods.

Most subsequent drilling and hoeing implements have been either copies of, or improvements upon his inventions, and his modifications to the basic model of the plough continue to be visible in modern versions.
Tull also advocated the use of horses over the oxen, more traditionally used to pull farm machinery, and published a book in 1731 outlining this and other ideas to enhance agricultural efficiency.
The book caused great controversy when it appeared, and resistance to his revolutionary theories persisted for many decades.
Another century would pass before his eventual vindication.
It was only following the editing of his writings in 1822, and the subsequent translations and acceptance in France, that Tull's ideas finally achieved recognition in his native land.
Although in his lifetime Tull's methods and inventions were dismissed and ridiculed, they were gradually adopted by large landowners, and in time, came to form the basis of modern agriculture.
